<H1>Gonorrhea
<H2>Definition

A. Gonorrhea is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI). Although most commonly seen in both male and female urogenital organs, Neisseria gonorrhoeae can thrive in both the oropharynx and the rectum.
<H2>Incidence

A. Gonorrhea is a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)-reportable infection. It is the second most commonly reported communicable disease. In the United States there are an estimated 1,568,000 new gonorrhea infections each year.
<H2>Pathogenesis

A. N. gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus, is the causative organism. The infection begins with adherence of N. gonorrhoeae to the mucosal cells in the genitourinary tract or endocervix. The incubation period is typically 2 to 5 days for urethritis and 5 to 10 days for cervical infection. Rectal and pharyngeal infections are often asymptomatic. Transmission during vaginal birth is possible and may result in conjunctivitis and blindness in neonates.
<H2>Predisposing Factors
A. History of STIs.
B. Multiple sexual partners.
C. Early age at first coitus.
<H2>Common Complaints
A. Dysuria.
B. Yellow, white, or mucoid urethral discharge in males.
C. Greenish, irritating vaginal discharge in females.
D. Menstrual irregularities.
E. Pelvic pain.
F. Fever.
<H2>Other Signs and Symptoms
A. Asymptomatic.
B. Uterine or adnexal tenderness.
C. Mucopurulent discharge from endocervix.
D. Polyarthralgias.
E. Necrotic skin lesions.
F. Rectal discharge.
<H2>Subjective Data
A. Elicit history of onset, duration, and location of symptoms. Note aggravating and alleviating factors and associated symptomatology.
B. Question the client about history of other STIs and sexual habits.
<H2>Physical Examination
A. Check temperature.
B. Inspect:
1. Inspect the skin for necrotic skin lesions.
2. Males: Inspect for anal and/or urethral discharge; elicit the latter by milking the penis.
3. Females:
a. Inspect the anus and introitus for discharge; milk the urethra.
b. Speculum examination: Inspect the vaginal walls and cervix for discharge and irritation.
C. Palpate:
1. Examine the joints for effusion and swelling.
2. Males:
a. Palpate the inguinal lymph nodes.
3. Females:
a. Palpate the inguinal lymph nodes.
b. Palpate the periurethral and Bartholin glands for exudate.
c. Bimanual examination:
i. Assess for cervical motion tenderness and friability.
ii. Assess for uterine and adnexal tenderness.
<H2>Diagnostic Tests
A. Culture, NAAT, and POC NAAT, such as GeneXpert (Cepheid) are screening tools available for genitourinary infection.
B. Culture is available for endocervical, urethral (men), rectal, oropharyngeal, and conjunctival gonococcal infections.
C. Gonococci can be recovered from the joint by aspiration for culture in patients that have a septic joint.
D. For persons diagnosed with gonorrhea, testing should also be performed for chlamydia, trichomoniasis, syphilis, and human immunodeficiency syndrome.
<H2>Differential Diagnoses
A. Gonorrhea.
B. Chlamydia.
C. Arthritis (rheumatoid or osteoarthritis).
<H2>Plan
A. General interventions:
1. All sexually active women <25 years old and older women at increased risk for infection should be screened annually.
2. Report positive test results to the health department.

3 Empirical treatment: People presenting with signs and symptoms of gonorrhea should be tested and treated for both gonorrhea and chlamydia at time of presentation to the clinic for care. NAAT swabs should be collected from all orifices exposed to sexual contact.
B. Client teaching: See Client Teaching Guide for this chapter, “Gonorrhea.”
1. Stress the importance of completing the medication regimen to prevent antimicrobial resistance.
2. Patients should abstain from sexual activity for 7 days after treatment and 7 days after their partner received treatment.
C. Pharmaceutical therapy:
1. Ceftriaxone 500 mg by intramuscular (IM) injection of a single dose for persons weighing <150 kg. For persons weighing >150 kg (300 lbs), 1 g of ceftriaxone IM should be administered.
2. If ceftriaxone is not available or resistance suspected: gentamicin 240 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 2 g dose orally. Or cefixime 800 mg orally in a single dose.
3. If chlamydial infection has not been excluded, treat for chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg orally 2 times daily for 7 days.
4. For clients with severe allergy to cephalosporins, gentamicin 240 mg IM in a single dose plus azithromycin 2 g dose orally.
5. Quinolones should no longer be used for treatment of gonorrhea due to their increased bacterial resistance.
<H2>Follow-Up

A. A test of cure is not indicated for patients who receive a diagnosis of uncomplicated urogenital or rectal gonorrhea who are treated with any of the recommended or alternative treatment regimens. Women should be retested 3 months after treatment.
B. Patients with pharyngeal gonorrhea should have a test of cure within 7 to 14 days.
C. Patients with a previous history of gonorrhea should be retested in 3 months regardless of if they believe their partner received treatment.
D. Providers are advised to report all treatment failures to the local or state public health department within 24 hours.
<H2>Consultation/Referral
A. Consult with a physician or refer the client if treatment with the recommended dosage fails and client noncompliance and re-exposure have been ruled out.
<H2>Individual Considerations
A. Pregnancy:
1. Pregnant clients with N. gonorrhoeae infections should be treated with both ceftriaxone 500 mg IM, single dose plus treatment for chlamydia if infection has not been excluded
2. Retest during the third trimester for women under 25 years of age or at risk.
3. Consult with infectious disease if the patient has a cephalosporin allergy.
4. Retest within 3 months of treatment.
5. Gentamicin should be used in caution in pregnancy because of the risk for neonatal birth defects, nephrotoxicity, or ototoxicity.
B. Adults:
1. There is insufficient evidence for screening among heterosexual men who are at low risk for infection.
C. Pediatrics:

1. Ophthalmia neonatorum prophylaxis: Perinatal exposure to the mother’s infected cervix during birth can cause gonococcal conjunctivitis, which can lead to blindness if left untreated. Accordingly, the CDC recommends a single application of erythromycin (0.5%) in each eye of an infant at birth.
2. Sexual abuse should be considered. Suspect chlamydia as a cause of conjunctivitis if the infant is 30 days old or younger.
a. Treatment:
i. If the presence of N. gonorrhoeae is confirmed, treatment with a single dose of ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IM or intravenously, not to exceed 250 mg, is considered the standard of care.
D. Partners:

1. Recent sex partners within the last 60 days should be referred for evaluation, testing and presumptive treatment. If the last sex exposure was >60 days before onset of symptoms or diagnosis, the most recent sex partner should be treated.
2. EPT can be delivered to the partner by the patient or collaborating pharmacy as permitted by law.
3. Partner treatment: oral cefixime 800 mg single dose if chlamydia infection has been excluded.
4. If chlamydia status is unknown, the recommended partner treatment is cefixime 800 mg PO + oral doxycycline 100 mg BID × 7 days.
5. If adherence of medication is a concern, give azithromycin 1 g oral, although it has lower efficacy rate.
E. Men who have Sex with Men:
1. MSM at higher risk for gonorrhea or HIV should be screened at all anatomical sites of exposure every 3 to 6 months.
2. At least annual screening is recommended for all MSM.
3. MSM have a higher risk of coexisting infections (HIV) among their partners and might have partners who would benefit from PrEP.

<H1>Herpes Simplex Virus
<H2>Definition

A. Herpes simplex is a lifelong, recurring viral disease that is transmitted by direct contact with the secretions or mucosa of an infected individual who is shedding the virus. The virus is usually characterized by painful vesicular lesions that form an ulcer, crust over, and then dry without scarring (Figure 20.2).
<H2>Incidence

A. Most cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV-2 however, there is rising rate of anogenital herpetic infections that are attributed to HSV-1. In the United States, about 11.9% of people between 14 and 49 years of age are infected with HSV-2.
<H2>Pathogenesis

A. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is the causative organism. Kissing, sexual contact, vaginal delivery, and autoinoculation are all possible routes of transmission. The virus remains dormant, and outbreaks can be stimulated by several factors, including stress, illness, sunlight exposure, and menstruation.
<H2>Predisposing Factors
A. Early age at first coitus.
B. Multiple sexual partners.
C. History of sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
<H2>Common Complaints
A. Dysuria.
B. Pruritus.
C. Burning.
D. Swelling sensation.
<H2>Other Signs and Symptoms
A. Primary episode:
1. Painful, itchy, vesicular, ulcerated, or crusted oral or genital lesion, singly or in clusters.
2. Flulike syndrome: fever, chills, headache, malaise, and myalgia.
B. Recurrent episode:
1. Less painful lesions and little or no systemic symptoms. Recurrent lesions in the same location as the previous outbreak is a significant clinical clue that the lesions are herpetic.
<H2>Subjective Data
A. Elicit history of onset of symptoms; their location, frequency, and duration; aggravating and alleviating factors; and associated symptomatology.
B. Question the client about history of other STIs and sexual habits.
<H2>Physical Examination
A. Check temperature.
B. Inspect:
1. Inspect the head, eyes, ears, nose, throat, and mucous membranes for lesions.
C. Palpate:
1. Palpate the neck and abdomen for lymphadenopathy.
2. Pelvic examination:
a. Assess the external genitalia, perineum, and anus for lesions.
b. Assess for inguinal lymphadenopathy.
<H2>Diagnostic Test
A. Testing
HSV NAAT assays are the most sensitive. Sensitivity ranges from 90.9% to 100% depending on the test.
In the absence of genital lesions, type-specific serologic tests can be used.
The sensitivity of viral cultures is low, especially as the lesion heals.
<H2>Differential Diagnoses
A. HSV.
B. Primary syphilis.
C. Chancroid.
D. Lymphogranuloma venereum.
E. Folliculitis.
F. Candidal fissure.
G. Vestibular vulvitis.
H. Mucocutaneous manifestations of Crohn disease.
<H2>Plan
A. General interventions:
1. Culture samples immediately to begin treatment
B. Client teaching: See Client Teaching Guide for this chapter, “Herpes Simplex Virus.”
1. Advise patients to abstain from sexual activity during prodrome or while lesions are present.
2. Condom use should be encouraged when sexually active.
3. Periocoital intravaginal tenofovir 1% gel decreases the risk of HSV-2 acquisition in heterosexual women.
4. Encourage patients to notify sex partners prior to engaging in sexual activities.
C. Pharmaceutical therapy: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends the following treatment regimens:
1. Primary episode:
a. Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID for 7 to 10 days.
b. Famciclovir 250 mg PO TID for 7 to 10 days.
c. Valacyclovir 1 g PO BID for 7 to 10 days.
2. Episodic Treatment for HSV-2
a. Acyclovir 800 mg PO BID for 5 days.
b. Acyclovir 800 mg PO TID for 2 days.
c. Famciclovir 125 mg PO BID for 5 days.
d. Famciclovir 1,000 mg PO BID for 1 day.
e. Famciclovir 500 mg once, followed by 250 mg BID for 2 days.
f. Valacyclovir 500 mg PO BID for 3 days.
g. Valacyclovir 1 g PO once daily for 5 days.
3. Daily suppressive therapy:
a. Acyclovir 400 mg PO BID.
b. Famciclovir 250 mg PO BID.
c. Valacyclovir 500 mg PO once daily.
d. Valacyclovir 1 g PO once daily.
e. Discontinue after 1 year of continuous use to reassess recurrence rate.
<H2>Follow-Up
A. Follow-up is not recommended unless it is warranted by clinical presentation.
<H2>Consultation/Referral
A. Consult or refer the client to a physician if they have prolonged ulceration unresponsive to therapy.
<H2>Individual Considerations
A. Adults:

1. Diagnosis is most often made via clinical presentation. Although viral testing is available, empirical treatment is recommended, versus first testing and then treating (see the “Other Signs and Symptoms” section).
2. Clients with HIV may have outbreaks of HSV lesions anywhere on their body. Do not limit the diagnosis based on the physical location of lesions.
3. Clients presenting with HSV-1/HSV-2 lesions should also be tested for HIV.
4. Failure to isolate HSV does not mean that the client does not have HSV.
B. Pregnancy:

1. Transmission of genital herpes from an infected pregnant female to the neonate is high, approximately 30% to 50%, when herpes is acquired during the last trimester or near delivery. The risk of transmission is much lower for pregnant females who have a history of HSV or first acquire the virus during the first half of the pregnancy.

2. All pregnant clients should be questioned and screened for HSV when they are admitted to the hospital for delivery. All pregnant clients with recurrent genital herpes lesions present at the onset of labor should be delivered by cesarean section to reduce the risk of transmission of the herpes virus to the neonate. Patients without prodrome symptoms or signs and symptoms of genital herpes can deliver vaginally.
3. Acyclovir and valacyclovir are considered safe to use during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
4. Suppressive acyclovir treatment starting at 36 weeks gestation reduces the frequency of cesarean delivery among patients who have genital herpes (Table 20.1).
5. Pregnant clients without genital herpes should be advised to avoid intercourse during the third trimester with partners known or suspected of having genital herpes.
6. Acyclovir allergy: No effective alternatives to acyclovir have been identified.
C. Partners:
1. Symptomatic partners should be evaluated and treated in the same manner as any client with genital lesions.
2. Asymptomatic sex partners of patients with symptomatic genital herpes should be offered type-specific serologic testing for HSV-2.
D. Pediatrics:

1. Transmission of HSV from mother to infant during birth is possible. The CDC recommends treatment of all infants born to mothers whose exposure to HSV was near term. Treatment is acyclovir 20 mg/kg intravenously Q8H for 14 days, unless there is disseminated disease or disease involving the central nervous system. In those cases, treatment should be extended for a total of 21 days.
E. Geriatrics:
1. Genital herpes is rarely seen in older adults. Recurrent infection of the buttocks region is not uncommon, especially in females.

<H1>HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS
<H2>Definition
The human papillomavirus (HPV) is a sexually transmitted infection (STI). There are 150 identified types of HPV and at least 40 affect the genital area.
<H2>Incidence
A. Most sexually active persons are exposed to HPV in their lifetime.
B. Types 16 and 18 account for 66% of all cervical cancers, whereas the 5 additional types targeted by the 9-valent vaccine account for 15%. Types 6 &11 cause 90% of genital warts.
<H2>Pathogenesis

A. Many types of HPV are sexually transmitted through anogenital contact, mainly during vaginal and anal sex. HPV can also be transmitted during oral sex and genital-to-genital contact without penetration.  In rare cases, a pregnant patient can transmit HPV to an infant during delivery.
B. Oncogenic, high-risk HPV infection (HPV 16 and 18) cause the majority of cervical, penile, vulvar, vaginal, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers and precancers.
C. Other HPV infections (HPV 6 and 11) cause genital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.
<H2>Predisposing Factors
A. Early first coitus.
B. Multiple sexual partners.
C. History of transmitted infections.
<H2>Common Complaints
A. Painless genital “bumps” or warts.
B. Pruritus.
C. Bleeding during or after coitus.
D. Malodorous vaginal discharge.
E. Dysuria.
<H2>Other Signs and Symptoms
A. Wart-like growths on the genital area that are elevated and rough or flat and smooth.
B. Lesions occurring singly or in clusters, from <1 mm to cauliflower-like aggregates.
C. Papillomas that are pale pink in color.
<H2>Subjective Data
A. Elicit history of the onset of symptoms, location, frequency, and duration; aggravating and alleviating factors; and associated symptomatology.
B. Question the client about history of other STIs, sexual behaviors, recent change in sexual partner, and partner’s history of STIs.
<H2>Physical Examination
A. Inspect:
1. Inspect the external genitalia, perineum, and anus for lesions.
2. Speculum examination in females: Inspect the vaginal walls and cervix for lesions.
3. Application of 3% acetic acid whitens lesions (not considered diagnostic by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC]).
<H2>Diagnostic Tests
A. Women 21 to 29 years of age should be screened every 3 years with cytology.
B. Women 30 to 65 years of age should be screened every 3 years with cytology alone or every 5 years with a combination of cytology and HPV testing.
C. Application of 3% to 5% acetic acid during colposcopy should cause affected areas to turn white indicating genital mucosa infected with HPV.
D. Diagnosis of genital warts can usually be made by visual inspection or confirmed by biopsy.
<H2>Differential Diagnoses
A. HPV.
B. Condylomata.
C. Molluscum contagiosum.
D. Carcinoma.
<H2>Plan
A. General interventions:
1. Make the diagnosis promptly to begin treatment.
B. Client teaching: See Client Teaching Guide for this chapter, “Human Papillomavirus.”
1. HPV vaccines can be administered regardless of history of anogenital warts, abnormal Pap test, or HPV test, or anogenital precancer.

2. Explain to the client that therapy eliminates visible warts but does not eradicate the virus. No therapy has been shown to be effective in eradication of HPV. Ablation of warts may decrease viral load and transmissibility.
3. Advise the client to abstain from genital contact while lesions are present.
4. Using commons and limiting the number of sex partners can reduce the risk of HPV.
C. Pharmaceutical therapy:
1. Therapy is not recommended for subclinical infections (absence of exophytic warts).
2. Recommended regimens for external anogenital warts:
a. Client-applied:
i. Imiquimod 3.75% or 5% cream. Or
ii. Podofilox 0.5% solution or gel. Or
iii. Sinecatechins 15% ointment.
b. Provider-administered:
i. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or cryoprobe. Or
ii. Trichloroacetic acid or bichloroacetic acid 80% to 90% solution.
iii. Surgical removal by tangential scissor excision, tangential shave excision, curettage, laser, or electrosurgery.
3. HPV vaccines
a. Vaccination can begin at 9 years old. Routine HPV vaccination for all adolescents should begin at age 11 or 12 years old.
b. The 2vHPV, 4vHPV, and 9vHPV vaccines protect against the majority of cervical cancers cases.  Only 9vHPV is available in the United States.

c. Catch-up vaccination is recommended for older adolescents and young adults through age 26 years. The HPV vaccine can be given to patients up to 45 years of age with shared clinical decision making.
<H2>Follow-Up
A. Anogenital warts typically respond within 3 months of therapy.
B. For abnormal pap tests, providers should follow the 2019 ASCCP Risk Based Management Consensus Guidelines for Abnormal Cervical Cancer Screening Tests and Cancer Precursors.
C. Long-term follow-up should include Pap smears per ASCCP guidelines and pelvic examinations. Encourage the patient to self-examine the genitalia.
<H2>Consultation/Referral
A. Consult or refer the client to a physician when lesions persist after six consecutive treatments or when cervical or rectal warts are diagnosed.
<H2>Individual Considerations
A. Pregnancy:
1. Pregnant patients should be screened for HPV at the same intervals as nonpregnant patients.  A swab, Ayre’s spatula, or cytobrush can be used for obtaining cytology test samples during pregnancy.
2. HPV vaccination is not recommended in pregnancy.
3. Podophyllum, podofilox, and sinecatechins are contraindicated during pregnancy.
4. Cesarean delivery is indicated for women with anogenital warts if the pelvic outlet is obstructed or if the vaginal delivery would result in excessive bleeding.
B. Partners:
1. Sex partners do not need to be tested for HPV.
2. Patients should inform their current partners about having genital warts.
3. Treatment of genital warts is recommended if visible lesions are present.
4. Partners might already have HPV despite no visible signs of warts; therefore, HPV testing of sex partners with genital warts is not recommended.
5. Female sex partners of men who disclose they had a previous female partner with HPV should continue screening at routine intervals.
6. Consistent condom usage can lower the chance of acquisition and transmission of HPV. However, the virus can infect areas not protected by condoms.
C. Adolescents:

1. Education regarding the Gardasil vaccine is recommended for adolescents 9 to 25 years of age to prevent acquisition of HPV. The vaccination may help clients avoid contracting strains of HPV that increase the risk of cancers discussed earlier.
D. Men who have Sex with Men:
1. Digital anorectal rectal exam.
2. Data is insufficient to recommend routine anal cancer screening with anal cytology.
E. Transgender and Gender Diverse People
1. Patients with a cervix should follow current screening guidelines for cervical cancer.
F. Geriatrics:
1. Verrucous carcinoma and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) can be indistinguishable from condyloma. Older females are more likely to have VIN or carcinoma.
2. Diagnosis is made by biopsy; colposcopy is strongly advised.
3. Immunocompetence should be investigated in new or recurrent condyloma.

<H1>Syphilis
<H2>Definition

A. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted systemic disease caused by T. pallidum. Syphilis is characterized into different stages that can occur over several years or decades: primary, secondary, and tertiary. T. pallidum can also infect the CNS, which can occur at any stage of syphilis and result in neurosyphilis.
<H2>Incidence

A. In 2019, there were 129,813 new diagnoses of syphilis in the United States, with 38,992 being primary and secondary syphilis. In 2019, men who have sex with men accounted for 41.6% of clients diagnosed with primary or secondary syphilis. There were 1,870 reported cases of children born with congenital syphilis in 2019.
<H2>Pathogenesis
A. Treponema pallidum, a spirochete bacterium, is the causative organism that infects the mucous membrane.
<H2>Predisposing Factors
A. History of STIs.
B. Multiple sexual partners.
C. Illicit drug use.
D. Prostitution.
<H2>Common Complaints
A. Genital lesion, generalized rash involving palms and soles, mucous patches, and condyloma latum are common.
<H2>Other Signs and Symptoms
A. Primary syphilis:
1. Chancre that is painless or minimally painful (Figure 20.3).
2. Round, indurated lesion with little or no purulent exudate.
3. Regional bilateral lymphadenopathy.
B. Secondary syphilis:
1. Generalized maculopapular rash that is nonpruritic and copper-colored on palms or soles; may be erythematous or scaly.
2. Mucous patches; painless, white, mucous membrane lesions.
3. Generalized lymphadenopathy; flulike syndrome, including fever, headache, sore throat, and malaise.
4. Patchy alopecia.
C. Tertiary syphilis:
1. Gumma: locally destructive granulomatous tumors involving various organs or systems; commonly seen on the liver but can occur on other organs (heart, brain, skin, bone, testis).
2. Cardiovascular: aortic involvement, aneurysms, and valve insufficiency.
3. Neurologic: Tabes dorsalis and general paresis.
D. Latent syphilis:

1. Latent syphilis acquired within the preceding year is referred to as early latent syphilis. All other cases of latent syphilis are classified as late latent syphilis or latent syphilis of unknown duration.
2. Latent infections are detected by serologic testing.
<unnumbered box>Latent-phase syphilis manifests itself after treatment failure or no history of treatment. Spirochetes can lie dormant for years.</unnumbered box>
E. Congenital syphilis:
1. Symptoms range from asymptomatic to fatal.
<H2>Subjective Data
A. Elicit history of onset, location, frequency, and duration of symptoms; aggravating and alleviating factors; and associated symptomatology.
B. Question the client about history of other STIs, illicit drug use, and sexual habits.
<H2>Physical Examination
A. Check temperature, pulse, respirations, and blood pressure.
B. Inspect:
1. Inspect the skin; note lesions and rashes.
2. Observe the head; note patchy alopecia.
3. Examine the mouth and throat; note lesions.
4. Inspect the genital and rectal area; note lesions and rashes.
C. Auscultate:
1. Heart.
2. Lungs.
D. Palpate:
1. Lymph nodes (neck, supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, and inguinal regions).
E. Neurologic examination:
1. Assess sensory functioning.
2. Test cranial nerves, first through twelfth.
<H2>Diagnostic Tests
A. The definitive method for diagnosing early syphilis and congenital syphilis is through darkfield examinations and molecular test for detecting T. pallidum from lesion exudate or tissue.
B. Diagnosis is made after two positive different serologic tests (nontreponemal or treponemal).
C. NAAT testing is not commercially available.
D. Diagnosis is reliant on the use of two laboratory serologic tests:
1. Nontreponemal test or
2. Rapid plasma regain (RPR) test and a treponemal test
E. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture to detect neurosyphilis.
<H2>Differential Diagnoses
A. Syphilis.
B. Herpes simplex virus.
<H2>Plan
A. General interventions:
1. Staging of the disease may be difficult but guides management decisions.
B. Client teaching: See Client Teaching Guide for this chapter, “Syphilis.”
1. Advise the client to abstain from sexual activity until treatment is completed.
2. Discuss the importance of partner notification.
3. Stress the importance of adhering to the follow-up regimen.
C. Pharmaceutical therapy: The CDC recommends the following treatment regimens:
1. Primary and Secondary Syphilis:
a. Adults: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units injected intramuscularly (IM) in a single dose.
b. Pediatrics: benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg, up to the adult dose of 2.4 million units, injected IM in a single dose.
2. Latent Syphilis:
a. Adults:
i. Early latent syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 2.5 million units IM in a single dose.
ii. Late latent syphilis: benzathine penicillin G 7.2 million units total, administered at 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals.
3. Neurosyphilis (manage with expert consultation):
a. Adults: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G18 to 24 million units daily, administered as 3 to 4 million units IV every 4 hours or continuous infusion for 10 to 14 days
i. Alternative Regimen: Procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once daily plus Probenecid 500mg orally 4 times/day, both for 10 to 14 days.
b. Pediatrics: penicillin desensitization, then treatment with the recommended regimen.
4. Primary syphilis, secondary syphilis, latent syphilis, or late latent syphilis in (nonpregnant) clients with penicillin allergy:
a. Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 2 weeks, or tetracycline 500 mg PO QID for 2 weeks.
5. Latent syphilis of unknown duration or late syphilis:
a. Treat with the aforementioned regimen for infections of less than 1 year in duration. If more than 1 year, treat with the aforementioned regimen for 4 weeks.
6. Pregnancy: Parenteral penicillin G is the only therapy with documented efficacy for syphilis during pregnancy.
a. For pregnant clients with penicillin allergy, penicillin treatment after desensitization is          recommended for the following reasons:
b. Penicillin is effective in preventing transmission and treating the infected fetus.
c. Doxycycline and tetracycline are contraindicated in pregnancy.
d. Erythromycin may not cure the infected fetus.
<H2>Follow-Up

A. Primary and secondary syphilis: Clinical and serologic examinations should be conducted at 6, 12, and 24 months. Absence of a fourfold decrease in the RPR titer within 12 months is indicative of treatment failure.

B. Latent syphilis: Clinical and serologic examinations should be conducted at 6, 12, and 24 months. Absence of a fourfold decrease in the RPR titer within 12 to 24 months is indicative of treatment failure.
C. Tertiary syphilis: Minimal evidence regarding follow-up exists. Follow-up largely depends on the nature of the lesions.
D. Neurosyphilis: CSF examination should take place every 6 months until the cell count is normal.
<H2>Consultation/Referral
A. Consult or refer the client to a physician when the recommended treatment fails and client noncompliance and re-exposure have been ruled out, or when neurosyphilis is diagnosed.
<H2>Individual Considerations
A. Pregnancy:
All pregnant patients should be screened at the first prenatal visit.

2. Retest at 28 weeks gestation and at delivery if at increased risk due to geography or personal risk (substance use, STIs during pregnancy, multiple partners, a new partner, partner with STIs). 3. Any client having a fetal death at more than 20 weeks’ gestation should be tested for syphilis.
4. Clients who are allergic to penicillin should be desensitized and treated with penicillin during pregnancy.
5. Follow-up: Perform serologic tests monthly until adequacy of treatment has been ensured.
B. Jarisch–Herxheimer
1. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute febrile reaction that occurs within 24 hours after the initiation of syphilis treatment.
2. This reaction occurs most frequently in early syphilis because the bacterial load is higher.
3. Symptoms include fever, headache and myalgia.  Antipyretics can be used to manage symptoms.
4. This reaction may induce early labor or cause fetal distress in pregnancy.
C. Pediatrics:
1. Congenital syphilis is caused by untreated infection or treatment failure in the mother.
2. Refer the client to a physician for infectious disease consultation.
3. Medication therapy: See the “Pharmaceutical Therapy” section.
D. Partners:
1. Sexual partners exposed to syphilis in the primary, secondary or early latent stages of syphilis should be evaluated and treated per recommendations.
2. Partners exposed to syphilis <90 days before diagnosis should be treated presumptively.

3. Partners who have been sexually active >90 days after diagnosis should be presumptively treated for early syphilis if serologic tests results are not immediately available or follow-up is uncertain.
E. Geriatrics:
1. Dementia, tremors, and pupillary changes are the result of long-term untreated syphilis2. The CSF should be tested using the FTA-ABS test. The VDRL is usually not adequate.
3. Syphilis is uncommon in the elderly in developed countries, but is very common worldwide.

<H1>TRICHOMONIASIS
<H2>Definition

A. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection (STI). It is easily passed between sex partners during penile-vaginal sex or through transmission of infected vaginal fluids or fomites among women who have sex with women. (Figure 20.4).
<H2>Incidence
A. Trichomoniasis is estimated to be the most prevalent nonviral STI worldwide, affecting 3.7 million persons in the United States.
B. Exact prevalence is unknown since trichomoniasis is not a reportable disease.
C. Rates are higher among women >24 years than women <24 years old.
<H2>Pathogenesis
A. Trichomonas vaginalis, a flagellated protozoan, is the causative organism.
<H2>Predisposing Factors
A. History of STIs.
B. Multiple sexual partners.
C. Less than a high school education.
D. Living below the national poverty level.
E. Concurrent infection with BV
<H2>Common Complaints
A. The majority of persons who have trichomoniasis have minimal or no genital symptoms.
B. Copious, yellow-green, or watery gray vaginal discharge with or without vulvar irritation
C. Vaginal odor.
D. Dysuria.
E. Dyspareunia.
F. Postcoital spotting or bleeding.
G. Abdominal discomfort.
H. Pruritus.
I. Urethritis
J. Epididymitis
K. Prostatitis
<H2>Subjective Data
A. Elicit history of the onset, location, frequency, and duration of symptoms; aggravating and alleviating factors; and associated symptomatology.
B. Question the client about history of other STIs or vaginal infections, changes and characteristics of vaginal discharge, and recent change in sexual partner.
<H2>Physical Examination
A. Check temperature.
B. Assessment:
1. Inspect the introitus for discharge and irritation.
2. Speculum examination:
a. Inspect the vaginal walls for discharge and irritation.
b. Inspect the cervix for discharge, erythema, punctate hemorrhages (strawberry-patch cervix), and friability.
C. Palpate:
1. Bimanual examination:
a. Assess for cervical motion tenderness.
b. Palpate for uterine and adnexal tenderness.
<H2>Diagnostic Tests
A. Wet mount microscopy: Easy to perform, but has low sensitivity (44% to 68%).

B. Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) are highly sensitive. Reliable samples include provider-collected endocervical swabs, provider-collected vaginal swabs, female urine specimens, and liquid Pap smear specimens collected in PreservCyt Solution (Hologic).
<H2>Differential Diagnoses
A. Trichomoniasis.
B. Bacterial vaginosis.
C. Vulvovaginal candidiasis.
D. Chlamydia.
E. Gonorrhea.
F. Pelvic inflammatory disease.
G. Foreign-body vaginitis.
<H2>Plan
A. General interventions:
1. Prompt diagnosis helps initiate treatment.
B. Client teaching: See Client Teaching Guide for this chapter, “Trichomoniasis.”
1. Advise the client to abstain from sexual activity until treatment is complete.
2. Untreated infections can last months to years.
3. Reiterate safe sex practices including condom use.
4. Men who have been circumcised might have a reduced risk for trichomoniasis.
5. Avoid douching as this can increase the risk for vaginal infections.
C. Pharmaceutical therapy:
1. Drug of choice:
a. Females: metronidazole 500 mg orally BID for 7 days.
b. Males: metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose.
c. Alternative treatment for males or females: tinidazole 2 g orally in a single dose.
d. Advise clients that alcohol and alcohol-containing products should be avoided at least 24 to 48 hours after the last dose of metronidazole is taken.
e. Inform the client of a possible metallic taste in the mouth during treatment.

2. Metronidazole gel is unlikely to achieve therapeutic levels in the urethra or perivaginal glands. It is a considerably less efficacious treatment than oral preparations and is not recommended for use.
<H2>Follow-Up
A. All women should be retested 3 months after treatment because of the high rate of reinfection.
B. There is insufficient data to retest men after treatment.
<H2>Consultation/Referral

A. Should treatment with the previous regimen fail in a client felt to be adherent with medication and not subject to reinfection, consult with or refer the client to a physician for assessment of metronidazole susceptibility.
<H2>Individual Considerations
A. Pregnancy:
1. Symptomatic pregnant clients, regardless of pregnancy stage, should be tested and treated. Metronidazole 500 mg BID for 7 days
2. Lactation: Metronidazole 500 mg BID for 7 days
3. Tinidazole should be avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding should be deferred for 72 hours after a single 2 g oral dose.
B. Partners:
1. Partners should be treated to prevent reinfection.
2. Partners should be advised to abstain from intercourse until treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved. Recommended treatment is metronidazole 2 g orally, one time.
2. Good faith treatment for partners is recommended without needing to see the partner.
C. Geriatrics:
1. Uncommon pathogen in postmenopausal clients.
2. Symptoms are vulvar irritation with discharge.
3. Diagnose with wet prep.
4. Treat with metronidazole 1 g in the morning and 1 g in the evening.
D. Clients with HIV:
1. Screen all females at the first visit and annually for trichomoniasis.
2. Treatment for trichomoniasis: multiple dose therapy: metronidazole 500 mg BID for 7 days.

<H1>CHLAMYDIA

<H2>PROBLEM Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted infection. Often, no problems are present, but you may notice a yellowish discharge from the penis or vagina, burning during urination, frequent and urgent urination, or pelvic pain.

Untreated chlamydia in females may lead to a condition called pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). PID is a leading cause of infertility, increased ectopic pregnancies, and chronic pelvic pain in females.
<H2>CAUSE Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium called Chlamydia trachomatis. This bacterium is spread through sexual contact and may infect the eyes, throat, vagina, penis, or rectum.
<H2>PREVENTION/CARE
A. Limit sexual partners.
B. Have routine screening tests for chlamydia prior to beginning a new sexual relationship.
C. Use condoms with sexual activity.
<H2>TREATMENT PLAN

Abstain from sexual activity until you and your partner(s) have completed your prescribed medication. Your healthcare provider is required to report this disease to the public health department. The health department may contact you.
Diet: As desired.
Medications: Chlamydia can be cured by the prescribed antibiotics.

You need to take all of your antibiotics. It is very important that you keep your follow-up appointment with your provider in 3 months: Your appointment has been scheduled for: ____________________________________________________________________________
You Need to Notify the Office If:
A. You are unable to take your antibiotics due to nausea, vomiting, or a reaction.

CLIENT TEACHING GUIDE
<H1>GONORRHEA

<H2>PROBLEM Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection. You may have the following symptoms: burning during urination, yellowish discharge from the penis or vagina, heavier menstrual periods, or pelvic pain.

Untreated gonorrhea in females can lead to a condition called pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). PID is a leading cause of infertility, increased ectopic pregnancies, and chronic pelvic pain in females.
<H2>CAUSE Gonorrhea is caused by an organism called Neisseria gonorrhoeae. This organism is spread through sexual contact and may infect the eyes, throat, vagina, penis, or rectum.
<H2>PREVENTION/CARE
A. Limit sexual partners.
B. Have routine screening tests for gonorrhea prior to beginning a new sexual relationship.
C. Use condoms during intercourse.

<H2>TREATMENT PLAN Your healthcare provider is required to report this disease to the public health department. The health department may contact you. Abstain from sexual activity until you and your partner(s) have completed your prescribed medications.
Diet: There is no special diet that needs to be followed.
Medications: Gonorrhea can be cured by the prescribed antibiotics.
It is very important that you keep your follow-up appointment that has been scheduled for you on:
All of the antibiotics need to be taken.
You Need to Notify the Office If:
A. You have any new symptoms.

F. Dry affected area thoroughly.

Activity: Stress is a trigger for an outbreak. Exercise may help with keeping your stress level down.

Medications: Antiviral medications are used to suppress the virus. They do not cure it but reduce the intensity of viral outbreaks.

Chapter 8: Persuasion
Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Distinguish between persuasion, manipulation, and influence in business contexts.
Apply the three classical rhetorical appeals—logos, pathos, and ethos—to shape strategic messages.
Use Cialdini’s six principles of persuasion to ethically motivate action.
Structure persuasive business messages using AIDA and PAS frameworks.
Critically evaluate real-world persuasive communication in fundraising, marketing, and leadership scenarios.
Craft credible, compelling, and audience-aware persuasive messages across formats.
Executive Summary

Persuasion isn’t deception. It’s not manipulation in a sharp suit or emotional coercion wrapped in polite language. At its best, persuasion is a partnership—a deliberate, ethical invitation for someone to see a new perspective or take meaningful action.

In the world of business communication, persuasive messaging is more than a useful tool—it’s the current that runs through everything. Whether you’re pitching an idea, proposing a change, advocating for a cause, or motivating a team, persuasion is your tool for impact.

This chapter explores the mechanics and strategies of persuasion, building directly on the foundational principles of ethical communication we explored in Chapter 7. We’ll begin with Aristotle’s classic appeals - logos, pathos, and ethos - and modernise the conversation with Robert Cialdini’s six principles of influence. From there, we’ll turn theory into structure with the AIDA and PAS frameworks.
This chapter will equip you with these powerful tools, anchored in integrity, guided by empathy, and built to earn trust.
Defining Persuasion: It’s Not a Dirty Word

In the previous chapter, we established the non-negotiable role of ethics in business communication. Now, we apply that foundation to persuasion—a skill that, more than any other, tests our commitment to those principles.

Persuasion is not manipulation. However, it is term that has been unfairly tarnished, often confused with its unethical cousins. To be an effective and respected communicator, you must understand the difference.

Influence is the broadest term. It is the capacity to have an effect on the character, development, or behaviour of someone or something. A respected leader has influence simply because of their position and reputation. Influence is typically passive.

Persuasion is active. It’s the intentional use of communication, through argument, evidence, or appeal. to guide an audience toward adopting a belief or taking action. It respects the audience's autonomy. It offers clarity. It invites a choice.
Manipulation, by contrast, crosses the ethical line. It seeks to control. It often plays on fear, distorts facts, or exploits emotions to serve the speaker’s interests, not the audiences.

The line between the three is integrity. Persuasion without integrity is manipulation. When you persuade, you are essentially asking someone to change. Whether it’s their behaviour, mindset, or priorities, you’re potentially creating cognitive dissonance. This is the discomfort people feel when holding two conflicting ideas. To reduce that discomfort, they must either change their mind… or reject your message.
Example: Persuasion Builds, Manipulation Breaks

Persuasion: “We’re under pressure this week. If we each put in two extra hours tonight, we can finish early and deliver ahead of schedule. That would give us a strong win to show the client, and I’ll make sure we recognise this effort at Friday’s team meeting.”
The team agrees. The request is clear, time-bound, appeals to shared pride (pathos), demonstrates credibility (ethos), and shows respect by promising recognition.
Manipulation: “Senior leadership is watching. If you don’t stay late, it’ll look bad for promotions.”
The team complies, but resentment builds. The request uses fear and implied punishment, eroding trust and morale.
Understanding persuasion means understanding how people make decisions. And for decades, we got that part wrong.
Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky famously challenged the idea that humans are purely rational actors. Their work in behavioural economics introduced the world to dual system thinking:
System 1: Fast, instinctive, emotional.
System 2: Slow, effortful, logical.
The catch? We use System 1 far more often. In many cases, System 2 just rationalises what System 1 has already decided.

So, what does this mean for you as a communicator? It means effective persuasion speaks to both systems. It respects logic, but it leads with resonance. Facts matter—but so does how those facts make people feel.
Pull Quote: Persuasion is not just trying to reverse someone’s beliefs. It’s the process of gradually influencing attitudes and behaviours and motivating the audience to act!
Reflection Prompt: Think about a time when you changed your mind. What shifted your thinking—facts, feelings, trust? Who or what influenced you, and how did it happen?
The Rhetorical Triangle: Logos, Pathos, and Ethos
About 2,300 years ago, Aristotle, in his book Rhetoric, gave us a framework that remains the bedrock of persuasive communication: the rhetorical triangle.

He understood that to persuade an audience, you need to appeal to them on three distinct but interconnected levels. A message that neglects one of these pillars is like a stool with two legs—unstable and likely to topple.
Ethos: The Appeal to Credibility and Character

Before an audience will listen to what you say, they must first trust who you are. Ethos is your foundation. It’s the credibility you project, signalling to your audience that you are knowledgeable, trustworthy, and have their best interests at heart. Ethos is not just about having a fancy title; it is actively earned and demonstrated. We can break it down into three components:

Competence and Expertise: You need to show that you know what you’re talking about. This can be conveyed through your credentials, your years of experience, your command of technical details, or the quality of the evidence you present.

Character and Integrity: This is the core of ethical persuasion. Do you come across as honest, fair, and principled? You build this by being transparent, acknowledging counterarguments, citing sources accurately, and, crucially, admitting what you don’t know.
Paradoxically, acknowledging a limitation or a potential risk in your own proposal can boost your ethos, because it signals honesty and confidence.

Goodwill and Dynamism: This is the audience’s belief that you care about them and are passionate about the topic. It’s conveyed through your tone, your enthusiasm, and your focus on shared benefits ("what this means for us") rather than personal gain ("what I want").
Pathos: The Appeal to Emotion

People are rarely rational. As much as we would like to think we are driven by logic, our feelings, values, and experiences play a large part in our decision-making. Think about buying a car, we should all be buying small hybrid cars, they are cheaper and easier to park! And yet, given the chance, we’d all be driving Ferraris!

Pathos connects with the audience on an emotional level. It makes your message more memorable and ultimately motivating. Storytelling is one of the most effective ways of using pathos. Storytelling transforms abstract ideas into relatable human experiences. We will explore the craft of storytelling in more depth in Chapter 9, but it is important to recognise that a well-chosen narrative can bring facts to life and help audiences connect to your message.
Ethical emotional appeals connect to universal values:

Appeals to Hope and Aspiration: Painting a vivid picture of a positive future. A CEO might use pathos to rally employees around a new vision, focusing on the pride and excitement of building something innovative together.

Appeals to Empathy: Telling a story that allows the audience to feel a connection to others. Charities excel at this, using stories of individuals to make large-scale problems feel more personal and relatable.

Appeals to Shared Values: Tapping into a sense of community, tradition, or principle. A manager arguing for a new sustainability initiative might appeal to the team’s shared desire to be a responsible corporate citizen.
However, pathos carries the greatest ethical risk. Appeals to fear, guilt, or pity can impair judgment if they aren’t grounded in sound reasoning. should enhance logic, not replace it.

The danger of pathos lies in using it to short-circuit logical thought, such as relying on fearmongering, flattery, or pity to get your way. Used properly, it inspires; used poorly, it’s manipulative. Emotional engagement should enhance logic, not replace it.
Logos: The Appeal to Logic

Logos is the appeal to reason. It’s built upon a foundation of clear logic and solid evidence. In a professional setting, logos is often the most heavily scrutinised appeal. Your argument must be able to stand up to questioning.
There are two primary forms of logical reasoning:
Deductive Reasoning: This moves from a general principle to a specific conclusion. It follows the structure: If A is true, and B is an example of A, then B is also true.

Business Example: "Our company policy (general principle) requires all client-facing reports to be approved by the legal department. This sales pitch is client-facing (specific case). Therefore, this document must be approved by the legal department (conclusion)."
Inductive Reasoning: This moves from specific evidence to a general conclusion. You observe a pattern and form a generalisation.

Business Example: "In Q1, our marketing campaign on Instagram had a 2% conversion rate. In Q2, the rate was 2.2%. In Q3, it was 1.9% (specific evidence). Based on this data, we can conclude that Instagram is not a high-performing channel for our business (general conclusion)."

Reflection Prompt: Which of the three appeals—logos, pathos, or ethos—do you naturally lean on most when trying to persuade? Which do you underuse? How might balancing them strengthen your next pitch, email, or proposal?
Pull Box: People don’t always believe what makes sense. They believe what feels true.

While Logos provides the rational backbone of an argument, we must not worship at the altar of logic alone. As advertising executive Rory Sutherland argues in his book Alchemy, some of the most powerful persuasive acts are those that don't make conventional sense. He calls this "psycho-logic."

Consider Red Bull. It’s expensive, comes in a small can and tastes "awful." From a rational perspective, it should have failed… and yet, these apparent “flaws” became its greatest marketing strengths. The taste and price signalled potency… “if it's expensive and tastes like medicine, it must work.”

Sutherland's point is that people do things for reasons they don’t always articulate. To persuade, you must sometimes appeal to the unstated, seemingly irrational desires that actually drive behaviour.
It’s not about abandoning logic, but you must recognise its limitations and respect the power of perception.
Analysing Your Purpose and Audience

Before you persuade anyone of anything, stop. Don’t write. Don’t design your slides. Don’t even open PowerPoint. First, get crystal clear on two things: your purpose (what you want to happen) and your audience (who you need to convince).
Your Purpose: What Do You Want Your Audience to Do?

A persuasive purpose is not the same as a general intention. “I want to update the board on our progress” might be polite, but it’s passive. It gives the audience no decision to make and no reason to act.

A persuasive purpose has a verb in its bloodstream. It’s targeted and measurable “I want the board to approve an additional £50,000 in funding to complete Phase 2 by the end of the year.” That’s a purpose you can measure against the outcome—and that your audience can say yes or no to.
Audience: Bridging the Gap

Once you know what you want, turn your focus on your audience. Persuasion is not a monologue, it’s a negotiation. That means understanding your audience so well you can meet them where they are, not where you wish they’d be.
Build a profile that covers three layers:
Demographics: Objective facts like age, job title, level of education, and professional background.
Psychographics: Their internal world of beliefs, values, goals, and motivations. What do they care about? What keeps them up at night?
Contextual Details: The immediate situation. What are their current pressures? What is their relationship to you? How much do they already know about your topic?
A key part of your audience analysis is anticipating resistance. People rarely change their minds without some friction. Common forms of resistance include:

Inertia: The easy way! the basic preference for keeping things the way they are. The best way to counter this is to highlight the risks and costs of inaction, making the status quo seem uncomfortable.

Scepticism: Distrust of you, your data, or your proposal. Counter this by building a stronger ethos, providing undeniable evidence (logos), and, whenever possible, using a credible third-party endorsement (Pro-tip: it's even more powerful if you use a source the audience already favours)
Apathy: They just don't care about the issue. To overcome this, connect your idea to something they already care about, often through a well-placed emotional hook (pathos).
Bias and Resistance:

One reason resistance is so stubborn is confirmation bias - the human tendency to favour information that supports what we already believe and dismiss what challenges it. A sceptical stakeholder won’t just question your data; they’ll instinctively notice every detail that undermines your case. To counter this, acknowledge objections openly. Provide evidence from sources they already trust. And wherever possible, frame your idea as building on what they already value, rather than attacking it.
Putting Analysis into Action: The Real Estate Pitch

Imagine you're a real estate agent selling a single, beautifully renovated character home in a transitioning urban neighbourhood. The property has many features, but you know you can't just list them all. You have to tailor your pitch.

Scenario 1: The Family A couple arrives in a minivan with a child's car seat visible in the back. Your instant analysis suggests their psychographics are centred on safety, community, and long-term stability. Their core emotional need is to find a secure and nurturing place to raise their family.

Your Persuasive Pitch: "As we walk through, you'll notice how quiet the street is. The park at the end of the block was just completely redone last year, and it’s become a real hub for local families on the weekends. We're also in the catchment for Northwood Elementary, which is one of the best-rated schools in the city. In fact, most of the neighbours on this street have young children, so there's a great sense of community here."

Why it Works: This pitch is almost pure Pathos. It doesn't focus on square footage or appliance brands. Instead, it paints a picture that speaks directly to the buyers' emotional needs for safety, belonging, and providing the best for their children.

Scenario 2: The Status Seeker: An hour later, a different buyer arrives in a flashy sports car. They are sharply dressed and checking market notifications on their phone. Your analysis suggests their psychographics are driven by financial upside, status, and strategic opportunity. Their core need is to make a smart, profitable decision.

Your Persuasive Pitch: "The key thing to know about this property is its location. This neighbourhood is on the cusp of a major transformation. Three new boutique coffee shops have opened within a five-block radius in the last six months, which is always a leading indicator of gentrification. Property values here have appreciated 15% year-over-year, and with the city's new zoning plan for this area, that trajectory is set to accelerate. This isn't just a home; it's a strategic asset."

Why it Works: This pitch is heavily weighted toward Logos. It uses data, trends, and financial language to appeal to the buyer's rational desire for a sound investment. The underlying Pathos is an appeal to their ego and the feeling of being a savvy, ahead-of-the-curve investor.
The house didn't change, but by analysing the audience, the persuasive strategy was completely transformed.

Group Activity: Choose a target audience (e.g., HR directors, small business owners, Gen Z consumers). Work in teams to build a mini-audience profile. Then brainstorm what tone, medium, and message structure would best reach them.
Cialdini’s Six Principles of Persuasion

In his 1984 book Influence, psychologist Robert Cialdini distilled decades of behavioural science into six principles that shape our decision making… in essence, he explains why we say “yes.”! They work because they tap into our fast, intuitive System 1 thinking. The same mental shortcuts we explored in Chapter 3 when we looked at bias and heuristics.

These cognitive shortcuts make persuasion feel effortless. However, these principles aren’t magic tricks. They’re psychological levers hardwired into human behaviour. That’s why these principles carry weighty ethical responsibility. Using them comes with a profound ethical responsibility. When used to enlighten and guide, they are tools of persuasion. When used to deceive or exploit, they become weapons of manipulation.
Reciprocity
What it is: We feel obliged to return favours, even unprompted ones.
Why it works: Fairness is baked into our social DNA. Across cultures, reciprocity underpins trust and cooperation.

Ethical business use: A consultant offers a free, valuable 30-minute diagnostic before pitching services—no hidden catch, no “gotcha” follow-up. The gift earns goodwill because it’s genuinely useful, not a setup for a sale.
Scarcity
What it is: When something is hard to get, we want it more.
Why it works: FOMO! Loss aversion makes us more motivated to avoid missing out than to gain something new.

Ethical business use: An internal announcement for a professional development course notes “only 15 spots available”—because it’s true. Faking scarcity (“last chance” every week) erodes trust faster than it builds urgency.
Authority
What it is: People tend to obey and trust figures of authority or credible experts.
Why it works: We have been socialised to trust that experts have superior knowledge – for example, professors!! It’s an efficient shortcut to making good decisions.
Ethical Business Use: A tech company features a testimonial from a well-respected independent industry analyst on its website. The analyst's credibility is transferred to the company.
Commitment and Consistency
What it is: People feel a powerful need to be consistent with what they have already said or done.
Why it works: Consistency signals reliability to others and to us. Breaking it feels uncomfortable. No one wants to be called a “waffler”

Ethical Business Use: A manager asks team members to voluntarily agree to a small goal, like "I'll submit my progress update every Friday morning." This small, public commitment makes it much more likely they will follow through, as they now see themselves as the "kind of person" who is reliable.
Liking
What it is: We are more likely to be persuaded by people we like or remind us of people we like.

Why it works: Similarity, compliments, and cooperation all increase our receptivity. This ties to the effect heuristic—our feelings about the person spill over into how we perceive their message. Sometimes this is conscious (“I trust her judgment”) and sometimes it’s subtle (“He reminds me of a teacher I respected”).

Ethical Business Use: A salesperson researches a client and discovers a shared interest—say, cycling. Mentioning it early builds authentic rapport, shifting the tone from “pitch” to peer-to-peer conversation. The connection is genuine, not engineered.
Social Proof (Consensus)
What it is: When we’re uncertain, we look to the actions and behaviours of others to determine our own.
Why it works: We assume that if a lot of other people are doing something, it must be the correct thing to do.

Ethical Business Use: Amazon uses this very effectively. Each product page on Amazon highlights detailed customer feedback. This signals to potential buyers that many others have purchased and been satisfied, normalising the decision without fabricating endorsements.
Quick Reference: Six Principles of Persuasion
People are more likely to say yes when…
Reciprocity → You gave first.
Scarcity → They might miss out.
Authority → An expert endorsed it.
Commitment & Consistency → They’ve already said or done something aligned.
Liking → They like and trust you.
Social Proof → Others are already doing it.
These aren’t tricks, they’re human defaults. Used ethically, they make persuasion smoother because they align your request with natural instincts. Used carelessly, they slip into manipulation.
Pull Quote: People don’t say yes because of facts alone. They say yes because of trust, belonging, and fairness.
Structuring Persuasive Messages: AIDA and PAS

Understanding the principles of persuasion is only the first step. Equally important is the ability to structure your message so that it guides the audience logically and purposefully from their current position to your intended outcome. Two long-established and widely applied frameworks, namely, AIDA and PAS. Frameworks which offer clear, adaptable pathways for achieving this.
AIDA: For Introducing Something New
The AIDA model is a classic in marketing and advertising. It's best used when you need to create awareness and generate excitement for something new, a product, an idea, or an initiative.
Attention: Hook your audience and pull them in. This must be sharp, surprising, or highly relevant.
Example: " The jacket you buy today shouldn’t be landfill tomorrow.
Interest: Now that you have their attention, explain why they should care. Connect the topic directly to their goals, challenges, or values.
Example: " Most outdoor gear ends up in a bin within a few years—worn out, broken, or replaced for the latest style. That’s not just bad for your wallet—it’s bad for the planet."
Desire: This is where you move from the problem to the solution. Paint a picture of a better future and make the audience want your solution.

Example: "Our New Premium Puff Jacket is built from 100% recycled materials, backed by our Ironclad Guarantee. If it ever fails, we’ll repair it—for life. It’s lightweight, weather-resistant, and warm enough for the summit or the school run."
Action: End with a clear, simple, and immediate call to action. Don't leave them wondering what to do next.
Example: " Choose well. Spend less.  And when you need gear that lasts, start here."
PAS: For Solving a Known Problem
The PAS model is more direct and is effective when your audience is already aware that a problem exists. It works by intensifying the pain of the problem before offering the relief of a solution.
Problem: State the problem clearly and concisely. Make sure it's a problem the audience recognises and relates to.
Example: " Finding it hard to stay productive? Do you often open your laptop with good intentions, only to end up scrolling through social media or getting pulled into emails that don’t matter?”
Agitate: This is the crucial step. Don't just state the problem—show them why it hurts. Use vivid language to highlight the frustration, cost, and negative consequences.

Example: “Every distraction costs more than time. It breaks your flow. Research shows it can take over 20 minutes to regain full focus after an interruption. That’s hours lost every week, deadlines slipping, and a constant low-level stress that follows you home.”
Solve: Now that you've amplified the pain, present your solution as the clear and obvious answer.

Example: “Our focus app blocks distractions, uses timed sprints to keep you moving, and gives progress reports that motivate. Try it free for a week and see how much more you can achieve—without longer hours.”
Application: Analysing Fundraising Appeals
Bringing it all together. The non-profit sector is a masterclass in persuasion. These organisations must build trust, evoke emotion, and drive action, often with limited resources.
Try this Exercise:
Visit the websites of a few charities, such as Save the Children, UNICEF, Red Cross, War Child, and Water.org. Analyse one of them.
To get you started, here is a brief analysis of what you might find on a site like the Red Cross:

Ethos: They establish immediate credibility through their globally recognised brand. The site is professional, and they often feature transparency reports on how donations are used, further building trust.
Pathos: The site will likely use powerful images of disaster relief and personal stories from both volunteers and victims. This creates a strong emotional connection and a sense of urgency.
Logos: They will provide clear statistics on the number of people they've helped or the scale of a crisis, giving a logical reason for the need for donations.

Cialdini's Principles: You might see Social Proof ("Join thousands of other Canadians in supporting this cause") and Scarcity ("Your donation will be matched, but only for the next 48 hours"). The very act of them helping people creates a sense of Reciprocity in the visitor.
Now, analyse your chosen website using the same lens:
How do they use logos, pathos, and ethos?
Which of Cialdini’s principles appear?
How does the site prompt action?
Which storytelling formats do they use (text, video, testimonials, images)?
Discussion Question: If you had £100 to donate, which site persuaded you most effectively? Why? What specific techniques made the difference?
Chapter Summary
Ethical communication is the foundation of persuasion; without integrity, influence quickly slips into manipulation.
In business, persuasion works best when it builds alignment rather than overpowering opposition.
Use the rhetorical triangle (logos, pathos, ethos) to create a balanced, credible appeal.
Understand your audience’s motivations and likely resistance, using tools such as Maslow’s hierarchy and principles of behavioural science.
Apply Cialdini’s principles thoughtfully and ethically—persuasion gains power when it guides, not when it exploits.
Structure your message with frameworks like AIDA or PAS to make your case clear, focused, and actionable.
Remember: ethical dilemmas are not always of your own making. Even when you inherit the problem, your choices in response shape your reputation.
What Can You Do Tomorrow?
Run an integrity check. Before sending a persuasive message, ask: ‘Am I being fully transparent? Does this empower my audience with truth, or does it mislead them?’
Rewrite the message using either the AIDA or PAS framework and see how it changes the flow and focus.
One-Minute Persuasion Checklist
Before sending your next persuasive message, ask:
Purpose: Is the action I want clear?
Appeals: Have I balanced ethos, pathos, and logos?
Principle: Which Cialdini lever am I using—and is it ethical?
Action: Is my call-to-action specific and easy to follow?

Setting the Stage

Every movement—from a simple breath to a complex athletic performance—depends on the harmony of body systems working together. Exercise is not merely about appearance or competition; it is a science of motion that connects physiology, nutrition, and mindset. Understanding how the body adapts to activity, responds to stress, and heals from strain allows us to train smarter, prevent injury, and sustain energy throughout life. Whether you are a casual exerciser, athlete, or health professional, learning to move with awareness and purpose is central to achieving lifelong wellness.

Purpose

By connecting physiological processes to behavioral and emotional well-being, this unit encourages a holistic view of fitness as an essential element of a long, healthy, and fulfilling life.
This chapter reinforces the concept that movement is not only about performance but about sustainability—helping individuals move well throughout every stage of life.
Learning Outcomes

Section 11.1: Wellness & Stress
Understanding Wellness and Stress

Stress is an inevitable part of life. It can serve as both a motivating force and a potential threat to wellness, depending on how it is perceived and managed. Hans Selye, often referred to as the “father of stress research,” defined stress as “the nonspecific response of the body to any demand placed upon it” (Selye, 1976). This means the body reacts physiologically to both positive and negative challenges in similar ways, releasing hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline to prepare for action.

While short-term stress (acute stress) can enhance performance and focus, chronic stress—when prolonged without adequate recovery—can disrupt homeostasis, impair immunity, and increase the risk for chronic diseases such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and depression (McEwen, 2007). In a fast-paced society, unmanaged stress has become a key factor influencing overall wellness among Americans.
Stress Management Determines Overall Physical & Emotional Well-Being

Rob Marmion, 2009, Shutterstock, Inc.
Rui Vale de Sousa, 2009, Shutterstock, Inc.
Types of Stress: Eustress and Distress

Stress is not inherently harmful; in fact, moderate levels can promote growth, focus, and motivation. This positive form of stress is known as eustress. Examples include preparing for an important exam, competing in sports, or starting a new job—situations that challenge one’s abilities but also build resilience (Quick et al., 2017).

Conversely, distress refers to negative, harmful stress that exceeds one’s ability to cope. Chronic distress can result from ongoing financial strain, work overload, or personal loss. Left unmanaged, it can manifest as sleep problems, anxiety, digestive issues, or weakened immunity (APA, 2023). Recognizing the difference between eustress and distress allows individuals to approach challenges with awareness and balance.
Physiological and Emotional Responses to Stress

When faced with a stressor, the body activates the fight-or-flight response, governed by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Adrenaline increases heart rate and blood pressure, while cortisol mobilizes glucose to fuel energy demands. Once the stressor passes, the body seeks to restore homeostasis (Sapolsky, 2004).

However, when stressors persist, the body may enter a prolonged state of tension. Emotional manifestations such as irritability, mood swings, or feelings of helplessness are common. Physically, individuals may experience headaches, digestive problems, muscle tension, or cardiovascular strain. Chronic activation of the HPA axis contributes to “allostatic load,” the cumulative wear and tear on the body’s systems (McEwen, 2007).
Common Manifestations of Stress
Coping and Stress Management
Effective stress management involves both problem-focused and emotion-focused strategies.
Problem-focused coping targets the source of stress directly—such as resolving a conflict or improving time management.
Emotion-focused coping helps manage one’s response to stress through relaxation, mindfulness, or social support (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984).
Practical approaches include:
Regular exercise to release endorphins
Adequate sleep and nutrition
Building strong social connections
Practicing mindfulness or meditation
Positive self-talk and reframing negative thoughts
Learning to view stress as a challenge rather than a threat can improve psychological resilience and health outcomes.

Section 11.2: Importance of Physical Activity
The Role of Physical Activity in Total Wellness

Physical activity is one of the most critical components of overall health and wellness. While many people approach exercise primarily as a tool for weight management, this narrow focus often overlooks the broader physiological and psychological benefits of movement. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2023), regular physical activity reduces the risk of chronic diseases, enhances mood, improves sleep, and strengthens the musculoskeletal and cardiovascular systems.

Weight loss goals may motivate short-term engagement in physical activity, but long-term adherence comes from recognizing exercise as a lifestyle practice that sustains energy, mobility, and mental balance. Individuals who integrate movement into their daily lives for stress relief, emotional regulation, or physical endurance often experience greater overall wellness and a more sustainable relationship with their bodies (WHO, 2020).
Redefining the Purpose of Physical Activity

Many people associate physical activity with “working off” excess weight or calories. This weight-centered mindset can make exercise feel like punishment rather than empowerment. In contrast, a wellness-centered mindset views physical activity as a tool for strengthening the body, supporting mental clarity, and improving quality of life.

Occupational and daily functional activities—such as walking, lifting, or cleaning—also contribute to physical fitness. Research suggests that non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT)—the energy expended in daily movement outside of structured exercise—can significantly impact metabolic health and body composition (Levine, 2004). This means that even individuals who do not frequent a gym may still be achieving meaningful physical fitness through their active lifestyles.

By reframing exercise as a mechanism to withstand, maintain, and build one’s lifestyle and career rather than a means of altering physical appearance, individuals can develop more positive, intrinsic motivation. Exercise becomes not just a tool for aesthetic goals but a foundation for longevity, resilience, and vitality.
Physical Activity and Mental Health

Beyond physical strength and endurance, regular activity profoundly impacts mental health. Aerobic exercise stimulates the release of endorphins and serotonin—neurotransmitters that reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression (Mayo Clinic, 2023). Engaging in consistent physical movement has been associated with improved self-esteem, cognitive function, and emotional regulation.

Additionally, physical activity can serve as a form of psychological relief—a way to process stress, clear the mind, and promote mindfulness through motion. Individuals who approach exercise with this perspective often find that movement becomes a form of therapy rather than obligation.
Nutrition and Physical Activity: A Complementary Relationship

Exercise and nutrition are interdependent. Physical activity supports nutrient metabolism, improves insulin sensitivity, and aids digestion. Meanwhile, adequate nutrition provides the energy and micronutrients necessary for muscle repair, hormone regulation, and recovery (Gropper & Smith, 2021).

In this way, exercise is not simply a counterbalance to caloric intake—it is a biological partner to nutrition that supports total metabolic health. Viewing physical activity as a supplement to nutrition rather than a punishment for eating fosters a sustainable and balanced approach to wellness.
Did You Know?

The World Health Organization (2020) recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week for adults. Yet, more than one in four adults globally do not meet these minimum guidelines—contributing to over 5 million preventable deaths annually from inactivity-related diseases.
Case Study: Redefining Fitness Goals

Marcus, a 35-year-old warehouse worker, walks an average of 12,000 steps per day and regularly lifts heavy boxes. Despite being physically active at work, he feels fatigued and discouraged by his lack of “gym time.” After consulting a wellness coach, Marcus learns to recognize his daily movement as meaningful exercise. He begins supplementing his routine with stretching and weekend bike rides rather than overexerting himself at the gym. Within weeks, his energy and mood improve—illustrating how reframing physical activity can promote both physical and mental well-being.

Section 11.3: Low, Moderate, and Extreme Impact Activities
Structure, Function, and Purpose of Movement Intensity

Everyday life involves a spectrum of physical activities—some intentional, others subconscious—that collectively contribute to cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and mental well-being. These activities can be categorized as low, moderate, or high (extreme) impact, depending on their effect on heart rate, oxygen consumption, and muscle exertion (ACSM, 2021).

Understanding the differences among these intensity levels helps individuals select appropriate activities that align with their abilities, health status, and goals. From a structural perspective, all forms of movement engage skeletal muscles and energy metabolism. Functionally, they strengthen the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, regulate metabolism, and maintain musculoskeletal health. Purposefully, they enhance longevity, resilience, and stress management—supporting both physical and psychological wellness.
Low-Impact Activities

Low-impact activities are gentle on the joints and require minimal energy expenditure but still stimulate circulation, flexibility, and muscle tone. These activities include leisurely walking, light household chores, yoga, stretching, and even playful movement such as dancing at a relaxed pace. Activities such as walking along the lakefront, gardening, or carrying groceries also fall into this category.

From a physiological standpoint, these activities modestly elevate heart rate and promote blood flow without overloading the body. They are especially beneficial for beginners, older adults, or individuals recovering from injury (NIH, 2022). Low-impact movement promotes consistency, mobility, and recovery—making it foundational for long-term wellness.
Moderate-Impact Activities

Moderate-impact activities elevate the heart rate and breathing more noticeably while still allowing for conversation. Examples include brisk walking, cycling at 10–15 mph, recreational swimming, or dancing at an energetic pace. These activities strengthen the heart and lungs, improve metabolic efficiency, and support healthy body composition (CDC, 2023).

The World Health Organization (2020) recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and depression. Functionally, this level of activity enhances endurance and improves the body’s ability to utilize oxygen—key components of aerobic fitness.
Different Types of Physical Activities
Dmitriy Samorodinov/Shutterstock.com
High (Extreme) Impact Activities

High- or extreme-impact activities significantly raise heart rate and challenge muscular and cardiovascular endurance. These include running, martial arts, uphill hiking, plyometrics, and high-intensity interval training (HIIT). Such exercises may fatigue the body within minutes but promote substantial physiological adaptation when performed safely and progressively (Mayo Clinic, 2023).

Extreme-impact exercises enhance anaerobic capacity, muscle hypertrophy, and bone density. However, due to their intensity, these activities require proper technique, hydration, and recovery to prevent injury or overtraining. The purpose of high-impact training is to push physical limits—developing strength, speed, and resilience.
Integrating Activity Levels into Daily Life

The diversity of physical activities available allows individuals to tailor their fitness regimens according to lifestyle, environment, and personal preference. A balanced program combines low, moderate, and high-impact movements to promote cardiovascular health, muscular endurance, flexibility, and stress relief.

Crucially, even routine daily tasks—such as walking at work, cleaning, or climbing stairs—contribute to overall energy expenditure and metabolic health. This reinforces the idea that all movement matters. Consistency in physical activity, regardless of intensity, supports cellular maintenance, growth, and repair—essential processes for health and longevity (Gropper & Smith, 2021).

According to the ACSM (2021), every minute of high-intensity exercise can provide benefits equivalent to roughly two minutes of moderate activity. However, overtraining without proper rest can impair immune function and muscle recovery.
