ACE inhibitors have been found to be effective at all stages of systolic dysfunction, unlike digitalis (which appears to benefit only those with severe LV systolic dysfunction). Several landmark studies (e.g., the Cooperative North Scandinavian Enalapril Survival Study, the Studies of Left Ventricular Dysfunction) have documented this broad spectrum of efficacy, demonstrating significant reductions in cardiac morbidity and mortality, as well as improvements in heart size, symptoms, quality of life, hospitalizations, and medication requirements. ACE inhibitors are able to slow the progression of systolic heart failure.

As noted, use of angiotensin blockade in patients with diastolic dysfunction has yet to demonstrate a mortality benefit under conditions of randomized controlled trial. Meta-analysis of data from available randomized trials and large-scale observational study do suggest such benefit, but more study is needed to confirm.

Despite their proven efficacy in systolic heart failure, ACE inhibitors are still not sufficiently prescribed. Surveys of community practice show underutilization by primary care physicians for persons with HF. This has prompted recommendations that ACE inhibitor use in HF be considered a quality measure.

<H4>Choice of Agent. Cost and convenience are the two major considerations; there is little evidence of other major differences among available agents. Generic formulations are now available for most once-daily preparations, making cost less of an issue than previously. In the few randomized, controlled studies directly comparing ACE inhibitors for the treatment of chronic HF, both longer- and shorter-acting preparations proved to be similarly effective, although the longer-acting agents tended to have a greater propensity to cause prolonged hypotension, especially when used in high doses.

<H4>Initiating Therapy and Minimizing Adverse Effects. ACE inhibitor therapy should be prescribed as first-line treatment for HF, starting with its use to treat risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, and coronary disease (stage A) and continuing as evidence of structural change develops, even before symptoms ensue (stage B). As noted, early treatment produces significant reductions in morbidity and mortality and helps to prevent disease progression.

<H5>Hypotension. Because hypotension is common at the onset of therapy (especially in the elderly), it is recommended to start with small doses (e.g., as little as 2.5 to 5.0 mg of lisinopril) and reduce any concurrent diuretic therapy. The dose is then increased gradually to the doses associated with a survival benefit (e.g., lisinopril 20 to 40 mg/d). Monitoring blood pressure is important not only to ensure adequate renal perfusion but also to minimize dizziness and falls. Most CHF patients are elderly and can be very susceptible to even mild degrees of cerebral hypoperfusion. Continuous blood pressure monitoring is needed because the onset of hypotension may be delayed for a few weeks and yet persist.

<H5>Renal Dysfunction. Patients with preexisting bilateral renal artery stenosis and those receiving very large ACE inhibitor doses are at greatest risk for renal impairment, limiting their use under such circumstances. Minor elevations in serum creatinine can be seen with the initiation of therapy due to changes in intrarenal hemodynamics, but these elevations are usually due to minor changes in intrarenal hemodynamics and are self-limited; they are not progressive. Monitoring of renal function (blood urea nitrogen [BUN], creatinine, urinalysis) is indicated. Any progressive deterioration in renal function requires dose reduction and close watching; rarely is the total discontinuation of therapy necessary unless there is renal artery stenosis or severe hypotension.

<H5>Hyperkalemia. Because ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone levels, the serum potassium may rise and should be monitored, particularly in patients with preexisting renal dysfunction or those receiving potassium supplementation, a potassium-sparing diuretic, or an aldosterone inhibitor. In many instances, potassium supplementation or use of a potassium-sparing agent can be discontinued or at least reduced.

<H5>Cough and Angioedema. A dry, irritant nocturnal cough affects as many as 10% of users. It is believed to be triggered by increased levels of tissue kinins associated with the inhibition of kinin metabolism in slow metabolizers. The cough can interfere with sleep, causing the patient to stop the drug. Angioedema is less common but is believed to develop by a similar mechanism; persons prone to idiopathic angioedema should avoid taking ACE inhibitor therapy. Those with unacceptable cough can consider a change in therapy.
<H3>Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers

These agents act at the receptor level to inhibit angiotensin II, which provides the vasodilating activity associated with angiotensin II blockade without increasing vascular endothelial kinins and triggering the bothersome cough and other kinin-attributed side effects associated with ACE inhibitor therapy. As such, they are considered a reasonable substitute for ACE inhibitor therapy in persons with systolic heart failure when the latter cannot be tolerated. Relief of symptoms, improvement in functional status, and reductions in heart failure–related hospitalizations are achieved. However, evidence of efficacy as regards enhancing survival in patients with systolic heart failure is not as strong as it is for ACE inhibitors, and there has been some question as to whether all these agents are equally effective, given differences in affinity for the target receptor (losartan having affinity less than candesartan or valsartan). While there remain no head-to-head randomized trials comparing ARBs, large cohort studies suggest no differences in all-cause mortality when comparing outcomes at full doses. Consequently, choice of agent can be based on cost. Initial dosing should start low (e.g., 25 mg/d losartan), but progress to full doses (e.g., 100 mg/d losartan as tolerated—systolic BP target can be as low as 90 to 100 mm Hg). Many of these agents have come off patent and are now available generically, making them preferred on a cost-effectiveness basis.

As alluded to earlier, angiotensin blockade is yet to demonstrate a survival benefit in persons with heart failure due to diastolic dysfunction, although hospitalizations are reduced and quality of life and exercise tolerance are improved. Results are similar for both ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Meta-analyses and large-scale observational study suggest a mortality benefit, but more study is needed to convincingly demonstrate it.

Combination therapy with an ACE inhibitor for enhanced angiotensin blockade reduces the hospitalization rate for heart failure and decreases LV size in, but not overall mortality; moreover, it markedly increases the rates of complications (e.g., hyperkalemia, worsening renal function, symptomatic hypotension). Systolic heart failure patients with elevated blood pressure despite full doses of an ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker might benefit from the addition of an ARB.
<H3>Adding Neprilysin Inhibition - Sacubitril/Valsartan

The application of angiotensin blockade achieves significant improvement in outcomes in patients with HFrEF, but many patients still remain severely limited by their symptoms and functionally impaired. Advances in the understanding of neprilysin (an endopeptidase that degrades important endogenous vasoactive peptides) and the effects of its inhibition have sparked interest in neprilysin inhibitors for treatment of heart failure. Early studies of the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril were limited by development of severe angioedema. Dual ARB/neprilysin inhibition appears to limit the risk and severity of the angioedema while preserving beneficial effects. In a major multicenter randomized trial involving 8,442 patients with class II to IV heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, comparing twice-daily enalapril with a twice-daily fixed combination of the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril and the ARB valsartan (PARADIGM-HF), significant reductions were achieved in the primary endpoints of cardiovascular mortality 3.3% vs. 16.5%), first hospitalization 2.8% vs. 15.6%), combination endpoint 1.8% vs. 26.5%), and all-cause mortality 7.0% vs. 19.8%). The most common adverse effects were hypokalemia and hypotension. Angioedema occurred in just 0.5%. Cough and elevated creatinine were also noted in a small percentage of patients. Subsequently, the FDA approved the combination angiotensin/neprilysin inhibitor preparation (Entresto) for patients with HFrEF.

Cost for the combination is substantial (six times that of generic valsartan), but the savings and patient benefits from fewer hospitalizations and improved clinical outcomes make use reasonably cost-effective (estimated QALY $47,531). Some have recommended this combination as first-line therapy, replacing angiotensin blockade alone, but more data on long-term effects are needed to determine safety of indefinite use—PARADIGM-HF was limited to 27 months. Animal models suggest the potential for neurocognitive and visual impairment due to inhibited metabolism of amyloid-beta peptide by the drug. No such adverse effects were noted during the course of the above-noted study.
<H3>Beta-Blockers

<H4>Rationale. Increased appreciation for the role of the sympathetic nervous system in the response to and perpetuation of HF has led to the application of beta-blockade for treatment. As discussed earlier, sympathetic stimulation is one of the major dysfunctional neurohumoral responses to heart failure, increasing with severity of disease and serving as an independent predictor of mortality. By blocking catechol-mediated myocardial stimulation and its adverse contributions to ventricular remodeling and hemodynamics (e.g., increased heart rate, increased peripheral resistance, decreased contractility), beta-blockers could reverse remodeling, slow disease progression, and enhance functional status and survival.

<H4>Efficacy. Many of hoped-for benefits have been observed with beta-blocker use in patients with and without reduced ejection fraction. Most importantly, survival is enhanced although hospitalizations for heart failure do not appear to decrease. Benefit accrues across the entire spectrum of disease stages and functional classes, although data on use in asymptomatic persons are more limited. Groups initially underrepresented in major studies (women, blacks, the very elderly) also appear to benefit. Persons with HF related to hypertension and coronary artery disease do especially well with beta-blockade, but so do those with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, with functional improvement related to changes in myocardial gene expression. Patients should be hemodynamically stable and relatively euvolemic at the time of initiating therapy.

Both cardioselective and nonselective beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol-XL, bisoprolol, carvedilol) have been shown to be effective. Use in combination with an ACE inhibitor achieves significant improvement in outcomes. Given their proven benefit, it is unfortunate that beta-blockers are underutilized in the treatment of HF, probably as a consequence of concern about side effects and the seemingly paradoxical idea of using a negatively inotropic agent to improve cardiac performance.

<H4>Adverse Effects. At the outset of therapy, there may be fluid retention (manifested by an increase in weight) due to decreased renal perfusion. Bradycardia and heart block may occur with the use of high doses, especially in persons with underlying sinus node or conduction system disease; low doses may be tolerated. Postural hypotension can be problematic, especially on the initiation of therapy with carvedilol, due to its alpha-blocking action; the problem decreases with continued use. Separating the daily intake for beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor administration can help to limit the risk of postural hypotension. The analysis of adverse effects and benefits associated with beta-blocker therapy finds, on balance, that the risks are well worth taking, given the likelihood of significant reductions in cardiac morbidity and mortality.

<H4>Choice of Agent and Patient Selection. The three beta-blockers studied to date (metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, carvedilol) span the spectrum of agents in this class, suggesting that differences among beta-blockers are less important than their similarities. On a theoretical basis, blockade of the entire adrenergic system should be more favorable hemodynamically than blockade limited to cardiac beta-receptors. In a large-scale, randomized, controlled study of this question (carvedilol vs. metoprolol, the Carvedilol or Metoprolol European Trial), carvedilol achieved a 15% greater reduction in mortality at 5 years but no significant difference in a combined endpoint of hospitalization and death. This survival advantage for carvedilol should be weighed against its greater tendency to cause orthostatic hypotension (see later discussion) and its high cost (about four times that of the branded long-acting formulation of metoprolol).

Contraindications to beta-blocker use in HF include severe bronchospastic disease (although modest doses of a cardioselective beta-blocker may be tolerated), symptomatic bradycardia, and advanced heart block. Diabetes mellitus and a history of bronchospastic disease are not contraindications.

<H4>Initiating Therapy. Patients need to be warned that symptoms may worsen a bit during the first few weeks of beta-blocker treatment and that it may take several weeks for clinical benefit to become evident. To minimize adverse effects early on, doses at first should be small (e.g., metoprolol succinate 25 mg/d, carvedilol 3.25 mg/d) and titrated upward slowly. The immediate goal is a resting heart rate of 50 to 60 beats/min. Diuretic therapy may be necessary to counter the fluid retention that can develop early on.
<H3>Diuretics (see also Aldosterone Antagonists)

<H4>Rationale. Diuretics are a key component of symptomatic therapy. They are directed at the volume overload that complicates heart failure. The degree of compensatory fluid retention in CHF is typically excessive, leading to pulmonary congestion and/or peripheral edema. In patients with mild to moderate HF, symptoms of volume overload respond acutely to diuretic therapy. However, diuretic therapy alone is usually insufficient for the chronic treatment of HF, in part because it stimulates the renin–angiotensin system and raises serum catecholamines, leading to increased afterload, reduced cardiac output, and further sodium retention. Consequently, concurrent ACE inhibition and beta-blockade are required.

Although diuretics may be effective in controlling peripheral edema and pulmonary congestion, most do little to prevent the progression of heart failure or improve prognosis. Overzealous use of diuretics can be counterproductive, producing prerenal azotemia or a dangerous fall in filling pressure (particularly important in diastolic dysfunction). Moreover, escalating diuretic therapy in mitral or aortic valve disease may inappropriately delay the timing of surgical therapy (see Chapter 33).

<H4>Thiazides. These are sulfonamide derivatives and are believed to inhibit sodium reabsorption in the cortical tubule. Although the number of thiazide preparations is large, they differ only in cost and duration of action. Most are very inexpensive and available generically (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone). Thiazides cause modest potassium depletion, which can be clinically important if there is underlying heart disease, especially in the setting of ventricular irritability, ischemia, or use of digitalis. Under such circumstances, careful monitoring for hypokalemia and assiduous potassium supplementation or use of a potassium-sparing diuretic may be needed. Mild hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia may result but are usually of little clinical significance (see Chapters 102 and 155). During the first 7 to 10 days of therapy, the serum calcium may rise, but it will stay elevated indefinitely only in patients with underlying hyperparathyroidism. Absorption from the gastrointestinal tract is rapid; the onset of action is 1 hour, and the half-life is 12 to 24 hours. For treatment of underlying hypertension, chlorthalidone is the more effective due to its more sustained duration of action (see Chapter 26).

<H4>Metolazone. This sulfonamide diuretic is similar to the thiazides in site of action (cortical tubule) but possesses a longer half-life and is more effective in patients with impaired renal function. The effective half-life is 24 to 48 hours, compared with 12 to 24 hours for the thiazides. Because it is a sulfonamide, it shares many of the same side effects, such as hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and hyperuricemia. The maximum daily dose is 10 to 20 mg.

<H4>Loop Diuretics. These potent agents act at the loop of Henle. Examples include furosemide, ethacrynic acid, bumetanide, and torsemide. With some of these drugs (e.g., furosemide), absorption can be erratic in HF; absorptions of torsemide and bumetanide are more consistent, exceeding 90%. For furosemide, the onset of action is 30 to 60 minutes and serum half-life is 2.7 hours; however, effects can last as long as 4 to 8 hours in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Serum half-life is longest for torsemide .0 hours) and shortest for bumetanide .3 hours).

Overdiuresis can be problematic and trigger countervailing mechanisms. After very vigorous diuresis, a period of postdiuretic sodium retention ensues, which, in the absence of dietary sodium restriction, may negate the natriuretic effect; it underscores the importance of limiting dietary sodium. A braking phenomenon in the setting of marked extracellular volume contraction has been described leading to less natriuretic response to each additional dose of loop diuretic. Purported mechanisms include activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic nervous system; nephron remodeling also appears to contribute.

Frequent urination is a common complaint; evening doses should be avoided if possible. The starting dose of furosemide is 20 to 40 mg/d. Prerenal azotemia (manifested by a BUN–creatinine ratio of >20:1), postural hypotension, light-headedness, and fatigue are clues to marked hypovolemia. Hypokalemia is the most serious metabolic consequence, necessitating careful monitoring of the serum potassium and supplementation should it fall to less than 3.5 mg/dL. Mild hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia may also occur. Ethacrynic acid is potentially ototoxic, especially when used in combination with an aminoglycoside antibiotic such as kanamycin. Audiograms should be obtained if ethacrynic acid is to be given for a prolonged period.

<H4>Combination Preparations. Combinations containing a thiazide and a weak potassium-sparing diuretic (e.g., amiloride, triamterene) are convenient to use and may facilitate compliance, but they are expensive and their fixed ratio limits dosing flexibility. Before prescribing such a preparation, the proper dose of each agent should be determined separately. The combination preparation is reasonable to use only if it can provide the exact doses desired. Many combinations contain subtherapeutic thiazide doses, and onset of action is slow; the full effect may take up to 1 week to become evident. They should be used with caution, if at all, in persons taking ACE inhibitors, because of the risk of hyperkalemia.

<H4>Selection of Diuretic Agent and Initiation of Therapy. When symptoms are slight (mild exertional dyspnea, minor ankle edema) or when the patient is asymptomatic but showing weight gain or x-ray findings indicative of early CHF, then diuretic therapy can be initiated with a thiazide (e.g., 25 to 50 mg/d of hydrochlorothiazide). The degree of dyspnea on exertion and weight change are the simplest clinical parameters to follow for gauging response to therapy in mild cases.

An increasing severity of symptoms is an indication for switching to a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide). Small doses of loop diuretics may also benefit patients with mild to moderate failure that cannot be adequately controlled by thiazides. Caution is warranted when treating a patient for the first time with a loop diuretic because a marked diuresis may be evoked, particularly with the use of a parenteral dose but sometimes with an oral dose. If a thiazide had been used previously, it should be stopped rather than continued in conjunction with the loop diuretic because the two agents are very potent when used together (see later discussion). If hypokalemia is a problem, potassium supplementation (see Appendix 32-1) or the use of a weak potassium-sparing diuretic (e.g., amiloride, triamterene) is indicated.

<H4>Use in Severe Congestive Heart Failure. In severe CHF, the absorption of oral loop diuretics such as furosemide declines, which accounts for the oft-noted reduction in efficacy during an exacerbation of heart failure. One can consider switching to a better absorbed, longer-acting loop preparation such as torsemide, but in head-to-head randomized trial among patients recently discharged for an exacerbation of heart failure, there was no significant difference in rehospitalization rates at one year or all-cause mortality at 3 years. The maximal effect of an oral loop diuretic can be achieved by using a large, single, daily dose rather than divided doses. Parenteral administration may be required to achieve diuresis. At times, supplementing oral therapy with an occasional parenteral dose in the office will suffice to counter worsening failure refractory to oral therapy. Adding a thiazide or metolazone to the loop diuretic program may be useful in refractory heart failure unresponsive to large doses of the loop diuretic alone. For patients with renal impairment, metolazone can be useful as the adjunct.

<H4>Diuretic Resistance. The onset of diuretic resistance, manifested by low urine sodium despite large oral doses of a loop diuretic, portends a poor prognosis. Intravenous administration, cutting back on ACE inhibition (which lowers natriuresis by lowering arterial pressure) in persons with HFpEF, and adding a second diuretic agent to a loop program (e.g., metolazone, referred to as “sequential therapy”) represent treatment options. Some argue that adding a second diuretic at low dose earlier in the course of heart failure will have a greater effect since it can precede nephron remodeling. Alternatively, one can add an aldosterone antagonist.

<H4>Monitoring Therapy. Monitoring postural symptoms and signs, potassium, BUN, and creatinine is essential to avoiding excess volume depletion, severe prerenal azotemia, and potassium abnormalities that may result from diuretic use and trigger complications. Such monitoring is especially important in the setting of drugs and conditions that affect or may be adversely affected by serum potassium, such as loop diuretics and combination diuretic programs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, digoxin, coronary ischemia, and renal failure. Magnesium level should also be monitored since depletion may also be triggered by diuretic therapy and contribute to refractory hypokalemia. Checking serum sodium periodically can help avoid hyponatremia that may ensue from potent diuretic therapy. Because volume status can be hard to ascertain, some have advocated selective use of a biologic marker such as the BNP to monitor and guide diuretic therapy, but results have been disappointing (see earlier discussion).
<H3>Mineralocorticoid (Aldosterone) Receptor Antagonists

Even with the use of ACE inhibition, aldosterone breakthrough can occur producing levels 20 times normal in persons with marked systolic dysfunction (EF < 30%). Such breakthrough underpins the rationale for adding a selective aldosterone blocker to standard first-line therapy. The selective aldosterone-receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) enhance sodium excretion and achieve 15% to 25% reductions in cardiac morbidity and mortality when used in conjunction with ACE inhibition, beta-blockade, and loop diuretics. Low doses usually suffice in the outpatient setting and avoid risking hyperkalemia. Their benefit may extend beyond enhanced sodium excretion to a direct beneficial effect on left ventricular remodeling. The nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid inhibitor finerenone has proved useful in heart failure patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease.

<H4>Indications for Use. In the context of marked LV dysfunction (EF < 30%) and inadequate response to standard first-line medical therapy, the addition of spironolactone or eplerenone should be considered. When small doses (e.g., 25 to 50 mg/d) of spironolactone or eplerenone are added to a program of maximal medical therapy, there are significant improvements in survival and rates of hospitalization, with benefits extending to persons across the spectrum of symptomatic disease (NYHA class II to IV)—one need not wait for symptoms to become severe before considering use in persons with marked reduction in LV systolic function. For HFpEF patients, use does not seem indicated at this time.

<H4>Adverse Effects and Monitoring Therapy. Serious hyperkalemia may occur, particularly in the setting of renal failure or treatment programs that include ACE inhibition, ARB therapy, or potassium supplementation. Use should be avoided in persons with a serum potassium ≥ 5,0 mEq/L. Close monitoring of the serum potassium is essential, and potassium supplementation should be stopped or limited to persons who manifest a serum potassium of less than 3.5 mg/dL despite therapy. These drugs should not be used in renal failure, because life-threatening hyperkalemia may ensue. Spironolactone has antiandrogenic activity which can lead to gynecomastia and breast pain in chronic users; eplerenone has less, and finerenone has none. There is also a question of increased risk of carcinogenesis with long-term use, but this is supported only by animal data.
<H3>SGLT2 Inhibitors
See Diastolic Heart Failure.
<H3>GLP-1 and GLP-1/GID Agonists
See Diastolic Heart Failure.
<H3>Vasodilators- Hydralazine/Isosorbide

Although largely replaced by ACE inhibitor therapy as first-line therapy, this combination vasodilator program has sufficient survival and hemodynamic benefits to warrant its consideration, especially as an addition to standard therapy in persons remaining unacceptably symptomatic. Benefit has been particularly noteworthy among severely symptomatic African-American patients, reversing left ventricular remodeling and reducing mortality—responses suggesting that nitric oxide, whose delivery is enhanced by this program, is an important pathophysiologic factor in heart failure among blacks and that adding the combination to standard therapy is a reasonable consideration in those with refractory disease. Cost is modest when these drugs are prescribed separately, but increased substantially with the use of a heavily promoted fixed-dose combination preparation. Disadvantages of the combination program include postural hypotension, the need for frequent dosing, and reflex tachycardia. There is a small risk of lupus-like syndrome with prolonged hydralazine use.

Nitrate monotherapy has been explored in a predominantly white patient population with preserved ejection fraction, but failed to demonstrate improvement in activity, quality of life, submaximal exercise capacity, or NT-proBNP levels.
<H3>Guanylate Cyclase Activation – Vericiguat

This activator of guanylate cyclase facilitates the vasodilating action of nitric oxide and improves outcomes in patients with acute decompensation. It is FDA-approved for use in HFrEF patients with decompensated heart failure. The initial dose is 2.5 mg once daily taken with food and doubled every two weeks as tolerated to reach a dose of 10 mg/day. The principal adverse effect is hypotension; nausea, dyspepsia, and anemia also occur. Hypotension can be considerable when used with other vasodilating drugs.
<H3>Digitalis

Once the centerpiece of treatment for HF based on the view that the drug enhances contractility, cardiac glycosides have been relegated to a minor role based on disappointing performance in major randomized, controlled studies (e.g., the Digitalis Investigation Group [DIG] trial), which failed to confirm a survival benefit at therapeutic serum levels as regards all-cause mortality, though there were fewer deaths related to heart failure. Another significant benefit (aside from rate control in atrial fibrillation—see Chapter 28) was a reduction in hospital admissions for severely symptomatic persons in sinus rhythm with marked systolic dysfunction (e.g., NYHA class III and IV disease, EF < 0.25, audible S3, marked left ventricular dilation). Post hoc analyses of the DIG trial data revealed increased mortality among patients with a serum digoxin level greater than 1.2 ng/mL (well within the traditional “therapeutic” range of 0.9 to 2.0 ng/mL for enhancing contractility) but a trend toward improved survival at lower digoxin levels .5 to 0.8). Such findings suggest that the benefit from cardiac glycosides might be more related to neurohumoral effects than improvements in contractility. A subsequent randomized trial in the setting of more contemporary therapy (DIGIT-HF) showed a significant reduction in the composite of hospitalization for heart failure and death from any cause (39.5% vs 44.1%, hazard ratio, 0.82; P=0.03), with more of the benefit due to reduction in hospitalization. The rate of serious adverse events was increased substantially (4.7% vs 2.8%).

<H4>Indications. It appears prudent to limit cardiac glycoside therapy to patients with marked systolic dysfunction who are already taking a full medical regimen of first-line agents (loop diuretic, ACE inhibitor, and beta-blockade) and not achieving adequate symptomatic relief. The cause for concern is the narrow therapeutic index of digoxin and risk of a serious adverse drug effect. Cardiac glycoside treatment has been helpful in the setting of cardiac decompensation associated with recent myocardial infarction. Other indications include heart failure induced by rapid atrial fibrillation (see Chapter 28), heart failure resulting from uncontrolled hypertension (but only for the short term and not as a substitute for blood pressure reduction [see Chapter 26]) or severe aortic stenosis (see Chapter 33). Efficacy in cor pulmonale is in question; the drug is occasionally beneficial, but the results are not impressive, and the risks of toxicity are increased in the setting of hypoxia.

Digitalis preparations are of little use in heart failure resulting from hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, be they idiopathic or due to longstanding hypertension (a common etiology among outpatients, especially women). Patients with idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis may experience worsening outflow tract obstruction with the use of digitalis. In addition, there is no proven benefit in cases of mitral stenosis (in the absence of atrial fibrillation) or during episodes of HF due to transient ischemia.

<H4>Choice of Preparation and Pharmacokinetics. Digoxin is the preparation of choice. In the past, some variation in bioavailability was noted among different brands, but this has long been corrected. The half-life of digoxin is 36 hours; the onset of action is 1 to 2 hours when taken orally. Absorption from the gastrointestinal tract ranges from 50% to 75% complete and remains adequate in HF but may fall in severe cases of malabsorption. Excretion is renal and decreases significantly with reduction in creatinine clearance.

Dose adjustments are sometimes necessary. Digoxin can be used safely in renal failure as long as renal function and serum levels are frequently checked and necessary dose adjustments made. Higher doses are not needed in obese patients because there is little lipid deposition. Thyroid disease can affect digitalis metabolism; hypothyroidism prolongs the half-life, and hyperthyroidism shortens it. The treatment of thyroid disease needs to be accompanied by an adjustment of digoxin dose. Similarly, amiodarone can increase serum digoxin levels both independently and as a consequence of effects on thyroid status.

<H4>Initiating and Maintaining Use. Initiation of therapy in clinically stable outpatients can commence with an oral maintenance dose and does not require loading doses. At a maintenance dose of 0.125 to 0.25 mg/d (determined by underlying renal function), one can attain a therapeutic serum level in 5 to 7 days (earlier, if the optimal therapeutic range suggested by the DIG study [0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL] is used). This has led to recommendations for a narrowing of the therapeutic range .5 to 0.8 ng/mL) and the use of smaller doses (e.g., 0.125 mg/d) both for loading and for maintenance.

Once initiated and if found to be of clinical benefit, digitalis should be continued chronically unless a reversible cause of pump failure has been fully corrected or there is no basis for using the drug in the first place. Patients who respond to digitalis clinically often deteriorate when the drug is withdrawn, even in the context of ACE inhibitor use.

<H4>Monitoring. Digoxin levels require careful monitoring because of frequently changing renal clearance in HF and the seriousness of digitalis toxicity. Serum levels should be measured at least three to four times per year, more frequently if there are changes in the patient’s renal or volume status or if the patient is taking amiodarone (which can raise serum digoxin levels). As noted, the conventional target range of 0.9 to 2.0 ng/mL is being supplanted by recommendations for the lower, narrower range of 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL. A serum sample should be drawn at least 6 hours after the last dose because there is a 4- to 6-hour rise in serum level after an oral dose. In most instances, it is best to have the patient omit the day’s dose when coming to the office for a serum determination.

The physician needs to monitor factors that increase the “sensitivity” of the myocardium to the toxic effects of the drug. Such factors include hypokalemia, abnormalities in serum calcium and magnesium, organic heart disease, and pulmonary disease with acute hypoxia. Digitalis-induced ST-T–wave changes on the ECG have no correlation with optimal or toxic dose levels and cannot be used for such determinations. Serum drug levels are necessary.

<H4>Digitalis Toxicity. The serum level of digitalis is not in itself diagnostic of toxicity because there is considerable overlap in serum concentrations between patients with and patients without evidence of toxicity, but if the digoxin level is greater than 2.0 ng/mL, the probability of encountering toxicity increases considerably.

Symptoms of digitalis toxicity can be divided into noncardiac and cardiac manifestations. Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, visual disturbances including yellow halos around lights, and, in rare instances, delirium have been described since the time of William Withering, the British physician who introduced the use of digitalis in the late eighteenth century. Arrhythmias are the predominant cardiac manifestation of toxicity. Digitalis can cause any type of rhythm and/or conduction disturbance because it affects the automaticity of myocardial tissues and the conduction system. Ventricular irritability (especially bigeminy), paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with block, and junctional tachycardia are particularly characteristic features of digitalis excess.

The unexplained onset of an arrhythmia in a patient on digitalis raises the possibility of drug-related toxicity. The drug should be withheld; a serum level obtained; potassium, calcium, and magnesium levels checked; and serious consideration given to immediate hospitalization for monitoring and parenteral antiarrhythmic therapy. The high incidence and mortality rate of this preventable and often treatable condition call for vigilance.

If the findings from the DIG study are confirmed, then the definition of digitalis toxicity may need to be extended from the well-described clinical syndrome to the increased mortality risk associated with serum levels greater than 1.2 ng/mL.
<H3>Oral Anticoagulation and Antiplatelet Therapy

Although heart failure per se in the absence of atrial fibrillation is not an absolute indication for oral anticoagulation, its presence is associated with a hypercoagulable state and potential for formation of left ventricular thrombus leading to systemic and cerebral embolization. The CHA2DS2–VASc score in heart failure patients correlates with rate of thromboembolic complications, but its predictive accuracy in the absence of atrial fibrillation proved only modest when tested (C-statistic 0.64); negative predictive 92%. Its clinical utility remains to be determined.

In randomized trial comparing aspirin with warfarin for prevention of embolic stroke in heart failure patients (ejection fraction ≤35%) in sinus rhythm (WARCEF trial), there was a significant reduction in the low baseline rate of ischemic stroke, but at the cost of a greater increase in risk of major hemorrhage, though not intracerebral hemorrhage. The low risk of cerebral embolism did not seem to warrant routine oral anticoagulation with its increased risk of serious bleeding.

Aspirin use in persons with coronary artery disease complicated by heart failure is associated with a nearly 30% reduction in 1-year mortality. However, there is some concern that the inhibitory effect of aspirin on prostaglandin synthesis might counter some of the beneficial effects of ACE inhibitors in HF, which appear to be prostaglandin- mediated (see prior discussion). Prospective cohort study suggests a dose-related blunting by aspirin of the ACE inhibitor survival benefit but no adverse effect with low aspirin doses (<160 mg/d).
<H3>Treatment of Iron Deficiency

With dyspnea being a major symptom of heart failure and iron deficiency (even in the absence of anemia) an important impairment of aerobic performance, interest in treatment of iron deficiency in persons with chronic heart failure has arisen. Intravenous iron infusion in moderately symptomatic systolic heart failure patients with iron deficiency was found in earlier study to improve symptoms, functional capacity, and quality of life, without significant adverse effects. A more recent large-scale, placebo-controlled trial of ferric carboxymaltose in patients with EF <40% found no significant difference in 6-minute walk distance or the composite of death, hospitalization for heart failure, or 6 minute walk. Given the differences in outcomes which could be related to degree of iron deficiency and degree of anemia, more data are needed to clarify benefit and for whom.
<H3>Statin Use

Statins have an uncertain role in patients with heart failure, even though many patients have underlying coronary artery disease and should benefit from statins. Most statin trials have excluded patients with heart failure due to theoretical concerns about potential adverse effects, such as reduced synthesis of coenzyme Q10 (impairing mitochondrial antioxidant activity) and increased production of selenoprotein (a potentially myopathic substance). Large-scale randomized trial of low-dose rosuvastatin in a mixed population of heart failure patients found no adverse effect or benefit on the combined outcome of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, and stroke, but there was a reduction in number of patients requiring cardiovascular hospitalization.
<H2>Medications for Diastolic Heart Failure
<H3>SGLT2 Inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin; see Chapter 102 for more details)

The serendipitous events which led to the application of these agents for use in HFpEF and the findings for reduction in hospitalization for heart failure, both in patients with HFrEF and those with HFpEF continue to beg the question of how they work. Nonetheless the accumulating evidence of efficacy and safety in both HFpEF and HFrEF, particularly in patients with diabetes or obesity, now places them as first-line treatment options, especially for HFpEF. Dosing is They are best taken in the AM to avoid nocturia and used cautiously with other drugs for hyperglycemia to avoid precipitating hypoglycemia. Adverse effects include polyuria and risk of urinary tract infection from increased glycosuria; Fournier’s gangrene is a rare complication. There may be a small reduction in eGFR (<5 mL/min/1.73m2). Starting dose for both empagliflozin and dapagliflozin is 10 mg daily in the AM.
<H3>GLP-1 and GLP-1/GIP Agonists (Semaglutide and Tirzepatide; see Chapter 102 for details)

The accumulating data of efficacy, particularly in HFpEF, suggest they will soon be added as first-line treatment options, given their ability to reduce risk of worsening heart failure and need for hospitalization obese persons as well as those with diabetes. Since these agents are proteins, they require parenteral administration (e.g., tirzepatide 2.5 mg/wk administered subcutaneously once weekly, or semaglutide 2.4 mg/wk administered subcutaneously once weekly).
<H3>Finerenone

The demonstrated ability to reduce heart failure hospitalizations in persons with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction argue for its consideration as first-line therapy. Its nonsteroidal composition helps it to avoid the androgenic inhibitory side effect of other mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. It is taken once daily at a starting does of 10 mg/day. As noted, its promotion of potassium retention requires avoiding use with a serum potassium ≥ 5 mEq/L and cautious use with other medications such as ARBs or ACEI which also result in potassium retention.
<H2>Nonpharmacologic Measures (107–123)
<H3>Salt and Water Restrictions

Sodium restriction has traditionally been an important component of advice given to patients who suffer from heart failure, given that volume overload is typically a prominent component of the clinical presentation and an often attributed precipitant of an exacerbation. However, the central role of sodium restriction in treatment of heart failure has been challenged by systematic review of available evidence, which finds no studies that address primary outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular- and all-cause mortality, stroke, and myocardial infarction) and only two involving outpatients, which show no effect on rates of hospitalization, length of stay, and change in NYHA functional class.

The paucity of relevant high-quality evidence has generated a call for caution about emphasizing sodium restriction as a foundation of heart failure management. While excessive sodium intake should be avoided, the value of its routine stringent restriction in heart failure should be viewed more agnostically. Some have hypothesized that inadequate potassium intake—a common accompaniment of high-sodium diets—is the responsible factor exacerbating myocardial dysfunction. In some studies, very low sodium intake is associated with adverse outcomes.

Given current uncertainties and pending data from well-designed studies, it seems reasonable to start with a no-added-salt diet (about 3.5 g sodium/d for the average U.S. diet). The patient and family are instructed to prepare and serve meals without the addition of salt and taught to avoid foods with inapparent but high salt content (e.g., cheese, cold cuts, canned soups, canned ham, bacon, catsup, and other processed foods). A DASH-style diet (see Chapter 26) should be strongly considered, since it also ensures adequate potassium intake and has other desirable cardiovascular attributes. Rarely should an extreme sodium restriction (e.g., 1 to 2 g/d) be urged on the patient because it is unrealistic, unpalatable, and demoralizing, not to mention unsupported by current evidence. Fluid restriction is reserved for severe cases that are complicated by hyponatremia. Instructing heart failure patients in dietary sodium and potassium at the time of hospital discharge achieves significantly better short-term outcomes (including fewer readmissions) than when such advice is omitted.
<H3>Lifestyle Modification—Diet and Exercise

The failure of most medical therapies to improve important outcomes in HFpEF patients and a better understanding of HFpEF pathophysiology (see earlier discussion) have stimulated renewed interest in weight loss and exercise. Study findings also have relevance for patients with HFrEF.

<H4>Diet. Obesity, its metabolic consequences, and their presumed link to diastolic heart failure are stimulating renewed interest in weight loss as an important component of a treatment regimen for HFpEF. Under study conditions, the combination of a weight loss program supplemented by exercise training achieves significant improvements in measures of exercise tolerance. To achieve sustainable weight loss and improve metabolic parameters, a Mediterranean-style diet should be considered; it can be melded into a DASH program (see Chapters 18, 26, and 235) in conjunction with an exercise program.

<H4>Exercise. Exercise intolerance and exertional dyspnea lead the list of heart failure symptoms and important causes of functional impairment and diminished quality of life. Exercise training has been reported capable of improving exercise tolerance, health status, and stroke volume, as well as reducing peripheral resistance, left ventricular hypertrophy, and number of hospitalizations. Benefits are most noteworthy in patients with HFpEF, which is to be expected given its pathophysiologic links to obesity, inactivity, and resultant metabolic consequences of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes, but also found in those with HFrEF. In HFpEF patients, who tend to be obese, the combination of diet for weight loss plus exercise achieves the best results as measured by peak oxygen consumption.

A modest but significant improvement in long-term survival is observed in patients with NYHA class II to IV disease with a program of 30 minutes of daily exercise on a treadmill or stationary bicycle most days of the week—a minimum of three times weekly—tailored to their functional capacity. Intermittent aerobic exercise with frequent rest breaks helps to maximize the training effect without inducing excessive cardiac stress. Although the ideal training regimen is yet to be defined, commonsense advice can be given for the activity prescription to be carried out at home. Referral to a formal exercise program can be considered in highly motivated persons who are hemodynamically stable and eager to improve their level of activity. Group classes (e.g., in Tai chi mind–body movement) can be helpful, enhancing both quality of life and functional capacity.

In older patients recently discharged from the hospital for heart failure, a randomized trial of physical rehabilitation using a tailored, progressive rehabilitation program achieved greater improvement in physical functioning than usual care, underscoring the value of such an approach.

<H4>Allowable Activity. The level of allowable activity needs to be tailored to the patient’s medical status, lifestyle, and responsibilities. The goal is to sustain if not improve daily functioning without overdoing it. As noted, a customized exercise program can enhance exercise tolerance and daily activity. Patients with symptoms of failure on moderate exertion (NYHA class II disease) should be encouraged to continue to work, provided that reasonable limits are placed on emotional and physical demands. It may be more stressful psychologically (and consequently physically) to have to quit one’s job than to continue working in a somewhat more limited capacity. In most instances, the amount of allowable activity can be determined from an office visit by a careful history that elicits the degree of exertion that precipitates symptoms. At times, the symptoms may be out of proportion to physical findings—taking a walk up a flight of stairs with the patient or performing a 6-minute walk test can provide helpful data regarding exercise tolerance. In the exercise-intolerant patient with both coronary disease and heart failure, a treadmill ECG test together with measurement of peak oxygen uptake can help determine the degrees to which ischemia and heart failure are contributing to the problem. Regardless of etiology, a daily period of physical and psychological rest period may be beneficial and complement a customized exercise program.

If weight, orthopnea, and exertional dyspnea are increasing, then activity should be further restricted. A few days of bed rest are often beneficial and may obviate the need for hospitalization. The patient with failure who is put to bed should use a footboard or get out of bed periodically to avoid prolonged venous stasis and risk of thrombus formation.
<H3>Caffeine

Despite the increased risk of serious cardiac dysrhythmias in patients with heart failure, especially those with reduced ejection fraction, there is no evidence of an increased risk of inducing such arrhythmias associated with caffeine intake. In a randomized trial placebo-controlled trial of short-term high-dose caffeine intake in patients with moderate or severe HFrEF, there were no significant increases in supraventricular or ventricular arrhythmias at rest or with treadmill exercise.
<H3>Treatment of Psychological Factors

Psychological factors are underappreciated and often overlooked. Major depression is common among HF patients who require hospitalization and is independently associated with increased rates of readmission and death. It is also a major cause of poor compliance with treatment regimens; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressants are well tolerated cardiovascularly (see Chapter 227), making antidepressant therapy a potentially attractive treatment option in HF. However, evidence of efficacy remains elusive. In large-scale randomized, placebo-controlled trial of the SSRI escitalopram in heart failure patients (MOOD-HF), there were no significant improvements in depression, all-cause mortality, or rate of hospitalization. A similarly designed trial of cognitive–behavioral therapy demonstrated efficacy with regard to depression but not for self-care of physical functioning.

Anxiety is also common but less well studied in HF. Its potential to impair quality of life (e.g., cause unnecessary restriction of activity) and exacerbate adrenergic stimulation argues for its consideration and treatment. There are few data to guide the use of specific pharmacologic therapy for anxiety in HF (although beta-blockade can help with the catecholamine excess, and SSRIs have some anxiolytic activity), but nonpharmacologic stress reduction measures may help and deserve consideration (see Appendix 226-1).

Emotional and social supports are essential. Long-term study finds that a lack of such supports is associated with increased risks of fatal and nonfatal adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Involving the family and arranging for community resources are essential. Transitional care services after hospitalization have been found cost-effective, with willingness-to-pay thresholds of $50,000/QALY. Nurse home visits proved more cost-effect compared to case manager calls and disease management clinics.
<H2>Management of Complications and Exacerbating Factors (124-134)

Attention to a host of complications and exacerbating factors is essential to successful management. These include acute renal failure and chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, and sleep apnea.
<H3>Renal Failure (see also Chapter 142)

Renal failure is a frequent accompaniment of HF, either as a precipitant or as consequence. About one third of HF patients have renal insufficiency, yet most studies exclude patients with significant azotemia, limiting evidence-based guidance. Nonetheless, some principles have emerged. They are expressed in terms of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which is routinely calculated automatically with reporting of routine chemistries and is based on the serum creatinine, age, and body weight. The equation as it stands is for men. For women, the weight is multiplied by 0.85. The equation is an imperfect formula—revisions have been proposed—but it is widely used and built into most GFR calculators. Cystatin-C based eGFR determinations are used for very thin patients (see Chapter 142).

As long as the eGFR remains greater than 60 ml/min/1.73m², all drugs used for HF can be used with minimal concern. Both SGLT2 inhibitors and the GLP-1 agonists help slow decline in renal function, particularly in HF patients with diabetes and should be considered. With a fall of the eGFR to the 30- to 60- ml/min/1.73m² range, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and beta-blockers can still be used reasonably safely without major concern, but in severe renal insufficiency (GFR < 30 ml/min/1.73m²), close monitoring of renal function and serum potassium is essential, and dose adjustment downward may be necessary. ARBs offer no advantage over ACE inhibitors in renal failure. Beta-blockers can be used safely in mild to moderate renal failure; those that are not renally excreted (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol) are probably easier to use. Aldosterone inhibitors should be used cautiously with close monitoring of serum potassium when GFR falls to less than 60 ml/min/1.73m², and avoided at a GFR of less than 30 ml/min/1.73m², mg/mL because of the high risk of severe hyperkalemia. Digoxin can be used in renal insufficiency but requires close monitoring of serum level and frequent dose adjustment. In later stages of chronic kidney disease, interventional therapies fail to prolong survival (see later discussion).
<H3>Atrial Fibrillation (see also Chapter 28)

Like renal failure, atrial fibrillation (AF) can be both a precipitant and consequence of heart failure. Persistent tachycardia is an important cause of ventricular remodeling, and heart failure is one of the leading causes of AF in community populations. Onset of AF can present as acute worsening shortness of breath and exercise intolerance.

<H4>Pathophysiology. Rapid AF reduces ventricular filling and triggers ventricular remodeling; loss of myocardial compliance and cardiomyopathic dilation (tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy) may ensue. As a consequence, cardiac output declines, exacerbated by any dilation-induced mitral regurgitation. Establishment of rate control or restoration of sinus rhythm can reverse these changes, but ventricular dilation may persist. Recurrence of tachycardia can lead to an acute drop in cardiac output, often by as much as 25% to 50%, greatest in persons with preexisting valvular disease or cardiomyopathy.

<H4>Prognosis. It remains unsettled as to whether development of AF directly affects prognosis or is simply a manifestation of advancing heart failure. The evidence for it being an independent predictor of survival and other outcomes is conflicting. Nonetheless, prevalence of AF increases markedly with advancing severity of symptoms 0% of NYHA class IV patients have AF), and onset can lead to acute clinical decompensation.
<H4>Treatment (see Chapter 28).
<H3>Sleep Apnea (see Chapter 45 for details)

Both obstructive and central sleep apneas are common in heart failure, with prevalence of 50% to 75% reported in persons with HFrEF. Central sleep apnea is estimated to occur in up to 40%; prevalence increases with severity of left ventricular failure and is associated with a poor prognosis; Cheyne-Stokes breathing is its clinical hallmark and a sign of increased risk.

CPAP has been shown to improve HF outcomes in patients with central sleep apnea and Cheyne-Storkes respiration, but not in those with obstructive sleep apnea. Those with Cheyne-Stokes respiration who do not respond to CPAP are candidates for adaptive-servo ventilation and need for consultation. For those with obesity as the cause of their sleep apnea, begin use of tirzepatide to achieve the marked requisite weight loss sufficient to improve airway patency.
<H3>Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes is an important risk factor for heart failure, and its effective treatment is an important component of the heart failure management program (see Chapter 102). Use of SGLT2 inhibition and GLP-1 GLP-1/GIP agents improve outcomes (see earlier discussion).
<H2>Management of Advanced Disease (135–157)

Patients with advanced disease (stage D, NYHA class III and IV) experience a very poor quality of life and increased risks of sudden death and death from progressive pump failure. Abnormal intraventricular activation (manifested by widening of the QRS on ECG, especially left bundle branch block) and electrical ventricular dyssynchronization are characteristic of this stage. Cardiac output declines, adverse ventricular remodeling progresses, and life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmias may ensue. Although dire, this stage of illness is amenable to interventions that can improve quality of life, reduce the need for hospitalization, and perhaps prolong survival.
<H3>Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy and Implantable Cardioverter–Defibrillators

Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) through implantation of an atriobiventricular pacemaker can alleviate dyssynchrony and its consequences in patients with evidence of marked left ventricular dysfunction (e.g., EF < 0.35, QRS > 150 msec). It is typically used in conjunction with an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) to protect against life-threatening dysrhythmias, which are prevalent in a failing heart. Data from randomized, controlled trials in symptomatic patients (NYHA class II to IV disease) show enhanced survival (by 20% to 40%) in conjunction with improvements in left ventricular remodeling, ejection fraction, exercise capacity, quality of life, and need for hospitalization. These findings have now been extended to minimally symptomatic persons (NYHA class I and II) having similarly depressed LV function and conduction delay. Resynchronization has no effect on rates of ventricular tachycardia (VT), fibrillation, or ability to cardiovert—for these problems, the ICD is required. Compared to ICD alone, combination therapy with CRT achieves better outcomes in terms of survival and need for readmission. Long-term outcome study comparing the two modalities in patients with HFrEF, a wide QRS complex, and NYHA class II or II heart failure shows a sustained survival benefit for CRT over ICD during a median follow-up of 14 years. Death occurred in 71.2% in the CRT group and 76.4% in the ICD group. Time to death was longer in the CRT group (acceleration factor 0.80; P=0.002).

Prophylactic implantation of an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator (ICD) in persons with marked LV ventricular dysfunction (EF < 35%) significantly reduces the risk of cardiac sudden death, which accounts for almost half of deaths among persons with systolic heart failure, especially those who have not reached advanced stages of symptomatic disease. However, those with end-stage disease experience no reduction in all-cause survival—survival is just as likely to be caused by pump failure. Patients with later stages of chronic kidney disease also achieve no improvement in survival from ICD implantation, but do experience increased rates of hospitalization. Compared to ICD, amiodarone shows no reduction in risk of sudden death in CHF patients (see Chapter 29).

<H4>Adverse Effects. It is important to keep in mind that CRT with or without ICD is technically demanding (requiring the implantation of a left ventricular pacing lead via the coronary sinus and coronary vein). Periprocedural complications reported under study conditions include coronary sinus dissection .0%), pneumothorax .7%), pocket hematoma requiring evacuation .3%), coronary venous dissection with pericardial effusion .5%), and need for repositioning of leads .0%). After 1 month, the adverse event rate is on the order of 4.5 per 100 device months. Complication rates in nonresearch settings are likely to be higher. Adding ICD implantation increases cost and complexity as well as its own set of adverse effects. The complication rate for ICD is 1.4% for infection, lead placement problems, and device malfunction and 1.2% for death during implantation. The rate of inappropriate discharges is 19% (see also Chapter 29).

<H4>Patient Selection. As noted, those obtaining the best survival results from combination resynchronization/defibrillator therapy are patients with early-stage systolic heart failure accompanied by marked systolic dysfunction (EF < 30%) and prolonged intraventricular conduction (QRS > 150 msec), especially when due to ischemia. Survival benefit has also been demonstrated in persons with more modest reductions in LV function (EF 30% to 35%) as well as relatively younger patients with nonischemic causes of heart failure. Patients with end-stage CHF or severe comorbid illnesses that shorten life expectancy are not reasonable candidates because there is no reduction in all-cause mortality.

As many as 30% of patients who receive these devices do not benefit and many who would benefit do not undergo implantation. To improve case selection, criteria are being developed, but remain in a state of flux as more outcomes data continue to emerge. Present criteria include the following:
For CRT: Ejection fraction less than 30% to 35% + QRS duration greater than 120 to 150 msec + symptomatic heart failure (NYHA class II to III), or
For ICD: Sustained VT or inducible nonsustained VT in the setting of an ejection fraction less than 35%

Disparities in access to ICD implantation have been noted, with men significantly more likely to receive an ICD than women. Only a small fraction of eligible elderly Medicare patients receive an ICD post myocardial infarction. Cost is very high for ICD/CRT placement, but cost-effectiveness is not prohibitive in properly selected patients ($61,000 per QALY—similar to that of other invasive cardiac interventions).
<H3>Surgical Interventions

<H4>Revascularization. Restoring blood flow to an area of ischemic but viable left ventricular myocardium can improve cardiac performance and outcomes. Randomized trial of coronary bypass and graft (CABG) surgery in conjunction with maximum medical therapy versus maximum medical therapy alone in patients with heart failure due to ischemic cardiomyopathy finds a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality, a 21% reduction in cardiovascular death, as well as significant improvements in hospitalization for any cause and quality of life. Ventricular reconstruction does not (see Chapter 30).

<H4>Transcatheter Mitral Valve Repair. A failing, dilated left ventricle displaces elements of the mitral valve apparatus, impairing valve leaflet apposition. Mitral regurgitation ensues, leading to worsening heart failure, increased rates of hospitalization, and shortened survival. Open surgical repair fails to improve outcomes and is fraught with complications, but transcatheter repair involving application of a clip to restore valve competence has been associated with reduction in hospitalizations and improved survival in carefully selected patients, typically those in whom maximal medical therapy and resynchronization have been exhausted.

<H4>Left Ventricular Assist Devices. These are surgically implanted mechanical devices designed to improve survival and quality of life for persons with advanced-stage heart failure; they also serve as a bridge to transplantation. Regressions of pathologic left ventricular enlargement and remodeling have been described in conjunction with improved functional status. Besides surgical implantation, anticoagulation is required due to a heightened risk of pump-associated thrombosis—stroke risk 0% to 20%) remains problematic. New LVAD designs (e.g., magnetically levitated vs. mechanical bearing) reduce stroke risk by 50% and need for reoperation by over 90%. Risks of bleeding and sepsis persist despite considerable advances in pump design. Heart failure patients with end-stage kidney disease are poor candidates, with many experiencing death within 3 weeks of LVAD implantation. Shared decision-making has been urged for use with late-stage HF patients being offered an LVAD, because many patients will prefer comfort and quality of life over prolongation of survival at a cost of considerable morbidity risk. Family members and others report much emotional stress caring for a patient with an assist device, especially at the very end of life when questions arise as to how and when to turn off the device and how to coordinate with palliative care and hospice.

<H4>Stem Cell Implantation. Transendocardial mesenchymal stem cells and mononuclear bone marrow cells have been applied to ameliorate left ventricular remodeling secondary to acute or chronic myocardial ischemic injury. Pilot results in persons with chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy are encouraging with respect to functional and anatomic parameters. More study will be needed to determine the role of this approach.

<H4>Cardiac Transplant. Heart transplant remains the last resort. Fitness for surgery and ability to comply with intensive medical treatment and follow-up are essential prerequisites. Candidacy is current determined by a categorical 6-status system, based mainly on treatment intensity. Other criteria are distance from a donor hospital, waiting time, status, and waiting time. Because of concerns that the current system is subject to manipulation, alternatives have been proposed. A novel US-Candidate Risk Score (US-CRS) was developed based on clinical and laboratory variables and found to outperform the 6-status system in terms of medical urgency and highest risk of death without transplantation.
<H2>End-Stage Care (158–160)

With the exception of ventricular assist devices (which remain investigational) and transplantation (which is available to only 2,500 HF patients per year in the United States), the management of end-stage disease is mostly supportive and guided by the same principles of terminal care that apply to most persons with end-stage diseases (see Chapter 90). Heroic measures that prolong survival without improving quality of life should cease. For example, persons who have implantable defibrillators should probably have them turned off because the frequency of disruptive overdrive pacing and defibrillatory discharges increases with the increasing frequency of serious ventricular dysrhythmias. There is no demonstrated value to intermittent outpatient intravenous infusions of vasodilators (e.g., B-type natriuretic peptide) or inotropic agents (e.g., milrinone), although they are promoted by some. Compassionate use of morphine for anxiety and dyspnea is perfectly reasonable and appropriate (see Chapter 90). Hospice care can be greatly comforting and improve quality of life for patients and those who care for them.
<H1>Patient Education and Monitoring (161–168)

Because the medical program for HF is often complex and the need for compliance is great, it takes the combined efforts of the entire primary care team working in conjunction with community-based resources to educate the patient and family and help monitor compliance and clinical status. Disease management programs for HF not linked to the patient’s primary care practice tend to fall short in reducing costs and improving outcomes such as readmission rates, but those that are centered in or coordinated with the medical home do considerably better though not in all parameters. In randomized trial, a comprehensive program centered in primary care practice and entailing a multidisciplinary team approach significantly reduced mortality and measures of depression, but made no impact on rates of hospitalization or measures of functional status, which improved in both groups. A collaborative care approach reduced depression and fatigue, but not heart failure-related overall health status. Meta-analytic study finds that home visits and multidisciplinary clinics have the best impact on all-cause readmission and mortality; structured telephone follow-up by the medical home team reduces heart failure readmissions. Other studies show that efforts limited to telephone contact from centralized, nurse-staffed, monitoring services or stand-alone educational program fail to reduce hospitalization rates.

Although stand-alone educational efforts are without merit, those incorporated into a comprehensive heart failure program centered in the primary care practice can help ensure safety and compliance. The objective is to enlist patients, household members, and families as partners in the care management effort. Surveys of HF patients find health literacy rates for their condition of less than 50%, which likely contribute to the high rates of avoidable exacerbations and hospital admissions. Key goals of the educational effort include an understanding of the rationale behind therapy and guidelines for activity, diet, and use of medication. Patients and their caregivers must know the identity of the medications being prescribed; multidrug regimens are common, which increases the risks of confusion, errors in administration, and noncompliance leading to complications and otherwise avoidable hospital admission. Medication booklets are invaluable, taping each tablet to the page alongside its generic and brand names, along with dose schedule, indication for use, and warning signs of toxicity. For patients with poor eyesight, a family member or visiting nurse should set aside the pills to be taken each day.

Shared decision-making becomes an important adjunct when considering interventional therapies, ranging from synchronized pacing to implantable defibrillators and left ventricular assist devices (LVADs). Especially for persons with late-stage disease, options for increasing survival at the potential cost of adversely impacting quality of life pose difficult choices. Eliciting patient values and preferences along with expected risks (including mortality) and benefits are essential to helping the patient express informed preferences. When done well, the clinician can recommend or endorse the preferred choice thereby unburdening patient and family of anticipated regret or guilt. All too often, studies show little conversation along these lines, limited by the assumption that any life-prolonging intervention is worth promoting enthusiastically. Patients choose LV assist devices less often when shared decision-making is carried out.

An important element of the partnership effort is to engage patients and their families in home monitoring. While telemonitoring has not realized its promise, home monitoring by patient and family makes important contributions to a comprehensive management program. Obtaining and recording a daily weight each morning before breakfast (so-called dry weight) are essential—a lesser frequency will suffice if clinically stable and compliant. If weight increases suddenly by more than 2 or 3 lbs (strongly suggestive of fluid retention and worsening failure), it should trigger a call to the medical home practice or implementation of a prearranged adjustment in the diuretic program followed by an office or home visit by a member of the care team. Such efforts have the potential for limiting avoidable exacerbations of HF leading to emergency room visits, hospitalizations, and readmissions (major sources of high cost for care of HF patients). As noted, the impact of HF disease management programs appears to depend on how well efforts are coordinated with and integrated into the patient’s primary care practice.

Novel approaches to automated home monitoring and transmission are under development, ranging from the implanted wireless transmitter of pulmonary artery pressure described earlier to less sophisticated devices reporting weight, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and other basic parameters. To date, their value has not been established, but their potential to facilitate care and reduce readmission rates if not improve survival bears watching.
<H1>Indications for Referral and Admission (168,169)

Patients with acutely worsening or refractory failure should be considered for hospital admission and cardiac consultation. For the patient with seemingly refractory disease, hospitalization provides the opportunity to observe the response to treatment under controlled conditions that ensure compliance with the medical regimen. Moreover, hospitalization helps to ensure the safe initiation of additional therapy and a search for a treatable underlying etiology that may have initially eluded detection. Cardiac consultation can be helpful when considering adjunctive pharmacologic therapy (e.g., aldosterone inhibition, digitalization) and is essential to exploring indications for pacemaker or defibrillator implantation. Relatively young patients failing maximal medical therapy may be appropriate for consideration of transplantation, provided renal, pulmonary, hepatic, and central nervous system functions are preserved. Other indications for admission include evidence of digitalis toxicity, renal failure, hypotension, and inadequate support and supervision at home. Even though much HF care can be carried out in the primary care setting, a close working relationship between the primary care team and the cardiac consultant helps optimize outcomes.
<H1>Therapeutic Recommendations (168,169)
<H2>Stage A—At High Risk; No Structural or Functional Abnormalities; No Signs or Symptoms
<H3>All Patients

Screen for and treat risk factors and underlying etiologies, including hypertension (see Chapters 14, 19, and 26), coronary artery disease (see Chapters 20, 30, and 31), diabetes mellitus (see Chapters 93 and 102), hypercholesterolemia (Chapter 27), high dietary sodium intake (especially in obese persons; see Chapters 26 and 235), hemodynamically significant valvular disease (see Chapter 33), thyroid disease (see Chapters 103 and 104), cardiomyopathy (see Appendix 33-1), and tachyarrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation; see Chapters 25 and 28).
Implement oral anticoagulation only if there is atrial fibrillation (see Chapter 28); omit if sinus rhythm persists.

Consider using the Framingham Heart Study scoring system (based on age, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG, evidence of coronary or valvular heart disease, diabetes, cardiomegaly on chest x-ray, and forced expiratory capacity) to determine the risk for CHF and the appropriate level of aggressiveness of preventive measures. Although useful for diagnosis, neither BNP nor NT-proBNP has proven effective to gauge timing or adequacy of therapy; do not use as treatment thresholds or targets.

Prescribe and strongly encourage dietary changes for moderating sodium intake, ensuring adequate potassium intake, losing excess weight, and lowering cardiovascular risk; recommend a DASH-type diet for sodium restriction (see Chapter 26) and incorporate elements of a Mediterranean-style diet (see Chapters 18 and 27) for weight loss and lowering of cardiovascular risk.

Prescribe and strongly encourage 30 minutes of gentle aerobic exercise to be conducted most days of the week (minimum of 3 days/week), customized to patient’s capabilities and preferences (see Chapter 18). Encourage maintenance as much as possible of one’s daily work and social activities and avoid unnecessary limitations; however, during periods of exacerbation as program is adjusted, consider reducing activity temporarily and recommending some rest.

Implement a comprehensive approach to CHF disease management, engaging the patient, household members, family, and community resources in the effort; integrate any disease management program into the primary care practice, using a multidisciplinary team approach to care, complemented by consultation with cardiology as needed.
<H2>Stage B—Early Structural Change; Minimal or No Signs or Symptoms—NYHA Class I Disease
<H3>Systolic Dysfunction (HFrEF)

Begin ACE inhibitor therapy, starting at a low dose in the elderly (e.g., 2.5 to 5.0 mg of lisinopril once daily) to minimize the risks of hypotension and hypoperfusion, and gently titrate upward as tolerated, monitoring blood pressure, potassium, and renal function. (Substitute an ARB [e.g., losartan 25 mg/d or valsartan 80 mg/d] if ACE inhibitor is not tolerated due to cough or angioedema.)

Begin low-dose beta-blockade (e.g., metoprolol succinate extended release, 12.5 to 25 mg/d; or carvedilol 3.125 mg BID), and gently titrate upward as tolerated, monitoring blood pressure, heart rate, and weight.
Begin low dose diuretic therapy for signs of volume overload. Monitor serum potassium and replete if low (see Appendix 32-1).
Consider early initiation of aldosterone antagonist therapy (e.g., eplerenone 25 mg/d—see stage C) if ejection fraction is less than 35%, even if patient is barely symptomatic.
Begin SGLT2 therapy if the patient has obesity or diabetes (e.g., empagliflozin or dapagliflozin, 10 mg QAM)
Consider adding GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP therapy for additional weight loss or glycemic control.

For patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy—especially if African American—consider substituting hydralazine (starting at 37.5 mg TID) plus isosorbide dinitrate (starting at 20 mg TID). Monitor closely for tachycardia and hypotension.
<H3>Diastolic Dysfunction (HFpEF)
Continue as for stage A and treatment of underlying etiology; recommend a DASH/Mediterranean-style diet and weight reduction if obese.
Begin SGLT2 therapy if the patient has obesity or diabetes (e.g., empagliflozin or dapagliflozin, 10 mg QAM)
Consider adding GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP therapy for additional weight loss or glycemic control (e.g., semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly subcutaneously; tirzepatide 2.5 g mg once weekly subcutaneously) .

Consider adding mineralocorticoid inhibition with finerenone (starting at 10 mg/day and increasing as tolerated to 40 mg/day), exerting caution and monitoring of serum potassium; hold for serum potassium ≥5 mEq/L.
Consider angiotensin-neprilysin inhibition with sacubitril/valsartan (starting at 24/26 mg BID and increasing to as high as 97/103 mg BID), especially for women

Treat risk factors aggressively. Start and advance use of an ACE inhibitor if there is hypertension or diabetes. Begin a beta-blocker if there is underlying coronary disease (especially previous myocardial infarction), hypertension, or atrial fibrillation (see Chapters 26, 30, 102). There is no role for oral anticoagulation if sinus rhythm persists.

Add a diuretic if there is evidence of fluid retention (e.g., starting with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg/d); monitor potassium, BUN, and creatinine; avoid overdiuresis and replete potassium if hypokalemic (K < 3.5 mg/dL).
<H2>Stage C—Structural Change; Symptoms and Signs Evident—NYHA Class II to III Disease
<H3>Systolic Dysfunction (HFrEF)
Same as for stage A and B plus:
Recheck for and treat specifically any amenable exacerbating factors (e.g., noncompliance, sodium excess, fever, anemia, atrial fibrillation, infection, ischemia, hypertension, diabetes).

Advance ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy to improve exercise tolerance and relieve congestive symptoms while continuing to monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renal function. If tolerated, advance to doses associated with best outcomes (e.g., lisinopril 20 to 40 mg/d; losartan 50 to 100 mg/d, or valsartan 160 mg/d).

Consider sacubitril/valsartan if response to advancing angiotensin blockade does not suffice.
