Health Promotion and Injury Prevention

Each time a child and their family visit an ED, there is an opportunity to discuss health promotion and injury prevention topics (McCain et al., 2023). The 2025 joint policy statement, Pediatric Readiness in the Emergency Department, highlighted the need for these discussions to occur throughout the ED visit as well as to ensure that they are incorporated into quality plans and community outreach and advocacy programs (Remick et al., 2025). Despite the work that has been done to decrease injuries in children, firearm injuries remain the leading cause of death in children older than 1 year and are a source of significant morbidity and healthcare costs (Bongiorno et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2023).

Integration of health promotion and child injury prevention strategies, in addition to use of screening tools such as HEAD-ED for adolescent patients (Cappelli et al., 2012) (Table <S>2-</S>3), creates a comprehensive approach to the health and development of children and can be completed during various interactions throughout the ED visit (Cappelli et al., 2020; Goldenring & Cohen, 1988; Salentiny-Wrobleski, 2019). Engaging children in these discussions increases their awareness of healthy practices and injury prevention from an early age and empowers pediatric patients to be participants in their own care. Various modalities for dissemination could include third-party or ED/facility-created videos, discussions, and digital and paper pamphlets that include information and links to vetted resources. Topics to start discussions could include the following:
<BL>Nutrition/food: Ask about favorite foods, with a focus on how options improve health rather than being good or bad choices.

Activity safety: What color is the child’s helmet or how fast do they think they can get their seat belt on? What kind of car seat do they have, and where/how is it positioned? Has the parent considered routinely placing an often-used item such as a phone or purse next to the car seat to prevent inadvertently leaving the child in a hot car? Did the child attend an e-bike safety course to understand the rules of the road?

Home safety: Have the parents anticipated the child’s ability to access medications, firearms (Lee et al., 2022) candles, or other potential hazards? Are smoke and carbon monoxide alarms present and tested? Does the child know two ways to escape from every room in the house if there is a fire?

Personal safety: For children with special healthcare needs, ask them about their medical condition and medications, if they are able to answer such questions. Ask about personal relationships with family, friends, and partners. What is the safest thing for the child to do if inadvertently separated from their caregivers? Is the child aware of where they live and/or the phone number of a trusted adult?

Health safety: Review immunization status and overall management of health and/or medical conditions. Review sexual health screening and possible need for sexually transmitted infection testing (Liddon et al., 2022). Promote awareness of safe sleep initiatives for infants (Moon et al., 2022).

Physical activity: Explore activity level, with the understanding that not all patients and families have a safe, outdoor area to be active in, and discuss alternatives. Does the child like to swim or run? What level of supervision and/or protective equipment is recommended based on the child’s age and the specific activity?
Resources: Provide phone numbers for the poison control center and suicide and/or mental health support services. Connect the caregivers with local resources for injury prevention initiatives.</BL>

When these conversations occur throughout the visit, it enables the ED nurse to provide education and information in smaller, more digestible segments rather than just during the patient discharge, which can overwhelm patients and families. These discussions can also assist the nurse in determining whether the patient and family need referrals for housing and/or food insecurity, safety concerns, social and support services, mental health services, establishment of a medical home, or changes in home healthcare needs.

Discharge Planning or Transfer to Definitive Care

Discharge planning or planning for transfer of the patient to definitive care should begin early in the pediatric patient’s visit (Salentiny-Wrobleski, 2019). Most children who visit EDs are discharged home, highlighting the need for high-quality discharge education for this population (Curran et al., 2019). Discussions or screening can occur during each patient and family interaction. Topics could include the patient’s plan of care, patient/family needs, the ability of the parent to safely care for the patient at home, psychosocial needs, transportation needs, and the need for additional medical equipment and/or medications. Determining the needs of the patient and family early in the visit enables the focus at discharge to be on the discharge instructions and education related to the reason for the ED visit.

Communication strategies such as Ask Me 3 (Institute for Healthcare Improvement, 2021) (Box <S>2-</S>2) and Teach Back (Brach, 2024; Hesselink et al., 2022) (Box <S>2-</S>3) have been shown to improve parent comprehension of discharge instructions, increase adherence to treatment plans, reduce unnecessary return visits, improve health outcomes for children, and improve health literacy (Brown et al., 2021; Curran et al., 2019; Dudley et al., 2019). Utilization of multimodal educational and communications strategies, in the learner’s primary language, optimized caregiver understanding (Glick et al., 2023).

The three questions are:

<BOX>
<BN>BOX <S>2-</S>3 <BT>Teach Back

Studies have shown that 40% to 80% of the information given to patients is forgotten immediately and nearly 50% is remembered incorrectly. The teach-back method, however, can improve patient comprehension, adherence, satisfaction, and outcomes. After providing the patient and family with any instructions, use variations on the following phrases to help assess their understanding. These can be prefaced with “This was a lot of information. I want to be sure that I explained things well.”
<BL>Describe the three things you will do within the next 2 days.
Can you show me how you are going to [administer the medication, clean the wound]?
In your own words, tell me what signs and symptoms you will watch out for.
When should you come back to the emergency department?</BL>
Other techniques include the following:
<BL>Highlight handouts during the teach-back session.
Use clear, plain language.
Make eye contact and sit at eye level.
Use a caring—not testing or judging—tone of voice.</BL>

Assessing the patient’s discharge readiness includes a review of the discharge instructions for completeness (e.g., clinical condition information, new medications and/or changes to home medications, signs and symptoms indicating the need to return to the ED, follow-up appointment information, focused care needs such as dressing/wound care, and home health contacts) and patient-centered communications with caregivers and/or patient focusing on any concerns related to discharge from the ED. Ensuring discharge readiness also includes a full reassessment of the patient’s vital signs, effectiveness of interventions, primary and focused assessment, and pain. To decrease barriers to continuity of care and adherence to discharge instructions, the patient and/or family are provided with a paper copy of the discharge instructions to reference once discharged and to share with their primary care or subspecialty providers who may not have access to the ED’s electronic medical record system.
Transfer to Definitive Care

Eighty-five percent of neonatal and pediatric patients present to general EDs rather than specialized pediatric EDs (Iyer et al., 2024), and in 2020 more than 13,000 severely injured children required transfer to higher level of care and specialty services (ACS, n.d.). To help bridge this gap and maximize positive outcomes for pediatric patients, general EDs should have written transfer agreements and relationships with pediatric referral centers. Early recognition of the need to transfer the pediatric patient, effective communication with the receiving center, and establishment of interfacility transfer agreements and guidelines are key components of pediatric readiness.
Regional Transfer Agreements and Guidelines

Interfacility transfer agreements are written contracts between a referring facility (such as a community hospital) and facility with a higher level of care and/or appropriate resources for the child (such as a specialized pediatric center). These agreements formalize arrangements for the consultation and transport of a pediatric patient to the facility offering a higher level of care.

Interfacility transfer guidelines are developed between hospitals—including out-of-state/territory facilities—and outline administrative policies and procedures for transferring critically ill pediatric patients to facilities with the resources to provide specialized pediatric care. Specific components of a transfer include the following:

<BL>A defined process for timely initiation of a transfer, including the roles and responsibilities of the referring facility and the referral center (including responsibilities for requesting transfer and communication)
The process for selecting the appropriate care facility
Consideration of a verified pediatric center to increase the probability of improved outcomes and survival (Newgard et al., 2023)
The process for selecting the appropriately staffed transport service to match the patient’s acuity level (e.g., level of care required by the patient, equipment needed during the transport)
The process for patient transfer (including obtaining informed consent)
Plan for transfer of the patient’s medical records, including imaging studies
Plan for transfer of a copy of the signed transport consent
Plan for transfer of the patient’s personal belongings
Plan for provision of directions and referral institution information to the family</BL>
Transfer Responsibilities

In the United States, transfers of unstable patients must be done in accordance with the provisions in the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA), which was passed by Congress in 1986. Under EMTALA, patients who present to an ED for care, including newly born infants, must be provided with a medical screening exam to determine whether a medical emergency exists; the ED must provide care for the patient until either the situation resolves or the patient’s condition has been stabilized within the facility’s capacity and capabilities. If the patient’s condition exceeds the facility’s capabilities, the patient can be transferred, as long as this transfer is done in accordance with the EMTALA regulations. EMTALA does not apply to the transfer of stable patients. When transferring an unstable patient, EMTALA requires the referring facility to do the following (EMSC et al., 2024):

<BL>Ensure a physician, or designee as defined by facility rules or regulations, certifies that the medical benefits expected from the transfer outweigh the risks or arranges transfer at the patient’s or family’s request after being informed of the hospital’s obligations under EMTALA and the risks of transfer.
Continue to provide care within its capabilities until the transfer occurs to minimize transfer risks.
Provide copies of medical records.
Confirm that the receiving facility has space and qualified personnel to treat the condition and has agreed to accept the transfer.

Arrange to transfer the patient with qualified personnel and appropriate medical equipment for the patient’s condition. When requesting transport services, special considerations such as the need for a neonatal transport team, use of emergency child restraint systems, ability of the family to accompany the patient, and need for bariatric or mental health transport services should be communicated.</BL>

Under EMTALA, hospitals with specialized services are obligated to accept transfers from other U.S. hospitals when the referring facility does not have the capability to treat unstable emergency medical conditions. Internationally, transfer responsibilities and regulations vary with few options for pediatric critical care in low resource settings (Losonczy et al., 2021).

Emerging Trends

Emerging trends in readiness for pediatric emergency care are focused on pediatric trauma, facility recognition programs, the Prehospital Pediatric Readiness Project, and paediatric care initiatives in Europe.
Pediatric Trauma

Ongoing efforts are needed in trauma centers to improve ED pediatric readiness in these facilities that treat the most critically injured children. Designation as an ACS-verified trauma center was found to not equate to a high WPRS (i.e., minimum score of 88) (Newgard et al., 2021; Remick et al., 2023b). Gaps in readiness identified in ACS-verified trauma centers include lack of interfacility transfer agreements for pediatric patients, failure to weigh children in kilograms, lack of pediatric-specific quality improvement metrics, and lack of comfort with some pediatric trauma-specific protocols (Genovese et al., 2021; Melhado et al., 2024; Remick et al., 2018). Efforts to improve pediatric readiness at non-pediatric trauma centers are crucial, especially in facilities that often transfer children to other facilities for ongoing care (Melhado et al., 2025). As of 2022, ACS requires that all ACS-verified adult and pediatric trauma centers work with ED-based pediatric champions to complete the NPRP Assessment, review the follow-up gap analysis, and create improvement plans to address identified gaps (EMSC Innovation and Improvement Center, 2021; Melhado et al, 2023).
Pediatric Readiness Recognition Programs

Pediatric readiness facility recognition programs are state-wide initiatives that identify EDs and EMS/fire-rescue agencies that have become pediatric ready. Facility recognition programs support improvements in care, enhance coordination, and ensure children receive appropriate treatment from well-prepared clinicians. EDs that participate in pediatric readiness recognition programs scored significantly higher (i.e., median WPRS 24 points higher) in the 2021 assessment than facilities not participating in recognition programs (Remick et al., 2023).

Prehospital Pediatric Readiness Project

Established in 2019, the Prehospital Pediatric Readiness Project (PPRP) aims to improve prehospital care for acutely ill and injured children across the United States. Pediatric patients account for approximately 10% of EMS volume, and the PPRP focuses on ensuring that EMS/fire-rescue agencies have the appropriate equipment, supplies, training, education, physician oversight, and policies to effectively provide emergency care to pediatric patients as recommended in the 2020 joint policy statement and technical report, Pediatric Readiness in Emergency Medical Services Systems (Moore et al., 2020; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2020).
Paediatric Innovation in Europe

In January 2025, the i4KIDS-EUROPE consortium, representing 16 European countries, published a white paper that served as a call to action for the European Union and national policymakers to improve the paediatric innovation landscape across Europe with a specific focus on medicines and medical devices. Anticipated actions resulting from this paper include boosting public funding dedicated to paediatric care, improving paediatric regulation navigation, incentivizing companies investing in and enhancing the visibility of children’s health, and creating a strong culture of paediatric innovation in hospitals (i4KIDS-EUROPE, 2025).
Summary

Initiatives such as the NPRP continue to demonstrate progress toward improving ED pediatric readiness globally. Continued readiness efforts are needed to ensure that all critically ill and injured children have access to timely, well-resourced, and effective emergency care regardless of where they reside (Glass et al., 2023; Newgard et al., 2022, 2023). Identifying an ED nurse PECC can strongly affect pediatric emergency nursing care. The PECC can improve outcomes by overseeing nursing-based aspects of pediatric readiness such as incorporating principles of PFCC; assessment and care of the pediatric patient; health promotion/injury prevention activities; disaster planning; best practices for the safe disposition of the pediatric patient to include transfer, admission, or discharge; and incorporation of pediatric performance measures into QI plans. Partnering with local emergency medical services and neighboring hospitals to create a community of readiness further improves outcomes for ill and injured children and reduces the fragmented and uneven care that currently exists in some parts of the world (Paediatric Emergency Medicine Special Interest Group, 2019; Remick et al., 2023a).

<AU>Jennifer Gold, MSN, BSW, RN, TCRN
<H1>Objectives
Upon completion of this chapter, the learner will be able to:
<NL>Integrate Pediatric Assessment Triangle findings into a categorization of “sick, sicker, or sickest.”
Identify pediatric considerations within common triage systems, identifying strengths and weaknesses.
Recognize pediatric red flags.</NL>
Introduction

The ability to prioritize patient care is essential to emergency nursing. Accurate prioritization is a skill that is built over time and with experience. Every minute, emergency nurses must decide which patient needs to be cared for first, which interventions and assessments must be completed immediately, and what tasks can safely wait; this is prioritization. Prioritization encompasses the initial formal triage, which assigns a patient acuity when the patient enters the department, and the ongoing triage of patient care based on patient workload and condition. The ability to prioritize accurately requires experience and skill often not attained until the nurse has achieved a level of experience and competence equivalent to what Benner (2001) would classify as proficiency. However, nurses in the emergency department (ED) are called upon to make these decisions on a daily basis. It is essential that the nurse be able to identify the often-subtle signs of pediatric distress or illness. Although multiple evidence-based tools are available to help determine acuity, studies have shown that racial disparities in the under-triage of children persist (Lee et al., 2024; Warren et al., 2024). Children and families who do not speak the most prominent language may experience inequities (Rojas et al., 2023). Other marginalized groups include minoritized populations and those with a disability.

The word triage, meaning “to sort,” in French, was first introduced to the medical arena on the battlefields of the Napoleonic Wars to quickly assess and determine the level of injury the soldiers sustained. This enabled those needing urgent interventions to receive prioritized care. Triaging on the battlefields has evolved into the triaging systems used in today’s EDs worldwide. Various systems and scales are used, but all establish patient acuity and prioritize the order in which patients are seen, thus controlling the patient flow in the ED (Robertson-Steel, 2006). Several triaging systems and scales are discussed in the chapter.

Triage is not a place but an ongoing process that can occur anywhere patients and their caregivers seek medical care. Prioritization can occur in an ED, doctors’ offices, urgent care facilities, clinics, or other out-of-hospital settings. Triage is also used during disaster management and mass-casualty incidents and events. Prioritization during such events facilitates the greatest good for the greatest number. Additionally, it is important to consider prioritization when transferring a patient from one department to another within a hospital or from one facility to another. Moreover, the patient needs to be continually reevaluated as the situation warrants. A patient’s condition and order of priority can change based on ongoing assessments.

Research regarding triage decisions and processes highlights the importance of nursing expertise and accurate prioritization. Evidence also emphasizes the need for critical thinking, intuition, and the nurses’ knowledge base to make accurate triaging decisions. When nurses lack knowledge and experience regarding a patient's population or disease process, they rely on intuition and past experiences (heuristics) to make decisions in complex situations (Aghajani et al., 2021). Intuition is more than a feeling. The nurse interprets subjective and objective findings to determine acuity and prioritization appropriately, using sensory perceptions embedded in nursing assessment, intuition, knowledge, and experience (Wilson et al., 2023).

Inaccurate triage of pediatric patients is common, particularly in general emergency departments (Geanacopoulos et al., 2025). In addition to previously mentioned disparities that lead to under-triage, other studies have identified certain chief complaints that are associated with inaccurate triage levels. For example, chief complaints revolving around nonaccidental trauma were most often under-triaged, while penetrating traumas were most often over-triaged, especially at non-trauma centers or general EDs (Ngo et al, 2024; Scaife et al., 2024). Triage accuracy is essential in delivering effective, equitable care to the pediatric population, especially with all their unique challenges. Pediatric patients can deteriorate rapidly. It is essential that the nurse accurately prioritizes the pediatric patient initially and consistently reevaluates the patient’s condition, to detect subtle signs of decompensation.

A validated, evidence-based tool can assist in initial and ongoing pediatric assessments. This helps get the right patient to the right place at the right time with the right personnel. The Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) is such a tool (Figure <S>4-</S>1). This tool can be vital in recognizing a decompensating patient and the need for re-prioritization.

Triage is an ongoing process that can occur anywhere, not just in the ED.

The Pediatric Assessment Triangle

The PAT is a relatively simple tool that enables the nurse to obtain a quick general impression of the patient’s physiological status. It is a rapid assessment of the patient’s general physiological stability and can be performed before engaging in direct physical contact with the patient. Its validity as a first step in the assessment process for the pediatric patient presenting to the emergency department has been supported by research (Masoumeh et al., 2023; Tørisen et al., 2024). It uses visual and auditory cues to identify acutely ill and injured pediatric patients. The tool enables the nurse to quickly determine if the pediatric patient’s general condition is “sick,” “sicker,” or “sickest,” guiding the decision-making around which patients receive the highest priority to be further evaluated or need life-saving interventions (Dieckmann et al., 2023). The PAT consists of three components:
<BL>Appearance
Work of breathing
Circulation to the skin</BL>

The three components are recognizable from the ABCs of basic life support (BLS), advanced cardiac life support (ACLS), and pediatric advanced life support (PALS). The significant difference is that the PAT components are quickly assessed without touching the patient. The PAT has been integrated into life support algorithms, protocols, and courses worldwide (Dieckmann et al., 2023).
<CLINICAL PEARL>
CLINICAL PEARL
<BT>Utility of the PAT

Whether the nurse is faced with multiple pediatric patients who need to be triaged upon arrival to the ED or peeking in to see whether the patients are okay, the PAT can help. The PAT is not always related to ED triage or priority. It is simply an effective tool that calls out critical physical assessments the nurse can see or hear in a moment.
</CLINICAL PEARL>
Appearance

The first thing the nurse sees when looking at a child is their general appearance, whether they walk in through triage, arrive via ambulance, or are in a room. This assessment is often performed without conscious thought. However, it is paramount in determining the severity of illness and injury and how urgently the patient needs attention. General appearance includes the child’s interactions with the caregiver or the surroundings, revealing much information regarding the adequacy of ventilation, oxygenation, and perfusion to the brain and central nervous system. Any alteration in general appearance should be considered a significant underlying problem until proven otherwise.

The mnemonic TICLS is a helpful way to remember what to look for when assessing a pediatric patient (Box <S>4-</S>1). A quick assessment of appearance using the five TICLS components tells a lot about the patient’s overall condition.
<BOX>
<BN>BOX <S>4-</S>1 <BT>TICLS Mnemonic

<UNL>T	Tone: Is the muscle tone demonstrated by the child appropriate? Is the child moving arms and legs, or does the child appear limp or flaccid? Are they older than 3 months and cannot hold their neck and head up?
I	Interactiveness: Does the child appear to interact appropriately with the environment and/or the caregiver? If age appropriate, does the child play with toys and/or interact with others?
C	Consolability: Is the child easily consoled or comforted by the caregiver or a blanket, toy, or pacifier, or is there no consoling the child?

L	Look/gaze: If the eyes are open, does the child appear to be alert or is the child staring into space? If the child’s eyes are closed, are they open to noise or sound, or is the child just sleeping?
S	Speech/cry: Is the child’s speech appropriate, is the cry loud, strong, and vigorous, or is the speech or cry weak or listless?</UNL>
</BOX>
<RED FLAG>
RED FLAG
Any alteration in mental status in a pediatric patient should be considered as the result of decreased cerebral perfusion, hypoxia, or hypoglycemia until proven otherwise.
</RED FLAG>
Work of Breathing

The next component of the PAT is the work of breathing, or how much effort the child exerts to breathe. The work of breathing reflects the oxygenation and ventilation status. Observing any abnormalities in respiratory effort will help the healthcare provider identify a possible attempt to compensate for other physiological abnormalities. Assess the child’s respiratory rate and effort.

Increased work of breathing may be seen as a change in rate from what would be normal for the child’s age—either tachypnea or bradypnea. Observe the child for abnormal positioning (tripoding or leaning forward with hands on knees to breathe), retractions (intercostal, clavicular, sternal, tracheal, or abdominal), nasal flaring, or head-bobbing, which can indicate increased work of breathing. Listen for any abnormal audible breath sounds such as stridor; wheezing; or a barky, prolonged, or persistent cough. These are telltale signs of increased work of breathing and may be suggestive of significant illness or injury.
Circulation to the Skin

The final component in the PAT is circulation to the skin. Look at the child’s skin color in central areas, such as the lips and mucous membranes. The palms of the hands and the soles of the feet are also good indicators of circulation. Changes from the patient’s normal color are a strong indicator of insufficiency of cardiac output and core perfusion. Is the child’s skin color normal, or is it pale, mottled, ashen, gray, dusky, or cyanotic? In children with darker skin tones, it is especially important to look at the lips, tongue, conjunctiva, mucous membranes, gums, nail beds, palms of the hands, and soles of the feet to identify problems with circulation (Mukwende et al., 2020). Although mottling can be a normal physiological response to cold caused by vasoconstriction, it can also be a sign of shock and decreased cardiac output (Dietrich & Widmeier, 2021). It is safest to err on the side of caution and assume that any mottling indicates poor cardiac output until proven otherwise. Observe for any unusual redness or rashes, which may indicate a need to isolate the patient.
<CLINICAL PEARL>
CLINICAL PEARL
<BT>Utility of the PAT with Patients with Darker Skin Tones

Flushed skin, pallor, and rashes may appear differently in darker skin tones, and darker pigmentation can mask redness. In lighter skin tones, cyanosis can appear with a blue or purplish hue. However, darker skin tones may appear gray or white (Dodd et al., 2023). The palms, sclera, and conjunctival areas should be examined to assess the significance of pallor or other skin changes (Shanmugavadivel et al., 2022).
</CLINICAL PEARL>
Sick, Sicker, or Sickest
After using the PAT, the nurse can classify the patient as sick, sicker, or sickest.
Sick

Even with no abnormalities in the PAT, because the patient presents for medical care, the patient is classified as “sick.” Someone, whether the child, parent, caregiver, school, or other provider, had a concern. The child needs to be evaluated by a medical professional. Because there is no apparent alteration in the PAT, the child can be placed in the queue for care and wait to be seen for a more thorough evaluation and focused assessment. <S>The components of the pediatric nursing assessment are discussed in Chapter 5, “Initial Assessment.”</S>
Sicker

If there is any deviation or abnormality in only one of the three components of the PAT, the child is considered “sicker.” The child may be showing signs of compensation. The “sicker” child takes priority over the child who is “sick” and should be placed ahead of them in the queue for care. Depending on severity, the child may require rapid intervention.
Sickest

If there is a deviation from normal in two or more of the components of the PAT, the child is considered “sickest” and often warrants a high acuity level rating. A child determined to be sickest is placed in an area where rapid treatment, including resuscitation (if indicated), can be initiated.
A “sick” or “sicker” child may change in priority after a more thorough assessment is completed. A formal triage assessment is still needed to assign acuity accurately.
Triage Assessment Tools

While the PAT can be used with every patient encounter, it is also the first step of a more formalized triage assessment to determine order of priority when children present to the ED. Multiple assessment tools are utilized worldwide to quickly and efficiently determine a pediatric patient’s acuity and the urgency of care. Triage systems are imperative to the function and patient flow in the ED. Globally, EDs face an influx of patients that often outnumber their capacity (Ingielewicz et al, 2024). Triage tools are designed to establish a hierarchy of prioritized care based on clinical risk, enabling the proper resources to be allocated to urgent patients. These scales distinguish which patients require urgent care from those who can safely wait, especially in times of overcrowding (Viana et al., 2023). Validated triage tools have also been linked to reducing the length of stay in the ED, improving patient outcomes, and saving hospital resources. Many studies have explored the reliability and validity of various triage tools (Berkowitz et al., 2023; Huabbangyang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Recznik et al., 2019; Sax et al., 2024; Simon et al., 2022). Four scales commonly used and found to be reliable and valid are the Australasian Triage Scale (ATS), Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS), Emergency Severity Index (ESI), and Manchester Triage System (MTS), all of which use a five-tier system. Table <S>4-</S>1 compares these triage systems.

No matter what tool is used, ongoing quality monitoring and performance improvement are needed to increase triage accuracy. Education is also essential to assigning accurate acuity (Butler et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Recznik et al., 2019). Most pediatric emergency patients receive care in general EDs and thus are triaged by general emergency nurses (Recznik et al., 2019). A combined approach of case reviews, matching experienced nurses with novice triage nurses, and high-fidelity simulation effectively improves accuracy among general ED nurses with limited exposure to pediatric patients (Berkowitz et al., 2022: Liu et al., 2022; Recznik et al., 2019). Both over- and under-triage can be harmful; over-triage may waste resources, while under-triage can result in adverse outcomes, life-threatening complications, treatment delays, increased length of stay, and return visits requiring admission (Ageron et al., 2021: Berkowitz et al., 2023).
Disaster Triage

In disaster situations involving a massive number of casualties, conventional triage tools can be impractical. Triage takes a different approach and mindset in the disaster setting. Instead of doing the most for the sickest patient, utilizing all available resources, it follows the adage of “doing the greatest good for the greatest number.” There is no exact number of victims that constitutes a disaster; it can be any event that exceeds the facility’s available resources. Disasters can be natural or manmade. In a mass-casualty event or incident, critical patients who have the greatest chance of survival take priority (American College of Surgeons [ACS], 2025Chapter 17).

Disaster triage matches the patients’ needs with available resources. The PAT can still be used to form a general impression, but the sick, sicker, sickest determination may not govern priority of care. Different decision trees, such as START and SALT, are used in disaster triage for rapid patient assessments (Chemical Hazards Emergency Medical Management [CHEMM], 2025d). Pediatric triage tape (PTT) is another tool used in many countries in conjunction with the decision tree algorithm that uses physiological measurements proportional to the child’s height, weight, and age to aid in rapid identification of patient’s condition (Yalcin & Anil, 2022). Be familiar with the facility’s disaster plan, including its roles, resources, and communication structure in emergency preparedness. Children have specific considerations, including developmental, anatomical, and physiological differences that need to be considered (Yalcin & Anil, 2022).

The aforementioned decision tree called START (Figure <S>4-</S>2) is used to facilitate rapid patient assessment in patients older than age 8 years (CHEMM, 2025c). Reevaluation

It is important to remember that triage acuity (regardless of which system is used) reflects only the patient’s initial presentation to the ED. Acuity is a determination often made before the patient is placed in a treatment room to be seen. The assigned acuity level is simply a tool to guide the healthcare provider in which patient to see first. Acuity can change if the patient deteriorates or decompensates, requiring increased, more urgent care and interventions. This does not necessarily mean the triage acuity level changes. The acuity level may be upgraded if a patient’s condition deteriorates before being seen by the physician or advanced practice provider. An acuity score should not be downgraded based on environmental factors such as high patient volumes (Wolf et al., 2023).

As previously stated, triage is not a place but a dynamic ongoing process. Because pediatric patients can deteriorate rapidly, frequent reevaluations are warranted. Many institutions have set standards and protocols regarding patients’ reevaluation frequency based on their assigned triage acuity rating. Any patient who has not received definitive care and/or had a medical screening exam within the prescribed maximum waiting time for the assigned triage acuity rating (using ATS, CTAS, or MTS) should be reassessed. Not all triage tools have maximum waiting times. Institutions using ESI may develop reevaluation standards based on a more in-depth assessment after the triage acuity assignment is made. Additionally, any time an intervention is instituted, a reevaluation of the patient’s status is performed to determine the effectiveness of that intervention. Follow your institution’s reevaluation policies.
Assessment Pearls
This section covers several additional assessments and prioritization pearls.
Make the Parent or Primary Caregiver Your Friend

One of the most important things to remember when caring for a pediatric patient is that the primary caregiver is, in most instances, the greatest source of information and an invaluable assessment partner. They know their children. If a parent or caregiver states that the child is not acting normally and is concerned, listen! Even if the child seems to be acting perfectly normally and not in distress, remember that a nurse unfamiliar with the patient does not know what is normal for that child. There are developmental guidelines and milestones based on age, but this does not mean every child reflects those norms. The parent or primary caregiver knows what is normal and the milestones they have achieved. A basic understanding of pediatric norms and the most common disease processes is vital when assessing a pediatric patient. It is impossible to have expert knowledge in every disease process. Utilize the parent or caregiver; do not hesitate to ask them questions. Make the parent or primary caregiver your ally. Actively listen and validate their concerns. It is invaluable.
<CLINICAL PEARL>
CLINICAL PEARL
<BT>Recruit the Caregivers

Recruit the patient’s caregivers to assist with ongoing patient reassessment. Teach the caregivers which signs and symptoms are concerning and warrant immediate notification of the healthcare team. This intervention can also relieve anxiety while waiting for treatment or results.
</CLINICAL PEARL>
Ask the Right Questions to Get the Right Answers

Another pearl that applies to all assessments, particularly when determining priority of care, is “You must ask the right questions to get the right answers!” Avoid yes/no questions. Instead, ask open-ended questions. You are much more likely to get information of significant value, especially during a focused assessment of a pediatric patient. This helps ensure the child, caregiver, and/or parent understand what you are asking, and it may lead to additional questions. Two commonly used mnemonics to assist the nurse with which questions to ask are SAMPLE (Box <S>4-</S>2; appropriate for patients of any age) and CIAMPEDS (Box <S>4-</S>3; slightly more in-depth and focused on the pediatric population).

The SAMPLE mnemonic is commonly used. The version in Box <S>4-</S>2 is slightly adapted to include immunizations and the last output. Decreased urination is a way to assess dehydration. This information is lost if the nurse does not ask about output. Ask about the frequency of wet diapers. The differentiation of urine and watery diarrhea in diapers may be hard to determine, so asking how many diapers and bouts of diarrhea, including color, is helpful to determine the child’s condition. Older children can be asked about the last time they used the bathroom, the color of their urine, or the frequency and color of loose stools. Using one or both mnemonics will assist the nurse in remembering which questions to ask when conducting a focused assessment, which will help prioritize the pediatric patient beyond “sick, sicker, or sickest.”
Additional Screening Questions

It is also becoming increasingly important to perform abuse, violence, substance use, suicide risk, and other safety screenings during the assessment of pediatric patients. These evaluations can often be initiated during the triage process after determining that the child is physiologically stable. Quickly assess injuries and maltreatment. If suspicion arouses during the focused assessment, having a process to communicate this suspicion is important. <S>Further discussion of child abuse and screening tools can be found in Chapter 16, “Child Abuse.”</S>

Behavioral health emergencies are considered when determining priority. This helps ensure the safety of patients and others. Several tools are used to determine the level of risk, such as the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). Suicide screening is mandated in some institutions by governing bodies (Walsh et al., 2025). Substance abuse has been another growing public health concern, with an increase in mortality from drug overdoses between 2013 and 2022 (Renny et al., 2024). Mortality rates, however, have gone down since 2022 (Ahmad et al., 2025). ACS (2023) recommends substance abuse screening for all trauma patients older than 12 years at verified trauma centers.

Several screening tools can be initiated in the ED, but do not necessarily occur during the focused assessment unless the chief complaint warrants further investigation. Screening for social determinants of health is an area that is being recognized (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, 2025). Health promotion and injury prevention assessments and interventions ideally will occur multiple times during a pediatric patient encounter. <S>See Additional information on social determinants of health can be found in the Emerging Trends section and  Chapter 1, “Children Around the World.”.</S>
Vital Signs: Now or Later?

If the child needs immediate care based on the PAT or other findings, obtaining vital signs may delay potentially life-saving interventions. Focus on the child, not the numbers. If the child appears to be physiologically stable, obtaining a complete set of vital signs aids in determining the patient’s triage acuity. Some emergency acuity tools use abnormalities in vital signs as a parameter for determining acuity. The challenge then becomes obtaining accurate vital signs, especially for young children. Attempting to get vital signs for a child crying, whether from pain, discomfort, or fear, is challenging. Having the appropriately sized blood pressure cuff and pulse oximetry sensor helps to ensure the accuracy of the measurements.

Learning to count respirations from afar, before the young pediatric patient even sees you or you touch them, is a valuable skill. The parent or caregiver may assist by lifting the shirt or positioning the patient. Also, remember that when measuring vital signs in an alert pediatric patient, especially a younger patient, the nurse should start with the least invasive vital sign first and then proceed to the most invasive last. In other words, start with the respiratory rate first, then the heart rate, then the blood pressure, and finally the temperature, especially if a rectal temperature is indicated.

Normal ranges for pediatric vital signs are quite different from what is seen in adults. Quick access to a pediatric vital signs reference based on age is also of tremendous value. A posted chart or normal vital signs reference embedded into an electronic health record is critical in determining whether the vital signs are abnormal. <S>Normal vital signs for specific age ranges can be found in Chapter 3, “Pediatric Differences.”</S>

When interpreting vital signs, consider the child’s clinical condition and context. The heart and respiratory rate will be slower when the child is calm or sleeping and faster when the child is active, in pain, anxious, or febrile. Children with chronic or underlying medical conditions may have vital signs outside the parameters for their age. Asking the parent or caregiver about the child’s norms may be indicated.
Size Is Everything!

A pediatric patient’s weight is vitally important because all pediatric medication doses and fluid replacements are based on the patient’s weight in kilograms. A scale that weighs kilograms only is an essential tool in any healthcare setting where pediatric patients receive care. Length-based resuscitation tapes can be helpful as an alternative to measured weights, but they should be used only when the child is too critically ill to obtain an exact weight measurement. Obtaining an accurate weight in kilograms for all pediatric patients as soon as possible is best practice and is supported by the American Academy of Pediatrics (American Academy of Pediatrics, 2021; Lubsch et al., 2023; Ward et al, 2023).
<PEDIATRIC READINESS>
PEDIATRIC READINESS
<BT>Length-Based Resuscitation Tape

The length-based resuscitation tape can also serve as a tool to help determine whether the correct-sized equipment is readily available and organized. Many institutions create a cart or bag that matches the resuscitation tape colors. It enables the healthcare provider to match the color to obtain the correctly sized equipment for the child’s weight.
</PEDIATRIC READINESS>
Crying Is Good—Or Is It?

An old adage in EDs is, “A crying child is a good child!” This is true up to a point because a crying child is usually responsive to the environment, which is one of the components of the PAT. However, a crying child presents many challenges for the nurse, especially when obtaining accurate vital signs or listening to lung sounds.

The most important element is the quality of the cry and whether the child is consolable. In younger, preverbal children, crying is the only way to communicate needs. Crying or fussiness can indicate discomfort caused by pain, hunger, frustration, comfort, or tiredness. In some infants, crying can reveal an abnormal condition (Carabelli et al., 2024). A healthy neonate can cry for 200 minutes a day. As the child gets older, the amount of daily crying decreases (Vermillet et al., 2022). The list of threats to a child that can cause crying is extensive; some of these can be identified with AH! IF IT CRIESS mnemonic (Box <S>4-</S>4) (Herman & Le, 2007).

The nurse assessing the crying child should consider the characteristics of the cry with the child’s general appearance and ability to be comforted. A child who cannot be consoled is concerning and needs further assessment. A quick head-to-toe assessment and a brief history can often help to identify the cause of the crying. The acoustics of a cry can help determine whether the child is healthy. An unhealthy child will have unique features in the tone due to certain diseases and effects on the vocal cords and respiratory or neurological system. If crying is weak, it can be a sign of a serious illness. A high-pitched, screeching, catlike cry in an infant can be indicative of increased intracranial pressure. A low-pitched, hoarse-sounding cry can be indicative of an upper respiratory illness (Wang et al., 2025). Otherwise, if the crying is strong, robust, and appropriate for the situation, it can be reassuring that the child is breathing adequately and has a patent airway. Crying is a normal part of development, but can be very distressing for parents and caregivers; they may need support and reassurance. <S>See Chapter 5, “Initial Assessment,” for more information on assessing children.</S>
<RED FLAG>
RED FLAG

If a parent or caregiver uses the term “fussy” or “fussiness” to describe difficulty in consoling the child, consider this a red flag for serious illness or injury. Other red flags in triage are discussed later in this chapter.
</RED FLAG>
Fever, Pain, and Rashes

Assessment of the pediatric patient for fever, pain, and rashes is an integral part of the initial triage of the patient beyond the PAT. Sometimes, these parameters can be partially assessed and recognized during the PAT. Crying may indicate pain. A child who appears flushed when assessing the skin color may have a fever, and skin rashes may also be noted during the application of the PAT. Evidence of these three parameters during the PAT warrants additional focused assessment.
Fever

Fever is a common presentation or chief complaint for children presenting to the ED. Some red flags associated with fever are pallor, mottling, and cyanosis; not interactive or responding to social cues; tachypnea over 60 breaths a minute; not arousable; lethargy; grunting; weak, high-pitched cry; increased work of breathing; dry mucous membranes; and poor skin turgor (Allen, 2025; Philbin & Hall, 2022). Children who are ill appearing or have vital signs outside the norm can be presumed to have severe illness, until proven otherwise. Fever above 38°C (100.4°F) in infants younger than 90 days is concerning. Weakened immune systems and immunizations are also a consideration (Ohns, 2025). Hypothermic temperatures in neonates and young infants of less than 36.1°C (97°F) rectally are considered a red flag and can be a sign of sepsis (Perry et al., 2021). <S>Causes and management are discussed in Chapter 11, “The Child with a Fever.”</S>
Pain

Children are often not able to communicate their discomfort. There are validated pain scales to determine a child’s level of pain. Research supports age-appropriate pain scales, such as the Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability scale (FLACC) and FACES (Peng et al., 2023). Children who receive inadequate pain management can suffer lifetime physical, social, and emotional consequences (Miller et al., 2020). Inadequate pain management can also be linked to racial/gender differences. Gender imbalances have also been noted in pediatric pain assessment and management, with male patients being more adequately treated for pain than are female patients (International Association for the Study of Pain, 2021; Reardon et al., 2021). The caregivers’ reaction to the child’s pain can also influence the provider’s decision-making in treating pain (Miller & Abu-Alhaija, 2019). Culture also influences pain assessment and thus management (Mahon et al., 2023). Assessment of the pediatric patient’s pain is a significant consideration when prioritizing care. Standardized and protocol-based orders are often used to facilitate prompt pain management. <S>Pain scales are discussed in Chapter 3, “Pediatric Differences.”</S>
Skin Rashes

There are multiple reasons a child may have a rash. A skin rash in a child with an abnormal PAT should be considered life-threatening until proven otherwise. A rash may or may not be identified during the PAT; its presence should be identified during the focused assessment. Isolate a patient with a rash until the cause is identified. Some rashes are easier to identify than others. Obtaining a vaccination, exposure, and travel history can be helpful in this determination. Follow institutional isolation guidelines and protocols.
Infection Prevention and Immunizations

Knowledge of the potential for spreading communicable diseases is an important consideration. Infection control practices are evolving. It is the nurse’s responsibility to identify risks and implement precautions in accordance with the most current guidelines. It is important to be aware of public health trends and the presence of communicable diseases in the area.

Isolation has always been a challenge for the pediatric population. Younger children may not be cognitively able to comply with infection control measures and may require special attention to limit disease transmission. Use of appropriate personal protective equipment by the nurse, the patient, and the family members is essential, along with easily accessible hand sanitizer, handwashing facilities, tissues, emesis containers, and appropriate disposal receptacles in the triage and waiting areas. In an ideal world, no child would have to wait for medical care. As this is not practical, limit the spread of infections in pediatric waiting rooms. Toys and books should be cleaned frequently or removed. Children with signs and symptoms of highly contagious disease should be isolated until they can be examined.

Determining the patient’s immunization status early is essential to protecting the child and promoting the well-being of all. Under-vaccinated children might warrant isolation for their protection. Familiarity with regional immunization recommendations and resources enables the nurse to assess and manage the risks involved with under-vaccination and provide education.

Children with Special Needs Require Special Attention

Children with special needs and chronic conditions require extra diligence and consideration when prioritizing and triaging. The child’s caregiver can be your best resource in determining what is abnormal and the specific red flags for the child. Do not hesitate to ask questions and gather the information needed to determine their acuity and specific needs. This information can dramatically improve the accuracy of the acuity. The child may not be fully vaccinated due to contraindications or may be immunosuppressed due to their condition, which is also an important factor. Isolation may be warranted for their protection. <S>More information can be found in Chapter 18, “The Child with Specific Healthcare Needs.”</S>

Emerging Trends

ED overcrowding, staffing shortages, and inpatient and psychiatric patient boarding are widespread obstacles to quality emergency care (Savioli et al., 2022). These factors add to the complexity of the triage nurses’ role and prioritization of care.

Although multiple evidence-based tools can be used to help determine acuity, studies have shown that under-triage still exists with racial disparities (Peitzman et al., 2023). One group subject to under-triage is those who do not speak the language considered standard or most socially acceptable (Rojas et al., 2023). This not only affects triage accuracy but can lead to inappropriate care decisions regarding patient placement (Peitzman et al., 2023). Self-reflection and decision analysis may mitigate this inequity (Valdez, 2024).

One concept that has become widely accepted is the link between social determinants of health (SDOH) and pediatric health care. Examples of SDOH are socioeconomic status, education, housing, food insecurity, financial difficulties, transportation issues, safety concerns, and health literacy. Addressing these concerns can improve a child’s health and minimize disparities (Randolf et al., 2024). Some institutions include screening during the initial assessment to help identify those with greater risk. Adding this screening during the initial encounter quickly identifies those with SDOH concerns. Additional screenings add to the complexity of the triage process. According to a recent study, there has been an increase in regulatory data collection during the triage process, which can inhibit the nurse from rapidly and accurately identifying patients at risk of deteriorating (Wolfe et al., 2024).

Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) computer programs are beginning to grow in popularity, and several studies are finding benefits in utilizing these tools to help improve triage efficiency when combined with nursing assessment (Fernandes et al., 2020; Halawani et al., 2025; Tyler et al., 2024). As AI in medicine evolves, further study is needed to explore ethical considerations and their long-term effects.
Summary

Prioritizing a pediatric patient’s need for care and the severity of their illness or injury is challenging. Several tools exist to help the ED nurse make these decisions. The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a simple, quick assessment of the patient’s overall physiological status before coming into direct contact with the patient. Determination of sick–sicker–sickest aids in prioritization and implementation of life-saving interventions promptly, as needed. A focused assessment of the presenting complaint helps to further identify the severity of the illness or injury and facilitate proper assignment of triage acuity. Utilizing a formal acuity scale enables further evaluation to determine the severity of the illness or injury and assign an acuity score. As with any skill, education and practice is essential. The pediatric patient’s condition can change rapidly, requiring ongoing reassessment for early identification of decompensation and the need to reprioritize.

<OBJ1>Learning Outcomes
After completing the chapter, you will be able to accomplish the following:
1.	Describe the communication process and identify factors that influence communication.
2.	Describe ways in which people communicate nonverbally.
3.	Discuss professional responsibilities when using electronic communication and other communication technologies.
4.	Describe the interrelation between communication and the nursing process.
5.	Identify patient goals for each phase of the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship.
6.	Use appropriate communication techniques when interacting with patients from different cultures.
7.	Use a standardized communication technique (e.g., SBAR) to communicate with other nurses and health care providers.
8.	Evaluate yourself in terms of the interpersonal competencies needed in nursing.
9.	Describe how each type of ineffective communication hinders communication.
10.	Describe strategies that counteract disruptive professional communication and behaviors.
11.	Establish therapeutic relationships with patients assigned to your care.
12.	Describe effective interventions for patients with impaired communication.</OBJ1>

A nurse who wishes to be an effective caregiver must first learn how to be an effective communicator. Good communication skills enable nurses to get to know their patients and, ultimately, to diagnose and meet their needs for nursing care. Nursing students who sit face to face with patients to obtain a comprehensive nursing history intuitively grasp the importance of the nurse’s communicator role. To adequately document the patient’s health history, the nursing student must understand and implement proper communication techniques. Communication skills are the building blocks of professional relationships between nurse and patient/family, nurse and nurse, and nurse and other health care team members. Refer to the Reflective Practice: Developing Professional Identity box (p. XXX).

Many experienced nurses identify the quality of their interpersonal relationships as the single most significant element in determining their helper effectiveness. On nursing units where nurses freely exchange ideas and information, solve problems together when something goes wrong rather than assigning blame, pay compliments to each other, and use humor creatively, staff morale is high and patient outcomes are met more often. On the other hand, when harassment or disruptive communication and/or behaviors occur in the workplace between health care professionals, the consequences can affect the emotional and physical well-being of those involved, the functioning of the organization, and the safety of patient care. The American Association of Critical-Care Nurses (AACN) provides standards for establishing and sustaining healthy work environments, and states the quality of the work environment is linked to excellent nursing practice and patient care outcomes (AACN, 2016). These standards include skilled communication: “Nurses must be as proficient in communication skills as they are in clinical skills” (AACN, 2016, p. 2). See Chapter 19. Effective communication supports collaborative relationships and continuous improvement in patient safety and quality of care (AACN; ANA & AONE, n.d.; Settani et al., 2019).
<H1>PROCESS OF COMMUNICATION

Communication is the process of exchanging information and generating and transmitting meanings between two or more people. It is the foundation of society and the most primary aspect of a nurse–patient interaction. Without communication, it would be impossible to share family experiences, gain knowledge, establish and maintain practice protocols, and enhance caregiving. By nature, humans are social beings, and human needs are met in collaboration with other humans. Human relationships enable us to meet our physical and safety needs. Communication also assists in meeting our psychosocial needs of love, belonging, and self-esteem. The ability to communicate is basic to human functioning and well-being.

David K. Berlo (1960) is credited with the classic description of the communication process, which involves a source (encoder), message, channel, and receiver (decoder). This communication process is initiated based on a stimulus, in this case, a patient need that must be addressed. The need might be due to a patient’s discomfort or desire for information or to address any uncertainty the patient might be experiencing. The sender or source (encoder) of the message is a person or group who initiates or begins the communication process.

Recently, I was accompanying a nurse in the ICU when I encountered some behaviors that I found to be unprofessional and lacking in interpersonal communication skills. We were caring for Mr. Randolph Gordon, a middle-age patient who was in end-stage liver failure and had been comatose for several weeks. The extent of drains, tubes, and technologies being used to care for Mr. Gordon was overwhelming. I was nevertheless taken aback when the nurse and some residents entered his room and immediately began to assess the technologic equipment, without any regard for or recognition of Mr. Gordon himself. They proceeded to have a conversation about his poor condition, unsightly appearance, and foul smell at the bedside in his direct presence. They did not speak to him and or otherwise interact with him, not even the slightest touch of a hand.

<RFBX_H1>Values and Ethics
<RFBX_H2>What from the Code of Ethics for Nurses (American Nurses Association [ANA], 2025) ought to inform the critical care nurses caring for Mr. Gordon?

The very first provision of the Code obligates every nurse to practice with compassion and respect for the inherent dignity, worth, unique attributes, and human rights of every person. It is also clear that each nurse is responsible to create and sustain an ethical environment where the nurse–patient relationship can flourish.
<RFBX_H1>Knowledge
<RFBX_H2>What knowledge and skills are essential in this case and how can the student nurse develop them?

Ideally, the student nurse will have had a course in pathophysiology with neuroscience and gained some understanding of the different stages of coma. We continue to learn more about different states of consciousness and what patients are likely able to experience. Regardless, it is always safe to presume that patients can hear us; we should therefore behave and speak appropriately.
<RFBX_H1>Nurse as a Leader
<RFBX_H2>How does the role of the nurse unit demonstrate leadership behaviors in this situation?

Modeling professional behaviors is an important element of leadership. The delivery of person-centered care that respects the dignity and worth of each individual person is not predicated on that individual engaging with the nurse. The student nurse has a unique opportunity to either request that the team engage with the patient briefly before working, or the student nurse could also simply engage with him herself. The nurse on the unit and others may not recognize their potential insensitivity; such modeling by the student nurse could be an effective, yet subtle reminder.
<RFBX_H1>Professional Comportment
<RFBX_H2>What would support the development of ethical comportment of the nurse on this unit?

No matter how busy any nurse is, there is always time to communicate respect and care to patients. Many have contrasted a task versus person orientation among nurses. This text is committed to urging you to always keep your attention and behavior oriented to the person/patient receiving your care. Keep in mind that the student nurse and the nurse assigned to the patient are working in tandem, and learning is not one-directional. Student nurses can elevate the practice on a unit by asking questions, adhering to the details of a policy, citing evidence-based resources, and spending extra time with patients. Ethical comportment is developed over time and may change in depth and breadth, even with very experienced nurses.

The message is the actual communication product from the source. It might be a speech, interview, conversation, chart, gesture, memorandum, or nursing note. The channel of communication is the medium the sender has selected to send the message. The channel might target any of the receiver’s senses. The message can be sent to the receiver through the following channels:
<BL>
●	Auditory—spoken words and cues
●	Visual—sight, observations, and perception
●	Kinesthetic—touch</BL>
Nurses use all three of these channels to communicate with patients and other health care providers.

The receiver (decoder) must translate and interpret the message sent and received. Through the translation of the message, the receiver must then make a decision about an accurate response. To be an effective communicator, the nurse needs to be considerate of the receiver, and select a message that appeals to the patient’s interests and that requires minimal effort and time to decode.
<BX>

<ch008_csimage003>Recall Randolph Gordon, the middle-age male who is comatose. When planning Mr. Gordon’s care, the nurse would need to incorporate knowledge about changes in mental status and their effect on communication. His current mental status mandates that the nurse and other health care providers communicate simply and clearly.
</BX>

Confirmation of the message provides feedback (i.e., evidence) that the receiver has understood the intended message. Noise—factors that distort the quality of a message—can interfere with communication at any point in the process. These distractors might be from the television, or from pain or discomfort experienced by the patient.

Communication is a reciprocal process in which both the sender and the receiver of messages participate simultaneously (Fig. 8-1). Messages might be influenced on either end by the person’s previous knowledge, past experiences, feelings, or sociocultural level.
