A vaccine containing a polyprotein expressing epitopes from EBV lytic and latency genes induced potent antibody and T cell responses in mice.157 A study of 14 HLA B*0801 EBV-seronegative adults randomized to receive an HLA B*0801 EBV EBNA3A peptide (FLRGRAYGL) and tetanus toxoid in a water in oil adjuvant showed that 8 of the 9 volunteers developed epitope-specific T cell responses.184 At 2-12 years after follow-up 1 of 2 placebo recipients developed IM, while 4/4 vaccinees that became infected with EBV did not develop IM. Vaccination of mice with virus-like and light particles that contain lytic and latent EBV antigens resulted in virus-specific T cells that controlled outgrowth of EBV, and particles containing EBNA1 protected mice from wild-type EBV in humanized mice.747 Vaccination of transgenic mice with adenovirus expressing EBNA1, following by boosting with MVA expressing EBNA1 resuled in protection both as a prophylactic and therapeutic vaccine to prevent or treat EBV lymphoma.621
<H1>Perspective

While we have learned much about EBV, many important questions remain. The precise mechanisms by which EBV is associated with malignancies, and how these relate to the establishment and reactivation from latency, are still being uncovered. Much remains to be learned about EBV gene regulation in newly infected and latently infected cells, including how long-range DNA interactions and epigenetic pathways control EBV programs. Knowledge remains incomplete of how EBV causes these cells to differentiate into memory B-cells, and whether these reservoir cells differ from uninfected memory B-cells. Many EBV lytic gene products remain poorly studied, and roles for miRNAs and circular RNAs remain to be fully characterized. It is not fully apparent why EBV IM is primarily a disease of adolescents and young adults, though humanized mouse models and human studies will continue to provide new insights. The types of immune responses needed to prevent EBV infection, EBV mononucleosis or virus-associated malignancies are uncertain. The role of EBV in multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune diseases is still unclear. While EBV-specific CTLs have often been effective in the treatment of EBV post-transplant lymphoma, these cells have been less effective in the treatment of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and EBV associated lymphomas, and improved virus-specific therapies are needed. Newer therapies to block EBV immune evasion mechanisms or to alter EBV genome programs to allow latently infected cells to be better recognized and killed by the immune system are needed. Finally, while small scale trials have shown that an EBV vaccine can reduce the incidence of IM but not the rate of infection, larger trials with more effective vaccines are needed to prevent EBV infection and/or disease. EBV continues to teach us about B cell biology, and studies of immune deficiencies that predispose to severe EBV infections inform us about how the immune system controls virus infections. Thus, the study of EBV continues to enrich our knowledge of human biology and virology and further progress should help to reduce the burden of EBV-associated cancer,

Figure 71.1. Schematic depiction of the linear Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) genome. Linear representation of the overall genome arrangement with the unique short (US) and unique long (UL) regions shown. Within the genome the terminal repeats (TR), internal repeats (IR1-4), and unique sequence domains (U1-U5) of the EBV genome are depicted in proportion to their overall size. The position of the cis-acting element for episome maintenance and replication in latent infection, oriP, is indicated. The origins for EBV DNA replication in lytic infection (oriLyt) are in U3 and U5 just to the right of IR2 and IR4, respectively. The deletions in B95-8 and P3HR-1 genomes are shown.253,304,316

Figure 71.2. Schematic depiction of the linear Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) genome with encoded open reading frames (ORFs). EBV ORFs are named based on their location (first ORF, second ORF, etc.) and direction (rightward or leftward) within the Bam H1 fragment (A, B, C, and so on, in decreasing size).27 The prototypic EBV type 1 genome DNA sequence (171,820 bp) found in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) is actually a composite of two viral genomes (B95-8 and Raji) due to deletions within the viral genomes during passage in tissue culture.27,530,555 Size and direction of the ORFs are indicated, as are the noncoding RNAs EBER1 and EBER2. The latency-associated ORFs or exons that make up these ORFs are colored purple. The early lytic ORFs are beige and late lytic ORFs are shaded with red. Yellow arrows depict ORFs of unknown gene class or are hypothetical. LMP2A and LMP2B are encoded across the circularized genome. The locations of microRNA (miRNAs) encoded by the genome are shown. Numbers refer to kilobase pairs. (From Sample JT, Marendy E, Hughes DJ, et al. The Epstein-Barr virus genome. In: Damania B, Pipas JM, eds. DNA Tumor Viruses. New York: Springer, 2009, with kind permission from Springer Science+Business Media B.V.)

<H1>Focusing on Patient Care
This chapter will help you develop some of the skills related to safety issues that may be necessary to care for the following patients:
Megan Lewis, an 18-month-old who has an intravenous (IV) access in her left forearm.
Kevin Mallory, a 35-year-old admitted with a severe closed head injury. He is intubated and reaches constantly for his endotracheal tube.
John Frawley, a 72-year-old diagnosed with Alzheimer disease who continues to try to get out of bed after falling and breaking a hip.
Refer to Focusing on Patient Care: Developing Clinical Reasoning and Clinical Judgment at the end of the chapter to apply what you learn.
</FPC_BX>
<OBJ1>Learning Outcomes
After completing the chapter, you will be able to accomplish the following:
1.	Perform a situational assessment.
2.	Implement nursing interventions related to reducing fall risk and risk of fall-related injury.
3. 	Implement nursing interventions to be used as alternatives to restraints.
4.	Identify guidelines for the use of physical restraints.
5.	Apply an extremity restraint correctly and safely.
6.	Apply a waist restraint correctly and safely.
7.	Apply an elbow restraint correctly and safely.
8.	Apply a mummy restraint correctly and safely.</OBJ1>

Safety is a paramount concern that underlies all nursing care, and patient safety is a responsibility of all health care providers. It is a focus in all health care facilities as well as in the home, workplace, and community. Guidelines to promote patient safety are provided by healthcare accrediting, professional, and governmental organizations and agencies. For example, The Joint Commission identifies National Patient Safety Goals (NPSGs) for varied patient care settings to improve patient safety, focusing on problems in health care safety and how to solve them. These goals are updated yearly and can be found at https://www.jointcommission.org/en/standards/national-patient-safety-goals/. The American Nurses Association (ANA) also provides guidance to promote patient safety. A position statement from the ANA defines the nurse’s role in reducing restraint use in health care. These recommendations are presented in Box 4-2 in Skill 4-3.

This chapter addresses skills nurses need when working with patients to monitor for safety, prevent injury, and to intervene when safety issues arise. The first skill addresses using a general patient and environmental survey to identify immediate patient concerns and safety concerns. The next two skills address injury prevention and discuss reducing fall risk and using alternatives for physical restraints. The remaining skills address how to use several types of physical restraints safely and correctly. Fundamentals Review 4-1 provides general guidelines for restraint use. Always treat patients with respect and protect their dignity.
<SK_BX4-1>
<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-1 <BX_TTL>Performing a Situational Assessment

Awareness of the patient’s environment and situation is an integral part of nursing care. Situational awareness in the patient care environment involves knowledge, attention, and responsiveness in relation to patient monitoring; knowing and understanding the elements of a given clinical situation and the significance of the interrelation of these elements; and awareness of patient safety (Avalos et al., 2021; Feller et al., 2023; Fukuta & Iitsuka, 2018; Green et al., 2017; Large & Aldridge, 2018). Situational awareness in nursing includes routine use of a general survey (observation) of the patient, family/caregivers, and environment, using input from all senses (Avalos et al., 2021). Integration of situational awareness as part of routine nursing care contributes to an understanding of the current situation, identifying and solving problems, and supports anticipation of potential problems (Avalos et al.; Connor et al., 2022; Feller et al.). Situational awareness promotes a safer patient care environment, reduces risks, and helps the nurse develop care priorities, acting correctly when things go as planned, and reacting appropriately when they do not (Avalos et al.; Feller et al.; Large & Aldridge).
</SK_BX>
<SK_BX4-2>
<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-2 <BX_TTL>Fall Risk and Fall-Related Injury Risk Reduction

Falls are the second leading cause of unintentional injury deaths worldwide, with older adults and children being at highest risk (World Health Organization [WHO], 2021). In the United States, falls are the leading cause of fatal and nonfatal injuries for older Americans and are associated with significant impact on quality of life as a result of fear of falling, limiting of activities, physical decline, depression, and social isolation (National Council on Aging, n.d.). Falls are caused by and associated with multiple factors. Primary risk factors related to falls are outlined in the Assessment discussion below.

An interdisciplinary approach that actively engages patients, families, and/or caregivers in assessment, intervention, and evaluation contributes to reduced risk of falls (Benning & Webb, 2019; Guirguis-Blake, et al., 2024; PSNet, 2024a; Tucker et al., 2019; WHO, 2021). Identifying at-risk patients is crucial to planning appropriate interventions to prevent a fall. Fall risk assessment is discussed in the Assessment section of this skill along with examples of fall-risk assessment tools. Table 4-1 identifies examples of fall risk reduction strategies for acute care based on fall risk assessment; interventions should be based on patient-specific risk factors to develop a personalized plan (PSNet, 2023; Reis da Silva, 2024). Providing patient education and a safer patient environment can reduce the incidence and severity of falls (The Joint Commission, 2015; Reis da Sliva; WHO, 2021).
<EFP_BX>
<BX_TYPE>EVIDENCE FOR PRACTICE
<BX_TTL>ENGAGING PATIENTS IN FALL PREVENTION EDUCATION

Providing patient education and a safer patient environment can reduce the incidence and severity of falls (The Joint Commission, 2015; Reis da Sliva; WHO, 2021). How can nurses engage older adults and their caregivers in fall prevention education to support effective implementation?
<EFP_H1>Related Research

Hill, A. M., Francis-Coad, J., Vaz, S., Morris, M. E., Flicker, L., Weselman, T., & Hang, J. A. (2024). Implementing falls prevention patient education in hospitals – older people’s views on barriers and enablers. BMC Nursing, 23(1), 633. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12912-024-02289-x.

This study explored the perceptions of older people and their caregivers about barriers to and enablers of implementation of an individualized hospital falls education program. Older adults (n=37, age range 64–89 years) who had been an inpatient in the hospital and their caregivers (n=9) participated in this qualitative study. A purposive sample was used to ensure a diverse range of participant characteristics, including types of hospital experiences, age, gender, and health status. Participants chose either a group or a one-on-one semi-structured interview. Participants were asked to review the revised Safe Recovery program (a patient falls education program) using a video and workbook and then provide feedback on how to implement the program in hospital settings. Member checking was performed at the end of each focus group or interview. The data was coded using reflexive thematic analysis. Two themes each with several subthemes emerged from data analysis: positive reaction to the program and practical suggestions to aid falls education delivery. Participants identified that the Safe Recovery program resources were of high quality, with clear information that enabled strong patient engagement and increased knowledge and awareness about fall prevention in hospitals. Practical suggestions to enable program delivery included timing of delivery around wellness and the patient’s mobility, tailoring messages for each older patient, and having key staff members assigned to lead program delivery. Providing resources in other languages and offering alternative shorter versions were suggested to support broad dissemination. The researchers concluded that valuable insights were gained to assist with implementation and support of effective falls education and address patient misconceptions related to fall risk and raise risk awareness.
<EFP_H1>Relevance to Nursing Practice

Limited awareness of and engagement in effective fall prevention may increase older adults’ risks for falls. Nurses have a key role to play in engaging patients in their health care. Programs that provide patients with information related to fall risk and fall prevention should be implemented during care points to address gaps in knowledge, improve patients’ experiences, and promote empowerment.
</EFP_BX>
<SK_BX4-3>
<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-3 <BX_TTL>Implementing Alternatives to Physical Restraints

Restraint-free care is the standard of practice and an indicator of quality care in all health care settings (American Nurses Association [ANA], 2012; Touhy & Jett, 2022, p. 221). Physical restraints do not prevent falls, and they increase the possibility of serious injury due to a fall (Taylor et al., 2027). Additional negative outcomes of restraint use include skin breakdown and contractures, incontinence, depression, delirium, anxiety, aspiration, respiratory difficulties, and even death. <na>Restraints should be considered only when less-restrictive interventions (alternatives to restraints) have been determined to be ineffective.</na>

Careful nursing assessment is the key to identifying appropriate alternatives to restraint use and finding an individualized solution (Taylor et al., 2027). ANA (2012) has approved a position statement defining the nurses’ role in reducing restraint use in health care. Their recommendations are included in Box 4-2. Nurses should collaborate with the health care team to implement less-restrictive alternatives to restraints (ANA, 2020). All alternatives used must be documented. Refer to Fundamentals Review 4-2 for additional guidelines for restraint use. The following skill outlines possible alternatives to restraint use.
</EFP_BX>
<SK_BX4-4>
<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-4 <BX_TTL>Applying an Extremity Restraint

Cloth extremity restraints limit the movement of one or more extremities (TIDI Products, 2024c). An extremity restraint may be applied to the hands, wrists, or ankles. It may be indicated after other measures have failed to prevent a patient from removing therapeutic devices, such as intravenous (IV) access devices, endotracheal tubes, oxygen, and other treatment interventions. <na>Restraints should be considered only when less-restrictive interventions have been determined to be ineffective. Ensure compliance with ordering, assessment, and maintenance procedures. Restraints must be applied safely and appropriately to reduce risks of injury.</na> Federal guidelines reinforce that in all settings, the primary responsibility is to protect and promote patient’s rights, and that restraints may only be used to protect the patient, staff, or others (Taylor et al., 2027). They must be discontinued at the earliest possible time.

Review the general guidelines for using restraints in Fundamentals Review 4-2 and Box 4-2 in Skill 4-3. See also Skill 4-3 and the Evidence for Practice resources at the end of Skill 4-3 for guidelines to minimizing and eliminating restraint use.

<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-5 <BX_TTL>Applying a Waist (Soft Belt) Restraint

A waist or soft belt restraint is applied to the patient’s torso, over their clothes, gown, or pajamas to secure them to a wheelchair, hospital bed, or stretcher (TIDI Products, 2024a). When using a waist restraint, patients can move their extremities, but the restraint limits their ability to move or exit unassisted. It may be indicated after other measures have failed to reduce the risk of unassisted movement or wheelchair, hospital bed, or stretcher exits. <na>Restraints should be considered only when less-restrictive interventions have been determined to be ineffective. Ensure compliance with ordering, assessment, and maintenance procedures. Restraints must be applied safely and appropriately to reduce risk of injury.</na> Federal guidelines reinforce that in all settings, the primary responsibility is to protect and promote patient’s rights, and that restraints may only be used to protect the patient, staff, or others (Taylor et al., 2027). They must be discontinued at the earliest possible time.

Review the general guidelines for using restraints in Fundamentals Review 4-2 and Box 4-2 in Skill 4-3. See also Skill 4-3 and the Evidence for Practice resources at the end of Skill 4-3 for guidelines to minimize or eliminate restraint use.

<SK_BX4-6>
<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-6 <BX_TTL>Applying an Elbow Restraint

Elbow restraints (immobilizers) are generally used on infants and children but may be used with adults and prevent patients from bending their elbows and touching incisions or therapeutic devices (Nationwide Children’s Hospital, n.d.; TIDI Products, n.d.). The patient can move all other joints and extremities. <na>Restraints should be considered only when less-restrictive interventions have been determined to be ineffective. Ensure compliance with ordering, assessment, and maintenance procedures. Restraints must be applied safely and appropriately to reduce risks of injury.</na> Federal guidelines reinforce that in all settings, the primary responsibility is to protect and promote the patient’s rights, and that restraints may only be used to protect the patient, staff, or others (Taylor et al., 2027). They must be discontinued at the earliest possible time.

<BX_TYPE>Skill 4-7 <BX_TTL>Applying a Mummy Restraint

A mummy restraint is appropriate for short-term restraint and temporary immobilization of an infant or young child to control their movements during examination or for a procedure involving the head and neck or care to one extremity (Kyle & Carman, 2025; Silbert-Flagg & Kennedy, 2023). <na>Restraints should be considered only when less-restrictive interventions have been determined to be ineffective. Ensure compliance with ordering, assessment, and maintenance procedures. Restraints must be applied safely and appropriately to reduce risks of injury.</na> Federal guidelines reinforce that in all settings, the primary responsibility is to protect and promote patient’s rights, and that restraints may only be used to protect the patient, staff, or others (Taylor et al., 2027). <H2>SUGGESTED ANSWERS FOR FOCUSING ON PATIENT CARE: DEVELOPING CLINICAL REASONING AND CLINICAL JUDGMENT

1.	Nursing interventions for Megan should include the use of distraction, such as play, toys, music, games, and so forth. (Refer to Skill 4-3.) Megan’s parent should be encouraged to stay with her to provide supervision and distraction, also. Cover the IV access site with a dressing and gauze or other covering. If all other alternatives to restraints are attempted, and maintaining the IV infusion is necessary, an elbow restraint (Skill 4-6) or hand mitt (Skill 4-4) would be the least-restrictive restraints to prevent dislodgement of Megan’s IV access.

2.	Implement as many alternatives to restraints as possible for Mr. Mallory. Refer to Skill 4-3. In addition, consult with the health care team to discuss a possible time frame for extubation. Increase monitoring frequency, repeat explanations, and provide distraction as part of the plan of care for him. Elbow restraints (Skill 4-6) would be a possible solution if restraints are determined to be necessary.

3.	Fall prevention is best achieved through the implementation of multiple strategies. Begin by assessing Mr. Frawley’s motivation for attempting activity unassisted. Provide reassurance and explanations related to care. If possible, he could be moved to a room closer to the nursing station to allow increased monitoring. Additional nursing interventions to try could include asking family members to stay with Mr. Frawley, providing distraction based on information from the family regarding his favorite activities, implementing more frequent rounding to ensure that his toileting and hydration needs are met. Adjust the bed to the appropriate height for Mr. Frawley to allow safe transition out of it and provide floor mats to reduce the risk for serious injury if he should fall. Refer to Skill 4-2 for additional intervention suggestions.

<BX_TYPE>Box 4-1 <BX_TTL>Patient Education for Preventing Falls in the Home
●	Talk with your health care provider about a plan for an exercise program. Regular exercise helps maintain strength and flexibility and can help slow bone loss.
●	Have regular hearing and vision testing. Always wear glasses and hearing aids, if prescribed. Even small changes in sight and hearing can affect stability.
●	Wear firm shoes with a back and a good grip on the bottom. Avoid wearing only socks or shoes with smooth soles.

●	Have handrails on both sides of stairs and make use of them when using the stairs. Try not to carry things when using the steps. When necessary, hold item in one hand and use the handrail with the other hand.
●	Install safety gates at the bottom and top of staircases to keep children from tumbling down.
●	Avoid using chairs and tables as ladders to reach items that are too high to reach.
●	Keep electrical and telephone cords against the wall and out of walkways.
●	Consider rails next to the toilet and in the shower or tub and raised toilet seats.
●	Use a cane, walking stick, or walker to help improve stability.
●	Keep home temperature at a moderate level. Temperatures that are too hot or too cold can contribute to dizziness.
●	Stand up slowly after eating, lying down, or resting. Standing too quickly can cause fainting or dizziness.
●	Ensure good lighting, particularly at the stairs.
●	Use a night light.
●	Remove clutter from walkways inside and outside the house.
●	Carpets should be fixed firmly to the floor to prevent slipping. Use no-slip strips on uncarpeted surfaces.
●	Use nonskid mats, strips, or carpet on surfaces that get wet.
●	Use rubber mats in the shower to prevent slips and falls from wet surfaces.
●	Check all medications, including prescriptions and over-the-counter drugs, herbs, and vitamins, with your health care provider and/or pharmacist to find out if any put you at risk for falling.

<CST>STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
<H1>THE COMMUNICATION PROCESS

All nursing practice revolves around the nurse–patient relationship, which is built upon verbal and nonverbal communication within a specific setting. The nurse–patient relationship differs from personal and social relationships because its foundation is the therapeutic use of self through communication skills. Nurses have a privileged role as a respected healthcare provider.  The relationship with patients is professionally intimate. In some situations, patients disclose information to their nurses that they do not even share with family members.  When taking the history, learn about personal physical concerns, spirituality, community, culture, and psychosocial limitations.

During health history taking, use special techniques and communication skills to gather complete and accurate data about the health state of the patient. This may feel awkward at first. As interviewing skills improve, conversation with patients becomes more comfortable. There are smooth transitions from question to question. Develop a comfort level with periods of silence and pause during the interview. Develop a style of communication that suits personality and values, blending the professional and the personal. Communication is one of the foundational components of the nurse–patient relationship.

The purpose of taking the health history is to collect subjective data from patients. Subjective data are based on the signs and symptoms that the patient reports. The individual and family histories describe past and current medical problems, surgeries, and risks for disease. Include information on behaviors and activities that promote health. In many settings, patients complete these long forms online in advance. Also review the form and ask questions about it.

Communication is a complex, ongoing, interactive process that forms the basis for building interpersonal relationships (American Association of Colleges of Nursing [AACN], 2025). It is a system of sending and receiving messages, forming a connection between sender and receiver (Fig. 2.1). This continuous and dynamic process is always subject to interpretation. The sender’s purpose is translated into meaning by the person hearing it. The receiver interprets the message, trying to understand the meaning of the verbal and nonverbal messages. Personal understanding greatly influences what is heard, both correctly and incorrectly.

Culture and judgments influence a person’s understanding. In many cultures, mental health disorders carry great stigma, so patients may describe psychosocial difficulties as a lack of sleep or as feeling tired. People living in some countries may speak loudly as an indication of confidence, whereas in other countries, speaking loudly signifies ignorance or disrespect.

Both nurses and patients bring perceptions about the relationship with them. A patient who has had positive personal experiences with the healthcare system may be more open to developing a relationship with the nurse than one who has had negative experiences. Therefore, it is important to be is aware of the patient’s comfort or anxieties.
<H2>Therapeutic Communication

Therapeutic communication is a basic tool used in a caring relationship with patients. In therapeutic communication, the interaction focuses on the patient and the patient’s concerns. This skill takes practice but can be learned with attention and awareness. It takes time to learn to listen for messages that might otherwise be unheard, but this careful listening contributes greatly to a therapeutic relationship. Learn to “read between the lines.” Assist patients to work through feelings and explore options.

Caring encompasses empathy for and connection with the patient. It also includes the ability to demonstrate emotional characteristics such as compassion, sensitivity, and patient-centered care. The nursing goal is to show warmth, care, interest, and respect-- and to value patients unconditionally and nonjudgmentally. Patients are more willing to discuss their health issues if they perceive the nurse as caring, understanding, and nonjudgmental.

Empathy is the ability to perceive, reason, and communicate understanding of another person’s feelings without criticism. It is being able to see and feel the situation from the patient’s perspective rather than a personal one. Being empathetic means asking questions to help patients express how they are feeling and what they are thinking. Empathy may be conveyed verbally or nonverbally. In some situations, such as death of a relative, it is possible to exhibit empathy simply by holding a person’s hand or offering a tissue. Through experience, learn to communicate empathy in a variety of situations.

A comfortable self-concept is important to be aware of biases, values, personality, cultural background, and communication style. Build  awareness through self-reflection and receiving feedback from others. Self-awareness helps to identify what is done well and what the challenges are. Self-reflection develops a genuinely therapeutic relationship with patients.
<H3>Nonverbal Communication Skills

Nonverbal communication is as important as—if not more important than—verbal communication. Physical appearance, facial expression, posture and positioning in relation to the patient, gestures, eye contact, tone of voice, and use of touch are all important components of nonverbal communication. For example, do not assume that touch is culturally acceptable to a patient. Instead, be courteous and ask permission: “Is it OK if I touch your hand?”

Physical appearance and facial expressions send messages to patients. Thus, it is important to ensure that  dress and appearance are professional, and facial expressions are relaxed, caring, and interested. Be aware that facial expressions common in casual social situations (rolling eyes,  showing shock, or grimacing in disgust) reduce trust and are thus inappropriate during interactions with patients. Posture is upright but relaxed and open.  Avoid “closed” positions, such as crossed arms, which may signal to patients lack of interest in them and their information. Use gestures intentionally to illustrate points, such as pretending to drink or pointing to the bathroom. Gestures are purposeful rather than distracting from the communication.

To facilitate the best eye contact, be at eye level with the patient. If standing while the patient is in bed, the nurse will be taller than the patient, in a position of power. Sitting on the patient’s hospital bed or examining table, however, may seem  unprofessional or too close in their personal space. Consider principles of infection control. Beds or tables contain bacteria and body secretions (such as urine or feces) that can be transported from one room to another. Avoid sitting on the patient’s bed since it could possibly be soiled. For patients seated on examination tables, be near eye level when standing. During the interview, it is important to balance soft eye contact with brief glances away. In some cultures, prolonged eye contact is considered threatening. However, no eye contact at all makes the nurse appear uninterested.

During the initial interview, there is only one chance to make a good first impression. Touch is an essential and a dominant component of the physical examination. Shaking hands, a gentle touch, and a smile can communicate caring. Consider cultural variations in terms of how much touch is appropriate because touching may not be acceptable in some cultures.

If positioned near the patient’s bed, speak carefully and maintain good eye contact so that the patient will feel that they are being heard. Appear confident, even if hesitant when learning a new skill, so that the patient has trust. In some situations, the instructor or assigned nurse can carry on the conversation. This provides a diversion for the patient and allows concentration on the skill.
<H3>Verbal Communication Skills

Learn effective interviewing skills through practice and repetition. Speech is of moderate pace and volume with clear words. A too-soft voice may indicate embarrassment or discomfort, whereas a too-loud voice may seem too powerful and controlling. Speech that is too fast indicates being rushed, whereas speech that is too slow may indicate a belief that the patient does not comprehend. For a patient with a hearing impairment, be in a position so that patients can lip-read. Picture boards are a good alternative for patients with hearing conditions (Fig. 2.2).
<Insert Figure 2.2 Here>

For patients with limited knowledge of the English language, use simple and clear language, but do not raise the voice. Instead of using complete sentences, speak in one or two words, such as “Pain?” Insert pauses in the conversation to allow patients an opportunity to speak.  Pauses facilitate trust, respect, and sharing. A pause of 5 to 10 seconds gives the patient the opportunity to consider the questions being asked. It seems like a long time at first, but it will become more comfortable with practice.
<BX6-CMA>
<BX6-TTL>Concept Mastery Alert

When using an interpreter, allow the interpreter time to speak and translate- and then allow pauses for the patient to reply. The best approach is to insert pauses so that the patient has time to think of the answer in the native language, translate into English, and speak.
</BX6-CMA>
<H4>Active Listening

Active listening is the ability to focus on patients and their perspective. It requires constant decoding of messages, including thoughts, words, opinions, and emotions. For example, if a patient is sad, it is appropriate to place a hand over the patient’s hand and to show a facial expression of compassion. If a patient is angry, listen to the reason for the anger, such as treatment failure. Rather than respond in turn with anger, attend to the patient’s feelings by pulling up a chair and taking the time to listen.

Try to uncover the hidden message and show concerned, appropriate body language. Talking about difficult feelings helps patients to heal. The nurse is not expected to solve all the patient’s difficulties but instead to therapeutically use self to assist patients by listening.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

<BX2-TXT-FIRST>If talking about a situation seems to increase rather than defuse a patient’s anger,  redirect the interview. If a patient is abusive or overly aggressive, it may be necessary to take a time-out by saying, “I understand that you’re very angry right now. I am feeling a little concerned/uncomfortable/unsafe, so I can either have someone else come in to talk with you or come back in 15 minutes. Which would you prefer?” Be aware of personal space, and if the patient becomes physically aggressive, leave the area to avoid harm. Keep a safe physical distance.
</BX2-SA>
<H4>Restatement

Restatement relates to the content of the communication. Make a simple statement, usually with the patient’s own words. The purpose is to ask the patient to elaborate. Restatement provides an opportunity for patients to further explain. For example, repeat the patient’s statement by saying, “So, you feel like there is a knot in your chest ….”
<H4>Reflection

Reflection is like restatement; however, instead of simply restating the patient’s comments, summarize the main themes of communication. Listen carefully to the different thoughts expressed and attempt to identify their relationship. With this technique, patients gain a better understanding of the issues that underlie their thoughts, which helps to identify their feelings. The following example illustrates how the nurse use reflection.
Patient: I really hate getting shots. Do I really need to get a flu shot? My friends never had it, and they didn’t get sick.
Nurse: You sound a bit nervous about getting an injection. (Pause)
Patient: The last shot that I had really hurt.

In this situation, the patient was not questioning the need for the injection but was expressing anxiety about it because of previous experience. The nurse now knows to direct the conversation toward dealing with the anxiety rather than teaching about the risk of influenza.
<H4>Elaboration (Facilitation)

Encouraging elaboration (facilitation) is a technique that assists patients to more completely describe difficulties. Use responses that encourage patients to say more and continue the conversation. This shows patients interest. Nod, or say, “Um-hum,” “Yes,” or “Go on” to cue patients to keep talking. Another technique is to let patients know that their thoughts and feelings are common, normal experiences and give them permission to discuss them. Say something like “Sometimes when patients are involved in a car accident, they have flashbacks or bad dreams.”
<H4>Silence

Use silence purposefully during the interview to allow the patient time to gather thoughts and provide accurate answers. Use silence therapeutically to communicate concern. Silence indicates interest in what the person is saying. It gives patients a chance to decide how much information to disclose. For example, a patient may be embarrassed to discuss how they contracted a sexually transmitted infection. A pause of quiet, and a caring expression can tell the patient that it is okay to share.
<H4>Focusing

Use focusing when patients are straying from a topic and need redirection. For example, “We were talking about the reaction that you had to the penicillin. Tell me more about that reaction.” This response connects the patient’s story to the initial need for information on the type of reaction, which is a safety issue needing further discussion. It keeps the conversation on track without changing the subject and  assists the patient in providing important information.
<H4>Clarification

Clarification is important when the patient’s word choice or ideas are unclear. For example, “Tell me what you mean by the evil eye.” Another way to clarify is to ask, “What happens when you get low blood sugar?” Such questions prompt patients to identify other symptoms or give more information to  better understand the situation. Use clarification when the patient’s history of illness is confusing. Putting data in time order or placing events in context can help make the story clearer. In the history of the illness, ask, “When you had chest pain, first you took three nitroglycerin tablets and then you called 911—is that right?”
<H4>Summarizing

Summarizing happens at the end of the interview, during the closure phase. Review and condense important information into two or three of the most important findings. Doing so helps ensure that you have identified important information and lets the patient know that they have been heard accurately. Summarizing includes the progress made toward problem solving and things to think about later. It also gives patients an opportunity to add information they wish to be included in the interview or that they may have unintentionally omitted. For example, “It seems that you are most concerned about your appetite and lack of energy. We have talked about adding some low-cost and high-protein foods to your diet. When you come in for your next visit, we can talk about how that worked.” Ask, “Is there anything else that you would like to add?”
<CST>SUBJECTIVE CUES
<H1>NONTHERAPEUTIC RESPONSES
<H2>False Reassurance

Often in social situations, people use nontherapeutic casual responses. Probably the most common example is false reassurance to minimize uncomfortable feelings. Providing false reassurance may indicates to patients that their concerns are not worth discussing. This situation enhances anxiety, which can increase a patient’s needs in other areas, such as pain medication, and diminish trust. Examples of false reassurance are, “It won’t hurt,” or “Don’t worry—it will be all right.”

It would be better instead to say, for example, “It will hurt a bit when I take off the bandage, but I’ll do it quickly,” or “It sounds like you’re concerned that your cancer might have returned. I will be here when you get your test results tomorrow.” This type of reassurance validates the patient’s concerns and reassures them of  support.
<H2>Sympathy

Sympathy is feeling what a patient feels. Being sympathetic is not therapeutic because it arises from a personal perspective. In contrast, empathy is feeling what a patient feels from the patient’s perspective. Keep the focus on the patient and listen. Avoid thinking about personal feelings of loss, grief, or anger. Step back from the situation and be mindful of the patient’s experience. Every person has walked a different path, and the patient’s experience is unique to them. Be curious and explore what it is like for them.
<H2>Unwanted Advice

Giving unwanted advice happens frequently in social situations. It is nontherapeutic in professional relationships because the advice is  from  a personal perspective, not the patients. Because the advice is based on personal experiences and opinions, it will not help the patient.

Giving advice differs from providing information. A patient may ask, “Do you think that I should have my knee replaced? I don’t really know what to do.” In this situation, understand that the patient is asking for an opportunity to discuss options rather than a personal opinion. Instead of telling the patient what to do,  state, “Tell me what you know about the surgery” or “You sound concerned about having knee surgery.”

Such responses give patients an opportunity to explore choices more fully, clarify any confusing points, and weigh risks against benefits. They also incorporate the patient’s perspective instead of adding potentially confusing or conflicting information or opinions. Patients then reach their own conclusions.

<H3>Biased Questions

Using leading or biased questions is often an unintentional nontherapeutic response. Biased questions carry judgment and lead patients to respond in a way that they think will be acceptable. Biased questions may also cause patients to feel guilty or inferior about unhealthy behaviors. An example of a biased question is, “You don’t use drugs, do you?”

To obtain a more honest response, ask objective questions, such as, “It is important that we know what drugs you are taking so that we avoid interactions with the medications that you are taking. What substances might you use to change how you think or feel?” In this way, place the need for information within the context of healthcare. Patients will then understand that information is needed for best care rather than to judge  unhealthy behaviors.
<H3>Changing the Subject

Avoid changing the subject when a situation is uncomfortable because of  personal experiences or coping mechanisms. For example, if a nurse recently experienced the death of a parent, it may be challenging at this time to talk with a family about a patient who has terminal cancer. Avoiding the subject is not therapeutic for the patient; recognize this as a personal coping mechanism. If distressing, seek support from others. An alternate approach is to be honest with the patient about the situation. If emotional control is too difficult, refer the patient to another nurse.

It is also common to change the subject unconsciously when  feeling rushed or stressed. When busy, it may be necessary to prioritize and block out time to use active listening when the patient needs to talk. Part of the plan of care may be “Allow 15 minutes of uninterrupted time every shift for therapeutic conversation.”
<H3>Distractions

Distractions in the environment contribute to nontherapeutic communication. Hectic and rushed work environments are common across healthcare settings and contribute to patient complaints about depersonalized care. Distractions come from various sources, such as equipment, other patients, colleagues, pagers, and cell phones. When equipment poses a potential source of distraction, tell the patient, silence the alarm, and resolve the problem before conversation. An equipment alarm indicates an immediate problem that usually takes priority over therapeutic communication.

When a patient’s roommate is asking for something, decide to either grant a simple request and then pull the curtains for privacy or ask them to wait by saying, “I’m listening to your roommate’s lungs right now. I can get you some water in about 5 minutes.”

Prioritize the importance of answering a page or cell phone based on the intensity of your conversation with the patient and the point in the interview. Answering a phone during the middle of a conversation is nontherapeutic; many patients may consider it rude. If answering a phone or pager is necessary, complete the topic being discussed and then ask for permission to answer by saying, for example, “I just received a call about a patient who needs pain medication. I’ll do my best to be back with you in 5 minutes or sooner.”
<H3>Technical or Overwhelming Language

Using too many technical terms or providing too much information is another nontherapeutic response. As medical vocabulary is developed, practice “back translating” from newly learned medical terminology back to lay language. For example, document “dysphagia” but ask the patient about “trouble swallowing.” Consider the knowledge level of the patient. Use more technical descriptions with a patient who is a physician, and simpler words with patients with limited English skills. Some ideas can be presented through visual or hands-on materials that illustrate points (Fig. 2.3).
<H3>Interrupting

Talking too much and interrupting are also examples of nontherapeutic communication. To exhibit caring behavior, choose words more carefully than in social situations. In the professional role as a nurse, listen more than talking. Communicate nonverbally through presence, facial expression, or touch. In healthcare settings, it is better to listen than to talk and to ask good questions rather than have all the right answers. A general guideline is to listen 80% and talk 20%.
<H2>Professional Expectations and Boundaries

Because it is easy to identify too much with some patients, especially those who seem familiar, it is important to establish clear professional boundaries. The nurse who becomes too involved with patients may experience burnout and decreased job satisfaction.

Nonprofessional involvement occurs when  boundaries are crossed to establish social, personal, or business ties with a patient (National Council of State Boards of Nursing [NCSBN], 2024a). Social talking about the weather or news may put patients at ease in the beginning, but too much chatting—especially about religion, politics, gossip, or personal finances—is unprofessional. Some disclosure may help establish a therapeutic relationship, but always present such information in the context of the patient. For example, a nurse is working with parents of a child who was recently diagnosed with asthma. The nurse’s son also has asthma. The nurse may use that information to say, “I have a child with asthma, too. I noticed that the cough would get worse at night. When is your child’s cough worse?” In this example, the nurse uses personal information to quickly redirect the conversation to focus on the patient and the family.

The use of social media sites presents challenges for maintaining professional boundaries with patients. Institutions have very rigid and specific policies that must be followed. Be very aware of crossing professional boundaries outside of the work setting. There are many ethical and legal consequences that may inadvertently arise through social media use outside of institutional and professional parameters (NCSBN, 2024b). Know the agency’s policy and follow it strictly.

Sexual contact is never acceptable within the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship and is considered sexual misconduct (NCSBN, 2024a). The NCSBN (2024a) states, “Professional sexual misconduct is an extreme form of boundary violation and includes any behavior that is seductive, sexually demeaning, harassing or reasonably interpreted as sexual by the patient.”

Visiting patients outside of the patient care role also breaks professional boundaries. At the end of the workday, trust that the healthcare system exists to meet ongoing patient needs. Although many times a nurse remembers and becomes attached to the first patients with whom they work, do not confuse the privileged intimacy associated with the nursing role with the intimacy involved in a social or personal relationship.
<H2>Culturally Competent Communication

Communication etiquette refers to the good manners used with patient contact. It is both the science and art of nursing to know which communication technique to use and when to use it. Intercultural communication refers to being polite and courteous with all types of people. This shows respect for everyone, even if their beliefs are different. Assess the degree to which each patient identifies with cultural norms or not. For example, if a patient notes “Asian” in the intake form, ask if they prefer a Chinese, Korean, Japanese, or American diet.
<H3>Patients With Limited English Skills

Obtain an interpreter if a patient uses a primary language other than English. However, interpreters cannot be involved continuously throughout a patient’s care because of cost and access. Develop other communication tools. For example, cover one concept at a time instead of overwhelming the patient with several ideas at once. Use simple words or phrases to facilitate understanding. At times, pantomime questions, such as pretending to be in pain or having a questioning look. Translation technology may also be of assistance.
When communicating with patients who have limited language proficiency, remember the following principles:
• 	Limitations in language are not a reflection of intellectual functioning. A patient may be highly literate in one language but functionally illiterate in another.
• 	Patients tend to think in their native language and translate, thus delaying their responses.
• 	Patients interpret the message that reflects their cultural beliefs, often changing the meaning, so be sure to ask for understanding. Say, “Tell me what you understand.”

A sheet with common phrases (e.g., “I am thirsty,” “I need to use the bathroom”) can be useful for patients who are literate in their native languages. Consider, however, that patients may not be able to read or write in their native language. Pictures are helpful for patients who can see but who cannot read. Audio assist technology and audio translation devices are used for those who hear well. It is also nice to know a few key phrases in a patient’s language.
<H3>Working With an Interpreter

Establish the need for an interpreter during the patient’s first contact. Even when a patient’s language skills are fluent, a trained medical interpreter is necessary for discussing sensitive topics, such as end-of-life care or permission for consent to treat. In inpatient settings, interpreters may check in with patients daily. In such situations, it is helpful to maintain a list of questions and areas for patient teaching to cluster the most important information during the time that the translator is available (usually for a 30-minute period). Other occasions for using an interpreter are the admission assessment, complex treatments, patient education, informed consent, and discharge planning. U.S. federal law mandates the use of a trained interpreter according to standards established by The Joint Commission (2025). Interpreters are chosen based on language, dialect, gender (for sensitive subjects), and social status (if this is likely to be an issue). Many agencies have a phone or video service for interpretation, although in this mode the nonverbal communication is lost.

Using children in the family, other relatives, or close friends as interpreters violates privacy laws because patients may not want to share personal information with relatives or friends. In addition, friends and family who are unfamiliar with medical terminology may misinterpret information. When possible, a trained medical interpreter is preferred. These interpreters also understand cultural health beliefs and practices and can help bridge the gap.

Interpreters are educated to remain neutral. Issues can arise if an interpreter adds their opinion or bias to communication. Be aware of nonverbal communication that seems inconsistent with the issues being discussed. See Box 2.1 for tips on communicating through interpreters.
