<H3>Gender and Sexual Orientation Bias

When working with sexual and gender minorities, be aware of societal biases. This population commonly reports discrimination and mistreatment in healthcare settings. Some members of the LGBTQ+ community choose to hide their gender identity or sexual orientation due to assumptions and fear of negative attitudes from healthcare providers, exclusion from services, lack of confidentiality, discrimination, and family conflicts (Rosendale et al., 2020).

Consider the simple intake question, “Are you single, married, or divorced?” Think of how a patient with an unmarried life partner may respond. A more inclusive, sensitive, and ultimately better question is “Do you live alone or with someone?” because it provides a more direct avenue for finding out about support at home.

An understanding of some basic terminology is also important. Gender identity refers to the individual’s self-identified gender, which may not correspond with the individual’s sex assigned at birth. Ask the patient to describe, in the patient’s own terms, their gender identity, and ask what pronouns the patient uses. Transgender describes individuals whose gender identity does not conform with societal norms and expectations associated with their sex assigned at birth. Keep in mind that gender identity does not define an individual’s sexual orientation.

An inclusive intake question is,  “We have begun asking all patients about their sexual orientation and gender identity so we can provide everyone with the best care possible. Can you tell me about yourself?” Some other questions are, “Do you think of yourself as straight, lesbian, gay, bisexual, or something else?” “What is your current gender identity?” and “What pronouns do you use?” Follow up with, “What sex were you assigned at birth?” and “What name do you use on your insurance card?” (). It is also important to be aware of specific health issues for this group. The LGBTQ+ population has a high incidence of smoking, excessive substance use, mental health issues, and suicide. Make sure to assess these in the history.
<CST>OBJECTIVE CUES
<H1>PHASES OF THE INTERVIEW PROCESS
<H2>Pre-interaction Phase

During the pre-interaction phase, collect data from the medical record before meeting with the patient. This includes the previous history of medical illnesses or surgeries, current medication list, and problem list. It is helpful to know about some of the past situations and responses to treatments before meeting. Review the record chronologically to detect patterns of illness such as declining functional status.
<H2>Beginning Phase

Introduce self with name and title and state the purpose of the interview. An example is, “Hello, my name is Sam, and I am going to be your nurse this evening.” At this moment, it is appropriate to ask the patient how they would like to be addressed. Simply say, “What name would you prefer me to use?” Listen carefully for the correct pronunciation and, if necessary, ask the patient for confirmation that the pronunciation is correct. Shake hands if that seems comfortable and is appropriate for the setting.

Continue the beginning phase with a discussion of some neutral areas, such as the weather, especially if the patient appears anxious. Move through such discussion quickly, however, and introduce the purpose of the interview. For example, “Mrs. Lewis, I need to ask you some questions about your personal and family history.” Make overall remarks that pertain to the patient’s record, such as, “You have been in the nurse’s office for a cold three times in the last 3 weeks. It doesn’t seem like your cold is going away.”

Privacy is essential, especially considering the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) guidelines (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services [USDHHS], 2022) for confidentiality of information. Pull drapes around patients if conducting the interview in a hospital room, and close the door if working in an examination room. In community settings where patients are disclosing personal information, identify an area where others cannot overhear the conversation before beginning the interview.
<H2>Working Phase

Collect data by asking specific questions during the working phase. Two types of questions used to collect information are closed-ended and open-ended questions. Each type has a purpose; choose which type will better help elicit the appropriate information.

Closed-ended or direct questions are best for specific information that yields yes-or-no answers, such as, “Do you have a history of heart disease?” Then during the interview, ask follow-up questions, and clarify information that is “yes”.

Open-ended questions require patients to give more than yes-or-no answers. They are broad and yield responses in the patient’s own words. Sometimes these answers are put in quotation marks in documentation. Examples of open-ended questions are “What does your pain feel like?” and “How are you doing with the low-salt diet?”

Closed-ended questions (e.g., “Is your pain sharp or dull?”) help cue patients who have had difficulty responding to an open-ended question. Closed-ended questions are also helpful for patients with communication challenges, such as those with dementia.

Avoid “why” questions because patients may find them difficult to answer. Avoid those that can be accusatory or judgmental. For example, “Why haven’t you stopped smoking?” is a nontherapeutic leading or biased question as compared with the more therapeutic question “Tell me about how difficult it is for you to stop smoking.”

Chart and document the patient’s history and health problems. The goal is to achieve a balance between listening and documenting. Sometimes, documentation is on paper; more commonly it is on a computer. When using a computer, be at eye level to maintain eye contact with the patient and the patient’s family. Record unexpected findings during the interview and then return to the form later to note the absence of findings. It takes practice to achieve a comfortable blend of recording assessments and listening.
<H2>Closing Phase

End the interview by summarizing and stating what the two to three most important patterns or problems might be. For example,, “It seems that you are most concerned about control of your pain. What other things are concerns?” Close the interview by letting the patient know the next steps, such as, “I’ll make sure to put in your plan of care to ask about your pain level every hour.”

Before leaving, ask whether the patient needs anything else. Doing so gives the patient a final opportunity to express needs and feel that they have been heard. The closing phase is a good time to review any checklists being used for completeness and to make notes about future interventions. Thank the patient for providing information as the interview is ended. Make sure the environment is returned to comfort and safety.

Keep in mind that the initial meeting and interview with the patient are critical to the visit or hospital stay. It is the patient’s first perception of the setting and care providers. In the acute care setting, the rapport that is developed sets the tone for the entire remainder of the patient’s stay.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

If an interview reveals confidential material, disclose those things required to be reported by law, such as suicidal thoughts, violence at home, or rape. Inform the patient at the beginning of the interview that these situations must be  reported. Notify authorities only after ensuring the victim’s safety.
</BX2-SA>
<H1>HEALTH HISTORY SOURCES
<H2>Primary and Secondary Data Sources

The individual patient is considered the primary data source. Charts and information from family members are considered secondary data sources. Subjective information is from the patient as a primary data source. Secondary sources are all other sources of information.
<H2>Reliability of the Source

Record the person who provides the information as well as their reliability. A reliable historian provides information that is consistent with existing records and is comprehensive in scope. If information differs from past descriptions or if details change each time, the patient may be unreliable or considered an inaccurate historian. Note any discrepancies and identify other sources (i.e., previous records) to confirm the history.
<H1>COMPONENTS OF THE HEALTH HISTORY

Usually, demographic data are collected first, followed by complete description of the reason for seeking healthcare. How much additional data is collected depends on the reason for the visit, pertinence of the data, and time restrictions within the setting. Determine which data to collect beyond the minimum required.

Data may be collected in an emergency, during a visit for a specific problem (e.g., shoulder pain), or during a wellness visit. Refer to Table 2.1 to compare emergency, focused, and comprehensive health histories. The following sections explain the components of the comprehensive health history.
<H2>Demographic Data

Depending on the healthcare setting, personnel at a front desk or admissions department often collect demographic data from patients, including name, date of birth, address, and billing information. Occupation and insurance may be sensitive issues for some patients. In such cases, explain the reason for asking about them. For example, “Sometimes people are concerned about how they will pay for their care. Do you have any insurance or financial concerns with which you might like help?” These can also be asked at the end of the interview.
<H2>Reason for Seeking Care

The reason for seeking care is a brief statement, usually in the patient’s own words, about why they are making the visit. Ask, “Tell me why you came to the clinic today,” or “What happened that brought you to the hospital?” Record this information in the subjective part of documentation; consider putting the statement in quotes. If a patient replies by giving a medical diagnosis, such as “heart attack,” encourage the patient to describe the symptoms, such as “shortness of breath and chest pain.” When taking the health history, record the symptoms, or subjective sensations or feelings of patients, versus the signs, or objective information, assessed during the physical examination.
<H2>History of Present Illness

Collect information about the present illness by beginning with open-ended questions and having the patient explain symptoms. A complete description of the present illness is essential to an accurate diagnosis. In addition, ask questions about the symptoms to assist the patient to be more specific and complete.
Use  a mnemonic to remember the elements that are important to assess for the presenting symptom. Examples are as follows:
• 	OLDCARTS (onset, location, duration, character, associated or aggravating factors, relieving factors, timing, severity)
• 	PQRSTU (provocative or palliative, quality, region, severity, timing, understanding patient perception)
• 	COLDSPA (character, onset, location, duration, severity, pattern, associated factors/how it affects the patient)
• 	Location, duration, intensity, description, aggravating factors, alleviating factors, pain goal, and functional impairment.
Regardless of the order of the data, redirect the conversation following the cues of the patient. Use a mental checklist to ensure assessment of all categories before the end of history taking.
<H3>Location

Ask, “Where does it hurt?” and observe the patient’s nonverbal cues. If the patient has difficulty describing the location, ask, “Show me where it hurts.” Note not only the location stated, but also nonverbal responses. For example, if a patient points with a finger to a location, the area of pain is more specific than use of the palm of the hand over a broad area.
<H3>Onset/Duration/Timing

Establish onset and duration by asking two questions: “When did you first notice the pain?” and “How long did it last?” Record the date and time specifically (month and year) instead of documenting “yesterday.” In this way, future healthcare providers can easily identify the date. Duration also refers to whether the pain is constant or intermittent, how long it lasts, and whether it goes completely away or cycles off and on. There are differences in the assessment of acute, chronic, and neuropathic pain.
<H3>Intensity

Ask the patient, “How bad does it hurt?” To provide a quantifying measurement, ask the patient to rate their pain on a 0-to-10 scale, with 0 being no pain and 10 being the worst imaginable. Other pain scales use faces and descriptors.
<H3>Quality/Description

Ask the patient, “What does the pain/discomfort feel like?” If the patient cannot describe it, provide cues by asking, “Is it sharp or dull?” or “Is it stabbing, sharp, or achy?” A question for associated symptoms is “Do you notice anything else when you have the pain?” If patients have difficulty understanding the question, you may ask, “When you have the pain, do you notice any sweating?” (which is common with chest pain) or “Do you notice a special feeling before you have a seizure?” (which is an aura).
<H3>Aggravating/Associated/Alleviating Factors

Uncover aggravating factors by asking, “Is there anything that you notice that makes it worse?” Assess associated factors by asking, “Is there anything that you notice that consistently causes or happens with the pain?” Assess for relieving factors by asking, “What seems to make it better?” or “What have you tried to make it go away?” Include settings in which the pain occurs, such as during gardening.
<H3>Pain Goal

Ask the patient, “What is an acceptable level of pain?” or “What do you hope that we can get your pain down to?” A pain goal should be set to allow patients to perform the most important activities easily. Usually, a goal of zero to mild pain (0 to 3 on a 10-point scale) is acceptable. Pain more than this is treated.
<H3>Functional Goal

Pain can affect the ability to perform common movements and tasks. Assess the effects of pain on the patient’s functional ability by questioning the patient about sitting, rising from a chair, standing for a while, climbing stairs, shopping, driving, and participating in sports. The patient may want to be able to run or jog without pain.
<H2>Past Health History

Past health history includes an assessment of medical and surgical problems along with the treatment and course. Some problems are acute, others resolve, and others are chronic. When the patient indicates a problem, follow up with questions on the details including the date of onset and when or if it was resolved. Include any treatments such as surgeries and any lasting effects of treatment. Complications of treatment may occur, or the condition may be chronic, such as arthritis, and require continued follow-up. Knowing the pattern and course of the problem gives a clearer idea about the current health status and what interventions are recommended now. Include the following sections in the health history.
<H3>Childhood Illnesses

Include in the record any childhood illnesses with potentially lasting effects (e.g., polio, varicella). Record the date of the most recent immunizations for tetanus, pertussis, polio, measles, rubella, mumps, influenza, covid, hepatitis A, B, and C, and pneumococcus. Note if there is a return to normal function or complications from the childhood illnesses.
<H3>Past Illnesses

Include a medical diagnosis, treatment, and what the treatment outcomes were for any past illnesses. Request a date by asking a follow-up question, such as, “What year was that?” Ask if the patient has ever been hospitalized and, if so, for what, when, and how long. Ask how the illness was treated, and if there were any complications from the treatment.
<H3>Surgeries

Document dates of initial diagnosis and surgeries—for example, “Appendectomy 2003; testicular cancer 1/2006; orchiectomy 2/2006; chemotherapy with cisplatin, etoposide, and bleomycin 3/2006; currently in remission.” Note if the surgery achieved the desired patient outcome.
<H3>Injuries and Trauma

Note any serious accidents and injuries. When documenting past medical and surgical history, it is important to note any long-term effects and ongoing problems. Chart events chronologically when possible so that others can easily identify the order. Note current problems on the problem list.
<H3>Obstetric History

Note the obstetric history for female patients, including the number of pregnancies (gravida) and number of births (para). Document the reason for any incomplete pregnancies (e.g., spontaneous abortion).
<H3>Health Screening

Ask about screening tests and the results, such as tuberculin skin test, Pap smear, mammogram, colonoscopy, stool for occult blood, cholesterol, and blood pressure. Document the date of the last physical assessment. This can show patterns of health promotion and interest in maintaining and improving a healthy lifestyle.
<H3>Genetics

Although nurses have always collected health histories, with increased knowledge of genetics, the nurse’s role in the thorough collection of family histories is more crucial than ever. Identifying genetic patterns in a patient’s history is essential to health promotion measures not only for the patient but also for their family and future generations.
<H2>Current Medications

Ask patients about current medications, including name, dose, route, and frequency. Identify the purpose of each medication because some drugs have more than one use. For example, one patient may take a beta-blocker for blood pressure control, whereas another may take the same drug to prevent a heart attack. In addition, query the patient about any over-the-counter medications, supplements, or herbal remedies in use. If the patient is confused about any medication, ask the patient or family member to bring in the pill bottles to ensure accuracy (Fig. 2.4).

For hospitalized patients, reconcile all medication lists with medications taken regularly at home so that patients continue using the correct drugs (). Medication reconciliation is creating the most accurate list of all medications a patient is taking (drug name, dosage, frequency, and route) and comparing that list against the physician’s admission, transfer, or discharge orders. It is important to explain to patients that any medications may interact with disease processes or with additional medications being given, for example, in the hospital.
<H2>Allergies

Verify allergies with patients and compare them with those stated in their medical records. When asking about allergies, it is essential to note the type of response, such as rash, throat swelling, difficulty breathing, or anaphylactic shock. Some patients may confuse an adverse effect or adverse reaction with an allergy. For example, a patient may become nauseous when given opiates. Note this response as an adverse reaction. Document throat swelling and difficulty breathing as an allergic reaction. It is critical to document both the medication and the patient’s reaction to it for future reference. Allergies must be appropriately noted in the chart, and the hospitalized patient must have a name band applied noting the allergy. If there are no known drug allergies, it may be noted in the chart as NKDA (no known drug allergies). NKA means no known allergies-- including drugs, foods, dust, and other allergens.
<H2>Family History

Ask the patient about the health of close family members (i.e., parents, grandparents, siblings) to help identify those diseases for which the patient may be at risk and to provide counseling and health teaching. The following familial conditions are important to note: high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, high cholesterol, stroke, cancer, diabetes mellitus, obesity, alcohol use disorder, drug addiction, and mental illness. In addition, obtain the health history of children and identify patterns of disease that might be genetically inherited. Ideally, the family history is recorded in a centralized area on a computer, and all healthcare providers can contribute.

A common tool used to understand family patterns is the genogram (Fig. 2.5). This graphic representation allows mapping of family structures to compile a large amount of information visually. Genograms make it easier to identify the complexity of families and validate patterns pertinent to patients. A complete family history can take as little as 15 minutes or as long as 2 hours. Each family member is represented in the diagram and linked to define relationships (e.g., parent–child). Deaths may be noted with an X or a slash mark through the individual’s symbol. A key is included to clarify the meaning of symbols. This graphic representation compiles information into a concise pattern of family history.
<H2>Functional Health Assessment

Functional health patterns (Table 2.2) are especially important to nursing because they focus on the effects of health or illness on a patient’s quality of life. The strengths of patients, as well as areas needing improvement, are assessed using this approach (). Some of the questions are personal and difficult to answer, so it is best to thread the questions throughout the history and address the more personal questions toward the end of the conversation. Integrate these questions into other activities, such as giving a bath or chatting before the next appointment, instead of sitting down and asking the questions in a structured and sequenced order. Identify issues that may be potential problems for patients and prioritize to ask those first.

Assess the patient’s ability to perform self-care activities, or activities of daily living (ADLs). These include behaviors such as eating, dressing, and grooming. Score these items based on whether the patient is totally independent, needs assistance from a person or device (e.g., a cane), or is dependent on others (see Box 2.2). These functional abilities help describe the impact of the problem on the patient’s daily life, and if they can stay at home, or how much help they may need.
<H2>Growth and Development

Developmental assessment of infants, children, and adolescents is especially important to determine the achievement of developmental milestones and to gain awareness of deficits to facilitate early intervention and management.

Psychosocial development is part of assessment for all age groups because even some adults have delays. For example, drug and alcohol overuse can interfere with relationships, employment, and housing. A patient who has a drug or alcohol problem may not reach the generativity stage but instead remains self-absorbed. For all patients, evaluate the cognitive stage. This is pertinent for those at either end of the life span. Assess if younger patients are appropriately developing abstract thinking skills and evaluate older patients for any signs of memory decline.
<H2>Review of Systems

The review of systems (ROS) is a series of questions about all body systems that help to reveal concerns as part of a comprehensive health assessment. When able, the patient fills out a form. Ask the patient about any symptoms related to each body system, such as a cough regarding the respiratory system. Integrate these questions during the physical examination of each region, such as asking about chest pain when listening to the heart. The systems review can vary in sequence and format depending on the setting, the acuity or degree of illness (and thus urgency of the problem), and the style of the nurse. In the ROS, data collected are subjective information. Objective data, completed in the physical assessment, are documented separately.

In addition to the problems covered in a ROS,  obtain information from the patient about health promotion practices. Begin with a general question, such as, “How is your appetite?” and progress to more detail, such as, “What types of foods do you eat to stay healthy?” In the review, document not only the presence of findings but also the absence of problems or symptoms, such as “No nausea, constipation, or diarrhea.”

It is good practice to logically organize the approach to the review. Most patients are unaware of the order, however, so they might include symptoms out of order. Just adjust and note this in the appropriate area.

Explain to the patient that, although the review is lengthy, it is an opportunity to double check for completeness and accuracy of past and current problems. When documenting findings, reorganize the information so that data regarding a problem are clustered. For example, if a patient is nauseous and vomiting, cluster together findings from the nutrition, hydration, skin, and abdominal assessments. This shows critical thinking about how urgent the problem is.

Box 2.3 presents a list of topics covered during the ROS. Note that the questions are not mutually exclusive. For example, weight gain or loss is part of the general health state, but it also provides information about fluid balance, edema, and appetite. Adapt topics to the patient and direct conversation in a way that is comfortable and logical. Omit topics that do not apply and add topics that seem pertinent. Although the list in Box 2.3 uses medical terminology, use common lay language so that the patient better understands the topics and questions. These topics are further explored in the individual chapters of this book.
<H1>PSYCHOSOCIAL AND LIFESTYLE FACTORS

Psychosocial and lifestyle issues may naturally arise during the ROS. Because many of these questions are personal, it is best to ask them at the end of the interview, after trust has been established. Some examples are mental health, risk for domestic violence, and drug use.
<H2>Social, Cultural, and Spiritual Assessment

Assess overall psychosocial well-being as part of the screening of the functional health patterns, including self-perception/self-concept, role/relationships, and coping/stress tolerance. Obtain more detailed information when patients have indicators of current distress. Assess cultural beliefs and health practices that influence care.

Assess spirituality and belief systems during the functional health screening with questions related to values or beliefs. In addition, assess rituals and practices that affect health status. Use this information to support the patient during times when hope and guidance are needed. Ask about religious preference so that referral to pastoral care can be initiated, if that is the patient’s preference.
<H2>Mental Health Assessment

If the patient is anxious, depressed, or sounds illogical, mental health requires a closer examination. Ask the patient, “Describe any changes that you have had in your mood or feelings” and “Have you ever been treated for any problems with your mood or behavior?” Note medications during the initial history and ask follow-up questions regarding the purpose and effectiveness of any psychiatric drugs. In addition,  use suicide risk assessments, depression screening tools, or a full mental status examination. When the primary concern is psychiatric,  perform a complete mental health assessment.

Assess alcohol and drug use by direct questioning. Observe behaviors that indicate impairment, such as slurred speech, nodding off, and unstable gait. Although this may be an uncomfortable area for beginners to ask about, most patients recognize that this is necessary. It is okay to be direct here. As an example, and to normalize the response, say, “A lot of college students like to party. Some of my patients drink a 12 pack every weekend. How much do you drink?” Assess smoking directly by asking, “Many people smoke marijuana, cigarettes, or vape. How much do you use?” Follow up with how much per day and for how long.
<H2>Neglect, Abuse, and Violence Assessment

Because of the high prevalence of physical abuse of children and females, especially during pregnancy, it is often the policy in healthcare agencies that nurses routinely question patients about this (). Because of the sensitive nature,  pose questions so that the patient feels comfortable talking. Examples include “Some women have experienced being hurt by someone. Within the past year, have you been hurt either physically or sexually by anyone?” and “Sometimes your mom or dad might get angry with you. What happens when your mom or dad gets mad?”

Suspect abuse if injuries are inconsistent with explanations, if the story changes over time, if the patient has delayed getting treatment, if there is a history of injuries or accidents, if there is associated drug or alcohol misuse, or if there is a history of mental illness. Commonly, the patient’s abuser is overly protective, may refuse to leave the room, or dominates the interview. Abused children may be overly attentive to please the parent or guardian.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

When child or elder abuse is suspected,  it is the provider’s obligation to report it to a supervisor.  Obtain assistance from social work or case management for further assessment. In some states, the permission of the victim of domestic abuse is required because of the increased risk when the abuser is aware. Document findings objectively in the medical record, avoid judgments, and do not make conclusions until investigated.
</BX2-SA>
<H2>Sexual History

This may be another uncomfortable area for beginning nurses to ask about, but recognize that these questions can provide information for health teaching. Consider sexual history and pattern as a topic for health promotion, especially in high-risk patients such as those with multiple partners or having unprotected sex. Introduce these questions during discussions of reproductive function or healthy behaviors or during the personal and social histories.

Ask, “As part of your physical examination, we like to provide information on healthy sexual practices. What would you like to know about?” Some other questions are “Have you had intimate contact, oral sex, or penile-rectal intercourse in the past year?” “How many sexual partners have you had in the past year?” “With which gender(s) do you prefer to have sex?” and “What measures do you take to protect yourself from sexually transmitted infections? Pregnancy?”

Provide opportunities for younger children to ask questions about sexuality; this can increase patients’ comfort level in discussing sexual topics with healthcare providers later in life. Do not omit the discussion of sexual history with older adults, who may remain sexually active.
<H2>Life Span Considerations

Parents, legal guardians, or other adult representatives serve as primary interview sources of healthcare information when patients are children. As they age and become more independent, children can participate more fully in interviews. Be sure to validate the roles of people bringing children to the attention of the healthcare facility. For example, a mother may be accompanied by a male partner who is not the child’s father; a stepparent may bring in a child; or a child may have two mothers or two fathers. In the beginning, ask, “Tell me about your relationship with the patient.”

It is important to address parents by the names they prefer. It is unprofessional to call parents “mom” or “dad.” Address children by their first names. Nonverbal communication is very important with young children, who may have limited verbal skills. Toddlers and preschoolers are quick to notice anxiety, pain, distress, or discomfort in either a caregiver or a nurse. Healthcare settings may provoke anxiety in children because many have had immunizations and tests that involved pain or discomfort. Instead of the formality found in other settings, pediatric and family practice settings are usually colorful, and many healthcare providers there wear playful bright clothing as well. These environments are childproofed, so parents and providers need to worry less about supervising their children for safety and feel more comfortable and relaxed and are thus more likely to provide accurate assessment data.

Collect the health history for infants from parents (Fig. 2.6). As children move into adolescence, interview the parent and adolescent together. The relationship between the adolescent and the parent determines how to collect data. It may be more comfortable and reliable to ask questions regarding sexual activity and recreational drug use with the parent absent. Ask parents to step out of the room for a short time.

For older adults, establish roles of others present during the interview . Introduce self and then ask what name they prefer to be addressed by. Refer to older adults by their preferred name instead of “auntie,” “honey,” or “sweetie.” Use a normal tone and pace initially and adapt later if the older adult patient is hard of hearing or has dementia.

With older adults, be aware of the increased risk for sensory deficits that might alter the history taking, such as loss of vision or hearing. Older adults may have more complex histories because of their increased prevalence of disease and may require some additional time to process information. It is important to identify the pattern of the illnesses and recognize how they might be related. In addition to the increased risk of illness because of family history, lifestyle choices also begin to influence health later in life. In the case of an older adult patient who has a family member along, focus the interview on the patient. Avoid assuming that the patient is an unreliable historian.
<H2>Challenging Situations

Patients may have special situations that require altering the usual approach to interviewing. Examples include hearing impairment, reduced level of consciousness, and the influence of drugs or alcohol. Adapt therapeutic techniques to complete the interview in these special cases.
<H3>Hearing Impairment

One in three adults older than 70 years has some type of hearing loss (). If a patient has a new or undiagnosed hearing loss, ask, “Please repeat what I said.” For patients using hearing aids, make sure that such devices are turned on and working. Gently touch or use visual signals with a hearing-impaired patient before speaking to them to verify that the patient is paying attention. Closing the door may help to limit background noise.

Many deaf patients communicate through a combination of methods, such as signing, writing, using speech, and moving the lips. They may sign with larger, quicker, and more forceful motions when expressing urgency, fear, or frustration. To facilitate lip reading, sit closer to the patient. Use regular speech volume and lip movement but speak more slowly. If the patient does not understand, use different wording because the sounds involved may be better understood.
<H3>Low Level of Consciousness

Patients with a low level of consciousness may be unable to communicate to provide answers to interview questions. In such cases, rely on secondary data sources and previous documentation. Physical examination and circumstances surrounding the reduced level of consciousness assume more importance until a complete history is collected.
<H3>Cognitive Impairment

Patients with dementia often have word-finding difficulties. As dementia increases, soundalike words and sounds make conversation difficult to track. Allow patients time to process as much as possible to avoid a one-sided conversation. Because it is easy to discount the communication as disordered or unreliable, many patients with dementia have unmet needs. Pain, hunger, thirst, and other basic needs that remain unaddressed may produce behaviors that others interpret as anxious or agitated. Perform assessments to help identify the source of the problem. Patients may need redirection and coaching on the organization and appropriateness of their communication.
<H3>Mental Illness

Patients with mental illnesses often have difficulty attending to and sequencing communication. Observe such patients for behaviors that indicate distraction, such as looking around the room or appearing to hear noises. Patients with mental illness may process communication better if it contains clear, short phrases that require one step in thinking rather than complex directions. Restatement, reflection, or focusing to redirect conversation to the health topic being assessed may be helpful.
<H3>Anxiety

Healthcare issues can cause great anxiety, which is an expected response to a threat to well-being. Behaviors that indicate anxiety are nail-biting, foot-tapping, sweating, and pacing. Voice may quiver, speech may be rapid, and language or tone may be defensive. These behaviors are an attempt to relieve anxious feelings. A mild level of anxiety heightens awareness of the surroundings and fosters learning and decision making. High levels of anxiety decrease perceptual ability and can progress to panic and immobilizing behavior. Active listening, honesty, and a calm and unhurried manner can be used to reduce anxiety. If anxiety is severe, teach the patient breathing and relaxation exercises, use therapeutic touch, and provide structure so that the patient knows that they will remain safe.
<H3>Crying

Health issues are sensitive; they sometimes pose sad situations for both patients and the nurse. When sensitive issues arise, use therapeutic communication techniques rather than progressing with additional interview questions. If  a patient is sad, say, “You look sad when talking about your prognosis,” to show empathy for the patient. Provide support through silence, acknowledging feelings, or offering a tissue (Fig. 2.7). Avoid giving false reassurance. Crying is therapeutic, and patients usually feel better after having a chance to express the associated emotions. Grief is an expected part of illness; it is therapeutic to express feelings of grief. At times, the nurse also feels emotional; in this case, it is acceptable to tear up. However, sobbing or frank expression of emotion by the nurse is not therapeutic.
<H3>Anger

When patients are angry, listen for the associated themes and avoid becoming defensive or personalizing the situation. It is common to feel bad but usually anger from a patient does not directly relate to the provider. Such emotion is usually a response to a situation in which the patient has lost control and feels anxious or helpless. Acknowledge the patient’s feelings by saying, “I understand that you are upset about being asked this question another time” or “I’m sorry that you’re so angry.” The nurse validates and encourages patients to express their feelings. The purpose of talking the emotion through is to help patients connect their emotions with related events.
<H3>Use of Alcohol, Drugs, or Mind-Altering Substances

Patients with chemical impairment have difficulty answering complex questions. Use direct and simple questions instead. Interview questions include the type of substance, amount ingested, and date and time of the last use. Explain that this information is important to provide accurate data regarding withdrawal. Patients who have used substances may provide an unreliable history with a story that changes over time. Be aware that memory may be impaired, and that substance use and withdrawal can cause confusion. As with patients who have reduced consciousness,  rely more on the circumstances and physical assessment data with patients who have substance use disorders. As the patient becomes sober and family members are available, discuss details about length of use, pattern of use, and related injuries or illnesses.
<H3>Personal Questions and Boundaries

When interviewing patients,  ask questions within the nursing role. Some patients do not understand the boundaries that define the nurse–patient relationship and instead may ask personal questions. In this situation, it can be difficult to know how much (if anything) to disclose. Briefly provide a response or choose simply to redirect the conversation, keeping it patient centered. For example,, “My husband is a welder. Tell me more about the occupational hazards that you have,” or simply, “I would rather talk about the occupational hazards in your workplace.”
<H3>Sexual Aggression

Sexual aggression includes inappropriate jokes, flirtatious comments, sexual suggestions, or sexual advances. Patients with low self-esteem may flaunt their sexual prowess to increase feelings of self-worth. Listen for these themes to understand why the patient is acting this way and, most importantly, set limits on these behaviors. Although these behaviors may provoke shock, embarrassment, or anger, confront sexual innuendos and make clear that such behavior is not acceptable. For example, “It makes me very uncomfortable when you make that type of joke. I would prefer that we talk about other things,” or “Yes, I have a boyfriend. Tell me more about your support systems.” If aggression is physical, it may be necessary to set limits, such as, “If you touch me there again, I will need to leave the room.”

<CJC-SUBTTL>Interprofessional Collaboration With Home Healthcare: What Can I Do?
<CJC-TTL2>Next Generation NCLEX Style Question
In many facilities, nurses initiate referrals for home care based on assessment findings. Requirements needed for home care services include the following:
•	The patient must be willing to participate in the plan of care, comply with the therapeutic regimen, and agree to work cooperatively at home.
•	If the patient requires shift care, there needs to be a family member or a trained and competent caregiver to assume care in the event the agency is unable to staff a shift.
•	Physical facilities and resources in the patient’s home must be adequate for proper and safe care.
•	The patient/family member agrees to keep privately owned medical and emergency equipment appropriately calibrated and maintained for safe and accurate delivery of nursing care.
•	There must be a plan to meet medical emergencies.
•	There is no duplication of services.

With Mr. Rowan, there are some concerns that his home is inadequate for proper and safe care. Further collaboration with Mr. Rowan is needed, including exploring his willingness to accept home health support. The following conversation illustrates how the nurse organizes the data and makes recommendations about Mr. Rowan’s situation.
SITUATION: “I’m Tom Fritz, a student who is working with the care team. They are listening in to the conversation and will help me share important information with you.”

BACKGROUND: “I am calling about Mr. Phil Rowan, a 56-year-old White man who is living in an assisted living facility. He was diagnosed with AIDS 2 years ago. His vital signs are normal, and he has been receiving meals and housekeeping as part of his services. The nurse has had ongoing contact with him to encourage him to take his medications and to assess his condition and needs. He has not been taking his antiretroviral medication regimen. He appears disheveled, depressed, and is feeling weak. His home is cluttered, and dressing and grooming are impaired.”
ANALYSIS: “We are becoming increasingly concerned about his safety and medication management, because he has further disease progression.”

RECOMMENDATIONS: “We want to continue with meal and housekeeping services and assess his medication regimen. We are considering increasing level of care to include daily hygiene, meal preparation, and housekeeping. When can you come to evaluate his need for shift care and increased support?”

<KP1>Key Points: You’ve Got This!
• 	Active listening, restatement, reflection, elaboration, silence, focusing, clarification, and summarizing are techniques to facilitate therapeutic communication.
• 	Nontherapeutic responses include false reassurance, sympathy, unwanted advice, leading or biased questions, changes of subject, distractions, too many technical terms, and talking too much.
• 	Nonverbal communication should be congruent with verbal communication.
• 	The phases of the interview process include the pre-interaction phase, beginning phase, working phase, and closing phase.
• 	Intercultural communication requires sensitivity to and knowledge of specific cultures, including language challenges, health beliefs, and gender issues.
• 	Assessment of newborns, infants, children, and the older adult includes the care provider and their relationship to the patient.
• 	Communication challenges include hearing impairment, decreased level of consciousness, cognitive impairment, anxiety, crying, anger, alcohol/drug use, personal boundaries, and sexual aggression.
• 	Nurses collect primary data from patients. They collect secondary data from other sources such as the chart or family members of the patient.

• 	An emergency assessment occurs when the patient’s condition is unstable; a focused assessment is narrower and more specific to the presenting problem; a comprehensive assessment covers all body systems for screening and health promotion.

• 	Components of the comprehensive health history include the reason for seeking care, history of present illness, past health history, current medications and indications, family history, functional health assessment, growth and development, and ROS.
• 	The history of present illness includes assessment of location, intensity, duration, description, aggravating and alleviating factors, functional impairment, and pain goal.
• 	A complete family history uses a genogram to illustrate family patterns.
• 	The functional health assessment includes health perception, nutrition, elimination, activity, sleep, cognition, self-perception, roles, sexuality, coping, and values.
• 	Nurses assess ADLs by asking about feeding, bathing, toileting, dressing, grooming, mobility, home maintenance, shopping, and cooking.

• 	A complete ROS assesses the history of all body systems, including nutrition/hydration, skin/hair/nails, head/neck, eyes/ears, heart, peripheral, vascular, breasts, abdominal, musculoskeletal, neurologic, genitalia, rectum, and endocrine/hematologic.
• 	Teaching is provided to promote health and reduce risk of disease.

<CST>STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
<H1>SAFETY PRECAUTIONS TO PREVENT INFECTION

During assessment, direct physical contact with the patient is expected. Thus, it is essential to follow infection control principles, including the current standard precautions, which include diligent hand hygiene (Fig. 3.1) and use of gloves and masks.

Healthcare environments contain many organisms that pose threats, especially for patients who are immunocompromised, those who have recently undergone surgery, and those who have indwelling medical devices (e.g., urinary catheters, endotracheal tubes, intravenous [IV] lines). Multidrug-resistant organisms, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), and other Gram-negative bacilli are common. Treatment of such pathogens is becoming increasingly difficult.  Take special measures to prevent the spread of infection before, after, and while conducting assessments.
<H2>Standard Precautions and Transmission-Based Precautions

The presence of disease-resistant organisms, emerging infectious diseases, and contagious coronavirus infections necessitate safety protocols. The following standard precautions (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2024b) are recommended for use in hospital settings:
• 	Perform hand hygiene.
• 	Use personal protective equipment (PPE) whenever there is an expectation of possible exposure to infectious material.
• 	Properly handle and properly clean and disinfect patient care equipment and instruments/devices.
• 	Handle textiles and laundry carefully.
• 	Ensure safety, including proper handling of needles and other sharps.
• 	Follow transmission-based precautions such as source control, social distancing, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette principles, and ensuring appropriate patient placement.

With standard precautions, all waste and contact are treated as potentially infectious. Use standard precautions with all patients to reduce the transmission of pathogens in both diagnosed and unknown infections. The intention of standard precautions is to prevent disease transmission during contact with nonintact skin, mucous membranes, body substances, and blood-borne contacts (e.g., needlestick injury). Because many patients are unaware of being infected, standard precautions help ensure that healthcare providers treat all patients equally.
See Box 3.1 for examples of healthcare work tasks with their accompanying exposure risk levels.
<H3>Hand Hygiene
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

The single most important action to prevent an infection is hand hygiene. Contact transmission from the hands of healthcare providers to patients is the most common mode of transmission because microorganisms from one patient are then spread to others (CDC, 2024b).
</BX2-SA>
Hand hygiene is implemented at specific occurrences for maximum effectiveness. Occurrences are as follows:
• 	Immediately before touching a patient
• 	Before performing an aseptic task (e.g., placing an indwelling device) or handling invasive medical devices
• 	Before moving from work on a soiled body site to a clean body site on the same patient
• 	After touching a patient or the patient’s immediate environment
• 	After contact with blood, body fluids, or contaminated surfaces
• 	Immediately after glove removal
Use of alcohol-based hand rubs is appropriate in the above situations. When using alcohol-based hand sanitizer:
• 	Put product on hands and rub hands together.
• 	Cover all surfaces until hands feel dry.
• 	This should take around 20 seconds.
Handwashing with soap and water is necessary:
• 	When hands are visibly soiled with blood or body fluids
• 	After caring for a person with known or suspected infectious diarrhea
• 	After known or suspected exposure to spores (e.g., Bacillus anthracis, Clostridium difficile outbreaks)
When washing hands with soap and water:

• 	Wet hands first with water, apply the amount of product recommended by the manufacturer to hands, and rub together vigorously for at least 15 seconds, covering all surfaces of the hands and fingers.
• 	Rinse hands with water and use disposable towels to dry. Use towel to turn off the faucet.
• 	Avoid using hot water, to prevent drying of skin.

Nails are trimmed to one-quarter of an inch or shorter. Artificial nails are not worn because they harbor bacteria. Polish is removed prior to going into the clinical setting. Open areas are covered with an adhesive bandage or protective barrier.
<H4>Skin Reactions

Nurses have a higher rate of skin reactions than the general population because of the higher frequency of hand hygiene. To minimize the adverse effects of hand hygiene and decrease transmission of pathogens, use alcohol-based rubs as the preferred method of hand hygiene to reduce the prevalence of hand eczema that can be caused by the use of soap and water.
<H3>Personal Protective Equipment

When selecting PPE, consider three things. First is the type of anticipated exposure, such as touch, splashes or sprays, or large volumes of blood or body fluids that might penetrate the clothing (CDC, 2024c). Second is the durability and appropriateness of the PPE for the task. Third is fit; PPE must properly fit the individual user. It is up to the employer to ensure that all PPE are available in appropriate sizes (CDC, 2024c).
There are four key points to remember about PPE use:
• 	First, put it on before any contact with the patient, generally before entering the room.
• 	Once the PPE is on, use it carefully to prevent contamination.
• 	When the task is completed, remove the PPE carefully and discard it in the receptacles provided.
• 	Immediately perform hand hygiene before going on to the next patient.
<H4>Gloves

The CDC (2024b) recommends that healthcare providers wear gloves (1) to reduce the risk of acquiring infections from patients; (2) to prevent the transmission of flora from healthcare workers to patients; and (3) to reduce transient contamination of the hands of personnel by flora that can be transmitted from one patient to another.

Wear gloves when touching blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, and contaminated items. Put on clean gloves just before touching the mucous membranes and nonintact skin of patients. Wear gloves when general contact with any “wet” body secretion is anticipated. For example, it is not necessary to wear gloves when taking an oral temperature, because only the thermometer cover contacts the patient’s oral secretions. However, wear gloves while assessing the back of a patient who has urinary incontinence to avoid potential contact with any urine that may be present. Wear gloves for personal protection and to avoid spreading organisms to other patients or from one body area to another.
<H5>When to Change Gloves
Change gloves in the following circumstances:
• 	Between tasks and procedures on the same patient after contact with a material that contains a high concentration of microorganisms (such as dressing changes or tracheostomy care).
• 	When going from a contaminated to a cleaner area.
<H5>Glove Removal

Remove gloves promptly after use, before touching noncontaminated items and environmental surfaces, and before going to another patient. Remove gloves before touching the computer, supply drawers, and equipment. Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal to avoid transfer of microorganisms to other patients and environments.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

Gloves are never worn from the room out into the hallway, to decrease the risk of carrying microbes from a “dirty” room to a “clean” area or from an infected patient to another person. Gloves are removed when going from the bedside to the computer. The computer is mobile. If gloves touch an infected patient, especially when soiled, and the computer moves into the hall and into another patient’s room. The infection is carried to another patient’s room.
</BX-SA>
<H5>Latex Allergy

Latex allergy usually results from repeated exposures to proteins in natural rubber latex through skin contact or inhalation. Reactions usually begin within minutes of exposure to latex, but they can occur hours later. Nurses and other healthcare workers are more likely to have latex allergy than the general population (8% to 12% among healthcare workers vs. 1% in the general population) (Occupational Safety and Health Administration [OSHA], n.d.).
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

Patients can develop an allergy to latex at any time, especially those who are frequently admitted to the hospital. Reactions may range from a mild rash to overwhelming anaphylaxis and death. Emergency measures must be available for persons with severe reactions.
</BX2-SA>

The best preventive action is to avoid contact with latex whenever possible. Healthcare facilities can establish latex-free zones for patients and staff. Take care to avoid carrying any latex substances into such zones, including stethoscopes, urinary catheters, and vials with rubber stoppers. To avoid increasing exposure to latex (which can increase allergy rates), institutions are encouraged to use powder-free, low-allergen gloves and latex-free equipment such as catheters and IV tubing.
<H4>Respiratory Precautions and Hygiene

The first step for respiratory hygiene is to wear masks and practice social distancing, both of which create a more hygienic environment. It is important for people to turn their head and cover their mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing, even when masked. Patients are taught to dispose of tissues directly into receptacles and perform hand hygiene after hands have been in contact with respiratory secretions. If a tissue is not available, cough etiquette encourages turning the head and coughing into the inner aspect of the elbow (CDC, 2024b).
<H5>Masks and Respirators

Masks and respirators provide different levels of protection depending on the type of mask and how it is used. Loosely worn woven cloth products (e.g., bandanas) provide the least protection. Layered finely woven products offer more protection. Well-fitting disposable surgical masks and KN95 masks offer even more protection. Well-fitting National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) approved respirators (including N95s for hospital use) offer the highest level of protection.

Whatever product is used it should fit well. This means it seals closely on the face (without any gaps along the edges or around the nose) and is comfortable enough when worn properly to keep it on when needed. Masks fully cover the nose and mouth, have a flexible nose piece, and are secured to the head with string ties or elastic (CDC, 2024c).
<H5>Physical Distancing

Healthcare delivery requires close physical contact between patients and providers. When possible, physical distancing (maintaining at least 6 feet between people) and masking are important to prevent disease transmission. Be aware that transmission can occur through unprotected exposures to asymptomatic or presymptomatic coworkers in breakrooms or via coworkers or visitors in other common areas (CDC, 2024a). Some strategies for physical distancing include:
• 	Limit visitors to the facility to those essential for healthcare.
• 	Encourage use of alternative mechanisms for interactions, such as cell phones or tablets.
• 	Schedule appointments to limit the number of patients in waiting rooms, or have patients wait outside or in their vehicle.
• 	Arrange seating in waiting rooms so patients can sit at least 6 feet apart.
• 	Modify in-person group healthcare activities (such as group counseling or group education) by implementing virtual methods when appropriate.
• 	Place a patient who contaminates the environment or who does not (or cannot be expected to) assist in maintaining appropriate hygiene or environmental control in a private room.
<H4>Eye Protection

Eye protection is recommended in areas with moderate to substantial community exposure. For areas with minimal to no community transmission, eye protection is considered optional, unless otherwise indicated as part of standard precautions. Additionally, take special precautions when working in very high versus lower risk settings and tasks (OSHA, 2021a).

Goggles provide barrier protection for the eyes (Fig. 3.2A). Goggles must fit snugly over and around the eyes or personal prescription lenses. Goggles with antifog features help to maintain clarity of vision (CDC, 2024c). Personal prescription lenses do not provide optimal eye protection and should not be used as a substitute for goggles. However, plastic covers for the sides of prescription eyeglasses may provide another option for barrier protection (CDC, 2024c).
<H5>Face Shields

When skin protection is needed or desired (in addition to mouth, nose, and eye protection), a face shield is used (Fig. 3.2B). A shield may be needed when irrigating a wound or suctioning oral or respiratory secretions. The face shield covers the forehead, extends below the chin, and wraps around the side of the face (CDC, 2024c).
<H4>Gowns

Consider how durable the body protection needs to be for the task; this will affect if a gown or apron is selected for PPE. A gown is a more durable option. If a gown is selected, decide whether fluid resistant, fluid proof, or neither is necessary.
<H4>Source Control

The six links in the chain of infection are the infectious agent, the reservoir, the portal of exit, the mode of transmission, the portal of entry, and the susceptible host. Three things are necessary for an infection to occur: places where pathogens survive (e.g., sinks, surfaces, person), transfer of pathogens, and a susceptible person with an entry for pathogens to enter the body. Infection is through contact, splash, inhalation, and sharps injuries.

• 	Contact moves pathogens by touch (MRSA or VRE). Hands become contaminated by touching pathogens present on medical equipment or patients. With poor hand hygiene, the pathogen is carried on the hands and spreads to a susceptible person.

• 	Sprays and splashes occur when an infected person coughs or sneezes, creating droplets that carry pathogens short distances (within approximately 6 feet). They also occur during wound care and surgical procedures.

• 	Inhalation occurs when germs are aerosolized in tiny particles that survive on air currents over distances. Airborne transmission can occur when infected patients cough, talk, or sneeze germs into the air, and when pathogens are aerosolized by medical equipment such as during suctioning.
• 	Sharps injuries can lead to infections (HIV, hepatitis) when bloodborne pathogens enter a person through a skin puncture by a used needle or other sharp instrument.

The safest practice is for everyone in a healthcare setting to wear source control. Source control includes the use of well-fitting cloth masks, face masks, or respirators to cover a person’s mouth and nose to prevent spread of respiratory secretions. Because of the potential for patient-to-patient transmission of pathogens, source control measures are recommended for everyone in a healthcare facility, even if they do not have symptoms. Educate others about the importance of performing hand hygiene, including immediately before and after any contact with their mask, shield, or respirator (CDC, 2024b).
<H4>Transmission-Based Precautions

The CDC developed transmission-based precautions for airborne, droplet, and contact routes of transmission (CDC, 2024d). Healthcare providers combine the use of these specific precautions with standard precautions. The general guideline is for healthcare providers to wear PPE whenever they are at risk for contacting body secretions from patients. Refer to Box 3.2 for a summary of transmission-based precautions.
