<H1>BASIC AND ADVANCED TECHNIQUES

The four techniques of inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation form the basis of physical assessment. Inspection is observation of the patient including general appearance. Specific inspection data are collected related to each body system. Palpation involves use of the hands to feel the firmness of body parts, such as the abdomen. Percussion—tapping motions of the nurse’s hands on the patient’s body—is used to produce sounds that indicate solid or air-filled spaces over the lungs and other areas. The stethoscope is a tool to perform auscultation, in which movements of air or fluid are heard over the lungs, heart, and abdomen.
<BX1-CS>
<BX1-H1>CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE

When doing an assessment, be prepared to follow up if findings are abnormal. Always use appropriate safety techniques. Use the correct order of assessment: inspect, palpate, percuss, and auscultate. An exception to the order is for the abdomen: inspect, then auscultate, percuss, and lastly palpate. Palpation is last as pressing the abdomen can stimulate the bowel and alter the findings.
</BX1-CS>
<H2>Inspection

The purpose of gathering data during this initial phase is to gain an overall impression of the patient and to assess the severity of the situation. Inspection is the first technique of both the overall general survey--and for each body part. The overall observation, called the general survey, is intentional and deliberate. First, perform a visual inspection by consciously observing the patient for physical characteristics and behaviors. Observe the patient for overall characteristics, including age, gender, level of alertness, body size and shape, skin color, hygiene, posture, and level of discomfort or anxiety. Listen for sounds such as wheezing. Use smell to observe for unusual odors. With experience, gathering data from inspection becomes automatic. Sight, hearing, and smell are used.

Following the general survey, proceed to assess specific body areas and systems. During focused inspection, expose each body part as necessary. Take measures to maintain the comfort and privacy of the patient through appropriate draping, especially over the breasts for females and genitalia for all patients (Fig. 3.3). Adequate lighting is essential to observe color, texture, and mobility. Inform patients of the need to look at the body part along with the rationale. Ask patients for permission before doing so, especially when assessments involve compromising the patient’s modesty. For example, “I need to look at your mastectomy incision to see how it is healing. May I lift your gown?”

Sometimes devices limit visibility, such as a splint over a knee. When possible, loosen or remove such devices to adequately observe the skin for any red, inflamed, or infected areas and to determine adequate circulation. For example, when inspecting the abdomen, note the shape (whether it is flat or distended), size, skin color, texture, and any bruising, veins, or prominent movements. A common technique is to consider overall shape first and then compare the two sides for symmetry.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

Be aware that some devices are placed to limit mobility, such as a brace for the back or neck. It is important to become familiar with guidelines for safe care and to have additional staff available to assist with splinting. If such devices are improperly released, damage to the nerve, muscle, or vasculature may occur.
</BX2-SA>

In addition to using the correct inspection techniques for each body system, it is important to label and document findings appropriately. It takes practice to identify details and subtle differences. Accurate medical terminology is essential for legal communication of findings. Each technique is followed by accurate documentation.

Pay attention to individual details. Note whether verbal, nonverbal, and inspection data match, and then identify any preliminary patterns or clusters. If the patient appears anxious, note facial expression, nervous gestures, body position or pacing, and voice characteristics. Inspection provides objective physical data leading to accurate diagnoses and treatment and allows for inclusion of the emotional state of the patient.
<H2>Palpation

Palpation is the use of touch to assess texture, temperature, moisture, size, shape, location, position, vibration, crepitus, tenderness, pain, and edema. Before performing this technique, inform the patient of the need to palpate the body part, along with the rationale, and ask for permission or consent to touch. For example, during abdominal assessment, say, “I know that you’re having some abdominal pain, but I would like to gently feel your abdomen to see if it is sensitive. Would that be okay with you?” Begin with a gentle and slow technique while inspecting the patient’s face for nonverbal indicators of discomfort, such as a furrowed brow or grimace.

Use different parts of the hand depending on the data that you are gathering. The fingers are best for some techniques, whereas the palms are best for others. Use finger pads for fine discrimination because they are the most mobile parts of the hand. Some examples of the need for fine discrimination include locating the pulses, lymph nodes, or small lumps and assessing for skin texture and edema.

The palmar surface of the fingers and finger joints is best for assessing firmness, contour, position, size, pain, and tenderness. The palm of the hand is best during abdominal assessment. If a patient reports being hot, use the dorsal (back) side of your hand to evaluate temperature because the skin there is thinner and more sensitive. Vibratory tremors can sometimes be felt on the chest as the patient speaks. These are best palpated with the ulnar (little finger) side of the hand.
<H3>Light Palpation

Begin with light palpation to allow the patient to become accustomed to gentle touch. If pain is present, say, “Let me know if this hurts you,” to gain trust and decrease anxiety. Avoid any tender or painful areas until the end. Ensure privacy by draping. If your hands are cold, warm them under running water or gently rub them together. Short and smooth nails are necessary to avoid causing discomfort. Palpation is difficult when patients’ muscles are tense, so use a gentle, calm, and easy touch to assist patients to relax.

Light palpation is appropriate for the assessment of surface characteristics, such as texture, surface lesions or lumps, or inflamed areas of skin (e.g., over an IV site). Place the finger pads of your dominant hand on the patient’s skin and slowly move the fingers in circular areas of approximately 1 cm in depth (about ½ in.) (Fig. 3.4). Intermittent palpation using this technique is more effective than a single continuous palpation, because the fingers sense the movement of skin and tissue beneath the finger pads. Patients may perceive this gentle light palpation as a light massage in the absence of pain. Communicate concern for patients verbally with conversation during the procedure and nonverbally through this caring touch.
<H3>Moderate Palpation

Use moderate palpation to assess the size, shape, and consistency of abdominal organs. Additionally, note any unexpected findings of pain, tenderness, or pulsations. The same gentle circular motion of light palpation is appropriate, but instead of your finger pads, use the palmar surface of the fingers. Pressure should be firm enough to depress approximately 1 to 2 cm. Observe the patient for any guarding, grimacing, or tension during moderate palpation.
<H3>Bimanual Deep Palpation
During bimanual deep palpation, place the extended fingers of your nondominant hand over the dominant hand to use the pressure of both hands. Use the same circular motion to palpate 2 to 4 cm.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT
Deep palpation should not be used over areas that pose a risk of injuring patients, such as over an enlarged spleen or inflamed appendix.
</BX2-SA>

As with other types of palpation, explain the purpose, touch gently at first, and ask about uncomfortable feelings. With deep palpation, say, “I’m going to touch you and push down more deeply than before. Let me know if you feel pain or want me to stop.” Watch the patient’s facial expressions. As palpation proceeds, continue the conversation, asking the patient about pain, presenting symptoms, or contributing factors while observing for nonverbal signs of tenderness or discomfort. As skill is gained, it becomes possible to palpate, question about symptoms, and teach all at the same time.
<H2>Percussion

The third technique of physical assessment is percussion. Percussion is used to produce sound or elicit tenderness. This is like the tapping of a drumstick on a drum. The vibrations that the fingers produce create percussion tones conducted into the patient. If the vibrations travel through dense tissue, the percussion tones are quiet or flat; if they travel through air or fluid, the tones are louder. The loudest tones are over the lungs and hollow stomach like a drum. The quietest are over bones. The two methods of percussion are direct and indirect.
<H3>Direct Percussion

For direct percussion, tap your fingers directly on the patient’s skin (Fig. 3.5). Examples include percussion of the sinuses in patients with sinus infections and percussion of the thorax in newborns to assess the air-filled lungs. Direct percussion is easier to learn than indirect percussion. Percussion that is too weak may not reveal important findings, whereas percussion that is too strong may elicit too much pain. Thus, moderate tapping is recommended.
<H3>Indirect Percussion

Rather than directly striking a patient, use your nondominant hand as a barrier between the dominant hand and the patient. This is known as indirect percussion. Place your nondominant palm on the patient and initiate a quick, moderately strong tap with the dominant hand. Use the ulnar surface of the fist to indirectly percuss the kidneys. As with direct percussion, practice until a comfortable strength is found.

The most common, and the most difficult sounds to elicit, are the indirect sounds. These are best differentiated by moving from area to area and listening to the changes in volume and pitch. It is easier to hear the difference from resonant to dull. Thus, when learning indirect percussion, it is easiest to go from the center of the abdomen with tympany (drum like) and move upward to the liver where dullness is percussed.

Indirect percussion requires coordination of both hands. Place your hyperextended middle finger of the nondominant hand firmly over the area to be percussed. Lift the other fingers on that hand from the patient and spread them slightly to avoid contact with the patient, which can dampen the sound of the striking finger. Then position the slightly flexed middle finger of the dominant hand approximately 2 to 3 cm (about 1 inch.) above the distal interphalangeal joint in contact with the patient. Using only the wrist of the dominant hand, raise the dominant finger 4 to 5 cm (about 2 inches) and quickly strike and raise your nondominant joint twice while listening for the elicited sound (Fig. 3.6). Then move the nondominant hand and strike twice in a new area.

First, practice to elicit a sound loud enough to hear. Practice on yourself until the sound is loud. The abdomen is a good place to start. Then, after getting the loud sound, listen carefully and compare sounds between body parts to identify dull, flat, or tympany differences. Some helpful hints when learning percussion are as follows:

• 	Most of your nondominant finger is touching the patient; otherwise, the sound transmission will be decreased. If only a little is touching, the sound will not have enough contact to make a sound; if too much of the hand is touching, the sound will be dampened and dull.

• 	The motion of your striking finger is quick, forceful, and snappy. The snapping finger must be brisk for a loud sound. The downward motion of the striking hand is from the wrist, not the finger, elbow, or arm.

• 	Because  the tip of your finger is used, nails are short and smooth. This is to avoid causing discomfort to the patient and to facilitate good contact. Using the pad of the finger dampens the sound. Use the tip.

• 	Position your striking finger at a 90-degree angle to the patient’s skin, to penetrate deeply rather than glance off the surface. While learning, begin by getting the two hands and fingers into position first, and then focus on the brisk motion.
• 	To avoid dampening the sound, immediately withdraw your snapping finger once the nondominant finger is struck. Make sure to strike the bony knuckle to get good conduction.
• 	Nurses with small hands and fingers need to strike more forcefully nurses with large hands.
<H3>Percussion Sounds
There are four different percussion tones in the body: flat, dull, resonant, and tympanic. In addition to intensity or loudness, listen to the pitch, duration, and quality of sound.

Intensity or loudness refers to how soft or loud the sound is. The louder the sound, the louder the intensity and the easier it is to hear. If air fills the structure, there is more ability to vibrate, and the sound is louder.

Pitch or frequency depends on how quickly the vibration oscillates. It is like music: if the frequency of the sound is fast, the pitch is high; if it is slow, the pitch is low. Both the lungs and the hollow stomach are loud. The lungs are low pitched, and the stomach is high pitched. See Table 3.1 for a list of percussion tones and their characteristics. Practice in all areas on others to see if these subtle differences can be identified. Each area of the body has a different medical label. It is important to learn these terms to properly document what is heard.
<H2>Auscultation

During auscultation, listen for sounds of movement from organs and tissues. A stethoscope is used to transmit normally unheard sounds. Auscultation requires a quiet environment with minimal to no distractions.

Common assessments involving auscultation include BP, lungs, heart, and abdomen. The BP produces sounds that correlate with the bounding of the pulse. Soft and rustling sounds in the lungs are from air moving in and out with each breath. The heart produces the typical “lub–dub” with the snapping closure of the heart valves. Peristalsis in the abdomen produces typical gurgling or growling sounds.

As with percussion, each area of the body has a different medical label. Sounds are described according to intensity, pitch, duration, and quality (Table 3.2). It is important to learn these terms to properly document and communicate what is heard.
<H3>The Stethoscope

The stethoscope conducts sound from the patient’s body to the listener and blocks environmental noise to more clearly pinpoint the patient’s body sounds. It does not amplify sounds—it only conducts them--so listen carefully to the minor differences between sounds that are often very soft.

The stethoscope includes the ear tips, earpiece, flexible tubing, and chestpiece with diaphragm and bell. To be effective, the ear tips must fit into the ear canal snugly but comfortably. Ear tips come in different sizes and firmness, so choose the type that works best depending on personal ear shape and size.

Earpieces are tilted slightly forward so that the angle on the earpiece is forward in the same direction as the nose (Fig. 3.7). This positioning directs the sound toward the tympanic membrane. It is difficult to hear if placed in the ear canal backward.

Tubing is thick to block environmental noise and short (55 to 69 cm [about 21 to 27 in.]) to increase transmission and reduce distortion of sound. Most stethoscopes have a diaphragm and bell on the chestpiece (Fig. 3.8A).

One type of stethoscope chestpiece swivels back and forth between the diaphragm and the bell. When the chestpiece is turned to the bell, the diaphragm does not conduct sound. Likewise, when the chestpiece is turned to the diaphragm, the bell does not conduct. Place the earpieces in the ears and gently touch the bell or diaphragm before auscultating to ascertain whether the chestpiece is turned toward the bell or diaphragm (Fig. 3.8B). Make sure to practice turning the chestpiece back and forth.

Other stethoscopes have only a diaphragm that changes between bell and diaphragm modes with pressure changes on the chestpiece. Use light contact to hear low-frequency sounds (like the bell) and press firmly for high-frequency sounds (like the diaphragm). The diaphragm is typically used for most sounds, such as lung and heart sounds, although the bell works best for detecting low-pitched heart murmurs. For this reason, heart sounds are usually auscultated with both the diaphragm and the bell.
Make sure to disinfect the stethoscope between patients to avoid spreading pathogens (Peacock, W.F., 2024). Patients in isolation will have their own stethoscopes.

Place the stethoscope directly on the patient’s skin so that complete contact with the skin surface is made. If there is a gap, which is common when measuring BP in the antecubital fossa, room noise is conducted, and the BP sounds are more difficult to hear. Have the patient straighten the arm to optimize contact.

Avoid listening to sounds over clothing. Make sure to listen to lung sounds directly on the skin under the clothes, because clothes make sounds that can sound abnormal. Listening to heart sounds over clothing dampens them and makes it difficult to hear extra sounds or murmurs.

When holding the chestpiece, place the endpiece between the index and the middle fingers, not on top of the stethoscope, which distorts the sound. Position the stethoscope such that tubing is away from objects that might brush against it, which produce extra noises that make it difficult to hear underlying body sounds. If the patient has a large amount of hair on the chest, it may be helpful to moisten the hair to avoid the crackly noises caused when the hair rubs against the stethoscope.
<H2>Advanced Techniques and Special Equipment

Some physical assessment techniques require special equipment. Examples include the ophthalmoscope, visual acuity chart, otoscope, tuning fork, reflex hammer, vaginal speculum, goniometer, and skinfold calipers.
<H3>Ophthalmoscope

The ophthalmoscope is a handheld system of lenses, lights, and mirrors that enables visualization of the interior structures of the eye (Fig. 3.9). The head of the ophthalmoscope attaches to the base, which is both a place to hold on to the ophthalmoscope and a power source with a rechargeable battery. The head contains the system of lights, lenses, and mirrors. When not in use, the base is plugged in for charging, while the head is stored to avoid damage.

Attach the head to the base by fitting the adapter of the base into the head and pushing down while turning the head clockwise. Turn on the ophthalmoscope by depressing the on/off switch. For routine use, the aperture commonly selected is the large full spot. Other choices include a small light spot for small pupils, a green light to filter out red, a grid used to locate structures and lesions, and a slit used to determine the shape of lesions.

Hold the ophthalmoscope firmly against your face, so that the eye looks directly through the viewing aperture. Both of your eyes must stay open, but the focus is on the view through the aperture. The lens selector dial focuses the ophthalmoscope, like binoculars. The black numbers (power of +20 to +140) focus on near objects, whereas the red numbers (power of −20 to −140) focus on objects far away. In this way, the ophthalmoscope adjusts for nearsightedness (myopia) or farsightedness (hyperopia). It does not, however, accommodate for astigmatism.

Darken the room to help dilate the patient’s pupils because the eye is visualized through the pupil. Eyeglasses obstruct visualization, so remove them from both yourself and the patient. When examining the right eye, grasp the ophthalmoscope with your right hand and use your right eye. When examining the left eye, use your left hand and left eye. This helps avoid bumping noses with the patient. Starting with zero, adjust the lenses using the index finger to bring the fundus (background) of the patient’s eye into focus. Moving the lens selector dial clockwise turns the magnification more positive, or closer, whereas moving the lens selector dial counterclockwise turns the magnification more negative, or further away.

Ask the patient to look at a distant fixation point while pointing the light of the ophthalmoscope into the pupil from approximately 25 to 30 cm (about 10 to 12 in.) away and slightly lateral to the patient’s line of vision. Visualization of the red reflex is the first step in examination of the eye.
<H3>Otoscope
The otoscope directs light into the ear to visualize the ear canal and tympanic membrane. The otoscope’s head and body connect and are activated in the same way as with the ophthalmoscope.

Select the proper-sized speculum, choosing the largest size that fits most comfortably into the patient’s ear, and place it on the otoscope. Hold the otoscope’s base between the thumb and the fingers upside down.
<BX2-SA>
<BX2-H1>SAFETY ALERT

Brace the ulnar surface or fingers of the hand against the patient’s cheek. This positioning allows you to move with the patient if the patient moves unexpectedly, as might happen with a child who has ear tenderness related to an infection.
</BX2-SA>

While inserting the speculum, straighten the adult patient’s ear canal by gently pulling the auricle up, back, and slightly away from the head (Fig. 3.10A). Insert the speculum gently into the ear canal, directing it slightly down and forward. Ask the patient to tilt the head toward the opposite shoulder to assist with visualization. With pediatric patients, pull the auricle down and back to straighten the ear canal; it may be easier to do this closer to the ear lobe (Fig. 3.10B).
<H3>Tuning Fork

The tuning fork is used in examinations of two anatomic regions: during a neuromuscular assessment, to determine vibration sense, and during assessment of hearing, to determine conductive versus sensorineural hearing loss. Depending on the design, tuning forks create vibrations that produce sound waves of low-pitched or high-pitched frequencies.

The tuning fork used to check for hearing loss produces a high-pitched tone of 512 to 1,024 Hz, within the range of human hearing (Fig. 3.11). While holding the fork at the base, activate it by briskly squeezing and stroking the outside of the tongs from base to tips or gently tapping the tongs against the knuckles to produce a soft ringing sound. Avoid touching the tongs once you have activated them, because this dampens the sound. If the fork is struck too harshly, the sound is too loud and takes too long to quiet to test the fine threshold of normal hearing. Gentle strokes or taps produce a softer sound for testing.

The tuning fork for determining vibration sense produces vibrations at a lower frequency of 128 to 256 Hz. Activate this lower pitched device by tapping it against the heel of the hand. Hold this fork at the base and apply the base to a bony prominence. The patient should feel a buzzing or tingling sensation.
<H3>Reflex Hammer

The neurologic reflex hammer is designed to test neurologic responses of the deep tendons to assess for abnormalities of the central or peripheral nervous system. The most common uses during the physical examination include assessment of the knee, ankle, brachial, elbow, and wrist tendons. There are several different types of reflex hammers. The Taylor hammer is most common. It has a triangular rubber mallet attached to a metal handle. The pointed end of the hammerhead is generally used on the upper body, whereas the flat end is used on the lower body. The hammer is gently swung using the wrist, in arc-like fashion, to strike the tendon.
<BX1-CS>
<BX1-H1>CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE

<BX1-TXT-FIRST>Hold the rounded part of the handle loosely with your dominant hand and allow it to swing between the fingers, causing a brisk tap over the tendon. Practice the technique on yourself or a partner to gain expertise.
</BX1-CS>

It may be more comfortable for the patient if the index finger of your nondominant hand is placed over the patient’s tendon before striking.  Use this technique when checking the smaller tendons of the wrist, ankle, and arm. Tap midway between the tip and second joint of your index finger, buffering the impact to the tendon. Responses are recorded as hypoactive, hyperactive, or normoactive.
<H1>EQUIPMENT FOR A COMPLETE PHYSICAL ASSESSMENT

Gather all equipment needed for the physical assessment before entering the room to avoid interruption and to increase the patient’s trust. Appropriate equipment depends on the type of examination. For example, if a patient has an appointment for a full physical assessment and Pap smear, lay out all the materials necessary for a complete physical assessment (Box 3.3), in addition to a speculum, gloves, material for cytology slide, lubricant, and fecal occult blood test materials. The vaginal, prostate, and rectal examinations are covered in the appropriate chapters.

For the general assessment in a hospital setting, the following equipment is needed: vital signs equipment (thermometer, alcohol, electronic or manual BP machine, timer, stethoscope), scale, flashlight, and materials for recording findings.
<H1>OLDER ADULTS

Older adults may become chilled more easily than younger patients, so consider offering them an additional blanket or drape. Older patients may also fatigue quickly, so it is important to perform the most important assessments in the beginning. When positioning older adults, slight elevation of the head of the bed or examination table may help facilitate breathing .
<H1>CULTURAL VARIATIONS AND HEALTH DISPARITIES

Each assessment must be individualized according to the patient’s cultural, religious, and social beliefs. Many patients are anxious prior to physical assessment. Anxiety may be related to fear of disclosing private or uncomfortable information, embarrassment about being touched or looked at, or worry about unexpected findings. If there is a language barrier, arrange for a trained medical interpreter.

Before starting the examination, ask the patient about their preferences, such as having a family member in the room or having a same-gender examiner. Perform less invasive assessments first, such as taking vital signs, and save the most personal assessments for the end.

Infectious disease and infection control workers provide advice to prevent the spread of infections among patients, among staff, and between patients and staff. These include preventive measures such as handwashing, cleaning, disinfecting, sterilizing, and vaccinating. An infection control referral is advised for:
•	diagnosis difficulties
•	specialized treatment and recovery such as an antibiotic-resistant infection
•	high or unexplained fever, which can predict a serious infection
•	chronic infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and hepatitis (Bhargava, 2020).

<KP1>Key Points: You’ve Got This!
• 	Hand hygiene is the most important action to prevent nosocomial infections.
• 	Nurses and other healthcare providers use standard precautions with every patient because many patients may not be aware that they are infected.
• 	Latex allergies are more common in nurses and in patients frequently hospitalized than in the public.
• 	Nurses wear gloves during anticipated contact with body secretions and remove them when going from contaminated to cleaner areas.
• 	PPE must fit and be used properly.
• 	Source control and personal distancing are methods to protect providers and others.
• 	Inspection, percussion, palpation, and auscultation are the four techniques of physical assessment.
• 	Inspection relies on vision and smell to assess general status as well as each body system.
• 	Nurses use light palpation to obtain an overall impression and deep palpation to assess pain, masses, and tumors.
• 	Percussion sounds vary based on tone, intensity, pitch, quality, duration, and location.
• 	Nurses identify sounds during auscultation of the heart, lungs, and abdomen with a stethoscope.

• 	An ophthalmoscope, visual acuity chart, otoscope, tuning fork, reflex hammer, vaginal speculum, goniometer, and skinfold calipers are equipment for advanced techniques used during the complete assessment.

Chapter 18: Outcomes Assessment in Advanced Practice Nursing in Cancer Care
Jessica MacIntyre, Kris Mathey, Deborah H. Allen, & Susan Yackzan
<H1>CHAPTER OBJECTIVES
By the end of this chapter, readers will be able to:
1. Understand the evolving role of advanced practice nurses (APNs) in cancer care.
2. Identify key competencies and their role in improving patient outcomes.
3. Review and identify key outcomes from literature related to advanced practice nursing in cancer care.
4. Analyze the clinical, quality and financial impacts of these outcomes.
5. Identify current challenges and opportunities for growth and improvement in outcomes assessment.
<H1>INTRODUCTION

Despite advances in cancer screenings, treatments, and technology, cancer remains the leading cause of death worldwide according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (NCI, 2024). In the United States (U.S.), cancer remains the second-leading cause of death, although declines in cancer-related mortality are attributed to early detection, treatment advances and decreased smoking rates (Siegel, Kratzer, Guiquinto, Sung, & Jemal, 2025).  By 2040, the number of new cancer cases per year in the U.S. is expected to rise to 29.9 million and the number of cancer-related deaths to 15.3 million. Furthermore, the overall market demand from 2012 to 2025 for oncology services in the United States is expected to rise 40% to 83.4 million oncology visits (Yang et al., 2014). This increased demand for service coincides with a predicted shortage of more than 2,200 hematologists and oncologists available to manage cancer care (Shih, Kim, & Halpern, 2020). Looking ahead to 2037, the supply of hematologists and oncologists in the U.S. is projected to increase by 7%, while demand is expected to grow by 15% during the same period (HRSA, 2024). Moreover, the number of cancer survivors is projected to increase from 18.1 (2022) to 26 million by 2040 (Tonoerezos et al., 2024). This widening gap leads to a crisis in the diagnosis, treatment, and surveillance of cancer. Oncology advanced practice nurses (APNs) are already vital members of the oncology care team and are increasingly recognized as a solution to the future provision of expert cancer care.
<H2>OVERVIEW OF THE PROFESSION

Oncology APNs include nurse practitioners (NPs) and Clinical Nurse Specialists (CNSs). Emerging in the 1950s, the CNS role was grounded in the work of Hildegard Peplau, who emphasized the importance of expert clinical practice, education, and consultation in specialized areas of nursing (Peplau, 1952; National Association of Clinical Nurse Specialists, n.d.). Formal education programs in the 1960s further solidified the CNS as a distinct and vital role within the healthcare system. CNSs have traditionally focused on system-level improvements, clinical education, and implementation of evidence-based practice among oncology teams. They often lead initiatives aimed at improving clinical protocols, ensuring quality improvement measures, and mentoring nursing staff. Their leadership focuses on improved patient safety outcomes, reduced hospital readmissions, and increased adherence to treatment guidelines.

In 1965, the first NP program was founded by Loretta Ford, EdD, RN, PNP, NP-C, CRNP, FAAN, FAANP, and Henry Silver, M.D., at the University of Colorado in response to the shortage of primary care providers. Since then, the NP role has significantly expanded into other specialties like oncology. When combined with Physician Assistants (PA), the number of advanced practice practitioners (APPs) in oncology could be as high as 7000 (ONS, 2018). Despite their essential role, oncology NPs constitute a relatively small percentage of the total U.S. NP workforce, approximately 1.2% of the more than 234,000 licensed nurse practitioners (Bishop, 2018). However, this number continues to grow in response to the increasing complexity of cancer care and the rising number of cancer survivors. Nevertheless, oncology NPs play are uniquely positioned to fill critical gaps in care, where oncologist shortages persist, especially in creating access to oncologic care for older adults and vulnerable populations.

Oncology NPs devote the majority of their time in patient care and conduct a wide array of patient services, from new patient visits to follow-up care, as well as more specialized services ((Bruinooge et al., 2018). They provide comprehensive patient care by diagnosing conditions, prescribing cancer-directed and supportive care treatments, managing treatment and disease related side effects, and providing palliative and survivorship care. Their ability to independently assess and manage patients plays a critical role in decreasing wait times, enhancing symptom control, and improving overall patient satisfaction.

Both the CNS and NP roles are recognized for fostering strong patient-provider relationships, emphasizing patient education, and advocating for psychosocial support. These factors not only improve patients’ quality of life but also enhance treatment adherence and reduce health disparities, particularly in underserved populations. Their specialized training in oncology equips them to address the unique needs of patients with cancer, such as managing complex symptom clusters, delivering difficult news with compassion, and coordinating multidisciplinary care. Ultimately, the integration and collaboration of NPs and CNSs within oncology teams strengthens the overall healthcare system’s ability to provide comprehensive, timely, and high-quality cancer care. Together, both oncology CNSs and NPs bring distinct skills within their roles that significantly influence patient outcomes.
<H2>COMPETENCY FRAMEWORK FOR THE ADVCANCED PRACTICE ONCOLGY NURSE

The Advanced Practice Registered Nurse (APRN) Consensus Model provides the foundation for advanced practice nursing by standardizing licensure, accreditation, certification, and education across four roles and six population foci, many of which align with oncology care (NCSBN, 2008). Building on this model, oncology-specific competency frameworks guide the development and evaluation of APN roles in cancer care, ensuring consistent, evidence-based, and patient-centered practice. A notable framework is the Oncology Nurse Practitioner Competencies from ONS (2019), which emphasize domains like assessment, diagnosis, and intervention, health promotion and education, communication, leadership, evidence-based practice and research, and resource utilization and quality of practice. These competencies support role clarity, performance evaluation, and interprofessional collaboration, empowering oncology APNs to demonstrate their impact, enhance care quality, and address the complex needs of cancer patients across diverse settings. By aligning professional practice through the APRN Consensus Model with a structured framework, institutions and individuals can contribute to more consistent and high-quality oncology care and equip oncology APNs to provide safe, high-quality, and population-focused cancer care.
<H2>ADVANCED PRACTICE NURSE ONCOLOGY CERTIFICATION

In addition to certification required for advanced practice licensing, advanced practice oncology nurses can obtain specialty certification to demonstrate expertise and commitment to oncology care. The Oncology Certification Corporation (ONCC) offers the Advanced Oncology Certified Nurse Practitioner (AOCNP®) credential for new and renewal certificate holders, while the Advanced Oncology Certified Nurse (AOCN®) and Advanced Oncology Certified Nurse Specialist (AOCNS®) credentials are available for renewal (ONCC, 2023). According to ONCC, there are currently 2,829 APNs certified in oncology. Certification eligibility criteria include graduate-level education, valid registered nurse (RN) and APRN license, and documented oncology advanced practice hours. Passing a rigorous examination ensures that certified nurses have validated competencies in areas such as cancer pathophysiology, treatment modalities, symptom management, and psychosocial care. These credentials support professional credibility, promote evidence-based practice, and may be associated with improved patient outcomes and career advancement. While many continuing education courses offer valuable information for supporting advanced oncology practice, they are not equivalent to formal certification; APNs should be mindful not to confuse these offerings with board certification.
<H1>LITERATURE REVIEW OF IMPACT

Oncology APNs play a critical role in cancer care delivery, system efficiencies, and improved patient outcomes.  Although the body of evidence remains limited and not fully up to date, existing research does demonstrate the meaningful impact of oncology APNs across the full continuum of cancer care.
Improved Access and Quality of Care

Oncology APNs expand access to cancer care. A study by Yang et al. (2014) projected a significant increase in the demand for oncology services, with an anticipated 40% rise in oncology visits from 2012 to 2025. This demand-supply gap is partially addressed by integrating oncology NPs and CNSs into practice settings.

Advanced practice nurses in oncology are increasingly involved in diagnosing, managing treatment plans, providing supportive and palliative care, and leading survivorship programs, thus ensuring patients receive timely and comprehensive services.
In multiple care settings, evidence has demonstrated the cost effectiveness, patient satisfaction, and quality care outcomes produced by NPs (Nevidjon, 2010).

Evaluations have clearly identified positive contributions with regards to improvements in supporting individuals with cancer, meeting their information needs, symptom management and a more streamlined access to appropriate services (Kerr, Donovan, & McSorley, 2020).
Impact on Patient Outcomes

Rohlfs (2022) examined the impact of an APRN-led discharge education program on hospital admissions among patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for melanoma. Their findings highlight the critical role of APRNs in bridging the transition from inpatient to outpatient care, which illustrated improved patient outcomes, reduced healthcare costs, and support for treatment adherence through proactive symptom management and patient engagement.
Patient Satisfaction and Quality of Life

Studies consistently show high levels of patient satisfaction with care provided by APNs. A systematic review by Newhouse et al. (2011) found that patients under APN care had higher satisfaction scores, better symptom control, and improved emotional well-being.
Improved outcomes have been documented in quality of life and cost outcomes in breast cancer care (Ritz et al, 2000).
Cost-Effectiveness

The integration of APNs into oncology practice models has been linked with cost savings. Their ability to manage common complications, reduce emergency department visits, and deliver preventive care reduces overall costs without compromising quality.

Overall satisfaction scores related to the patients’ experience of services were improved when the role of the CNS contributed to their care, with reports of moderate cost benefits (Kerr, Donovan, & McSorley, 2020).
Leadership in Care Innovation

APNs play a leading role in developing evidence-based protocols, managing quality improvement initiatives, and mentoring nursing staff, all of which indirectly improve system-level outcomes like treatment adherence, infection control, and patient safety.
<H2>CLINICAL OUTCOMES

Cancer Care Delivery: Oncology APNs strive to provide comprehensive, equitable, patient-centered, evidence-based care with a goal of improved clinical outcomes and well-being. Cancer treatments continue to evolve and expand due to many factors including new knowledge of receptors and cell signaling pathways, genomics and precision medicine advances, and an increased understanding of cancer-immune system interactions. Clinicians must adapt and incorporate new treatments, and they must do so within a capacity-constrained healthcare system experiencing a vast shortage of oncologists. All factors provide opportunities for innovations in care delivery with Oncology APNs leading these innovations:
Transitions of care:

In a group of patients with melanoma receiving ICI therapy, an APN-led program of pre-discharge education followed by a series of three post-discharge telephone sessions resulted in decreased hospitalizations (Rohlfs, 2022).

An APN-led telehealth intervention focusing on patients with advanced stage cancer who declined hospice at the time of discharge resulted in decreased hospitalizations compared to historical controls (Rosa et al., 2025).
Specialized clinics and services

APN’s providing specialized oncology-specific urgent care and acute symptom management reduce healthcare costs, decrease emergency room utilization and improve symptom management (D’Avella et al., 2024; Gould Rothberg et al., 2021)

APNs providing protocol-driven care in a subspecialty oncology procedure clinic for patients with leptomeningeal carcinoma resulted in improved survival as compared to historical control (Leese et al., 2021).

APNs deliver tailored comprehensive survivorship care addressing the multifaceted needs of cancer survivors like in post-allogenic hematopoietic cell transplantation (Baer et al, 2021). Additionally, Spears et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review comparing survivorship care provided by APRNs to other models. The review found that APRN-led care was associated with improved patient satisfaction, enhanced quality of life, and increased process and cost efficiency.
Oncology Palliative Care
An APN-led integrated model for palliative care, co-located with an oncology clinic, resulted in decreased symptom severity (Benson et al., 2023).

A six-year experience with an embedded palliative care NP within an oncology clinic resulted in improved documentation of goals of care, increased referrals to psychosocial oncology and hospice, and decreased hospitalization within the last six months of life (D’Ambruoso et al, 2021).

Symptom Control and Impact on quality of life (QoL): The symptom experience and its impact on QoL varies across the cancer care continuum from cancer diagnosis, treatment, or persistence beyond treatment conclusion.  The interpretation of patient reported symptoms and QoL impact is a vital role for the APN in assessment for acute and chronic management.  Patients with cancer frequently report experiencing fatigue, nausea and vomiting, pain, sleep disturbances, and cognitive impairment.  Additional symptoms may be related to specific treatments, such as radiation therapy or immunotherapies, like dermatological conditions or hormonal imbalances.  Through routine reassessment of symptoms and their impact on QoL across the cancer continuum, the APN can continue to provide patient-centered care by monitoring symptom improvement, resolution, or worsening, which may prompt specialist referrals. PROs in nurse-led services are comparable to those reported in physician-led models of care (Drury, Boland, & Dowling, 2024). Additionally, the APNs' ability to build sustained therapeutic relationships has been shown to facilitate timely interventions and foster trust, which can enhance communication about quality-of-life concerns. Integrating APNs into oncology teams has also been associated with reduced unplanned hospital visits and better continuity of care, both of which are valued by patients and reflected in improved PROs (McCorkle et al., 2011). These findings highlight the essential role of APNs in improving communication and early symptom management which can lead to less hospitalizations and costs for organizations.
<H2>QUALITY OUTCOMES

Patient satisfaction scores & patient perception of care: Metrics from patient-reported surveys regarding their perceptions of their recent health care encounters drive improvements in healthcare team performance and models of care.  The most common survey used, the Hospital Consumer Assessment of Health Providers and Systems (HCAHPS) survey, was developed by Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ).  In addition to patient reports on surveys, qualitative interviews with health care team members and patients have substantiated the impact APNs provide to the patient’s health trajectory. The experience of the care provided by the APN is viewed positively, with APNs responding to the needs of the patient both directly and indirectly through coordination of care, monitoring and management of toxicities and symptoms, provision of counseling and referrals, and delivery of patient and family education and promotion of safety. Teams and patients consider APNs essential to cancer care (Serra-Barril, et al., 2023). Furthermore, CNSs play a vital role in streamlining patient pathways and ensuring continuity of care, often serving as key decision-makers in multidisciplinary teams (Wilkinson et al., 2020). These roles not only improve patient satisfaction but also contribute to safer and more personalized care delivery.
<H2>FINANCIAL OUTCOMES
Revenue Data (Professional Billing and Downstream Revenue):

Professional Billing: Oncology APNs practicing in both inpatient and ambulatory settings contribute to productivity and revenue generation. Inpatient procedures, such as lumbar punctures and central line removal, can be performed independently and billed (SullivanCotter, 2024). In the ambulatory setting, APNs provide direct patient care for professional billing, as well as participation in care coordination (non-patient facing care) through lab value follow-up, patient phone calls, prescription refills, and prior authorizations (SullivanCotter, 2024). These strategies to optimize and integrate the APN to oncology practice are essential to improve access to quality and affordability.

Charge Capture: APNs also enhance revenue cycle management by ensuring accurate documentation and charge capture, thereby maximizing reimbursements and minimizing lost revenue opportunities. Utilizing tools like daily charge reports and oncology-specific evaluation and management (E&M) scorecards further supports improved financial performance (Association of Community Cancer Centers, 2005).

Downstream Revenue: APNs in oncology play a pivotal role in generating downstream revenue for cancer centers through care coordination activities that, while not always billable, lead to significant financial benefits. By expediting treatment planning, obtaining prior authorizations, managing symptoms, and directly coordinating chemotherapy schedules, APNs help reduce delays and optimize infusion suite utilization; leading to more efficient throughput and increased volume of billable services such as drug administration, laboratory testing, and imaging. Their involvement in triaging patients, managing side effects, and preventing treatment-related complications reduces emergency department visits and hospital admissions, further conserving system resources and enabling ongoing outpatient revenue generation. Additionally, APNs contribute to timely enrollment in clinical trials and supportive care services, which can be linked to grant funding, institutional reimbursements, or bundled payments.
<H1>TRACKING AND DEFINING OUTCOMES
<H2>CLINICAL OUTCOMES TRACKING

Cancer Care Delivery: APNs contribute significantly to system-wide efficiencies in oncology care through their impact on care coordination, patient outcomes, and resource utilization. In terms of care provision, concordance with guideline-based care is an outcome that could be measured, tracked, and improved. Some examples include: adoption of biomarker testing to inform treatment, adherence to guidelines in the prescription of treatment regimens and the use of appropriate supportive care such as antiemetics in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. In the lung cancer screening setting, the use of decision aids and the process of shared decision making is another example. Timely care resulting from interventions that improve screening, early detection or access and those that mitigate barriers to care promote best practice. The volume of visits, number of positive screening findings, and the actual time from initial biopsy to definitive treatment can be measured, tracked, reported, and benchmarked for comparison. Readmission rates, hospitalizations, length of stay, and emergency department utilization for potentially preventable conditions are other additional examples of trackable outcomes.

Symptom Control and QoL: Measuring the outcomes of APNs in the outcome of symptom control and QoL requires robust tools and standardized metrics that capture both clinical (patient facing), administrative (non-patient facing), and patient reported data. Common methods include:

Patient Reported Outcome Tools: Tools such as Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy (FACT-General, Diagnosis-Specific, and/or Symptom-Specific questionnaires), Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS), European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) questionnaires, PROMIS, NCCN Distress Thermometer, Clinically Aligned Pain Assessment and Behavioral Evaluation (CAPABLE), and MD Anderson Symptom Inventory are a small list of available symptom assessment and impact on QoL.  Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS®) can be used to measure fatigue, physical function, emotional distress, and social role participation that have a major impact on quality of life (NIH, 2025). Studies have shown that oncology APNs contribute to improvements in symptom control, treatment adherence, and patient satisfaction through comprehensive, patient-centered care. APNs are well-positioned to assess and respond to PROs due to their advanced training in symptom management and holistic care.
Electronic Health Records (EHR): Data on hospitalization rates, treatment delays, and symptoms management interventions can be monitored to ensure adherence to guidelines in APN practice.

AI tools: AI-based tools are being used beyond lung cancer screening to support APNs across various areas of oncology care, including incidental findings, hereditary risk, and survivorship. These platforms automate patient tracking, flag follow-up needs, and embed clinical guidelines to streamline complex workflows. By streamlining care coordination and reducing missed follow-ups, they support APNs in delivering consistent, high-quality cancer care. The data generated also enables real-time monitoring of care delivery metrics and supports continuous quality improvement.
<H2>QUALITY OUTCOMES TRACKING

Press Ganey/Qualtrics: Press Ganey is a widely used tool in healthcare for measuring patient satisfaction through standardized surveys and feedback mechanisms. For oncology advanced practice nurses (APNs), Press Ganey scores can offer valuable insights into how patients perceive their care and identify areas for improvement. By tracking and monitoring these results regularly, APNs can showcase the value from patients directly and implement targeted strategies to enhance patient-centered care and satisfaction.

Data from accreditations and quality programs: American Society of Clinical Oncology Quality Oncology Practice Initiative (QOPI). Commission on Cancer (CoC) accreditation, Foundation for the Accreditation of Cellular Therapy (FACT), and others can provide information on the role of APNs in adhering to high-quality care standards.
<H2>FINANCIAL OUTCOMES TRACKING

Professional Billing and Downstream Revenue: Tracking professional billing can be done through organizational billing systems, using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes and ICD-10 codes tied to each encounter. Developing periodic financial reports or dashboards can break down individual provider productivity, charge capture, and reimbursement. In reference to downstream revenue this can be tracked through EHR-integrated business intelligence tools to map referral and service utilization patterns by APNs (like oncology infusions, radiology studies, and surgical referrals) that yield high return on investment (ROI).

Productivity Benchmarking:  Comparing productivity within an organization or against industry standards can provide valuable insights into the APNs contribution and performance to oncology care (Krause et al., 2022). Several associations and companies provide benchmarking of APN productivity including, but not limited to, SullivanCotter, Vizient, and the Medical Group Management Association (MGMA).  Institutions may also assess APN value using Relative Value Units (RVUs) comparing them to national or internal benchmarks.
<H1>IMPACT OF OUTCOMES ASSESSMENT
<H2>CLINICAL IMPACT

Outcomes assessment is fundamental in oncology for improving patient care, demonstrating the effectiveness of advanced practice nursing and optimizing cancer care delivery. APNs have significantly contributed to these efforts through:

Symptom Control: Outcomes assessments have shown that oncology APNs improve symptom control through timely interventions and evidence-based symptom management (e.g., reducing unplanned hospital visits by managing mucositis, nausea, or neutropenia proactively).

Coordination of Care: Abundant literature confirms that the implementation of APN roles improves the care of patients with cancer, especially regarding information, coordination of care, accessibility of services, and patient’s active participation in decision-making (Serra-Barril et al., 2023).
<H2>QUALITY IMPACT
Patient Satisfaction: Press Ganey and other patient-reported outcomes data consistently show high satisfaction scores for APNs, especially in communication, time spent, and emotional support.

Benchmarking: By tracking outcomes like timely chemotherapy initiation, adherence to clinical pathways, and advance care planning documentation, APNs contribute directly to meeting quality metrics required by accrediting bodies such as CMS, CoC, and QOPI.
<H2>FINANCIAL IMPACT

Revenue Generation: APNs contribute to the financial sustainability of oncology practices through revenue generated from billable procedures and services. Research has shown that APNs in academic oncology settings can produce substantial revenue, with combined earnings from direct and bundled services ranging from approximately $77,000 to $141,000 per clinical full-time equivalent (cFTE), averaging over $111,000 annually (Moote et al., 2012). Moreover, APNs can bill for specific reimbursable services such as care plan oversight (CPO), which involves supervising patients receiving home health or hospice care and is reimbursed by Medicare under designated HCPCS codes (G0181 and G0182) (Oncology News Central, 2023).

System-wide Efficiencies: While APN services may be reimbursed at a professional billing level, the true financial impact is often seen in the broader system efficiencies and increased downstream revenue generated through coordinated oncology care delivery. Collectively, these contributions underscore the dual clinical and economic value of APNs in oncology care delivery
<H2>CHALLENGES IN OUTCOMES ASSESSMENT
Several barriers hinder effective APN outcomes assessment in cancer care, including:

New and varying APN roles in cancer care: Evolving roles like clinical trial APNs will take time to develop and produce outcome measures. Additionally, APN roles vary across institutions and settings. For example, APNs may focus on survivorship care while others work in infusion centers. As a result, comparing outcomes across different roles/setting becomes difficult and undermines benchmarking efforts.

Variability in Training and Experience: Although all APNs have the same training and education, when evaluating outcomes there may be variability in years of experience in cancer care, which may not reflect a consistent standard of advanced oncology care.

Technology and data collection limitations: Many organizations with APNs practicing in cancer care may use different EMRs and metrics, which make it difficult to standardized/collect information that is quantitative or qualitative. Additionally, most EMRs are not configured to capture APN specific contributions or workflows. Most financial analyses focus on professional billing which does not capture the full downstream of system or system-level impact of APNs. Consequently, this can lead to inadequate tracking and underreporting of APN activities and outcomes, especially for non-billable yet critical services, like care coordination.

Lack of standardized metrics: There are no universally accepted set of outcome measures specific to APN practice in cancer care which can hinder meaningful data collection and cross-institution comparisons.

Research gaps: Underrepresentation of oncology APNs in large-scale studies and there is limited research and/or reviews on advanced practice nursing roles and outcomes. Additionally, it is often difficult to isolate APNs from the larger interdisciplinary team in oncology. For example, data on NPs are often combined with Physician Assistants (PAs); making it hard to assign value to APNs specifically.
<H2>OPPORTUNITIES FOR GROWTH

Innovations in data analytics and reporting: Predictive analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) are emerging as powerful tools to analyze vast amounts of data. Leveraging AI for specific APN metrics can help develop better visualization of metrics via dashboards that capture real time decision making and care. Additionally, natural language processing (NLP) can be used to extract outcome data from clinical notes written by APNs, which can provide qualitative patient care insights. All of this will ease data analysis and shift reporting from manual to automatic.

Scope of practice advocacy: Supporting full practice authority and equitable reimbursement will expand autonomy and the ability to implement outcome-driven programs.  Advocating 100% reimbursement on services would standardize collections, support financial sustainability, and validate their impact on outcomes across all APNs delivering cancer care.

Research collaboration: There is a growing need for APN-led research in this area. By partnering with nurse scientists, APNs can contribute to the development of high-quality, real-world data that reflects the complexities of cancer care

Professional development: Encouraging APNs to pursue specialty certifications and advanced training represents a significant opportunity to enhance both individual competencies and overall cancer care outcomes. Continuing education programs and fellowships (see Table 18.1) or post graduate certificate programs in oncology can equip APNs seeking to provide advanced oncology care to produce measurable outcomes over time.

Expansion of APN roles in care models: Expanding roles to the care at home, survivorship clinics, clinical trials, palliative care, remote patient monitoring, genetic counseling and more offers opportunities for tracking and improving outcomes ties to quality, satisfaction, and cost.
<H1>EXEMPLARS
<H2>THE IMPACT OF APNs IN PREVENTION: LUNG CANCER SCREENING
<H3>Introduction to Lung Cancer and Its Significance

According to the U.S Department of Health and Humans Services, Centers of Disease Control (CDC), cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease, death, and disability in the United States (2014) and the most modifiable risk factor for the development in lung cancer (US Public Health Service Office of the Surgeon General, 2020). Lung and bronchus cancer is the third most common cancer diagnosis and is responsible for the most cancer-related deaths (Siegel et al., 2025).  Despite serious consequences of lung cancer, disparities in cancer screening and tobacco cessation persist. Oncology APNs are uniquely equipped to bridge this gap by providing timely lung cancer screening and targeted education, which facilitates earlier diagnosis, faster time to treatment, and improved patient outcomes.
<H3>Role of Oncology APNs in Early Detection

Lung cancer screening provides an opportunity for early detection of lung cancer. According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), individuals eligible for lung cancer screening with low dose computed tomography (LDCT) must be age 50-77 years, asymptomatic for lung cancer, have at least a 20-pack per year tobacco smoking history, and be a current smoker or quit smoking within the last 15 years (Jensen, et al., 2022). Eligible participants must undergo counseling and a shared decision-making healthcare visit prior to receiving the LDCT. This visit prompts the patient and APN to work collaboratively towards a medical decision regarding smoking cessation and appropriate treatment.  In this visit there must be documentation of : 1) beneficiary eligibility shared decision-making with one or more decision aids, 2) counseling on the importance and adherence to annual lung cancer LDCT screening, 3)impact of comorbidities and ability or willingness to undergo diagnosis and treatment, 4)counseling on the importance of maintaining cigarette smoking abstinence if a former smoker, or the importance of smoking cessation if a current smoker, and 5) if appropriate, providing information on tobacco cessation interventions (Jensen et al., 2022).
<H3>Management and Treatment Contributions

Care Coordination: Lung Cancer Screening visits provide an opportunity to optimize smoking cessation education and interventions with the APN. Smoking cessation can improve both immediate and long-term health outcomes, reduce cancer occurrence, and reduce overall mortality (Davis et al., 2020). Care coordination after lung cancer screening visits is also crucial to patients and their ultimate outcomes regarding lung nodules findings. The APN has the knowledge and skills to evaluate the LDCT results and refer the patient to pulmonology and/or thoracic surgery for further diagnostics and work-up.

Monitoring: The Lung Imaging Reporting and Date System (Lung-RADS) is a standardized classification system developed by the American College of Radiology (ACR) to help radiologists interpret and report LDCT lung cancer screening exams. The oncology APN evaluates the radiology reports and provides recommendations for monitoring. A plan for follow-up is established such as short interval follow up imaging, annual imaging, or in some cases patients may be released from follow-up screening. The LDCT Lung-RADS monitoring stratifies patients by cancer risk as low or high-risk and the aides the oncology APN to make informed, evidence-based decisions, and provide coordinated care and monitoring.
<H3>Outcomes From APN-led Care

Oncology APNs are at the forefront of lung cancer screening, providing education to high-risk patients on the importance of screening as well as the importance of tobacco cessation. The overall 5-year survival rate of lung cancer is less than 5%.  However, if lung cancer is found at an early stage, it can have a 70% cure rate (SEER Cancer Fact Stats, 2024).

Clinical Outcomes: Oncology APNs help ensure that patients receive timely diagnostic follow-up when needed after cancer screening, including procedures like lung nodule/mass biopsies that may lead to a cancer diagnosis.

Quality Outcomes: Patient education to individual patients and the community at large by APNs leads to adherence to lung cancer screening and follow-up as well as education on the risks of tobacco use and the development of lung cancer.

Financial Outcomes: By diagnosing lung cancer at early stages, APNs reduce the high costs associated with advanced disease management. The annual per-patient cost of medical services for patients with lung cancer ranges from 12.2 to 118 thousand dollars annually, with the greatest financial burden occurring at the time of initial diagnosis and the last year of life (Cancer Trends Progress Report, 2025).

Advancing Outcomes Assessment: Oncology APNs play an integral role in tracking lung cancer screening outcomes through metrics such as: 1) Rates of early detection and staging, 2) Patient adherence to follow-up care, 3) Long-term survival and recurrence rates, 4) Financial impact through cost savings in early-stage intervention, 5) Enhancing state and national surveillance and outcomes by reporting lung cancer cases to the state registry, and  6) Improvement of smoking cessation rates.

By leveraging evidence-based guidelines, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, and prioritizing patient education, Oncology APNs demonstrate measurable improvements in preventative care. These outcomes highlight their pivotal role in improving survival results in this disease.
<H2>THE ROLE OF ONCOLOGY APNs IN PREVENTION OF EMERGENT CARE
<H3>Introduction to Cancer Care and the APN role in Avoidable Emergency Department (ED) Visits

Cancer is increasingly viewed as a chronic disease with opportunities for proactive and expert symptom management and care coordination (Gallaway, et al., 2021; Pituskin, 2022). The role of Oncology APNs as providers of that care is increasing.

Up to 83% of patients with cancer experience ED encounters (Fleshner, et al., 2023; Lash et al., 2017). Inpatient admissions are more likely to result from cancer, as compared to non-cancer reasons for ED visits (Rivera, 2017). EDs should be utilized when appropriate but if the nature of the condition allows, alternative options should be considered. Additionally, avoidance of the ED could mitigate potential risk of ED-environmental exposures in immunocompromised patients, and care can be delivered by clinicians with oncology subspecialty expertise. Although definitions may vary, some ED visits in the cancer population can be classified as avoidable or potentially preventable with appropriate and timely outpatient management (Fleshner et al., 2023; Tabriz et al., 2024). The CMS classifies and publicly reports ten such diagnoses within 30 days of outpatient chemotherapy administration: anemia, dehydration, diarrhea, emesis, fever, nausea, neutropenia, pain, pneumonia, and sepsis (CMS, 2024). A recent review of over 35 million ED visits in the cancer population classified the majority (51.6%) as potentially preventable (Tabriz et al., 2023).
<H3>Management and Treatment Contributions

Proactive Coordination and Care: APNs can design and provide sub-specialty and treatment-specific interventions that avoid ED visits. Programs of patient and caregiver education and support in the lung cancer population (Stewart et al., 2021) or among patients receiving ICI therapies for melanoma are examples (Rohlfs, 2022).

Provision of Acute Care Services: Ambulatory or hospital-outpatient departments that provide same-day, acute-care services are increasingly offered in cancer programs. APN’s and Physician Assistants (PAs) are the most frequently reported providers of this care. Standard operating procedures include the identification of patients who are appropriate for the specialized acute care service and those who should be referred for admission or to the ED. A triage assessment by an oncology provider or nurse may be part of the workflow.  Patients can be evaluated by the provider and then efficiently receive prescribed fluids, antiemetics or other medications, electrolytes and blood products for many of the more common conditions associated with cancer and cancer treatment.
<H3>Outcomes from APN-led Care

Clinical Outcomes: Oncology APNs ensure the provision of prompt evaluation and management by those with knowledge of oncology-specific treatments, symptoms, and side effect management. Management of acute needs that is integrated within the cancer program may provide enhanced coordination among oncology specialties and supportive care services such as psychosocial oncology, navigation and palliative care. The mitigation of symptoms by prevention as well as early intervention with guideline-concordant care can improve clinical outcomes and patient experience.
Quality Outcomes: Oncology APN initiatives focused on care coordination and provision of acute care can decrease readmission and ED utilization for potentially preventable conditions.

Financial Outcomes: Initiatives that decrease healthcare utilization can decrease overall healthcare costs to patients and insurers. In addition, efforts to avoid unnecessary ED visits and hospital admissions improve capacity, freeing up constrained resources.

Advancing Outcomes Assessment: Oncology APNs play an integral role in avoiding unnecessary ED visits through tracking outcomes like 30-day readmission rates, ED utilization, hospital admission rates, cost avoidance, number of urgent oncology/same day visit managed by oncology APNs, and time from patient-reported symptom onset to APN led intervention.
<H1>CONCLUSION

Outcomes assessment is fundamental for improving oncology patient care, demonstrating the value of APNs, and enhancing the efficiency of cancer care delivery. By utilizing evidence-based practice, standardized outcome metrics, and collaborative care models, oncology APNs can address key challenges, highlight their measurable contributions, and drive innovation in cancer care. As the complexity and volume of oncology patients continue to grow, APNs will play an increasingly vital role in ensuring timely, high-quality, and patient-centered care; ultimately reducing disparities, improving access, and shaping the future of oncology practice.
