Understanding and Constructing Cinematic Language:
Camera Movement and Camera Support
Static Shots versus Moving Shots

The decision to use a static shot versus a moving shot—such as a tracking, dolly, or handheld movement—has a profound effect on storytelling, tone, and the way an audience perceives a scene. A static shot, with its fixed perspective, conveys stability, control, and focus, while a moving shot introduces fluidity and energy, pulling the audience into the scene by replicating natural movement or shifting points of view.

In the earlier chapters on Understanding and Constructing Cinematic Language, our primary focus has been on static shots where the camera remains still for the duration of a shot, without any movement. This is achieved by locking a camera to a fixed position typically with a tripod or fixed mount. One of the main advantages of using a static shot is, it provides complete control over the detailed mise-en-scène, enabling precise framing, composition, and blocking while also allowing for stylistic choices like symmetry.  Directors such as Wes Anderson typically employ static shots with symmetrical compositions to create a distinctive visual style. The Grand Budapest Hotel, Moonrise Kingdom, The Royal Tenenbaums, and most recently The Phoenician Scheme are just a few of his movies where he uses this approach to emphasize the films’ typical whimsical tone and intricate world-building

With static shots we also allow the audience to concentrate fully on the subject without distraction. This can be particularly effective in highlighting an actor’s performance when the viewer’s attention can be drawn to subtle facial expressions, body language, and emotional nuances. Similarly, in dialogue-heavy shot-reverse-shot sequences, where visual consistency and clarity between characters are crucial, static shots help keep the conversation as the central focus.

Example: No Country for Old Men (2007) – In the scene between Anton Chigurh and the gas station attendant, the camera remains completely static, with no movement throughout the exchange. This fixed perspective intensifies the unease of the moment, forcing the audience to remain locked in the tension of the dialogue without the relief or distraction that camera movement might provide. The lack of motion mirrors the suffocating inevitability of the encounter, amplifying both the menace of Chigurh’s presence and the helplessness of the attendant.

Our main emphasis in this chapter however, will be on camera movement and moving shots. We will be examining how shifts in the camera’s position or angle within a shot can do more than simply modify the frame and perspective. We are going to understand how camera movement can subtly and effectively enhance the cinematic language and guide our audience’s attention to ensure a seamless and immersive viewing experience. In that sense, we are going to recognize that camera movement not only enhances visual storytelling, but it also influences the emotional and psychological impact of a scene and contributes to narrative depth.
Camera Movement and Storytelling

As we talked about earlier, moving the camera with purpose helps guide the viewer’s attention and makes the experience feel smooth and immersive. In this section, we will break down common types of camera movement—such as pans, tilts, tracking shots, and handheld shots—and explore how each one helps tell the story, connect us to the characters, and add visual impact to a scene.
Pivot Move
A pivot move is a camera movement that adjusts or change the viewer’s perspective while staying fixed on a tripod or a stable surface.
Pan:  The camera moves horizontally left or right from a fixed position. We typically use pans to follow a subject, reveal new information or build tension.

Darjeeling Limited (2007) : In this scene, instead of relying on simple cuts, Anderson uses pans as the camera moves between characters, infusing the scene with rhythm and momentum. This approach along with his signature symmetrical framing keeps the audience engaged and enhances the visual story telling.

Psycho: (1960)  Towards the end of this brutal scene, slow pan follows the blood trail, moving from Marion's lifeless face to the swirling blood going down the drain. As the camera slowly pans and dissolves into the drain, it mirrors the life draining from her body, emphasizing the finality of her death, highly effective in building emotional impact and visual symbolism. (starting at 2.02 min.)

The speed of the pan movement depends on the context of the scene and what we are trying to convey. For instance, a slow pan can build anticipation whereas a fast pan can heighten the energy of a shot.

Swish Pan (Whip pan): A very fast pan that blurs motion, creating excitement, urgency and an energetic or seamless transitions. Swish pans can also build or emphasize the relationships between characters.

Whiplash (2014) In this scene, the camera shifts between Andrew and Fletcher in sync with the music’s rhythm. The fast, blurred movement adds a surge of energy that reflects the intense drumming and sharp pace of the scene. It doesn’t merely depict tension—it makes you experience it. The whip pan directs attention back and forth between drummer Andrew and conductor Fletcher, visually highlighting their tense and confrontational dynamic. This isn’t just camera movement; it’s a deliberate, powerful exchange of control.

Tilt:  The camera moves vertically up or down while remaining in a fixed position. We generally use tilts to follow action, establish scale, reveal details gradually about a character or a setting, or convey power dynamics. A tilt can give a character a sense of power by tilting up or vulnerability by tilting down. Similar to the pan, the speed of the tilt depends on the context of the scene and what we are trying to convey.

Blade Runner (2017) In both of these tilt shots in Blade Runner, the camera movement creates a visual connection between the character and their surroundings or the object they’re interacting with. These shots give us a clear sense of scale and help highlight the significance of what the character is observing or positioned near.
Dynamic Move

Dolly Shot – In a dolly shot the camera is placed on a wheeled cart, and it moves smoothly toward, away from, or alongside a subject. In dolly shots we often use tracks to ensure a controlled and fluid motion. As with every tool we use in visual storytelling, there are different reasons to use different dolly movements.

Push in: The camera moves toward the subject or action, creating a sense of intimacy or emphasis on a specific detail. This can be about an important detail, a moment of realization or internal conflict.  It heightens the dramatic tension of a scene, and it signals to the audience that what they are seeing is important.

Pull out: The camera moves away from the subject or action, often used to reveal a larger context in terms of setting or characters, give the audience a sense of detachment or abandonment or convey passage of time.

Joker (2019) The pull-out shot after the alley beating is subtle but deeply effective as it shows Arthur as small, powerless, and abandoned. It visually distances us, echoing how society has emotionally abandoned him.

The speed of movement in both of cases depends on the context of the scene and what we are trying to convey. For example, a gradual push-in can evoke a sense of intimacy or build tension, gradually pulling the audience closer to a character's emotional state and intensifying the connection. On the other hand, a swift pull-out can create a moment of sudden realization, shock, or awe, instantly altering the viewer's perspective.
Tracking/Trucking:  The camera moves often to follow action or characters as they move through space, giving the audience a sense of depth and motion in the scene.
These types of shots convey a sense of fluidity, and continuity and immerse the audience in the action particularly in long takes.

Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri (2017) In this sequence, we track Officer Jason Dixon crossing the street, climbing a set of stairs, violently assaulting Red by throwing him out a window, and then calmly returning to the police station. This uninterrupted tracking shot adds intensity to what we are seeing, making the brutality feel disturbingly real, leaving no room for us to disengage or be reminded that it’s fiction.

Arc Dolly: An arc shot is a distinctive camera movement where the camera travels in a circular or semi-circular path around a subject. This type of movement can emphasize a subject's importance or create a dynamic relationship between the subject and its surroundings. Since our focus typically is centralized on the subject or subjects, these types of shots can be used to convey a sense of intimacy, heroism even panic.

The Avengers (2012) - The arc shot highlights the Avengers as a cohesive, unified team, not just separate heroes. As the camera circles around them, it visually reinforces their strength as a group, reflecting the film’s central theme of unity and teamwork. Hero shot at 1.21 min.

Boom Shot: In a boom shot the camera moves vertically up or down to reveal or conceal aspects of the scene, or to give the audience a different perspective on the subject or environment. We can use them to showcase large environments, crowd scenes, or landscapes as well as epic stories, action films or sweeping dramas. Typically, cranes, jibs or pedestals are utilized to create these shots. Even though they are similar in their utility their use depends on the scale and the budget of the production.

Crane – A crane is used to move a camera vertically, horizontally, or in sweeping arcs. It consists of a long arm mounted on a pivot placed on a moveable platform, allowing for smooth, controlled movement over a large range. They are often used for grand, cinematic shots emphasizing vast settings, large crowds, or grand reveals. They can also make a character seem powerful by craning up or vulnerable by craning down.

La La Land (2016): The scene starts with a crane shot revealing the full scope of the setting and the vibrant energy of the freeway dance performance. As the sequence unfolds, the camera transitions into a Steadicam as well, weaving through the dancers
Please click on Behind the scenes to get a sense of the challenging filming process.

Jib - A jib shot is a type of camera movement where the camera is mounted on a jib arm (a small crane) that allows it to move vertically, horizontally, or in an arc with smooth motion. Jibs are often used to achieve dynamic, cinematic camera moves that would be difficult to execute with handheld or dolly setups.

Pedestal – In a pedestal shot the camera moves vertically up or down while staying on a fixed point. Unlike a tilt, a pedestal shot physically raises or lowers the camera position. We can see various examples of this in The Royal Tenenbaums directed by Wes Anderson. The movement can be used to reveal or conceal aspects of the scene, or to give the audience a different perspective on the subject or environment.  And just like the jib and crane shots, we can use pedestals to enhance or diminish character presence by making them powerful or small/vulnerable.

Steadicam: A Steadicam shot is achieved using a Steadicam rig, which allows the operator to capture smooth, stable footage while moving. The rig consists of a camera stabilizer system with a harness and an articulated arm that isolates the camera from the operator's movements, reducing shakiness and creating fluid motion. Since Steadicams provide smooth, stabilized movement even when the operator is walking, running, or navigating obstacles, they offer greater freedom of movement than traditional dolly shots. This flexibility makes it possible to create immersive long takes and dynamic tracking shots that follow characters through complex spaces.

Goodfellas (1990): In this classic sequence, the camera follows Henry and Karen in one long take as they walk through the back entrance, kitchen, and into the club. Because there are no cuts, we feel like we’re right there with them with a first-person perspective of his power and influence. The smooth camera movement helps show how powerful and confident Henry is, reinforcing the glamour and excitement of his life.
In movies like Sam Mendes’s 1917 (2019) Steadicam plays a crucial role in maintaining fluid camera movement and reinforcing the illusion of a single, continuous take throughout the narrative.

Handheld: A handheld shot is where the operator holds the camera without the support of a stabilizing device like a tripod, Steadicam, or gimbal. This creates a raw, shaky, unpolished movement, adding realism, tension, or urgency to what we are seeing, creating an immersive effect, making the audience feel like they are part of the scene.

Since handheld shots allows the operator to move freely, we can have spontaneous framing and a more intimate, subjective perspective. This technique can be applied across a range of situations: in action sequences, handheld shots can heighten intensity by creating a visceral, chaotic experience, while in character-driven moments they can convey psychological unrest or emotional instability. For example, in Saving Private Ryan (1998), handheld camerawork captures the battle scenes with a documentary-like quality, adding realism and immediacy that immerse the audience in the chaos of combat.

Saving Private Ryan (1998): In this sequence, the unsteady handheld camerawork evokes a documentary aesthetic, heightening the sense of realism. The erratic motion positions the audience within the scene, making them feel as though they are experiencing the intensity and chaos of war firsthand.

Found Footage Horror can be considered a subset of Handheld camera style as it mimics amateur camerawork with mostly first-person point of view for authenticity. The Blair Witch Project (1999), which was shot entirely in a shaky, first-person point of view is one of the earlier examples of this style. Depending on how heavy or large the camera is, camera operators often use simple support tools like shoulder mounts or an Easy Rig to help reduce strain and to have better control over how much the camera shakes.

Roll shot: In a roll shot the camera rotates along its z-axis, causing the horizon line to tilt and spin. This creates a dynamic, disorienting effect, often used to heighten tension, confusion, or stylistic flair. It can range from subtle to extreme—a slight roll may create unease, while a full 360° rotation can evoke a sense of chaos or surreal disorientation. Commonly used in dream sequences, action films, horror, or sci-fi to simulate dizziness, loss of control, or altered perception.

Inception (2010) – In Inception, director Christopher Nolan and cinematographer Wally Pfister, use the roll shot in the rotating hallway fight scene where Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s character fights in a gravity-shifting corridor that reinforces the film’s theme of shifting realities, making the audience feel as if they’re experiencing the dream world’s instability.
Please click on Behind the Scenes at 4.27min. to get a better sense of how this effect was achieved in Inception.

Black Panther (2018) – In Killmonger’s throne room scene, a slow roll shot is used to reflect his rise to power and the shift in control. The scene begins with the world literally turned upside down, and as he takes his seat, the camera slowly rotates upright, symbolizing his claim to the throne and his mission to reshape the world. This powerful visual reflects the complexity of his character: seen as a villain driven by aggression and power, yet also as someone deeply motivated by injustice, trying to correct what he believes is wrong.

We can create a roll shot effect in several ways: by rotating a handheld or gimbal-mounted camera, using a Steadicam with roll-axis control, or even a subtle roll by slowly tilting the camera on a fluid head tripod with a dutch-angle effect.

Vertigo Shot (Dolly/Zoom): In a vertigo shot we dolly in or dolly out while simultaneously zooming in or out in the opposite direction. This technique produces a surreal effect: the subject remains the same size in the frame while the background appears to expand when zooming out while dollying in, or contract when zooming in while dollying out. The effect works best when the zoom speed is carefully matched to the dolly movement. It is a powerful tool for storytelling as it can capture the shock of sudden realization, build an atmosphere of dread or unease, or convey a character’s disconnection from their world. Since it bends reality itself, it can also transport us into the surreal, heightening dreamlike or otherworldly moments.
Vertigo (1958) – This is the first major use of dolly/zoom, representing the character’s acrophobia or fear of heights.

Bohemian Rhapsody: In this concert scene, we watch Freddie Mercury’s bond with the audience grow. As the scene goes on, the crowd appears larger and moves closer to him while he stays the same size, highlighting his powerful connection with them.

In the end, camera movement is far more than a technical decision—it is a storytelling device that forges a powerful bond between audience and story. By choosing and executing movement with intention, we shape the emotional tone of a scene, guide the audience’s response, and draw them deeper into the lives of the characters and the unfolding narrative.

Making It Work: Creative Camera Techniques on a Student Budget

While student productions may not always have access to the specialized equipment, creative adaptation can go a long way. By making the most of the tools at hand, we can create similar effects and bring dynamic movement into our storytelling.
Here are a couple of examples:

Tripod Boom Method: Extend a sturdy tripod and use it like a mini-jib, holding one leg while tilting the camera up or down. For smoother motion try using a counterweight like a sandbag on the opposite leg. We can use this for small-scale vertical reveals such as from feet to face.
Another method is to extend a sturdy tripod to its highest point and tilting it up or down smoothly while panning. We can use this for short jib movements and reveals.
Monopod as a Mini Jib: Attach a camera to a monopod and raise/lower it in a controlled arc. For added stability, use a counterweight a sandbag or water bottle attached to the bottom.
Works well for small-scale crane movements such as revealing objects on a table.

Gimbal + Handheld Lift: If we have access to a gimbal, we can use it to lift the camera vertically while walking smoothly. This can mimic a jib-up or jib-down effect while keeping the shot steady. We can create fluid, floating camera effects, especially when tracking a character and we can add slow-motion for extra smoothness.
C-Stand or Boom Pole: We can mount a lightweight camera on a C-stand arm or boom mic pole and raise/lower it carefully.

Ladder or Chair Lift: Have a steady-handed operator stand on a ladder and smoothly tilt up or down. For a moving jib effect, use a rolling chair. Start tight on the ground and jib up to unveil a grand setting. This works well in establishing shots such as revealing a location or a crowded scene.
Tripod
Even though our primary focus in this chapter is camera movement. We need to also go over key components of a tripod as it helps stabilize and control the camera for smooth and precise shots.
Here’s a breakdown of the main parts of a tripod:
1. Tripod Head (Controls camera movement)
Fluid Head – The most common type for filmmaking, allowing smooth pan and tilt motions.
Pan Handle(s) – Long handles extending from the tripod head, used to control panning and tilting smoothly.
Quick Release Plate – A detachable plate that mounts the camera to the tripod for quick setup and removal.
Tilt Lock & Pan Lock – Locks the tilt and pan movements in place when needed.
Counterbalance System – Helps maintain stability, especially for heavier cameras.
2. Tripod Legs (Supports the camera)
Leg Sections – Usually adjustable in 2-3 segments, allowing height customization.
Leg Locks – Twist locks or flip locks that secure the leg height in place.
Spreader – A support structure (mid-level or ground) that keeps legs evenly spaced and stable.
Rubber Feet / Spikes – Rubber grips for indoor surfaces; retractable spikes for outdoor use.
3. Center Column / Bowl Mount (Adjusts height and leveling)
Center Column – Some tripods have an adjustable central post for additional height control.
Bowl Mount – A leveling mechanism (usually 75mm or 100mm diameter) allowing quick camera leveling without adjusting the legs.
Leveling Bubble – A small spirit/bubble level for accurate horizontal alignment.
4. Additional Accessories
Dolly Wheels – Attach to the tripod legs for smooth rolling movement.
Weight Hook – A hook at the bottom of the center column to add weight for extra stability.
Choosing the Right Tripod for Filmmaking
Lightweight tripods (mechanical/frictional) – Good for run-and-gun shooting but less stable, most of them not practical and smooth for pans and tilts.
Heavy-duty tripods (gear heads)– Exceptionally smooth, best for cinema cameras and controlled studio setups.
Fluid head tripods – Essential for smooth cinematic pans and tilts.
CHAPTER SUMMARY
Static vs. Moving Shots
Static shots (e.g., tripod-mounted) focus attention on composition and performance. Used in scenes requiring emotional subtlety or precise blocking.
Example: Wes Anderson’s symmetrical frames or tense dialogue scenes in No Country for Old Men.
Moving shots provide immersion, shift perspective, and guide audience focus. These can reflect emotion, momentum, or narrative shifts.
Types of Camera Movements and Their Storytelling Impact
Pivot-Based Movements
Pan (horizontal movement)
Used to follow action, reveal space, or shift perspective.
Example: The Darjeeling Limited uses pans instead of cuts to maintain rhythm and flow between characters.
Tilt (vertical movement)
Used to reveal vertical space, suggest scale, or show dominance/vulnerability.
Example: In Blade Runner 2049, tilt shots connect characters with towering environments, reinforcing their isolation or insignificance.
Whip Pan / Swish Pan
A rapid pan that creates blur and urgency, often used to build intensity or make energetic transitions.
Example: Whiplash uses whip pans in rehearsal scenes to visually capture the intensity and competitive tension between characters.
Dynamic Movements (Camera physically travels through space)
Dolly Camera is placed on a wheeled cart, and it moves smoothly toward, away from, or alongside a subject
Push-In
Camera moves closer to the subject, often used to emphasize realization, intimacy, or tension.
Example: A slow push-in can signal a character’s internal shift or emotional moment.
Pull-Out
Camera moves away from the subject to reveal isolation, broader context, or a change in emotional distance.
Example: In Joker, after Arthur is beaten in the alley, the pull-out highlights his isolation and society’s indifference.
Tracking / Trucking Shot
Camera follows a character’s movement, creating immersion and continuity.
Example: Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri features a long take tracking Officer Dixon across multiple locations, intensifying the brutality of the scene by refusing to cut.
Arc Shot
Camera circles around a subject to emphasize importance, unity, or emotional momentum.
Example: The Avengers uses an arc shot to unify the team visually and thematically.
Boom / Crane / Jib Shot
These elevate the camera to provide dramatic reveals or large-scale perspectives.
Example: La La Land opens with a sweeping crane shot that introduces the setting and energy of the freeway musical number before transitioning to Steadicam for more intimate movement.
Pedestal Shot
Camera is raised or lowered in a straight vertical line—useful for subtle reveals or perspective shifts, often used in controlled, studio environments.
Specialty Movements
Roll Shot
Rotates the camera along the z-axis, disorienting the viewer.
Example: In Black Panther, Killmonger’s throne room scene begins upside down and slowly rotates upright, symbolizing his shift in power and ideology.
Vertigo Shot (Dolly Zoom)
Combines dolly movement with an opposite zoom to create spatial distortion, reflecting psychological tension.
Example: Vertigo (1958) pioneered this to represent fear of heights; Bohemian Rhapsody uses it to show Freddie Mercury’s growing bond with the audience.
Handheld and Stabilized Movement
Steadicam
Offers smooth movement with more flexibility than a dolly. Often used in long takes, tracking characters through environments while maintaining a stable image.
Example: Goodfellas features an iconic Steadicam shot as Henry Hill takes Karen through the back entrance of the Copacabana—immersing us in his world.
Handheld Camera
Creates a raw, spontaneous, and intimate feel. Shakiness adds realism, often used in war films, horror, or emotional scenes.
Example: Saving Private Ryan uses handheld shots to mimic documentary-style combat footage, pulling the viewer directly into the chaos of battle.
Found Footage Style
A subgenre of handheld cinematography used in films like The Blair Witch Project to create authenticity through a first-person point of view.
Making It Work on a Student Budget
Professional tools like cranes and Steadicams may be beyond the reach of student productions, but similar effects can be achieved with creativity and resourcefulness:
Tripod Boom Method – Extend and pivot a tripod for basic crane-like moves.
Monopod Mini-Jib – Use a monopod with a counterweight for controlled lifts.
Rolling Chair / Ladder – Create vertical motion by moving or elevating the camera.
Gimbal Lift – Use gimbals for stabilized floating movement and vertical tracking.
Boom Pole Mount – Use a C-stand or boom pole to simulate high-angle shots.
The goal is to match the intention of professional tools, not to replicate them exactly—creative execution matters more than expensive gear.
Tripod Fundamentals
Tripods are essential for stable shots and controlled movement.
Components:
Tripod Head – Controls panning and tilting.
Fluid Head for smooth motion.
Pan Handles for directional control.
Quick Release Plate for fast camera attachment.
Tilt/Pan Locks to hold position.
Counterbalance System for heavy rigs.
Legs and Spreader – Provide height, stability, and flexibility.
Adjustable legs with flip or twist locks.
Rubber feet or spikes depending on terrain.
Spreaders stabilize the structure.
Center Column / Bowl Mount
Bowl Mount allows quick leveling.
Leveling Bubble ensures horizontal framing.
Optional Accessories
Dolly wheels for rolling camera moves.
Weight hooks for extra stability in windy or uneven conditions.
Conclusion

Understanding camera movement is not simply a technical detail—it is a powerful visual storytelling tool. With every type of movement—from subtle pans to dramatic crane shots—we can guide viewer attention, shape emotion, enhance tension, and contribute to the rhythm and flow of a film.

INTRODUCTION

In this book, everything has always been about the patient! Indeed, the overarching theme has been to deliver value to the patient. Yet, as discussed in Chapter 3, healthcare organizations have multiple customers, including payers, accreditation agencies, certification organizations, and the community.

Healthcare organizations must undergo accreditation and/or certification on a regular basis. Accreditation and certification validate an institution and may bring distinction for high standards. In this chapter, we review the ways healthcare organizations and provider groups achieve accreditation, and we describe the most notable healthcare award in the U.S. We also discuss how organizations can become more consistent and reliable.

ACCREDITATION

Accreditation is a rigorous, and comprehensive validation process that examines the systems, processes, and performance of healthcare organizations. It is performed by impartial outside groups to ensure that business is being conducted in a way that meets national quality standards (Table 13.1). In order for an organization to receive federal payment from Medicare or Medicaid, it must have a certification called Conditions of Participation (CoPs) or Conditions for Coverage that complies with the government’s health and safety requirements. Accrediting bodies must have quality standards and a survey process that meets or exceeds Medicare and Medicaid requirements. The process that CMS uses to recognize an accreditation body that can evaluate a healthcare organization is called “deeming.” CMS monitors and validates the surveys of these entities with “deeming authority.” In this section, we will look more closely at three accrediting bodies: The Joint Commission (TJC), Det Norske Veritas (DNV), and the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA).

The Joint Commission (TJC)

In 1951, the American College of Physicians, the American Hospital Association, the American Medical Association, and the Canadian Medical Association joined the American College of Surgeons to create the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Hospitals (JCAH), whose main purpose was to provide voluntary accreditation. The Social Security Amendment of 1965 created two major healthcare programs in the United States: Medicare and Medicaid. At the time, only hospitals accredited by the JCAH were “deemed” to be in compliance with the Medicare CoPs and could participate in the Medicare and Medicaid programs. In 1987, JCAH was renamed the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations (JCAHO), and in 2007, the name was shortened to The Joint Commission (TJC). Currently, this agency accredits and certifies more than 22,000 healthcare organizations in the United States. TJC accreditation or certification is recognized as symbolizing quality and an organizational commitment to meeting certain performance standards (The Joint Commission, 2024c). A basic tenet of TJC is that healthcare organizations can go beyond accreditation and achieve exemplary safety records. Their program called “Leading the Way to ZeroTM” helps healthcare organizations change the way they work to prevent patient harm. Zero harm does not mean that mistakes never happen. It means that systems and processes are put in place to catch errors before they cause harm (The Joint Commission, 2024d). The Joint Commission has expanded its survey process to non–hospital-based services. Many payers now require accreditation as a condition for reimbursement.
How Is Accreditation Achieved?

TJC standards form the basis of an objective survey process that uses the tracer methodology to evaluate healthcare organizations (Box 13.1). The survey process is data-driven and focused on the evaluation of the actual care processes that affect patients. Trained surveyors perform an onsite assessment every three years for hospitals and health systems (every two years for lab accreditation), checking for compliance with standards founded on the most current evidence-based practices. The surveys are unannounced. Following the path of care throughout a hospital stay, the team can randomly select patient records to evaluate the quality of care provided against TJC-established criteria. After the survey, the “findings” or areas of non-compliance with national standards are shared with the organization. The organization is required to develop a “plan of correction” to ensure they can meet the standard and depending on the severity of the finding, TJC can return to repeat parts of the survey and verify compliance.

Performance Measurement

TJC works with CMS and other experts to identify and implement standardized performance measures. TJC distinguishes between accountability and non-accountability measures and places a greater emphasis on the former (The Joint Commission, 2024a). Accountability measures are the best indicators of improvement on patient outcomes and must meet the criteria for process indicators outlined in Chapter 4: evidence-based, reflecting the quality of the process itself, directly related to outcomes, proven safe, systematic and timely, stable, and valid.
Benefits of Accreditation
There is consistent evidence that ensuring standards compliance improves healthcare organizations’ care processes (Jha, 2018). But, in addition, there are benefits to the organizations themselves:
Helping to organize and strengthen patient safety efforts.
Strengthening community’s confidence in care provided by the institution.
Providing education to enhance staff performance.
Building a framework for organizations to structure safety and quality efforts.
Providing a thorough and in-depth review of care processes.

Another accrediting agency that has been gaining traction worldwide is Det Norske Veritas (DNV).
DET NORSKE VERITAS

Det Norske Veritas is an international accrediting certification body headquartered in Norway. It provides a variety of services across multiple sectors, including healthcare. It has been accrediting hospitals since 2008. Like TJC’s, its accreditation standards, National Integrated Accreditation for Healthcare Organizations (NIAHO®), follow closely the Medicare CoPs and cover (DNV, 2024):

Quality management system and governance: These standards guarantee that the governing body establish and sustain a robust quality management system. The system must be data-driven and focus on quality improvement with measurement (outcomes, process, and patient perception), assessment, corrective and preventive actions, and monitoring. The system should conform to the ISO 9001 standard (see later section in this chapter) within three years after the initial accreditation.

Proactive risk management: These standards call for the identification and management of risks threatening patient safety. They include medical errors and adverse patient events. Once detected, these risks should be reported and their sources investigated. Preventive and corrective actions should ensue, and the effectiveness of these actions should be continuously monitored.

Higher risk services: Services such as anesthesia, obstetrics, nuclear medicine, and emergency rooms present higher levels of risk. Special procedures must be in place in these areas to ensure utmost proficiency and safety.

Medication management: The organization seeking accreditation should have pharmacy services with written policies and procedures based on best practices for patient care. The policies cover ordering, storage, handling, dispensing, and administration.

Patient rights: The organization should abide by the nondiscrimination provisions of the ACA, inform patients and/or representatives of patients’ rights before providing or discontinuing care, tell them about their visitation rights, and allow them to develop advanced directives. These rights should be communicated in the patient’s chosen language.

Physical environment: Construction, layout, equipment, and maintenance of the facility should promote patient safety. Multiple maintenance strategies (e.g., preventive vs. corrective) can be implemented, but their use should be justified based on equipment type and safety risk.
TJC and DNV have very similar standards, leading to similar health outcomes and patient experience (Box 13.2).

National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA)

Founded in 1990, the NCQA is a private, not-for-profit organization dedicated to improving healthcare quality (NCQA, 2024b). NCQA accredits health plans, provider groups, and health insurance organizations. The accreditation process is an on-site, rigorous review of more than 60 standards performed every 3 years. Every year, health plans must report on their performance. These performance reviews are tracked, and assessment scores, based on a set of clinical measures and consumer experience, are reported to the public.
When NCQA reviews a health plan, provider group, or health insurance company, it looks at structure, organization, and results in these areas (NCQA, 2024a):
Quality management and improvement using:

Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS) with measures comprising five domains: effectiveness of care, access/availability of care, utilization and risk-adjusted utilization, health plan descriptive information, and measures reported using electronic clinical data systems.
Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (CAHPS) performance measures.
Utilization management
Population health management
Network management
Credentialing and re-credentialing of providers
Members’ rights and responsibilities
Member connections
Medicaid benefits and services

Any health plan sold on the health insurance exchanges as outlined by the Affordable Care Act (ACA) requires accreditation through NCQA, but many unaccredited plans are still sold through employers or in the private market. NCQA scores are posted, and consumers can compare plans according to these parameters.

In contrast, certification focuses on programs or functions (e.g., heart disease care; Table 13.3). A highly regarded certification agency is the International Organization for Standardization (ISO).

The International Organization for Standardization (ISO)

The ISO, a nongovernmental agency counting over 160 member countries, established ISO 9000 certification in 1987, with the latest version of the 9001standard released in 2015. The ISO provides standards to organizations wanting to ensure that their products and/or services consistently meet consumers’ requirements and that the quality continuously improves. It is thus consistent with DNV’s requirement that ISO 9001 certification be required for reaccreditation.

ISO 9001:2015 builds on the PDSA cycle (Chapter 1) and centers on the documentation and review of effective quality management practices in leadership, process interactions, human resources management, service continuum, sustainability, and measurement-analysis-improvement activities (American Society for Quality (ASQ), 2024a).

In healthcare, ISO certification covers various sectors: patient safety, streamlined supply chains, and innovations in digital health and sustainability. It is based on seven principles that help build a quality management system for healthcare organizations (American Society for Quality (ASQ), 2024a; Table 13.4).

MALCOLM BALDRIGE NATIONAL QUALITY AWARD (MBQNA)

Unlike accreditation or certification, which indicates that specified standards are being met, a growing number of healthcare organizations are trying to differentiate themselves by seeking awards. Awards suggest that an institution is not just meeting the standards but exceeding them in certain ways. Achievement of this type adds luster to an institution’s image, sets it apart from the competition, and is a focal point for employee pride.

There are numerous national, regional, and state awards in healthcare, but the Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award (MBNQA) is especially coveted. The U.S. Congress established this award in 1987 to recognize all types of companies that have implemented successful quality management systems (ASQ, 2024b). The MBNQA is the only presidential award for performance excellence in the United States. The National Institute of Standards and Technology manages the award, and the president of the United States presents it annually. There are now seven categories of awards representing different segments of the economy, and an independent board judges the competition:
Manufacturing
Service
Small business
Education
Healthcare
Nonprofit
Community

The Baldrige Excellence Framework provides a comprehensive performance management approach that focuses on results, learning, and sharing of information (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2024a). It does not tell leaders how to run their organizations but instead helps guide the assessment of systems and outcomes. Similar to the balanced scorecard (Chapter 4), the framework stresses an integrated approach to deliver ever-improving value to customers, develop organizational capabilities, and promote personal learning. This framework encompasses excellence criteria covering seven areas of organizational management and performance (Figure 13.1):

Leadership: The leaders do not just need to lead the organization well. The MBNQA goes beyond that and is interested in how the organization leads within the community.

Strategy: The organization must have a planning process that defines its direction and delineates how the strategy will be implemented. Strategic planning should lead to positive action, and the strategic plans should not just sit on the shelf.

Customers: The organization must show that it values its customers and builds strong and lasting relationships. These relationships are put in the context of the market as a whole. In healthcare, this means putting the patient at the center of its focus, but customers of various processes, such as physicians and other staff, are also valued.

Measurement, analysis, and knowledge management: The organization must be able to collect and use data to support its decisions, improve key processes, and manage performance. The organization must turn data into information that can be used to drive its business.

Workforce: Organizations that value their human resources train them and empower them to do their jobs are more resilient and flexible. Workforce morale spills over into taking care of customers and organizational excellence. Organizations taking care of their people tend to perform better and maintain higher efficiency.

Operations: Operations management determines how well the organization is run. Excellent organizations are interested in identifying the processes that matter, designing them well, managing the variables, and continuously improving so that the outcomes are enhanced.

Business/organizational performance results: Organizations that focus on results have a broad portfolio of performance indicators: customer satisfaction, finance, human resources, supplier and partner performance, operations, governance and social responsibility, and competitiveness. Healthy organizations learn from comparing themselves to others and strive to adopt best practices.
Leadership

The first criterion of the MBNQA, and possibly the most important, is an evaluation of leadership. Let us explore this concept a bit further. Although there is no specific leadership style that defines Baldrige leaders, the Baldrige Foundation Institute for Performance Excellence (Strahan, 2019) found some common behaviors that leaders of high-performing organizations display. These leaders: (1) create and maintain a focused vision for their organization, and (2) ensure the effective execution of that vision (Table 13.5). Achieving a focused vision involves clarifying and aligning strategic priorities and defining performance criteria. For these leaders, the organization’s mission, vision, and values are more than words on paper; they are the compasses that guide the organization’s actions. This happens through effective communication and consistency of action at all levels.

Exceptional leaders encourage innovation to address difficult problems. They provide a safe environment to share new ideas and challenge the workforce to think creatively. Lean Six Sigma methodology can be used to foster innovation since the most effective way to improve a process is to eliminate areas of little value, augment existing value, and produce areas of new value (Hansen, 2018). Enhancing quality while decreasing costs requires innovation.

Leaders of exceptional organizations must model desired behaviors. They must be consistent with their actions and words. They model the organization’s mission and courageously stand up in tough situations. These leaders truly believe in the mission of their organizations and use continuous improvement to realize their vision of excellence.

Ensuring effective execution of the organization’s vision is how Baldrige leaders achieve their goals. A clear theme articulated by Baldrige leaders is the importance of data and using objective metrics to incentivize the desired behaviors within their organizations. Tracking performance measures, using comparative data, and having a structure to select meaningful metrics are vital to operating an organization while improving efficiency and effectiveness.

Baldrige leaders are also committed to leadership development at all levels within the organization. The organization benefits by having expertise throughout its ranks and allows for both personal development and improved competencies of staff.

Leaders must understand their organizations and how the different components work together. Indeed, healthcare organizations must be appreciated as a system, the components of which work together to provide high-quality care. The many leaders within the organization (the governing body, the chief executive and other senior leaders, and the leaders of the licensed independent practitioners) should also work well together.

As institutions evolve, leaders must grow and change. Leaders do not have to know the answers to all the questions, but instead, they need to create an environment where the right questions are asked (Box 13.3). At times, it may be uncomfortable to ask or respond to hard questions, but it is important to take all questions seriously and try to answer them honestly (Figure 13.2). Greater institutional tolerance and diversity of thought lead to higher performing organizations. The best leaders view every situation, no matter how challenging, as an opportunity to learn. If leaders are not willing to take a hard look inward and are willing to assess their own strengths and weaknesses, they will find it difficult to create an organizational culture where assessment is the norm.

The Governing Body

In Chapter 1, you may remember that when Kimberly Mitchell took over as BAMC’s chief executive officer (CEO), one of her first actions was to discuss her plans with the board of directors. The commitment to patient safety and quality must start with the governing body or board of directors. A component of Baldrige’s leadership development is the education and monitoring of board performance. A strong and capable board helps the organization maintain a constant focus on excellence and motivates leaders to achieve their vision. Delivering quality healthcare is increasingly recognized as a corporate responsibility, and the healthcare organization’s board must be fully engaged. In order to hold senior management accountable for the performance of the institution, the board must be involved in identifying the quality and safety goals. Boards must prioritize quality and safety agendas and commit sufficient resources for the implementation of continuous improvement programs.

Strategy

By now, you probably realize that the contents of this book parallel the Malcolm Baldrige performance framework. In Chapter 1, you learned how to take into account the organization’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT). Based on the SWOT analysis, a strategic path is chosen, and the primary functions within the organization—marketing, operations, finance, human resources, and information technology (IT)—must align their strategies with the business strategy. As per the cumulative model, building a strategic advantage in operations means competing on the basis of quality, cost, timeliness, and flexibility, with quality as the building block for overall excellence.
Customers

The ultimate customers of the chain of interconnected healthcare processes are known collectively as the “market.” They define the meaning of quality. In Chapter 4, you learned how to capture the voice of the customer (VOC). The VOC reflects the customers’ opinions and perceptions regarding the service provided by the organization. In healthcare, the VOC often captures the following service characteristics: responsiveness, reliability, communication with providers, empathy, courtesy, ease of making an appointment, and tangible aspects of the service such as lighting, noise, cleanliness, and so on. The house of quality framework helps ensure that the VOC is translated into the voice of the process (VOP) and is measured through quality indicators along the three stages of the healthcare delivery system: structure (or input), process, and outcomes (or output). Many of the tools described in this text are designed to measure, analyze, and improve a process so that the customer’s needs and wants are met.
Measurement, Analysis, and Knowledge Management

Throughout the chapters, you were introduced to tools and methodologies that can be used to diagnose and improve workflows and processes. These tools and methodologies are summarized in Appendix B. LSS tools help signal problems, identify opportunities for improvement, and design targeted corrective actions. They are especially useful for systematically communicating to others within the organization what is needed to align activities with performance.
Workforce

LSS is much more than a collection of tools. It is based on a system-wide collaboration of individuals in all functions of an organization—marketing, finance, IT, operations, and human resources— working together to support the overall organizational goals. TQM and LSS (Chapters 1 and 2) stress employee respect and empowerment. Similarly, some of the process design principles in Chapter 10 emphasized employee autonomy and collaboration, increased flexibility through job enlargement, cross-training, and job enrichment. Supervisors and leaders must learn from those actually doing the job and allow them to solve problems and improve processes when they see fit. Respect is a fundamental value in a continuously learning organization.
Operations

Process management is the core of operations. Processes must be designed to support the organizational strategy. At the beginning of this text, you learned about the Institute of Medicine’s call to design a system that makes it harder to do something wrong and easier to do something right. This idea paralleled Deming’s point #3, which advocated productive systems geared toward prevention of errors rather than correction. Chapter 10 presented several process design principles, which were built upon this concept as well as TQM and LSS paradigms. The principles urge organizations to emphasize mistake-proofing, simplification, integration, collaboration, and reduction of variability to achieve world class performance.

In the dynamic healthcare environment, processes cannot be static. Rather, they must evolve to continue to support changing strategies. Change is hard! Sometimes, even the simplest process modifications are met with harsh resistance (Box 13.4).

Business/organizational performance Results

In Chapter 11, the BAMC dashboards showed marked improvements in several performance metrics. The lower door-to-doc time leads to a lower LWBS rate and increased revenue. The ALOS was drastically shortened, boosting throughput and revenue. The lower number of travel nurses FTEs slashed labor costs. The higher top box percentages in patient experience and the better health outcomes increase Medicare reimbursements and enhance the organization’s image, ultimately leading to increased revenue and lower costs of poor quality. Furthermore, the enhanced working conditions for staff with less waste and higher skill utilization are likely to lower turnover costs. Therefore, over time, the added value to processes and their outputs triggers financial benefits. This is one of the requirements of the MBNQA: to translate quality improvements into significant business outcomes. This is another reminder that a systems approach to quality yields an end result greater than the sum of its parts. This was illustrated in our balanced scorecard (Figure 4.11). Listening to the VOC and developing the human capital of an organization improve processes, which in turn, enhance the financial health of the organization. When quality is the driving force of an organization, and the Malcolm Baldrige framework for performance excellence is achieved, business success follows (Box 13.5). Deming taught that strong, visionary leadership is needed to drive organizational learning and cooperation (Deming, 1986). But leadership alone cannot lead to a quality organization. It takes a culture of quality and continuous improvement throughout the organization to achieve excellence in healthcare.

The Highly Reliable Organization

Healthcare is a complex world with constant change and high risk. Doctors, nurses, and technicians work hard to deliver the best possible care. But in an environment of frequent and routine interruptions, patient variability, and occasionally emergent situations, it is difficult to consistently provide quality care or the “right care for the right patient at the right time—every time” (Clancy, 2009). As healthcare providers focus on improving quality and safety, they have turned to other industries that share characteristics of complexity and risk to learn how to avoid accidents. Industries such as aviation, nuclear power, and the military have studied past disasters to develop practices leading to improved safety. Weick and Sutcliffe (2007) demonstrated how the concepts of high reliability apply to healthcare and help prevent errors and avoid crises.

Highly reliable organizations (HROs) work to decrease or eliminate errors that can lead to patient harm despite operating in complex and risky domains. The only way that organizations can become highly reliable is by putting time and resources into what they value. For example, the airline industry values airplanes not crashing. Consequently, 2023 was a record-breaking year for safety with a fatality risk rate of 0.03 per million flight sectors dropping to 0.03 fatality per million flights (Flight Safety Foundation, 2024). However, airlines still occasionally lose a traveler’s bag. This doesn’t mean that the individuals in baggage claim are not good at their jobs; it likely suggests that out of all of the airline’s competing priorities, traveler safety ranks higher than baggage handling. Organizations must decide where they want to excel and put time and resources into the effort. Determining an organization’s strategy and priorities defines the areas where resources are targeted. In an organization that has quality as a core strategy, resources can be allocated to designing thoughtful processes to aid employees reduce error, building a culture that is collaborative and information sharing, and developing surveillance systems to identify mistakes early.

In Chapter 6 (rolled throughput yield), we looked at the concept of reliability, or the probability that each step will function effectively, without error, for a determined period of time. We will now explore how health systems can become highly reliable organizations.
Common Principles of Highly Reliable Organizations

Weick and Sutcliffe (2007) studied complex, high-risk organizations that coped well with sudden disasters and adapted in ways that prevented future catastrophes. They found that the culture of these organizations was constantly organizing and planning to handle the known, expected events, but they were always alert to the fact that unexpected things could happen. They were prepared to manage the unexpected. It was based on strong principles that were embraced at all levels of the organization and went beyond the process improvement concepts explained in Chapters 10 and 11 when we talked about the Improve stage in the DMAIC process. The principles were as follows (Figure 13.4):

FIGURE 13.4 Principles of highly reliable organizations.

Sensitivity to operations: Leaders in HROs need to be aware of how processes and systems affect the organization. They appreciate that employees involved in direct patient care understand best the state of the equipment and the adequacy of the processes to care for patients. HROs ensure that leaders and staff at all levels become aware of the risks to patients and work collectively to correct problems to improve the quality and safety of the care provided.

Being sensitive to operations means being aware of how messy reality is in most processes and identifying abnormalities around them. When individuals are involved in a complex activity, they often lose sight of what is going on around them. However, in an HRO, everyone must learn how to notice. For example, a laboratory manager saw data that several environmental services workers had sustained needlestick injuries while cleaning her department. She went to the blood drawing area and observed the venipuncture technicians depositing the used needles in the sharp's container. A few of the needles fell out of the sharps container into the trashcan that was positioned below. The manager moved the trashcan location away from the sharp's container, and the needlestick injuries stopped occurring.

In HROs, clear focus on problematic processes leads to important observations that can result in improvement. Employees must be able to ask questions and challenge assumptions. If everyone is clearly observing what is actually happening, problems can be identified sooner.

Reluctance to simplify: LSS taught us that simplifying processes leads to improved quality and decreased variability. Then, why should we be reluctant to simplify? When analyzing a problem (not a process), it is important to understand the complexity of issues surrounding failures and not link the solution to a simple cause. Broad, rational excuses are often used when something is not working well. Assigning blame to a single staff member, faulting inadequate training, citing poor communication, and so on may be easy, but the true reason for the failure will not be found and corrected unless (a) all possible causes, including the seemingly insignificant ones, have been identified and evaluated, and (b) the underlying causes of symptoms have been unearthed. People often jump into simple explanations for problems, but it does not get them closer to solving them. For example, attributing low patient satisfaction scores to an increase in emergency room admissions that had delays in transfers to a bed seems logical. But examination of data can suggest alternative reasons for the problem. Groups must be resistant to accepting the first possible answer and should dig deeper to uncover other potential causes. Brainstorming sessions must have a diversity of perspectives, and there must be trust within the group so people feel free to question and speak up.

Preoccupation with failure: Every organization has failures. In HRO organizations, employees are encouraged to look at their work processes and ask themselves, “What could possibly go wrong.” This shared attentiveness is constant. When issues are identified, employees are encouraged to come forward, and the focus is then placed on how to safeguard the process (Box 13.6).

HROs de-stigmatize failures and consider the identification of failure points as a success. When issues are identified, they are communicated across the organization to help other areas correct a failure point or stimulate ideas to improve more processes. For example, during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals were fearful of not having enough personal protective equipment to keep their employees safe. Multidisciplinary groups brainstormed about what to do if N95 facemasks ran low. Other health systems were called, and potential solutions were compiled. One health system decided to stave off the risk of running out of N95 facemasks by assigning labeled facemasks to individuals and re-sterilizing them as needed. This prevented a shortage that could have resulted in staff exposure to the virus.

HROs also focus their attention on the little problems in order to prevent bigger mistakes. These small issues are viewed as symptomatic of underlying problems that need more attention. The Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) tool (Chapter 9) is especially well suited to engage teams in identifying all points of possible failure and mistake-proof the system accordingly.

Deference to expertise: In every organization, some people are technical experts on processes or technology. The experts know how things work and the risks that patients face. Leaders of HROs must understand that these are the individuals who must be drawn into the conversations if they want to build a culture of high reliability. Leaders (without the expertise) should not call the shots when circumstances call for those with specific expertise to direct the way. Often, these experts do not have the most seniority and need to be encouraged to speak out. The worst thing that a leader can say is “I know that.” This will shut down communication, and people will stop voicing their concerns and ideas. In order to build an HRO, leaders and supervisors must listen to staff and create a culture of openness.

Resilience. There are always unexpected events. Leaders and staff in HROs are trained and prepared to respond when system failures occur. The capacity to recover quickly from unexpected events is called resilience. Resilient leaders design redundancy into their systems so that there will not be a single point of failure. Emergency situations are discussed, and the organization learns from errors. Planning efforts are organized so that all employees know their roles and have personalized plans of action so that they are not crippled when errors occur (Box 13.7).

With the rapid changes occurring in healthcare, such as delivery redesign, increased data reporting, and more rigid payment models, physicians and other providers are experiencing increased stress. In order to achieve high-quality care, a resilient and well-supported clinical team is paramount. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019) recognized the importance of preventing clinician burnout and improving well-being and resilience. The result was a collaborative platform entitled “Action Collaborative on Clinician Well-being and Resilience,” which focused on individual approaches to increase personal resilience and organizational approaches to reduce stressors.
<INSERT BOX 13.7 HERE>

For example, in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, health system administrators and clinicians needed to quickly and significantly change their workflow throughout the organization. Universal virus testing, masking, closing of patient care units, acquisition of increased numbers of ventilators and protective personal equipment devices, transition from in-person clinic visits to telehealth, modifying infection control strategies, etc., stressed all personnel. The organizations that had incorporated high-reliability methods into their cultures were able to adapt and continue to provide quality care.
The Importance of Mindfulness in HROs

The aforementioned five principles are interrelated and must be understood by everyone in the organization in order to have a collective “mindfulness.” Mindfulness is a rich awareness of detail that allows one to discover and correct errors that could escalate into a crisis. Performance can be improved by paying attention to one’s surroundings and actively working to eliminate distractions. Inattention to detail caused by stress and fatigue creates conditions that lead to errors. In HROs, everyone is engaged in the mission and strives to identify ways to improve the workings of the organization (Box 13.8).
<INSERT BOX 13.8 HERE>

So, what actually happened in the incident narrated in Box 13.8? A young recruit saw a piece of paper fly onto the flight deck. He saw the paper and could anticipate that something bad could happen as a result. Anticipation encompasses three of the five concepts of HROs:
Preoccupation with failure: The recruit was actively looking for signs that could indicate an error.

Reluctance to simplify: Foreign-object debris on the flight deck is a hazard. It can be sucked into jet engines and cause failure. The recruit saw the piece of paper and did not convince himself that the paper was too minor to cause problems.
Sensitivity to operations: The recruit understood how jet engines are able to draw foreign objects into them and how damage to engines and personnel can result.

Anticipation can also make healthcare safer. Imagine that instead of a young recruit on an aircraft carrier, you see a young nurse in the medical intensive care unit. She is helping a physician insert a central venous catheter, a catheter that is placed in a large vein and is at high risk for infection. The nurse, using the sterile technique, has set up all of the equipment needed for the catheter insertion. The doctor comes into the room and puts on sterile gloves. But the nurse notices that he has not washed his hands. Her mind is racing. She can anticipate that the error of not washing hands can result in a potentially life-threatening infection. In an HRO, she must speak up and stop the catheter from being placed. Anticipation is more than sensing early events that will lead to a problem; it also includes acting on observations to prevent future events from occurring. That is related to the Lean concept of jidoka.

Anticipation is important, but errors do happen. Unexpected events or mistakes, no matter how carefully one tries to avoid them, occur. HROs are able to respond appropriately when errors occur to contain the damage. The last two principles of HROs are related to containment:

Deference to expertise: In the last example, the physician must defer to the expertise of the nurse and respect her ability to see errors that will lead to infection. Even though the nurse did not have the same number of years of training, she did have the knowledge and experience to call out the error.

Resilience: The nurse and physician must regroup, absorb any strain, and preserve a professional relationship as they gather the necessary materials to restart the catheter insertion under sterile conditions. Both parties must also learn and grow from the episode.

HROs act mindfully to manage the unexpected. Note that we say “manage” and not “expect” the unexpected. Always expecting the unexpected is very stressful and signals that there is no expectation of stability within the organization. In managing the unexpected, HROs organize themselves to anticipate and notice aberrations to stop the development of errors. If they cannot halt mistakes, they focus on containment. If an event cannot be contained, HROs work to restore system functioning as soon as possible.

This book has been about a relentless pursuit of quality. But in the end, it is about being able to respond effectively and quickly to dramatic changes. It is the “obsession” with quality that prepares the organization to be responsive to patients’ needs, and the efficient use of resources that allows it to react to the most unanticipated changes. Embracing the concepts of HROs will help you create a better healthcare organization.

SUMMARY

This chapter does not really conclude our journey toward excellent quality because, as you know, it is a continuous pursuit. The chapter simply provides an overview of the rewards reaped from a commitment to excellence. Accreditation testifies to the organization’s adherence to stringent, evidence-based standards of quality. Awards, whether they are granted at the community, regional, or national level, demonstrate that a healthcare organization’s performance has surpassed that of all others. As such, it can be considered a role model. Becoming a highly reliable organization requires a fixation on safety and quality to prevent errors from occurring in the first place or being prepared to recover if they unexpectedly occur. The HRO essentially takes this quality journey full circle as you remember from Chapter 1 the IOM’s insistence on building processes that make it difficult for errors to occur. We hope this book has given you the motivation to do just that.

A student asks how circulating neutrophils can fight bacteria in tissue. You start explaining neutrophil recruitment.
<Prompt>
What is the first step of neutrophil recruitment?
<BACK>

The steps of neutrophil recruitment include tethering, rolling, adhesion, crawling, and transmigration. Initially, endothelial cells are activated when they encounter pathogens, which then upregulate the surface adhesion molecules P and E selectin from Weibel-Palade bodies.  These selectins bind to their ligands on rolling neutrophils, capturing them, which starts neutrophil rolling across endothelium.

<KP>Key Point: Neutrophil recruitment includes tethering, rolling, adhesion, crawling, and transmigration.  Damaged or inflamed endothelial cells upregulate adhesion molecules which mediate neutrophil capture and rolling.

You are giving a lecture to medical students about B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, explaining that patients commonly present with elevated white blood cells. A medical student asks why these patients are prone to infection.
<Prompt>
Along with T cells, B cells play a major role in what kind of immunity?
<BACK>

Lymphocytes (B and T cells) are the basis for adaptive immunity, which respond to specific antigens.  Once foreign pathogens are identified, the innate immune system is activated first, utilizing macrophages, neutrophils and the complement system.  The adaptive system is activated secondarily. B cells make antibodies against antigens via clonal selection, whereas T cells help provide signals for B cell proliferation, or act locally at sites to kill infected host cells or induce other cells to do the same.  In leukemia, only a single B cell clone proliferates against one antigen, often ineffectively, not allowing a full B cell response to the many pathogens faced every day.
<KP>Key Point: B and T cells are part of adaptive immunity, which can respond to specific antigens and pathogens in infected cells and can product a memory response against them.

A 12-year-old female who was recently diagnosed with ulcerative colitis presents to hematology clinic with neutropenia that has persisted for one month. Her medications include Tylenol as needed, cetirizine, and sulfasalazine daily.  She is otherwise well with a benign physical exam.

<BACK>

Sulfasalazine is utilized in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis and has been implicated in drug induced neutropenia. A 6-month-old male is currently hospitalized for a blood culture positive for Serratia marcescens. He has also been treated previously for Aspergillus pneumonia and Staph aureus abscesses. Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is a predominantly X-linked primary immunodeficiency causing a defect in Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase. Previously diagnosis was done through Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) testing. The gold standard for CGD testing is now dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry whereby neutrophils show reduced oxidative burst capability. Burkholderia cepacia sepsis is pathognomonic for CGD.  Therefore, prophylaxis with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim and itraconazole are critical. A 2-year-old female is referred to hematology clinic for workup of thrombocytopenia and anemia. She has had a 6-month history of cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and bicytopenia.
<Prompt>
What testing should be included to diagnose this condition?
<BACK>

Peripheral flow cytometry to check for double negative T-cells (CD4 and CD8 negative T cells) are one of the two required criteria for the diagnosis of Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome (ALPS).  The second is a 6-month history of chronic lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly.  A definitive diagnosis is completed with the presence of both required criteria plus one primary accessory criterion.  A probable diagnosis is based on the presence of both required criteria and one secondary accessory criterion.
Primary Accessory Criteria (need at least 1) for definitive diagnosis
Evidence of defective lymphocyte apoptosis in two assays,
Evidence of a somatic germline mutation in FAS, FAS-LG, or CAS10.
Secondary Accessory Criteria (need at least 1) for probable diagnosis
Elevated plasma sFasL or IL10
IL18 or plasma B12.
Additionally, patients can have immunohistological smears consistent with ALPS, other autoimmune cytopenias like hemolytic anemia or neutropenia with an elevated IgG, or a positive family history.
<KP>Key Point: A definitive ALPS diagnosis requires one of either an increased double negative T cell population, or a 6-month history of lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly.

A 2-year-old male presents with jaundice, splenomegaly, and severe anemia requiring transfusion.  Significant history includes upper respiratory symptoms and rash which resolved in the past week.  After recovery, parents inquire about the spleen size.
<Prompt>
When is splenectomy indicated for this condition?
<BACK>

Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) presents with splenomegaly, jaundice, and anemia during illness.  Spherocytes are prematurely destroyed in the spleen and phagocytosed by macrophages, causing splenomegaly; this usually improves after acute illness.  If patients have severe anemia requiring frequent transfusions or splenomegaly that affects quality of life, splenectomy may be indicated, especially if patients have complete deficiencies in alpha spectrin or band 3.  However, if the symptoms are mild, then it may be preferable to defer splenectomy to avoid the increased postsurgical and infectious complications of asplenia. Patients undergoing splenectomy should receive vaccinations against polysaccharide-based organisms including pneumococcal, Hib, and meningococcal.

<KP>Key Point: Not all patients with HS require splenectomy as there are post-surgical infectious complications that arise with asplenia.  Severe presentations of HS requiring frequent transfusions may need splenectomy.

ABSTRACT

Chapter 7 provides a comprehensive overview of time management, offering insights into various aspects related to optimizing productivity and achieving a healthy work-life balance. It explores the dimensions and properties of time, presents principles of effective time management, discusses interfaced systems, time laws, time traps, self-care, and the role of technology in time management. By understanding the finite nature of time and implementing strategies such as prioritizing tasks, organizing schedules, and utilizing time effectively, individuals can make the most of this valuable resource. Effective communication, collaboration, and coordination with others are emphasized as crucial elements of interfaced systems for efficient time management. The chapter also addresses common time traps that hinder productivity and provides strategies to overcome them. Recognizing the importance of self-care, it highlights the significance of maintaining physical, mental, and emotional well-being to sustain high energy levels and focus. Additionally, the role of technology as a valuable tool for time management is explored, with examples of various technological solutions to streamline processes and enhance efficiency. By implementing the principles and strategies discussed, individuals can develop effective time management skills, maximize productivity, and achieve greater balance in their personal and professional lives.
