<TX>In 25% of cases, pleural effusion results from malignant disease. In another 20–40% of cases, biochemical testing, bacteriologic examination, and pathologic cytology of the pleural fluid fail to identify any underlying cause of disease. In such cases, either cytology is repeated, or a pleural biopsy is performed.77

<TX>Additionally, helpful tests to assess the patient include pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation and ABG analysis to assess oxygenation and ventilation. Tissue sampling via closed pleural biopsy for histologic assessment is performed in some cases and can reveal granulomas of tuberculosis or tumor cells from malignant processes.89
Treatment and Management

<TXL>Treatment of the underlying disease is the principal therapy for fluid in the pleural space. Emergency procedures are required when there is a large amount of fluid, when breathing is impaired, when cardiac function is compromised, or when pleural bleeding resulting from external injury cannot be controlled. Drainage of the pleural space is instituted promptly in cases of acute thoracic empyema.77 If the initial thoracentesis reveals a complicated parapneumonic effusion with pleural fluid pH < 7.20 or a glucose level ≤ 40 mg/dL, an immediate chest tube thoracostomy placement is required. Chest tube insertions for complicated effusions must be done under imaging guidance because the added cost for the procedure is expected to be more than compensated by the increased success of drainage.79

<TX>Only in a few specific circumstances is a thoracentesis not warranted; for example, if there is a strong suspicion of heart failure as a cause of the effusion(s), then a trial of medical therapy for heart failure can be done prior to a thoracentesis.79

<TX>The palliation of dyspnea in persons with recurrent malignant fluid accumulation is an important therapeutic goal. The instillation of agents such as talc, tetracycline, doxycycline, or bleomycin into the pleural space (<KT>sclerotherapy</KT>) following chest tube drainage may be effective in fusing the pleura (<KT>pleurodesis</KT>) and preventing the recurrence of the effusion. The type of malignancy involved, however, directly influences the success of pleurodesis, regardless of the sclerosing agent used, with mesothelioma and lung cancer particularly prone to failure.77,90
Prognosis

<TXL>Prognosis varies in accordance with the underlying disorder and subsequent response to directed therapy. The outcome in malignant effusions invariably carries an extremely poor prognosis, with survival typically measured in months. While management in malignant effusion is primarily palliative, therapeutic options, including thoracentesis, tube thoracostomy, chemical pleurodesis, and thoracoscopic powder poudrage, can result in a significant response.80 Parapneumonic effusions, on the other hand, when recognized and treated promptly, normally resolve without significant consequence. Most patients recover, but the mortality rate for parapneumonic effusions and empyema remains at approximately 10%. Approximately 15–25% of patients require surgical intervention, including decortication and/or an open drainage procedure.91
Air in the Pleural Space

<TXL>Pneumothorax is a relatively common disorder involving the abnormal presence of air or gas within the pleural space. Pneumothorax is traditionally referred to as spontaneous when it occurs in the absence of indirect or intentional trauma in an individual with or without the presence of pleural or lung disease. Normal intrapleural pressure is negative (less than atmospheric pressure) because of inward lung and outward chest wall recoil. In pneumothorax, however, air enters the pleural space from outside the chest or from the lung itself via a virtual check-valve-like mechanism through mediastinal tissue planes or direct pleural perforation, causing intrapleural pressure to increase and lung volume to decrease.
Definition/Diagnosis

<TXL>Spontaneous pneumothoraces can be divided into a primary or idiopathic form that occurs in persons without a previous underlying lung disease and a secondary form occurring in individuals with a known underlying lung disease.92 Other forms of pneumothorax that are sometimes separately described include catamenial, iatrogenic, traumatic, and tension pneumothorax.

<TX>A spontaneous <KT>pneumomediastinum</KT> refers to the presence of free air (extraluminal gas) in the mediastinum that happens without traumatic injury or known underlying disease, resulting from alveolar rupture. A secondary pneumomediastinum, on the other hand, refers to free air introduced into the mediastinum following medical procedure complications or trauma, commonly occurring following perforation of the tracheobronchial tree or esophagus, or gas leaking into the thorax from the neck, chest wall, or abdomen.93
Clinical Signs and Symptoms

<TXL>The main symptoms of pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum are chest pain and dyspnea, which usually begin abruptly. Pneumomediastinum can manifest with variable signs and symptoms. The severity of the symptoms depends on the volume of air and the degree of the underlying disease. Box <S>5-</S>11 presents some common physical signs of pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum.

<TX>A small amount of air in the pleural space may not manifest with any symptoms and have a normal physical exam. The triggering factors for pneumomediastinum include precipitating factors such as the Valsalva maneuver, illicit drug ingestion, vigorous vomiting or cough, and activities leading to barotrauma (e.g., scuba diving, flying). A forceful cough from asthma is one of the most common triggers of spontaneous pneumomediastinum.94
Etiology

<TXL>In some cases of pneumothorax, air enters the intrapleural space without preceding trauma and without an underlying history of lung disease. This type of pneumothorax is commonly referred to as <KT>primary spontaneous pneumothorax</KT> (PSP). There are times when a pneumothorax is diagnosed as PSP; however, the patient has subclinical lung disease that can be detected only by CT scanning. These patients are typically between the ages of 18 and 40 years, are tall and slim, and often smoke tobacco.92

<TX><KT>Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax</KT> (SSP) occurs in people with a wide variety of parenchymal lung diseases. These lung diseases cause structural alterations that allow air to enter the pleural space via distended, damaged, or compromised alveoli. Iatrogenic pneumothorax is a type of traumatic pneumothorax resulting from pleural injury.92 In this type of pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space because of a diagnostic or therapeutic medical intervention. Pneumomediastinum may occur spontaneously or because of trauma.
Epidemiology

<TXL>Pneumothorax is estimated to occur in more than 20,000 individuals in the United States and costs over $130 million annually in added healthcare expenses. The estimated annual incidence of PSP is between 7.4 and 18 cases per 100,000 persons in men and 1.2–6 cases per 100,000 persons in women, whereas the incidence estimate of SSP is 6.3 cases per 100,000 persons annually in men and 2 cases per 100,000 persons annually in women.92 While difficult to accurately determine, it is likely that the incidence estimates for spontaneous pneumothorax are underestimated. PSP occurs less commonly in children than in adults. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) involving primarily emphysema is the most common cause of SSP and carries an estimated incidence of approximately 26 cases per 100,000 persons.

<TX>Spontaneous pneumomediastinum typically occurs in young adults, healthy individuals with no serious underlying pulmonary disease who are between 20 and 40 years of age. There is a slight predominance for men.92
Pathology/Pathophysiology

<TXL>Spontaneous pneumothorax occurs mostly from the rupture of blebs and bullae. This is thought to be related to increased shear forces in the apex (apical pleural blebs), especially in tall, young people without parenchymal lung disease. Spontaneous pneumomediastinum occurs when air leaks through small alveolar ruptures to the surrounding bronchovascular sheath.93 Air escapes into the surrounding connective tissue and dissects further into the mediastinum. Less commonly, pneumomediastinum results from air escaping from the upper respiratory tract, intrathoracic airways, or gastrointestinal tract (e.g., esophageal perforation). Esophageal trauma or elevated airway pressures may also allow air to dissect into the mediastinum. Air may then travel superiorly into the visceral, retropharyngeal, and subcutaneous spaces of the neck and can then continue throughout the body.

Complications

<TXL>Complications can take place in all forms of pneumothorax and are usually categorized as either acute or long term. Acute complications include air leaks due to continued leakage of air from the lung into the pleural space or air leaking around the chest tube insertion site; they are more common in SSP than in PSP. Failure of the lung to reexpand may complicate pneumothorax from a persistent air leak, an endobronchial obstruction, a trapped lung, or a mispositioned chest tube. Reexpansion pulmonary edema may occur when the lung is rapidly expanded following a relatively extended collapse. Other associated difficulties include bilateral pneumothorax, hemothorax, empyema, and acute respiratory failure. Problems that are more likely to occur in the long term include persistent pneumothorax (failure of the lung to reexpand) and pneumothorax recurrence. In most cases of complications for pneumomediastinum, the movement of air into the subcutaneous tissues prevents the buildup of pressure in the mediastinum. Occasionally, air leaks into the pericardial space, causing pneumopericardium.93
Diagnostic Testing

<TXL>Standard radiographic findings in pneumothorax are dependent on the presence or absence of coexisting lung disease and tension pneumothorax. The chest x-ray examination in pneumothorax uncomplicated by underlying pulmonary disease or adhesions typically reveals the margin of the lung as a thin, outwardly convex line separating the collapsed lung from the chest wall (Figure <S>5-</S>25).

<TX>Patients with mild pneumothorax usually present with mild hyperventilation, causing ABGs to commonly display a lowered Pao2 and Paco2 with an increased pH, consistent with acute respiratory alkalemia. Mild-to-moderate hypoxemia (reflecting an increased ventilation–perfusion [V/Q] shunt) is usually dependent on the extent of physiologic impairment. Acute ventilatory failure can result from inadequate alveolar ventilation and abnormal gas exchange, especially with life-threatening tension pneumothorax or with significant secondary pneumothorax.

<TX>ECG findings in pneumothorax characteristically reveal decreased QRS amplitude and electrical axis shift in addition to tachycardia.95 Electromechanical dissociation may occur in extreme cases, as with tension pneumothorax.

<TX>Left-sided pneumothoraces greater than 30% are often associated with right-axis deviation, diminution of the QRS complex amplitude, T-wave inversion, and loss of R waves in the precordial leads.95 Rarely, 12-lead ECG findings may be suggestive of acute myocardial infarction. Right-sided pneumothorax less often produces diminution of precordial chest R waves, inversion of precordial T waves, diminution of QRS amplitude, and rightward shift in the frontal QRS axis.95 In general, characteristic changes encountered in pneumothorax return to normal with the resolution of pneumothorax.
Treatment and Management

<TXL>The management options are dependent on the severity of the pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum, the predisposing state, and the underlying disease. Persons that present with a small, uncomplicated, asymptomatic pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum with no underlying lung disease present may (1) be monitored by careful observation in either the inpatient or the outpatient setting only, (2) undergo small-catheter pleural aspiration, (3) undergo small chest tube placement attached to a flutter valve (for pneumothorax), or (4) undergo chest tube drainage to evacuate the air (for pneumothorax).96

<TX>More complicated presentations generally require chest tube insertion attached to negative-pressure evacuation and underwater seal. Because recurrences of PSPs are common after the initial evacuation treatment, additional therapy may include chemical pleurodesis, open thoracotomy with pleural abrasion, or VAT in which blebs are stapled.96 A pleurodesis may be necessary with pleural abrasion, parietal pleurectomy, or talc insufflations after recurrence of pneumothorax. The use of supplemental oxygen in all cases (spontaneous pneumothorax and spontaneous pneumomediastinum) causes an increase in the gradient between nitrogen in the pleural space and nitrogen in the pleural capillary blood, promoting the movement of nitrogen out of the pleural space.92,93 When no evidence of reaccumulation of air is confirmed on chest radiograph following an adequate period of observation, the catheter can be removed.

<TX>Uncomplicated spontaneous pneumomediastinum is managed conservatively with analgesia, rest, and avoidance of maneuvers that increase pulmonary pressure (Valsalva or forced expiration, including spirometry). Asthma or another underlying lung disease is treated as indicated.93
Prognosis

<TXL>SSP is associated with a higher mortality and morbidity than PSP. The presence of pneumothorax in patients with HIV is thought to be an ominous sign and is associated with poor outcome. Pneumothorax occurs in 1–2% of hospitalized HIV patients and is associated with 30–34% mortality.97 Pneumomediastinum is generally considered a benign entity of little clinical importance with a good prognosis.98

<EOC_H1>Chapter Summary</EOC_H1>

<TXL>The thorax is a body cavity that contains the lungs, heart, great vessels, esophagus, trachea, nerves, and blood vessels that supply blood to these vital organs. Surrounding and protecting these organs is the chest wall, made up of the rib cage, sternum, spine, respiratory muscles, and diaphragm. The lungs are covered by thin, transparent double membranes that are in close contact with each other and cover the lungs and inner chest wall. Between these two thin flexible layers, there is normally about 10 mL of fluid surrounding each lung. Alterations of any of these structures can have major effects on the ability of the respiratory system to operate effectively, leading to respiratory distress and possibly failure. These alterations may come from direct trauma to the chest wall, chest wall deformities, infectious diseases, CHF, cancer, and other systemic diseases. The effects on the respiratory system may be immediate, as with chest trauma; may take days or weeks to develop, as with infectious diseases; or may take years to develop, as with chest wall deformities. The pulmonary effects depend on the severity of these disorders.
<EOC_H1>Key Points</EOC_H1>
<EOC_NL>

1.	The primary survey for chest trauma consists of assessing the airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure (ABCDEs of trauma care) of the trauma patient, looking for life-threatening injuries and addressing them immediately upon discovery.
2.	The secondary survey for chest trauma is a methodical examination of the respiratory system, looking for injuries that may have been missed with the primary survey.
3.	Chest trauma comes in several forms, but most cases are blunt injuries, penetrating injuries, or a combination of both.
4.	Chest trauma causes a local inflammatory response, and severe or multiple trauma evokes a systemic inflammatory response that can lead to ARDS and multiorgan failure.
5.	Chest wall deformities can lead to respiratory insufficiency by limiting the ability of the chest to expand while overworking the diaphragm.
6.	Obesity is a form of chest wall deformity because it limits chest expansion, decreases chest compliance, and increases the work of breathing.
7.	Limited movement of the chest wall manifests in reductions of lung volumes and appears on PFTs as a restrictive defect.

8.	Once the type of pleural effusion (exudative, transudative, parapneumonic, empyema) is determined by the drainage and evaluation of the fluid, the underlying disorder causing the disrupted physiologic condition can be treated.
9.	Transudative pleural effusions are caused mostly by CHF.
10.	One-quarter of all pleural effusions are due to a malignant process; many more go undiagnosed.

ABSTRACT: The weight of nursing’s voice and the growing evidence of nursing’s influence in shaping policy are transforming care and health, including the definition of health. But how do we continue to reform healthcare and advance global population health? The immediate answer is individually and collectively. This chapter provides an overview of policy, politics, and the interconnected barriers, challenges, and opportunities to address the geopolitical determinants of health. The power to shape policy exists in every role in nursing, from providers in the community and at the bedside to advanced practice providers, researchers, academia, boards, political action committees, and professional organizations. The chapter’s Policy Challenge describes the policy journey of an individual whose career is evolving into nursing with a focus on policy. Nursing’s power to shape policy is essential to all facets of health. The chapter highlights selected examples of nurses' diverse roles, which are often overlooked when discussing advocacy and politics.

CHAPTER 11: Applying the Nursing Lens to Shape Policy
GREER GLAZER AND ANGELA CLARK
The nursing lens . . .“is not simply a matter of parity. . . It’s a matter of perspective. Without the nurses’ voices and nursing lens, needed change cannot occur.”
—Joanne Disch, Past President, AARP, American Academy of Nursing
<H1>OBJECTIVES
Understand the interconnectedness among policy, politics, health policy, voting, and health reform.
Identify pathways for influencing policy at multiple levels (institutional, organizational, governmental: local, state, national, international).
Formulate strategies for expanding influence and commitment to policy engagement.
Model commitment to eliminating structural racism in the classroom, workplace, organization, and/or government.

Nurses and midwives account for just under 30 million individuals in the global health workforce (WHO, 2025). In the United States, there are over five million nurses, which is four times larger than the next biggest group of providers. The strength of nursing’s voice and the increasing evidence of its influence on shaping policy are transforming care and health, including the very definition of health. How can we continue to reform health care and advance global population health? The immediate answer lies in both individual and collective efforts. This chapter presents an overview of policy, politics, and the interconnected barriers, challenges, and opportunities that exist to address the geopolitical determinants of health. The power to shape policy resides in every role within nursing—from providers in the community and at the bedside to advanced practice providers, researchers, academics, boards, political action committees (PACs), and professional organizations. This chapter’s Policy Challenge outlines the policy journey of a millennial nurse.
<unnumberedbox>
<H1>POLICY CHALLENGE
The Nursing Lens of a Millennial
Marcus D. Henderson, MSN, RN, FNAP
PhD Candidate, Johns Hopkins University School of Nursing
Lecturer, University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing, Philadelphia, PA

My nursing career was inspired by my experience in middle school as a caregiver for my great-grandmother, who had Alzheimer’s disease, and my great-aunt, who had Down syndrome. I saw firsthand how home care, hospice, and acute care nurses helped maintain their dignity at the end of life, motivating me to pursue a career in nursing. Numerous strong women were my role models: partner, mother, grandmother, aunts, great-grandmother, and great-aunts. They provided me with resources of love and support, shaping me and my career as a nurse.

Mentorship has been important at every stage of my career. It started with a high school teacher, Jessica Way, a nurse. The mentor/mentee relationship gives each person perspective and can result in long-lasting relationships.

During high school, I began my activism by becoming the president of the Pennsylvania chapter of HOSA-Future Health Professionals. Its creed became my north star: “I believe through service to my community and the world, I will make the best use of my knowledge and talents” (HOSA-Future Health Professionals, 2020). I attribute my rapid professional development to the foundation provided.

At the start of my BSN program, I joined the National Student Nurses Association (NSNA), its state affiliate, and the school chapter. I attended the state convention that fall and was elected to the Student Nurses Association of Pennsylvania (SNAP) board. I served on its board for four years, as president from 2015 to 2017, and served on the NSNA board from 2016 to 2017. My SNAP/NSNA experience exposed me to the American Nurses Association (ANA) and the use of evidence to inform policy and decision-making. Throughout my undergraduate career, my mentoring network grew.

Initially aspiring to be a geriatric nurse, my focus shifted to community and psychiatric nursing when I was a research assistant at Penn Nursing's Center for Health Equity Research and had a clinical rotation at a local public high school. These experiences exposed me to social and structural health determinants, fueling my desire to help individuals and families thrive in their communities.

My professional involvement gave me the skills, leadership, and vision to compete for a $100,000 Penn President’s Engagement Prize (with my friend, Ian McCurry) for the project Homeless Health and Nursing: Building Community Partnerships for a Healthier Future in 2017. I witnessed the structural inequities disproportionately affecting underserved and marginalized populations. These men faced higher rates of unaddressed mental and behavioral health problems. I pursued psychiatric nursing to understand better the mental health care system, factors contributing to poor mental health, and mental health disparities. Working on an inpatient child and adolescent psychiatric unit, I observed high rates of mental health issues and hospitalizations, and the heavy burdens placed on families resulting from system deficiencies. This breadth of experience (see LinkedIn https://www.linkedin.com/in/marcushenderson1) and access to mentors shaped my nursing lens.
</unnumberedbox>
<H1>THE POWER OF NURSES TO SHAPE POLICY

Nursing’s power to shaping policy is crucial for all aspects of health. Policies exist at the unit (microsystem), organizational, and societal levels. These policies may emerge from individual efforts or collective actions. They can tackle social issues, organizational effectiveness, or health outcomes. Historically, the involvement of nurses in policy development and implementation across these three levels has been inconsistent. However, there is an increasing call to adopt a broader perspective to improve population health at the societal level. Population health, defined as the “health outcomes of a group of individuals, including distribution of such outcomes within the group,” provides a platform for individuals, healthcare systems, agencies, and organizations to work together in enhancing health outcomes in their communities (Kindig & Stoddart, 2003). Policy plays a significant role in advancing improvements in population health. Nursing boasts a rich history of leaders who have addressed population health issues. For example, Lillian Wald, recognized for founding public health in the late 1800s, established the Henry Street Settlement to support marginalized populations, with a focus on the social determinants of health (SDOHs). Public health nurses have carried on her legacy by striving to improve population health and achieve health equity within communities through health promotion, disease prevention and control, and advocacy.

Key healthcare organizations' policy definitions clarify the scope of efforts to improve health. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2015) defines policy as “a law, regulation, procedure, administrative action, incentive, or voluntary practice of governments and other institutions.” The WHO (2021) defines it as a complex dynamic process that requires key elements of engaging stakeholders, situation analysis, and priority setting, bringing it all together, from vision to operational, costing plans, monitoring, and evaluation. Broadly, health policy focuses on individual and population health and health equity, where “everyone has a fair and just opportunity to reach their full health potential.”

Equity and inclusion are essential to improving population health. Policy groups and think tanks have identified essential goals for improving health. The Institute of Medicine (IOM, 2001) identified six aims for healthcare improvement: safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. The Institute of Healthcare Improvement (IHI) has called health equity the forgotten aim (Feeley, 2016).

Health in All Policies (HiAP) is an approach to policy development that incorporates the health of all communities and individuals to promote and achieve health equity (CDC, 2016). HiAP expands the definitions of health policy by properly emphasizing the impact of policy on the SDOH, which are the “conditions in the environments in which people live, learn, work, play, worship and age that affect a wide range of health, functioning and quality of life outcomes and risks” (Department of Health and Human Services [DHHS], n.d., para. 1). These conditions include economic stability, social and community context, health and health care, education, and the built environment.

While social determinants of health were prominently included in the Future of Nursing 2020-2030 Report and most nurses understand what they are, the term political determinants of health (PDOH) were not mentioned. Few nurses are aware of this foundational concept. Political determinants of health “involve the systematic process of structuring relationships, distributing resources, and administering power, operating simultaneously in ways that mutually reinforce or influence one another to shape opportunities that either advance health equity or exacerbate health inequities” (Dawes 2020). Political determinants of health are at the root of social determinants of health and the policy choices that have shaped them. The PDOH create social drivers that impact our health. The three categories of PDOH are voting, government, and policy. Holding policymakers accountable through voting is vital to addressing PDOH.

Voter registration, a non-partisan activity that directly impacts public investment in health and health care, is foundational to our nursing practice as patient advocates for health and health care for everyone. Safe and equitable access to voting is a PDOH, a fundamental right and responsibility for each of us. Bipartisan voter registration efforts should be viewed as our professional duty. Since 83% of people in the United States visit a medical facility yearly, and 62% of unregistered voters have never been asked to register, healthcare settings offer an opportunity to assist eligible individuals in registering to vote (Vot-ER, 2024). States with greater voting access report better health outcomes (Vot-ER, 2024). It is concerning that marginalized populations are less likely to vote compared to the general population, and registered nurses are 10% less likely to vote than the general population (Vot-ER, 2024). Though this varies by state, nurse researchers in Ohio analyzed the voting turnout of Ohio nurses compared to the general population for the general elections in November 2020, 2022, and 2023. Nurses consistently exhibited a turnout of roughly 10-12% higher each year, with APRNs showing the highest turnout and LPNs the lowest among nurses (Ludwick, Zalon, Patton, and Baughman, 2024). While turnout in the state is higher than in the general population, only 71% of Ohio nurses are registered to vote (Zalon, Ludwick, Patton, 2024).
<H2>THE CURRENT ENVIRONMENT

Current executive orders and shifting state laws that prohibit diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts create dilemmas for nurses in practice, education, administration, and the community. The ANA Code of Ethics (ANA, 2025) requires nurses to advocate for underserved populations, confront implicit bias, provide anti-racist care and education, and acknowledge as well as address health disparities and health inequities. The American Academy of Nursing remains steadfast in its mission to improve health and achieve health equity by influencing policy through nursing leadership, innovation, and science (www.aan.org). The ANA-Ohio Board of Directors has reaffirmed its commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion and continues to use these terms without hesitation.

Improvements in the social determinants of health (SDOHs) cannot occur without policy changes. The groundwork for addressing SDOHs is laid out in Healthy People 2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the United Nations (UN). Healthy People 2030 provides a framework for addressing SDOHs (see Figure 14.2 in Chapter 14). Nurses must engage in organizational, local, state, and federal policy, applying a HiAP strategy to achieve health equity goals and ultimately eliminate health gaps (DHHS, n.d.). The UN SDGs, totaling 17, offer a roadmap for improving SDOHs from a global perspective (see Chapter 14). The SDGs, signed by all UN member nations in 2015, focus on ending poverty and other deprivations; they must be included in efforts to “improve health and education, reduce inequality, and spur economic growth” while also addressing climate change and preserving oceans and forests (UN, n.d., para. 1). Health reform through policy development and political implementation significantly enhances health equity and population health. The CDC attributes the last century's Ten Great Public Health Achievements to the interplay between policy, politics, and health. However, addressing health reform requires political connectedness at all levels (CDC, 2011).

Given their various roles across sectors, nurses are uniquely positioned to lead and shape policy through advocacy for health reform. They need to leverage their 23-year first-place ranking in honesty and ethical standards among professions not for bragging but as an opportunity to influence policy (Saad, 2020). In a survey on Americans’ values and beliefs regarding national health insurance reform conducted by the Commonwealth Fund, The New York Times, & Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2019), Americans generally did not trust major interest groups other than nurses to improve the U.S. healthcare system. Americans trusted nurses (58%) to lead healthcare reform, 28 percentage points higher than physicians, who were trusted to improve the healthcare system at 30%.

Nurses need to use their influence to get seats at policy tables. The future of health and health care is in the hands of nurses, but there are challenges. The fractured public healthcare system in the United States is buckling under the multiple epidemic threats and a system plagued with implicit bias and structural racism. The United States spends 16.9% of its gross domestic product on health care (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, 2024), more than any other country! Despite this, the United States has the most significant income inequity, the highest poverty rates, and some of the poorest health outcomes among the developed countries (Tikkanen, 2020). People of color and low socioeconomic status experience more disease burden and decreased life expectancy (Andrasfay & Goldman, 2021; Woolf & Schoomaker, 2019). Nurses have a front-row seat to this fractured public health system, and with their nurse lens, they need front-row policy seats. Former Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm (n.d.) pointed out, “If they don’t give you a seat at the table, bring a folding chair.” If necessary, we must bring our folding chairs in work settings, organizations, boards, and local, state, and national governments.
<H1>THE NURSING LENS

The nursing lens, based on understanding of nursing history, education, and practical experience, differentiates nurses from others when they engage in the political process. The nursing lens is a “viewpoint from which someone sees things holistically, considering the person, population or community in the larger context” (Disch, 2012, p. 170). The prevailing perspective is that the history of nursing is founded on social justice, health equity, public health, and community advocacy.

In nursing’s history, this lens has also been grounded and limited by a Eurocentric, White viewpoint, negating the experiences of many nurses and patients. Regrettably, most nurses know little about other historic nurses who were persons of color (POCs) because this history is not part of textbooks, publications, or education. Nurses know about Florence Nightingale. She is credited with establishing nursing as a profession, a holistic approach to health promotion, evidence-based practice, and recognizing the impact of the physical and social environment of health (precursor to the concept of SDOHs). Her status was recognized by the WHO in 2020—the 200th anniversary of Nightingale’s birth—as the International Year of the Nurse and Midwife.

Yet some researchers posit another angle from which to view Nightingale: “What is often unknown and rarely discussed in nursing history is Nightingale’s racism and her political role in the genocide of Indigenous people under British rule” (Stake-Doucet, 2020, “Nightingale and Colonialism”). The New Zealand Nurses Organization did not celebrate Nightingale in 2020 due to her role in advising their governor (late 1800s), who fueled the harsh repression against Māori anti-colonial uprisings. Nightingale’s contemporary, Mary Grant Seacole, a Black Jamaican nurse, also served in the Crimean War, but despite being recognized for her selfless treatment of wounded soldiers, she was never given an official position by Nightingale. While it is beyond the scope of this chapter to provide a more comprehensive picture of the many contributions of nurse leaders who were POCs, we recommend Darlene Clark Hine’s Black Women in White: Racial Conflict and Cooperation in the Nursing Profession 1890–1950 (Hine, 1989).

More national initiatives are changing the narrative of our historical, narrow view of nursing. The national commission to address racism in nursing was established in 2021 by ANA (American Nurses Association), NBNA (National Black Nurses Association), NCEMNA (National Coalition of Ethnic Minority Nurse Association), and NAHN (National Association of Hispanic Nurses) to focus on the impact of racism on nurses, patients, communities, and healthcare systems “to motivate all nurses to confront individual and systemic racism” (www.nursingworld.org). Recommendations for individuals include understanding what racism is, discovering how pervasive racism is in nursing, hearing directly from other nurses about their experiences, sharing stories, and learning how to make a difference daily.

The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation funded a national study involving 980 nurses to gain insights into their experiences and perceptions of discrimination (RWJF, 2023). Disheartening findings revealed that 79% of nurses reported witnessing or experiencing racism or discrimination from patients, while 59% faced it from colleagues. Fewer than 25% of nurses formally reported the racism or discrimination they encountered to management in their workplaces. Furthermore, eighty percent of nurses believe that zero-tolerance workplace discrimination policies, clear consequences, and reporting anonymity would improve the ability to retain racially and ethnically diverse nurses (RWJF, 2023).

While many nursing organizations have developed reconciliation statements, the American Academy of Nursing (AAN) adopted a reflection statement (rather than a reconciliation statement) to emphasize progress and illustrate the journey that has shaped us through societal context, individual conscious and unconscious bias, and organizational policies (Scott, November 2, 2024, aaninfo@aannet.org). Other contemporary reports and documents that influence the nursing lens include the revised American Nurses Association Code of Ethics for Nurses (ANA, 2025). The Code outlines all nurses' ethical obligations and responsibilities to address social justice in nursing and health policy (see Chapter 2) (ANA, 2025).

Another significant report is The Future of Nursing 2020-2030, which urges all national nursing organizations to establish a shared agenda for addressing social determinants of health and achieving health equity, with clear priorities for nursing practice, education, leadership, and health policy engagement.

The nursing lens is rooted in more than our history. It is grounded in the education we receive and our practice (skills and setting). Nursing programs prepare students to view individuals holistically, considering their families and communities. Our educational system emphasizes the importance of the patient perspective, focusing on strengths, person-centered care, compassion, and health equity. We demonstrate our skills in listening, assessment, interpersonal communication, ethical decision-making, critical thinking, etc., across various practice settings (e.g., homes, hospitals, community health centers, schools, workplaces, retail clinics, and places of worship). Both educational and practical perspectives enhance nurses’ capacity to find personalized solutions that are both practical and attainable.

When nursing history, educational preparation, and clinical practice are integrated, the nursing lens offers a multifaceted understanding of care recipients from a holistic, broad perspective that reflects an awareness of the intersectionality of factors determining health. The nursing lens embodies the understanding, articulation, and advocacy of individual and community perspectives, aiming to achieve maximum health for all. They can quickly assess situations and individuals. The nursing lens centers on the guiding question, “What is in the patient's best interest?” as its north star. Health and healthcare equity are our goals. With the nurse lens, nurses grasp the human condition's intricacies and complexities. Consequently, nurses can develop solutions or access resources where none appear to exist.

The following sections highlight selected examples of the diverse roles nurses hold that are often overlooked in discussions about advocacy and politics. These nontraditional roles can be overlooked because some mistakenly believe that nurses in these positions have abandoned the nursing perspective and are no longer “real nurses.” Nurses themselves may assert they could not consider such atypical positions because it would mean “giving up nursing” and the opportunities to advance nursing. However, leaders who began their careers in direct patient care have discovered many opportunities to positively impact both patients and fellow nurses in their less conventional roles.
<H1>INFLUENCING POLICY THROUGH EMPLOYMENT

The path to nurse policy involvement often begins at work, frequently through volunteering for a committee or responding “yes” when asked to serve. Policy work is an excellent way to make a difference; it affects not only the lives of the public that nurses serve but also their work environment. Whether one is a new nurse or an experienced professional, a direct care provider, a leader on a unit or in the C-suite, an educator, a researcher, or holds an advanced degree, every nurse can play a role in policy. Various roles allow for active and varied engagement in policy including its analysis, creation, implementation, evaluation, and/or modification. Active engagement also encompasses role modeling and mentorship. Those with advanced degrees and formal leadership positions are expected to take on policy roles. Nurses without a special title or credentials can encourage a colleague to start on a policy journey by highlighting the importance of an issue, attending meetings, or participating in a policy project.

Committee work is a good starting point. It not only offers opportunities to build political skills but also helps develop essential networking skills, strengthens existing connections, and provides chances for mentorship. Organizations frequently seek members and chairpersons to lead committees or task forces, both in the workplace and in local communities. When starting committee work, begin by finding a mentor and clarifying expectations. Without guidance, committee members may lose focus on the work at hand and or valuable start-up time. Both seasoned and new members can benefit from formal orientations to any new committee.

Often though, the first step is to express interest—and often just to show up. Highlighted here are three nurses, Kevin Sowers, Antoinette Hays, and Linda Thompson, who share their stories of how they became involved in policy work and now strive to influence policy beyond nursing.

Kevin W. Sowers, MSN, RN, FAAN, president of the Johns Hopkins Health System (JHHS) and executive vice president of Johns Hopkins Medicine (JHM), is first a nurse. His lens is framed by the commitment that patients and their loved ones are central to everything in health care despite frequent changes in technology, care models, and organization disruptions. He is committed to thinking through policy at all levels to support and balance this tenet.

Sowers understood the need for and importance of hard work. He spent his formative years growing up in poverty and focusing on voice and piano. He spent summer days working at the county nursing home, providing music therapy, and evenings at his second job as an orderly, feeding people, bathing them, and assisting with nightly routines. He fell in love with making a difference in people’s lives and was inspired to make a career change to nursing, a decision that did not reflect the workforce when men were not as prominent in the field. Sowers’s supportive mother was foundational to him. She saw he had the passion and compassion to create change and make a real difference for patients and nurses alike. Sowers started out as an oncology staff nurse at Duke University Hospital System in 1985. He took on nurse manger roles before accepting a vice president role and then a senior vice president role at Duke.

Sowers’s contributions include extensive publications and consultations on leadership, mentorship, and organizational change. He is active among professional organizations and boards, both current and past, including the American Hospital Association (AHA) Health Systems Council, Maryland Hospital Association Executive Board, the Vizient Board of Directors, and the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) Council of Teaching Hospitals and Health Systems Administrative Board, to name a few (Johns Hopkins Medicine, n.d.; Rossbach, 2018).

Sowers attributes his success to relationships, collaboration, succinct message delivery, intent, rationale, and an outcome-oriented approach. “You must be able to tell your story. When I go into any legislator’s office, I always begin with ‘as a nurse.’ I’ve found the power behind being a nurse, and having people know I’m a nurse is immensely helpful. It begins a different dialogue and a different listening session because I’m coming from the place of a nurse versus an administrator.”

Sowers has standing meetings with the legislators because “it’s important to have an ongoing dialogue. Every conversation can’t come with an ask.” He suggests instead to remain collaborative and use language that emphasizes partnership. When negotiating, you will never get everything you want. Look at the resources around you; most organizations have government affairs departments that can help provide discussion data points. Understand a politician or senior official’s beliefs and agenda. Develop a strategy for managing communication before you enter the room and negotiate.

An example of this strategy is his approach to healthcare delivery disruptions from COVID-19.  Sowers, only in his role as JHHS president and JHM executive vice president for two years, intentionally learned the region’s history that contributed to contemporary social determinants of health because “It’s important as one responsible for influencing and shaping policies to understand the linkages of the past to the present before making decisions that will resonate for generations to come.” Sowers recognized how decisions impact people and why it is vital to hear the voices of those affected by our choices. He believes that as leaders, we must appreciate the dynamic nature of the places in which we live and work.

Sowers led a public/private stakeholder partnership traditionally viewed as competitors. Together, these representatives from the private payor industry, academia, healthcare organizations, as well as state and local leaders, created avenues to engage the community and drive decisions, developing plans and policies focused on education, communication, vaccinations, and the flow of COVID-19 patients throughout the region. Sowers shared, “We also realized that it was within our collective interest to manage resources and make decisions jointly.”

Another approach was to show the value of academic medical centers and their importance to the community and the public at large. The Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health quickly established a COVID Resource Center, a vital tool for tracking COVID-19 cases worldwide. Educators developed remote learning capabilities. Researchers uncovered how COVID spread and developed vaccines rapidly. Leaders used data to identify vulnerable groups—such as the elderly, those in nursing care facilities, and communities of color—who were disproportionately affected by the pandemic. This included increased COVID cases reported in these populations and groups whose lives were significantly impacted financially by the closure of schools and businesses. The public/private partnership addressed immediate needs and influenced evolving policies during that time, affecting the social determinants of health for years to come.

Patient care policies also were developed to manage the flow of COVID-19 patients regionally, ensuring that no single facility was overwhelmed. This approach allowed for continued services for non-COVID patients. JHHS collaborated to convert the Baltimore Convention Center into a 250-bed field hospital, serving as a site for COVID testing, mass vaccination, and an infusion center that administered FDA-authorized monoclonal antibody therapies for COVID patients. Policies were established to guarantee that patients at this facility received the same quality of care as those at JHHS hospitals and clinics. The ability to share data and resources was crucial in this effort. JHHS also engaged local hotels, which had remained empty due to business closures, to serve as recovery facilities for unhoused people who needed safe places to heal.

Sowers was also concerned about his team’s resilience and ability to navigate so many challenges simultaneously. His leadership team organized a town meeting for staff to connect with leaders from Johns Hopkins to discuss social justice matters, what they were already doing, and what they could do further in this area. They also created modules to help managers engage in conversations with their team members. Because the COVID crisis affected already vulnerable communities, they learned that some staff had family members whose jobs had been impacted by business closures. They were struggling to feed their families, pay bills, and care for children and elderly loved ones who were home all day due to COVID restrictions. The team developed a program that allowed JHHS employees to apply for financial support and/or computers to assist children who had to switch to remote learning. They also established local, entity-level food banks, creating places for staff to get free food for their loved ones.

Despite numerous challenges, crises can create an opportunity for leaders across industries to showcase their collective ability to care for the people in their communities. For Sowers, it clarified the value of nursing in a global society. Sowers says, “When I began my career at the bedside, I never dreamed that one day I would stand at the helm of one of the top health systems, leading at the forefront of a worldwide pandemic. My experience is a true testament to the extraordinary power of a nursing career in preparing future leaders. My 40 years as a nurse prepared me to lead during the COVID crisis. It set the foundation for me to sit at the table with leaders representing the interests of governments and industries, working together to develop human-focused policies that will shape the world of tomorrow.”

Antoinette Hays, PhD, RN, became the 10th President of Regis College in Weston, Massachusetts, a comprehensive liberal arts institution, in 2011. She firmly believes that her experiences as a nurse were key motivators and laid the groundwork for her current role. As a BSN student at Boston College, she learned to advocate for her patients using a person-centered approach, understanding the critical role of patients in care decisions. Upon graduation, she worked in geriatrics because she saw the incredible gaps in long-term care, the challenges of managing multiple medical comorbidities, and the need to enhance the quality of care for older adults. Very quickly, she experienced two profound realities in geriatric care: first, the essential skill of multitasking, as she was often the only registered nurse on a clinical unit, and second, how ageism influenced the social, economic, and policy injustices related to the care of older adults. Equally important, she acknowledged the social and economic injustices within the nursing profession.

Antoinette’s passion for influencing change and policy ignited in 1976 when she enrolled in the Geriatric Nurse Practitioner Program and master’s program in Gerontology and Community Health at Boston University (BU). Partnering with the medical team, she launched the Geriatric NP role at the Boston Visiting Nurses Association (VNA), creating a linkage between the new role of the APRN in the care of the geriatric client across the care continuum from home to hospital to long-term care and back to home.

Hays’s academic career significantly evolved through this experience. In 1979, she began as an assistant professor in the graduate Geriatric NP Program at the BU School of Nursing, with a joint appointment in the Department of Geriatric Medicine. In that role, she developed and launched a new Multidisciplinary Acute Geriatric Consultation Program at BUMC. She designed curricula across disciplines (nursing, medicine, and social work), engaged in clinical research, presented at conferences, and authored peer-reviewed publications. By 1980, this program had become a national model for acute geriatric care, integral to the inaugural Geriatric Medical Fellowship Program and a mandatory rotation for all medical residents at BU Hospital.

Her next goal was to pursue a doctoral degree at the Heller School of Social Policy at Brandeis University in Waltham, Massachusetts. It provided a pathway to enhance geriatric healthcare through research and education. She often witnessed healthcare providers feeling helpless as victims in the policy arena. It was evident to her that nurses need to be at the policy table with data to advocate and focus on changes rather than remain frustrated onlookers.

During Hays’s doctoral studies, she helped launch a new Nursing Leadership and Advanced-Practice program at Regis College, incorporating a curriculum designed to prepare future nursing leaders and advanced nurse practitioners within a policy research and practice framework. In 1993, she was hired by Regis College as an assistant professor and subsequently advanced to the position of dean of the School of Nursing, Science, and Health Professions from 2006 to 2011, before being selected as the college’s president in 2011. Throughout this period, she actively participated in the Massachusetts Association of Colleges of Nursing (MACN). As a board member and treasurer of MACN, the Nursing Deans and Directors began meeting with the Massachusetts Chief Nurse Executives (CNOs) through joint meetings of the MACN and the Massachusetts Organization of Nurse Executives. Hays’s perspective on systems enhanced the group’s understanding that academia could not advance without practice and vice versa. Massachusetts emerged as a leader in operationalizing academic-practice partnerships in the mid-2000s.

Hays’s evolving career often presented her challenges to launch new, innovative roles or programs. Although this was sometimes daunting, she cherished the chance to “step out of the box” and challenge the norm, always viewing the situation through a nursing lens as she evaluated how systems could be improved to enhance practice experiences and the quality of patient care outcomes. She recognized the critical role of system analysis and research in persuading others of the importance of innovation in practice. This principle became integral to her work, whether on clinical teams, with faculty partners, administrators, or global partners in Haiti, striving to improve health care and higher education outcomes.

Recognizing that change could only occur with the support and buy-in of others, Hays prioritized her role as a consensus builder. Excellence tempered by gentleness had always characterized Hays’s approach as a provider, teacher, and leader, which continues to serve her well as an innovator in the United States, Haiti, and now, as a university president. Her years in nursing practice and education provided the foundation through which she became a strategic partner, policy advocate, and change agent. She applies her system assessment daily regarding the interconnectedness of a healthcare organization, a community, or a related industry. Interdependence and partnerships are central to policy, whether in patient care, education, business, or global outreach. Hays values the power of collective intelligence in enhancing outcomes in patient care, student success, and a university’s success.

However, Hays believes that influencing workplace policy does not require holding a leadership position; every nurse needs to participate in policy development, implementation, and evaluation. Nurses can initiate and join unit committees to create policies that will enhance patient outcomes and prioritize their health and well-being. Similarly, nursing faculty can start and engage in committees at their schools or colleges to improve student learning and success, as well as those that support their own health and well-being. When nurses begin at the local level, they build the confidence and experience necessary to expand their policy involvement.

Linda Thompson, PhD, RN, FAAN, is the President of Westfield State University. Linda Thompson was not born with the proverbial “silver spoon in her mouth.” Her early years were quite the opposite. Thompson hails from Detroit, where her mother was a single parent relying on welfare. When her mother became too ill to care for her, Thompson entered foster care. She often faced teasing about the differences between her and her foster mother, and says that despite being in “…a very loving foster family who tried to manage my anxiety,” she often “felt like a target.”
She compares her life then to that of her two older sisters, noting, “They got into trouble with the justice system, so I saw the impact of that on their life.”

From the early adversity of her childhood and witnessing her sisters' lives during those years, Thompson knew she wanted to help others and make a change. That drive centered on at-risk youth, their circumstances, shifting delinquent behaviors, and working to promote healthy outcomes. When speaking of her sisters, who both experienced teen pregnancies, Thompson says, “I started to see the link between education…when you don’t have a good education and the outcomes and the pathway to a criminal life or the justice system. I started to be concerned about what are the factors (characteristics, issues) that lead a person to go into that pathway.”

Thompson has focused her career on improving the lives of children, especially foster kids, those with special needs, and those in juvenile justice systems, through nursing, education, and public policy. Significant policy positions include working in Baltimore City’s cabinet in the '90s as Director of Occupational Medicine and Safety. She oversaw programs and policies that promote workforce health, including hard issues like HIV prevention and substance. She next served at the state level as Special Secretary of Children, Youth and Families for Maryland, overseeing a budget of $350 million while continuing her work to improve the quality of care for vulnerable children (e.g., foster care, special education). Unlike some of the leaders in this chapter, Thompson’s career trajectory moved to academia after early public policy positions.

However, she did not abandon policy. Her groundbreaking research on incarcerated youth and their need for mental health assessments led to the development of a national policy requiring mental health assessments for all detained and sentenced youth. She is widely recognized for creating integrated multidisciplinary models for vulnerable children that enhance their health and safety. Her more recent research emphasizes promoting healthy lifestyles to combat childhood obesity, a field where significant new policy work is emerging. Many of the programs to which she has contributed have been replicated both nationally and internationally.

Even after publishing over 100 articles, books, etc., receiving numerous awards, serving on innumerable boards and commissions, and obtaining multimillions in grant funds, she remains dedicated to improving the lives of vulnerable children and fostering collaborations to promote that ideal. The following quote illustrates her lifelong philosophy about policy, which is more critical today than ever before: “If the United States is to retain its position as an economic and social force in the future, it must focus more attention on the well-being of children. Indeed, if children, families, and communities are to prosper into the next century, all children must be given an opportunity to grow up in a caring, nurturing, and safe environment, be educated, and have a sense of hope for a bright future” (Thompson, 1999).
<H1>INFLUENCING POLICY THROUGH ORGANIZATIONS

Organizations are like people in that they possess values, a mission or purpose, and a vision. They can be shaped by those involved or associated with them. Leaders often play a significant role in determining the values, purposes, visions, and strategic actions within their organizations. These elements guide the organization's positions and establish recommendations on important issues, forming the foundation on which they will seek to influence matters or policies.

Organizational values influence policies. Some values are central to the organization's mission and vision; thus, they endure over time. For example, ANA collaborated with the nursing community in 1991 to develop Nursing’s Agenda for Health Care Reform (Betts, 1996), which was updated in 2008. Previous organizational positions and recommendations guided ANA’s policy stance that healthcare is a basic human right and that all individuals deserve access to essential healthcare services. Nursing’s Blueprint for Healthcare Reform, backed by an overwhelming majority of specialty nurses’ associations, was a guide for developing the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA), which was enacted in 2010.

Pam Cipriano, PhD, RN, FAAN, International Council of Nurses President, the 35th president of the American Nurses Association (ANA), and a former dean, is a highly accomplished global leader. Growing up as the youngest of three children in a traditional Italian family significantly influenced her. She stated that she learned a lot as the youngest sibling (raised in the 1940s and 1950s) by observing her older brother and sister. Cipriano shared, “As first-generation college students, we had supportive parents, my father in particular. He said I could do whatever I wanted, but I had to choose a college that was not expensive. I started at a basic liberal arts college for two years, and I hated it. It was out in the middle of nowhere in rural Pennsylvania, and I wasn't doing well. I had been a Medtech major; I’d taken chemistry and biology classes, and I said, what can I do with that? I knew I had to leave.

My parents weren’t happy, and I didn't really have a plan. In the spring of my sophomore year, my mother's best friend's daughter was a faculty member at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania Diploma School, and she convinced me to go there. While not attending a baccalaureate program was a mistake then, this was still an incredible learning experience in many ways. I got very involved right away in the Pennsylvania Student Nurses Association.

My diploma experience helped me realize that to truly advance in nursing, I first needed to return to school. I became involved in the Philadelphia chapter of the National Student Nurse Association (NSNA) and later in the state chapter. I traveled across the country and was elected as the first Vice President of NSNA at a national meeting. The following year, I became president. Those were significant formative steps in shaping my career and aspirations. The motivation for joining the NSNA chapters was that membership was mandatory in the nursing program. It was common for students to become members, especially in diploma schools automatically.”

Cipriano became excited about attending meetings and, in that first year, volunteered for the Breakthrough to Nursing project, which focused on recruiting nursing students into the profession, developing leadership skills, and offering mentorship. This initiative became a national program in 1964 (www.nsna.org). In her second or third year, it transitioned into an HRSA-funded program that still exists today (Breakthrough to Nursing, https://www.nsna.org/breakthrough-to-nursing-committee.html).
NSNA provided another opportunity for Pam.

“At the time that the NSNA president had a very intimate role with the ANA. I was on the Commission of Education, and I was given significant responsibilities. I also met with all the leaders of both ANA and NLN. I met Jesse Scott, an RN, the Assistant Surgeon General of the United States, who directed the Nursing Division of the United States Public Health Service (PHS). Scott testified before Congress about nursing education needs, and some of her testimony resulted in the creation of the Nurse Training Act of 1964.

Further, even attending NSNA conventions was life changing. I heard the well-known speaker, Judith Blackfeather, who made such an impression on me to learn about different things, how people responded in life, how health care affected their lives, and how we as nurses needed to think about those differences and effects.”
Pam also noted that when she got her BSN, there was only one black person in a class of 100, which made her wonder how there was such a mismatch among nurses and people served.

In our interview, Cipriano reflected on the importance of health policy. “I think of policy as encompassing both the Big `P’ (public or governmental policies) and the little ‘p’ (private or non-governmental policies),” she said, although she now tends to focus on the Big “P.” This is primarily due to her career experiences, as those represent the guiding principles, requirements, and rules for how we function as a society. However, her Big “P” work has been informed by little ‘p” work as a CNS in adult critical care in the unit where she worked and within the organization.

At the Big “P” level, Cipriano’s work as ANA president (2014-2018) is significant. She was president during the Ebola outbreak and became the face of calm, accurate information for the public. Her policy work involved advocating and collaborating with physicians and the American Hospital Association to provide the media with appropriate details regarding quarantine, suitable treatment, and requirements for all nurses and frontline emergency medical providers, including emergency care and the emergency department’s response to screening, detection, and all matters related to Ebola. This visibility immediately escalated nursing's role, with a wide range of information being shared. It combined a public health emergency response with policy approaches simultaneously.

Other significant policy issues championed under Cipriano’s presidency were firearm safety and the Healthy Nurse Healthy Nation (HNHN) Initiative. She guided the ANA board in creating policy statements on firearm violence and sensible firearm legislation. The HNHN program was initiated by ANA to prioritize nurses' well-being. The program connects and engages nurses and now partner organizations to take action on mental health, physical activity, sleep, nutrition, quality of life, and safety (https://www.healthynursehealthynation.org/).

As ICN President, Cipriano has demonstrated relentless advocacy for safe nursing environments, the well-being of the global workforce of nearly 30 million nurses, and the visibility of the nursing profession through policy and advocacy, leadership development, and disaster response. The depth and breadth of Pam’s policy expertise has made her a sought-after thought leader, recognized globally as a highly regarded collaborator and an effective spokesperson for the world’s nurses and consumers. As a testament to these qualities, she has been appointed co-chair of the Universal Health Coverage (UHC) Steering Committee (UHC2030) for the United Nations. (See Figure 11.1.) This important and prestigious appointment places her on the international stage, working with multiple stakeholders to enhance the global commitment toward UHC. During her tenure, ICN has released multiple new position statements (see examples: Health care in conflict: the nursing perspective, 2025; Nurses, climate change and health, 2024; and Gender equity in health and healthcare, 2023 https://www.icn.ch/what-we-do/position-statements).

Pam’s superpower is the ability to advance the nursing profession in healthcare, enhancing care quality, fostering economic growth, and improving health outcomes. Cipriano describes this success as grounded in being credible, honest, a quick thinker, and a good listener who often uses questions as a tool. “You must pay attention to what people say and respond tactfully...Ask more questions, never criticize the individual, and avoid attacking someone at their core. That’s a leadership skill everyone should cultivate. You can discuss behaviors you dislike without labeling them as intrinsic to the person. It's about responding tactfully in the moment and being able to challenge a statement, position, or action. To influence at any level, we need persistence to do the right thing.”

Beverly Malone, PhD, RN, FAAN, President and CEO of the National League for Nursing, exemplifies an American nurse who has significantly influenced health policy through her leadership in three major national and international organizations: the ANA, the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) in the United Kingdom, and the National League for Nursing (NLN). She has received numerous recognitions like inclusion in Modern Healthcare’s list (2020) of the “100 Most Influential People in Healthcare,” marking four times in last ten years that she appeared there.
Her great-grandmother, a healer in the community, served as her earliest role model: “She required everyone to eat before drinking and taught me how you work with the community.”

Malone’s experience as a psychiatric–mental health nurse, clinical specialist, administrator, and faculty member shaped her nursing perspective about the importance of relationships. She believes that policy is deeply intertwined with relationships. Being a nurse means that Malone embodied policy, just as all nurses do: “How do you walk into a room and end up doing something personal with a patient and family if you don’t have the ability to relate in an incredibly personal way?”

Malone’s nursing lens as an African American nurse emphasizes equity and the crucial need to ensure that everyone is cared for, including those unable to care for themselves, and individuals facing mental health challenges.

While Malone was working on her doctorate, her mentor, Dr. Hattie Bessent, encouraged her to go to Washington, D.C., to gain a better understanding of federal policy in the policy arena. In 1979, she worked for one summer as a legislative intern for Senator Inouye (D-HI), becoming the first African American nurse on Capitol Hill.

She returned the following summer, having gained a deeper understanding of policy and how to collaborate with the government. Her relationship to Inouye was important and he called on her for help. He asked Malone to find funding to build a rehabilitation center in Hawaii. She requested the deputy assistant secretary for the money, but he replied that he did not have any funds available for this project. When she reported that back to Inouye, he instructed her to verify if it was true that the administrator had no money. Malone discovered that there were funds, and she was directed to call the secretary and inform him that he was lying.

As a skilled psychiatric nurse, Malone called and said, “It seems there was a misunderstanding: we need the $500,000 that you have for the center in Hawaii. The senator said that if you don’t put the money in your proposed budget forward, then you won’t have any money at all.”

The money was located, and the rehabilitation center was built. Malone utilized her interpersonal communication skills as a nurse and refrained from calling the appointed officer a liar, which would have likely ended their conversation. Malone had developed the relational skills necessary to get things done.

Malone has a favorite saying, “I can be delayed but not defeated.” She shares an example of perceived failure from her time as Interim Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University in 1994, where she had served as a dean and professor since 1986. During her term as interim vice chancellor, she led a successful Southern Association of Colleges and Schools (SACS) accreditation visit and a Family Science and Environment accreditation process, and when it opened, she applied for the permanent position. Unexpectedly, she did not get it. Initially, she thought her career was over. Then she realized it was merely delayed: “Sometimes you have to get to a place, turn around, and look back to see the opportunities.”

Malone needed this twist in her plans and a closed door to reach her next big opportunity: becoming the president of the ANA in 1996, a role she held until 2000. She served on ANA’s board of directors as second vice president, chair of the Legislation Committee, vice chair of the Ethnic Minority Fellowship Program, and as a member of the Finance Committee. “You don’t just become president of an organization one day without having provided prior significant service in the organization,” said Malone, who had previously served in leadership roles at the state level.

As president of the ANA, she represented the association on issues affecting the nation’s health care and the professional requirements of a diverse nursing workforce to ensure safe, quality care. She worked closely with the President of the United States’ Office and Congress, providing consultation and testimony, and serving on numerous federal commissions, committees, and taskforces. Significant achievements during this time include serving on President Clinton’s Advisory Commission on Consumer Protection and Quality in the Healthcare Industry (1996–1998), where she helped develop the Patients’ Bill of Rights, the National Forum for Healthcare Quality Measurement and Reporting (1998–1999), and her appointment by President Clinton to the World Health Assembly (1998, 1999). She represented nurses and nursing at various press conferences in support of the Patients’ Bill of Rights and the Patient Safety Act.

At the end of Malone’s ANA presidency, she was appointed Deputy Assistant Secretary for Health from 1999 to 2001, serving as the senior advisor to the Assistant Secretary of Health. She also provided advice and counsel to the Secretary of Health and Human Services (DHHS) on public health and science issues. Her portfolio included mental health, international healthcare, food safety, disaster relief, and any public health issues that arose.

Opportunity knocked in 2001 when Malone became the general secretary of the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) in the United Kingdom, the largest professional union for nursing staff in the world; she held this position until 2007. As chief executive, reporting to the elected RCN Council across the U.K., Malone provided leadership to over 1,000 staff, transforming the organization to better meet the needs and desires of its members. Her intensive influencing and legislative activities included regular meetings with government figures like the prime minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and politicians from all major U.K. political parties, among others. During Malone’s tenure as general secretary, Prime Minister Tony Blair appointed her to the World Health Assembly from 2002 to 2003, which led to an invitation to a state dinner where she was seated next to then-Prince Charles (King Charles).

Malone returned to the United States in 2007 as chief executive officer of the National League for Nursing (NLN), a position she still holds today. Dedicated to excellence in nursing education, the NLN is a membership organization for nurse faculty and leaders in nursing education. In this role, Malone has testified before Congress, subcommittees, and federal agencies on Title VIII appropriations (funding for nursing education) and funding for the Nurse Education Act.

Malone’s prolific policy contributions through her leadership in national and international organizations have always been viewed through her nursing lens, emphasizing equity, service, and placing people at the center of her work. She is dedicated to caring for others and believes in fostering excellent relationships and communication: “Nurses are committed to taking care of patients and creating a better place for them.”

She believes that any nurse can engage in policy work, noting “It is a cinch by an inch, and it’s hard by the yard. Understand we are the healers; even doing policy, we are in the business of healing.”
Malone reminds us that we do not exist as nurses without patients: “We are who we are because of our patients.”

Catherine Alicia Georges, EdD, RN, FAAN, is the professor and chairperson emerita of the Department of Nursing at Lehman College, City University of New York, and serves as an exemplar for service leadership by shaping policy through boards and organizations, functioning as a conduit for community and population health. Georges was raised in the U.S. Virgin Islands, where her godmother delivered many of the children on St. Thomas, and her family maintained strong connections with local nurses. Inspired by these relationships, she graduated from Seton Hall School of Nursing in New Jersey and then transitioned to work in one of the most underserved areas of the Bronx. Her involvement grew in health promotion, restoration, and prevention for vulnerable populations. Georges networked extensively and built relationships with community stakeholders and politicians in the Bronx. She later earned her Master of Arts with a focus on community health nursing administration from New York University and a Doctor of Education from the University of Vermont. One of her nursing educational experiences reflecting systemic racism included being required to submit a picture with a certain school application, which led her to decide against applying to that school.

Georges’ nursing lens encompasses a holistic view and a clear understanding of the intersectionality of social determinants of health (SDOHs). Her pragmatic approach to problem-solving complemented her background in public health nursing, enabling her to advocate effectively for community members' needs. One example of her early work involved preparing Bronx, NY, community members for testimony on budget items about what communities needed and why they needed it from a HiAP perspective. She pointedly explained that an ambulance cannot get down the street in an emergency because of potholes and the elderly cannot walk on a sidewalk with a walker, exercise, or easily get groceries because of deteriorating sidewalks. She amplified her influence and that of the community by serving on the Bronx Community Board #12, where she gained insights into news and the inner workings of the city that shaped policy. “Many elected officials don’t know or have a sense of the health issues and social determinants. Nurses know the impact. Talk about it and bring forward the hard data. Nurses need to speak out.”

Georges discusses the struggles and opportunities during the COVID-19 pandemic to speak out and influence the glaring disparities that emerged from it. The loss of life in Black and Hispanic communities, particularly among those in lower socioeconomic strata, was incredibly revealing. The pandemic's impact had a devastating effect on these communities that continues to reverberate across the U.S.

The lives of many, including family and colleagues, were disrupted. In Bronx, NY, this disruption was evident in healthcare facilities providing services to a section of New York City (NYC) that was severely affected by COVID-19. Each night, it was disheartening to hear about the number of people who were hospitalized or who had lost their lives. The data in NYC and nationally indicated that Black individuals were disproportionately represented in both morbidity and mortality statistics. Georges decided she needed to do more to assist her community during these challenging times.

As COVID-19 rapidly escalated in the Bronx, a concerted effort was needed to inform Bronx residents. Part of this involved dispelling myths about homemade remedies and addressing circulating conspiracy theories. Joining other Black health professionals in webinars to provide accurate information was one of the strategies employed. When the vaccine became available, it was crucial to hold healthcare facilities accountable for ensuring access to the vaccine for Bronx residents. It became evident that certain groups were prioritized for receiving the vaccine while the most at-risk population struggled to access available slots.
