By engaging with local officials and senior hospital staff, more slots were made available to communities of color.

“The chronicity of racism was evident during the pandemic. The fact that some communities were given preferential treatment in receiving the vaccine exemplifies the racism that existed and continues to exist. The COVID-19 pandemic left indelible marks on communities of color. We observed how the prior lack of addressing the social determinants of health negatively impacted our community. The nurses who suffered the most from stress and the subsequent loss of lives were practicing in large urban settings. These institutions had not been receiving their fair share of available resources. The COVID-19 pandemic strengthened my resolve to continue fighting for health equity and social justice by speaking out and joining others who are working for the same outcomes,” said Georges.

As an active at-large member of the board of directors for the New York Black Nurses Association, Georges communicated the needs of residents of lower middle-class areas in the Bronx. She expanded her role within the New York Black Nurses Association by serving as treasurer, participating on Governor Cuomo’s advisory board, and later becoming the president and founder of the National Black Nurses Day on the Hill. She held the positions of vice president and president of the National Black Nurses Association (NBNA), served on the DHHS Advisory Council on Nursing Education and Practice, and was a member of the AARP board of directors from 2010 to 2020.

Her ambitions were fueled by the tremendous Black nurses she met, like Drs. Betty Smith Williams, Rhetaugh Dumas, Gloria Smith, and Mary Elizabeth Carnegie, who talked with her about the history of Black nurses and mentored her. Early on Georges had no idea that these women were “big shots,” because they were so nice. She feels obligated to mentor others because of their mentorship. Her efforts have resulted in research and program funding, speaking engagements around the globe, and invited proceedings to empower a culture of health and policy change. During momentous advancements in leadership roles, Georges has remained constant in her efforts to partner and advocate for African Americans and aging communities while addressing the structural and racial barriers to health care.

Service and policy advancements have led to Georges’ recognitions, including but not limited to the American Academy of Nursing (AAN) Living Legend, Women Who Lead Vitas Black History Month, Outstanding Women by New York Senator Larry Seabrook, and the ANA Minority Fellowship Program Public Service Award. Georges’ father used to say, “The best you can do is give service to mankind.” Georges does that by continuing to show up, volunteer, speak out, offer suggestions and solutions, and remain connected.

Deborah Trautman, PhD, RN, FAAN, is the president and chief executive officer of the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN). From a young age, Trautman knew she wanted to make a difference and improve the lives of those in her community. In a conversation with her, one is struck by her genuine kindness and humility. While working as an aide in a long-term care facility, she recognized the quality of work done by one of the nurses and knew she wanted to be like her: “She was a leader, organizer, and fun.” Although her career did not initially focus on formal policy development and she doesn’t recall taking policy courses during nursing school, her nursing lens is rooted in health reform and enhanced by her natural ability to build relationships and communicate evidence.

Trautman’s experiences as an ED nurse, staff instructor, and manager provided her with the expertise to lead in policy. She believes that much of what made her a good nurse also prepared her well for the policy arena. Early in her career, she noticed that nurses were often brought in after policy development and implementation “to clean things up,” yet she thought, “if you just had nurses at the table in the first place.”

While in the ED, her boss contacted her to serve as a representative for a statewide trauma system initiative in Pennsylvania. During her doctoral studies, she had the opportunity to expand her role in domestic initiatives by serving on an interprofessional, diverse committee aimed at reducing domestic violence for the state of Maryland. She advocated for better protections for women and safeguards to protect individuals. Her mentor, Dr. Jackie Campbell, was instrumental in helping her develop her dissertation study on domestic violence screening. Trautman compared an electronic computer-based screening with an in-person screening to determine which yielded better results. The computer screening provided superior information for detecting violence, which contradicted prevailing beliefs. Her mentor suggested she continue her efforts to drive evidence-based health reform and apply for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (RWJF) Health Policy Fellowship.

Trautman was awarded the fellowship and served as Assistant to the Honorable Nancy Pelosi, Speaker of the House. Her role as a senior health policy staffer included advising the Speaker and the House on healthcare issues, current and pending legislation, and strategic policy considerations to advance health and healthcare. She coordinated activities with the Congressional health policy committee staff and Congressional offices and engaged in public speaking while liaising with professional associations, trade organizations, and constituents. While working on the ACA, Trautman was struck by the absence of health professionals at the table and noted that those present were most often advocating for their own profession. When a member of Congress sought to impose penalties on individuals who did not adhere to ACA policies, Trautman effectively communicated that such penalties would be discriminatory. Trautman’s interactions with patients and families, along with conversations with members of Congress, all came together to guide her in collaborating with the team that crafted appropriate language for this component of the bill.

After the legislative language was released and just before the House was set to vote, Trautman received a call from a freshman member of Congress who was hosting a town hall. Five hundred people, both red and blue constituents, were expected, and he requested that she sit behind the curtain to help answer questions. The first question was posed by an elderly woman who reminded Trautman of her great-grandmother; she shared that she had just lost her husband of 50 years and was concerned about navigating the health system. Trautman felt relief that she seemed to have a supportive audience. The next person had a more aggressive approach: “How could he dare support legislation to take control away from doctors and nurses and place it into policymakers’ hands?” Trautman’s thoughts shifted to the possibility that the audience might be more combative than she had initially thought. The congressman informed his audience that “he just so happens to have a nurse here that can provide more information.” Trautman was surprised to learn that she would now be answering questions. However, she rose to the occasion with her usual command of interpersonal communication and positivity. Trautman helped explain the issues they were trying to address; she was prepared to have these difficult conversations because her nursing experience provided her with knowledge and human competencies. “Nurses will do whatever it takes to get the job done; we’re less worried about the lane we’re in and see boundaries differently.”

While working on the ACA, strong disagreement prevailed, and people were defensive. Trautman felt that not enough had been done to educate individuals and that “policies fail because people are not ready for it.” This realization led to Trautman’s next role as the executive director of the Johns Hopkins Medicine Center for Health Policy and Healthcare Transformation. The center’s mission is to generate and disseminate knowledge and promote effective health policy. Reflecting on her work in policy at the federal level, Trautman posits that her roles in nursing—staff nurse, clinical nurse manager, director of nursing, vice president of patient care services—and her experience in handling any uncertainty that comes through the door conditioned her to shape policy. Trautman advised that it’s important for nurses to remember that “we are not the only profession that has humanism; it may be more in our DNA than others and a lot of it is in our education and preparation, but we don’t have to stand alone. We need to have the wisdom and confidence in our abilities to bring people together.”

Trautman continues to influence policy in her role as president and CEO of the AACN. Under her leadership, the AACN has revised its Essentials document to prominently feature diversity, equity, and inclusion. Through speaking engagements, congressional testimony, research, and dissemination, she remains a committed policy advocate for nurses. She belongs to numerous organizations and professional affiliations, including the ANA, Sigma Theta Tau, the AAN, Academy Health (as an advisory board member), and the Nursing Organization Alliance, and serves as chair of the Interprofessional Education Collaborative and secretary and treasurer of the Federation of Associations of Schools of the Health Professions. In addition, Trautman is part of the Nursing Advisory Council at the Joint Commission. She believes that participation in professional organizations is essential for enhancing one’s influence and amplifying nursing's voice. She expresses concern that fewer than 10% of RNs and advanced practice nurses in the United States are members of the ANA, and she strongly encourages every nurse to join their professional association or organization.

Cole Williams, BSN, RN, founded Pride and Plasma (prideandplasma.org), a new organization aimed at advocating for revisions to FDA blood guidelines that prevented queer men from donating blood in 2022. Cole spearheaded the initiative as a 21-year-old BSN student at the University of Cincinnati. Pride and Plasma garnered national attention in May 2023 when the FDA altered its guidelines (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2023) for blood and tissue donation to incorporate gender-inclusive language and individual-based risk assessments for blood donor eligibility. This significant change occurred just one month after Cole presented it to the FDA’s Blood Products Advisory Committee, https://ojin.nursingworld.org/table-of-contents/volume-30-2025/number-1-january-2025/using-research-to-fight-for-policy-solutions/.

The group expanded its efforts after successfully altering blood donation guidelines to address the FDA’s tissue ban on queer men, which had been in place since 1994, as well as deferment policies affecting trans and nonbinary donors. Using a similar strategy to their advocacy for blood donations, they submitted two research briefs to the FDA’s Cellular, Tissue, and Gene Therapies Advisory Committee in 2023. In May 2024, Pride and Plasma provided testimony to the Blood Products Advisory Committee regarding the lack of federal guidelines for screening, testing, and interacting with gender-diverse blood donors. Arguments presented to the FDA emphasized the necessity for inclusive policies for gender-diverse blood donors and addressed the FDA's 5-year queer tissue ban, along with a brief on the tissue ban and the need for policies that recognize and screen gender-diverse blood donors, which are available on their website. They gathered data from blood centers across the nation to assess current practices and conducted a literature review. They are “here to fight discriminatory policies impacting the queer community in health care” (prideandplasma.org). This group has been highly successful in changing policy at the national level.
All the leaders in this section were selected for their key organizational roles. Each believes in the strength of joining together through organizational membership, advocacy, and leadership.
<H1>INFLUENCING POLICY THROUGH BOARD SERVICE

It is well known that nurses possess extensive knowledge about the challenges and issues on the frontlines of health care. Yet, too often, their expertise is underutilized, frequently going unheard or unconsidered when redesigning health care to make it cost-effective, safe, quality-driven, and person-centered. To address the leadership gap for nurses in the boardroom and in response to the Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health report’s (IOM, 2011) recommendations, the Nurses on Boards Coalition (NOBC, 2021a) was established in 2014. This national organization focuses on recruiting and recommending nurses for board positions. Its nationally coordinated approach has successfully advanced a nursing perspective into America’s boardrooms (See Chapter 1). The following individuals’ stories illustrate the importance of having nurses at the table, where their voices and votes help influence critical decisions that affect patients and their communities.

Melanie Dreher, PhD, RN, FAAN, is the dean emerita of Rush University College of Nursing. Coming from a family of nurses with Irish political roots, Dreher is an influential nursing leader with expansive, big-picture views shaped by years of diverse experience. She has made it her mission to forge connections, serve as a decision-maker, and advocate for policy change through her board service. Her unique nursing lens was shaped by her training as an anthropologist and as a student of Margaret Mead: “For nurses to have [the] capacity to create policy, they have to stand back and look through a different lens, the skill of policy starts with an assessment of your own profession on the world stage—its strengths and its limitations (most of which are self-imposed).”

Dreher’s early work in anthropology took place in Jamaica, where she examined the use of cannabis. Engaged in studying norms and values, she recognized that nurses were missing an incredible opportunity: “Helping people live well is a huge undertaking.” Armed with a deep understanding of the needs and standards (values and norms) of individuals and communities, she used her board positions to advocate for a focus on health and the patient experience. When discussions in board meetings centered around the need to cut expenses by reducing nursing staff, she succeeded in achieving consensus that high standards of care were a value most would expect and agree upon. Her board colleagues identified a better solution once they grasped that the “real business of hospitals is 24-hour vigilance by expert nurses.”

Dreher’s extensive experience in Jamaica shaped her lens on the importance of nurse confidence. “I observed a nurse intercept a physician while he was writing discharge notes on a patient and quietly offered, ‘Doctor, I need to make you aware that this patient is not ready to go home at this time.’ The physician simply stopped writing, closed the chart, and said, ‘Ms. Jones, you know more about this patient than I. Please keep me informed on his progress.’ She didn’t begin her sentence with ‘I think’ or ‘I believe.’ She was secure in her assessment to advocate for the patient’s welfare effectively…Nurses have to be visible. Make yourself heard beyond academia. Join the Rotary, the Chamber of Commerce, and identify yourself as a community resource, available to impart your wisdom to individuals and groups. Write letters to the editor of the newspaper...People will see you and recommend you for all kinds of opportunities in policy leadership.”

While serving as dean at the University of Iowa, a business colleague suggested to Dreher that the nursing profession could greatly benefit by participating on influential corporate boards. For her, that primarily referred to the health insurance industry. Focusing on how to accomplish this objective, she approached a banker new to Iowa City, seeking to establish his reputation, and asked if he had any connections that could help her secure a position on the Des Moines Board of Blue Cross Blue Shield. Within two months, she was interviewed and offered a seat on its subsidiary board, where she continued to serve even after relocating to Chicago. A few years later, she was “promoted” to the Wellmark Inc. board, where she still serves. In the meantime, she was recruited for the board of directors of Trinity Health, which became the second-largest private hospital/healthcare system in the country. According to Dreher, “board success requires showing up and showing what you got, armed with data and the rich experience that nurses bring.”

As a dean, Dreher’s voice shaped policy on the boards of Sigma Theta Tau International, the AACN, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). In retirement, her policy work has continued with board service at various organizations such as Wellmark, Trinity Health, the Chicago Board of Health, AvaSure Inc, Patients Out of Time, the Loyola University Board of Trustees, and the University of Minnesota School of Nursing Visiting Committee. Her innovative programs at Rush University have shaped the future of nursing education (Callahan, 2019; Clarke & Dreher, 2017).

While engaged in leadership roles and extensive board service, Dreher maintained an active research program related to the use of cannabis for more than 50 years. Her work in this area has both promoted social justice and transformed public opinion. Although the nursing academic community did not especially welcome her research, she found an eager audience in social science, education, psychiatry, and medicine. Her work was cited in the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and even the High Times and Rolling Stone. These publication outlets created opportunities for public awareness, visibility for nursing, and policy change beyond what was usually available in traditional academic journals.

Bobbie Berkowitz, PhD, RN, NEA-BC, FAAN, is the dean and professor emerita at Columbia University School of Nursing. For anyone who knows Bobbie, it is hard to believe that she once described herself as very shy and introverted. She realized that these traits would not lead her to where she wanted to go, so she worked hard to become comfortable taking the initiative. Her story illustrates how she overcame her introversion and became a leader in nursing. As a second grader, Berkowitz was hospitalized with rheumatic fever. Her lengthy hospitalization led to isolation, and the nurses caring for her became her world. It was then that she discovered her passion for the field of nursing. Although her parents were not college-educated, they supported her decision to attend college to become a nurse and pursue a PhD. They would say, “We don’t understand it, but we know you do. If this is what you want, we are there for you.” Berkowitz persevered throughout her education, initially becoming a candy striper and nurse’s aide before attending the University of Washington for nursing. Despite her passion for public health, Berkowitz accepted a position as an oncology nurse in Seattle after graduation. Once she realized that this was not the right fit for her, she eagerly seized the opportunity to work as a public health nurse, visiting families, serving as a school nurse, and working at the public health clinic.

The nursing director and health officer of the health department had great confidence in Berkowitz’s ability to interact with all types of people and recognized her gift for managing complex situations. They supported her return to school for her MSN. After her graduation, she returned to the local health department and became its nursing director. As Berkowitz continued her education, pursuing a PhD, she transitioned to a more senior leadership role as the nursing director at the Seattle King County Department of Public Health. At that time, the governor of Washington sought to create a universal health plan for the state. He established a task force to develop the framework for a universal health plan that could be presented to the legislature for approval. Berkowitz was appointed to the task force, and when the plan was completed, it was passed by the legislature. Berkowitz's nursing lens was grounded in public health nursing. “You see what the world looks like from the eyes of those you work with,” she observed.

This experience led to her appointment as the Deputy Secretary for the Washington State Department of Health. Berkowitz had numerous meetings with legislators and learned about their priorities regarding public health: “There is limited understanding of the role of public health and why it is so critical to people. This legislation helped raise the visibility and value of public health.”

During her time at the Washington State Department of Health, she was approached by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation to lead a program called “Turning Point.” This would be a 10-year grant aimed at modernizing states’ public health statutes, improving health quality, enhancing information technology, creating performance management systems, and fostering public health leadership. To implement the grant, she left the state health department and joined the University of Washington School of Public Health faculty. Over those 10 years of the grant, she became the Department of Psychosocial and Community Health chair at the University of Washington School of Nursing. When the grant ended, she took a sabbatical to reflect on her next phase. Columbia University recruited her to become the dean of the Columbia University School of Nursing. During that time, she also served as the president of the AAN (2015–2017).

Berkowitz retired from Columbia University in 2018 and moved back to Seattle. She believes strongly that serving on boards is essential for nurses. She serves on the board of advisors of the University of Washington School of Nursing, the board of trustees for the Swedish Health System, the National Advisory Board of the University of California Davis Health System, and the board of directors of the Nurse-Family Partnership.

“Nurses need to lead through boards, that is where we can have a significant impact in shaping policies. And nursing must be part of corporate board work where board members have a major leadership role,” she contended.

Drs. Dreher and Berkowitz exemplify how board membership and leadership influence policy from the nursing lens. Board membership allows nurses to serve as advocates and ambassadors for healthcare agendas while providing opportunities to oversee the strategic direction of nonprofit and for-profit organizations. Recently, the NOBC has begun promoting the impact of the nursing profession and documenting board service. Although discussed in Chapter 1, it is important to note that since its inception, the NOBC has expanded its mission to include placing nurses on boards outside of healthcare, including corporate boards. Our nursing lens on boards is essential for fostering healthier communities.
<H1>INFLUENCING POLICY THROUGH RESEARCH

Health policies are often promoted and developed without research to support or challenge a particular stance. Likewise, many researchers have focused on designing, implementing, and analyzing their studies without considering policy. Nursing research offers a unique perspective on patients' experiences within the healthcare system, providing crucial input during each stage of the policy process. The following highlighted leaders demonstrate how nurses can intentionally influence policy through research.

Peter Buerhaus, PhD, RN, FAAN, FAANP(h), states that becoming a nurse was his best decision. His father worked as a hospital administrator and managed a community hospital. His parents often invited candidates for hospital positions to their home for dinner with the family. Influenced by these discussions and the experiences of his older sister, who is a nurse, Buerhaus chose to pursue nursing as a career. He served as a staff nurse and head nurse at a small hospital in New Hampshire and then attended graduate school at the University of Michigan, focusing on nursing health services administration, before going to Wayne State University for advanced education in healthcare economics and nursing.

Stints at the University of Iowa, a fellowship at Johns Hopkins, a Robert Wood Johnson program in finance, and the Public Health School at Harvard followed. There, he met colleagues with whom he collaborated on early studies who were enormously influential in shaping private and public policy. Buerhaus believes his career success was based on his background as a nurse researcher, economist, and policy expert. He describes his nursing lens as understanding the nurse's role in addition to drawing on his background as an economist and health services researcher. He understands the outcomes that nurses can achieve clinically and can explain nuances about what is going on to nonclinical team members. His nursing lens focuses on clinical outcomes, quality, and cost. Buerhaus says that it is important for nurses to understand that their job is about patient care and that they should excel clinically, but their role is also to improve outcomes and keep the cost the same or lower. He believes that, from their first care plan, nurses should consider clinical conditions, quality, and cost for every person.

Buerhaus is best known for his research on the nursing and physician workforces in the United States. Five of his 150-plus publications are designated as “classics” by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Patient Safety Network. Based on Buerhaus’s research expertise, he was appointed chair of the National Health Workforce Commission established under the ACA in 2010. This commission was formed to advise Congress and the administration on health workforce policy, provide data and analysis on issues facing health care, and align federal healthcare workforce resources with national needs. Two important points about the Workforce Commission are worth noting. First, Buerhaus, the only RN appointed to the commission, was selected as chair of a 15-person group that included a variety of experts. His research expertise secured him a seat on the commission, and his appointment as chair likely stemmed from fairness. Second, although the commission was established and members were appointed, Congress never funded it and thus it never became operational because federal spending was not approved. This underscores a frequent occurrence: a significant piece of legislation establishing a program, activity, or agency is authorized and passes in Congress; however, the second step in the process—appropriation of funding—never takes place. We need to remain aware of this and continue advocating through the appropriations process.

The influence of Buerhaus’s research on policy presents outstanding examples. Due to its significant impact in multiple areas, we highlight his team’s publication, Nurse Staffing and Quality of Care in Hospitals in the United States (Needleman et al., 2002). It contributed to (a) Medicare’s adoption of recommendations for changing how inpatient complications are coded to distinguish between community-acquired and hospital-acquired complications, and (b) the language used in The Nurse Reinvestment Act (DL 107-205), sponsored by Representative Lois Capps (D-CA) and signed into law in August 2002. Unfortunately, the 107th Congress adjourned in November 2002 without appropriating funding. The following year, Congress authorized appropriations for all programs, which have continued to this day.

Loretta Sweet-Jemmott, PhD, MSN, RN, FAAN, was struck by a car when she was seven years old. During her lengthy hospitalization, she realized that the nurses in white uniforms were supportive and made her feel better. This experience marked the beginning of Jemmott’s journey into nursing. When she enrolled in a local public university to pursue her nursing degree, she encountered discrimination and racism, including being reprimanded by a professor in front of a large class. Together with other Black nursing students, she endured many painful experiences of racism that hindered their pursuit of nursing degrees at that institution. Determined to become a nurse, she transferred to Hampton University, a Historically Black College and University (HBCU) she cherished. She was actively involved in student leadership there.

After graduation, Jemmott volunteered at a local adolescent community sexual health clinic, where she was asked to teach classes to reduce teen pregnancy. One year later, she became the clinic’s executive director. She did not understand why teens knew how to reduce their risk of pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections but refused to take action. She enrolled in the adolescent psychiatric and mental health nursing master’s program at the University of Pennsylvania, followed by a PhD program in education, focusing on sex education. Although she worked in a private psychiatric–mental health office in downtown Philadelphia and wanted to be the “Black Dr. Ruth,” she moved to New Jersey for her first faculty position at Rutgers University, becoming the only Black professor in the nursing school and the first to achieve tenure. From there, she went to Columbia University and shortly thereafter transferred to the University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing, where she remained for 20 years, becoming the first and only Black faculty member promoted to the rank of full professor and the first to hold an endowed chair.

Jemmott is best known for her theory-driven, culturally competent, translational, and community-engaged research on HIV/AIDS prevention. As an expert in health promotion research, she has led the nation in understanding the psychological determinants of reducing sexual risk-related behaviors. Her premier contribution is developing knowledge on how to best facilitate and promote positive changes in health behaviors.

Jemmott describes her nursing approach as caring, sincere listening, and being present. “If you design an HIV/sexually transmitted infection (STI) risk reduction intervention and the teens get a sense that you genuinely care about them, all the theories and concept of caring are taken to the next level. The adolescents want to know that you see them, that you hear them, that you understand them, that you really care about them, and would advocate for them. They need to know that you are just not giving them the knowledge to be safe sexually. You are also building up the confidence (self-efficacy) to be safe sexually while preparing them with the skills and the positive attitudes and beliefs needed to do it.”

Jemmott and her husband, John Jemmott III, have received over $150 million in funding from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to design and test interventions aimed at reducing the risk of HIV and other STIs among diverse populations worldwide. As a translational researcher with global impact, she has transformed her NIH-funded evidence-based research outcomes for real-world applications. To date, eight of her evidence-based interventions have been designated for national and international dissemination by the CDC and the DHHS Office of Adolescent Health. Three of her evidence-based interventions have been developed into programs by community-based organizations and clinics in high-risk urban areas. Her research has influenced public policy regarding theory-driven, culturally appropriate, evidence-based HIV risk reduction interventions in community and clinical settings. She was invited to present her research to the U.S. Congress, at an HIV Prevention Briefing, as well as at the NIH’s Consensus Development Conference on Interventions to Reduce HIV Risk Behaviors. Jemmott’s research expertise earned her the U.S. Congressional Merit Award and election to membership in the IOM, an honor bestowed upon very few nurses.

The Jemmotts’ work with abstinence-based education demonstrated a greater delay in the initiation of sexual activity among middle school children compared to other types of sex education. This finding was later used to support policies for school-based abstinence-only sex education programs implemented by President George Bush. However, it is important to note that the Jemmotts’ research differed from other abstinence-only programs in that they did not instruct adolescents to abstain from sex until marriage; the curriculum does not mention marriage or morality. Upon this realization, the White House team ceased using this evidence-based program because they preferred pure abstinence-only-until-marriage programs instead of abstinence-based programs. This example highlights how research results can be politicized and exploited by others for purposes never intended by the researchers.

Jemmott’s nursing lens has been influenced by her experiences as a Black woman in the United States, including facing racism and exclusion throughout her life, particularly in her nursing career. Her advice to others is to be strong and keep pressing on. “You can’t let oppression and institutional racism block your success. You must have faith, determination, and resilience to push on and succeed despite whatever comes your way. You have to speak up, stand up, and advocate for yourself when others do not want you in the room or at the table.” She believes she has successfully shaped policy at the federal level thanks to what her mother calls gumption, the fire in her belly that propels her through the door when people try to close it. It is this spirit that keeps her going, and her belief that “This is a lifelong journey and God sending His angels.” Her nurse mentors, including Angela McBride, Rhetaugh Dumas, Nancy Bergstrom, Ada Sue Hinshaw, Beverly Malone, Neville Strumpf, and Linda Burns Bolton, were always there for her, pushed her out of her comfort zone, encouraged her, and introduced her to other successful scholars. Early on, they told her she would be an “up-and-coming star,” and she certainly accomplished that.

Drs. Buerhaus’s and Jemmott’s research on health policy has had an extensive impact. All nurse researchers should identify the policy implications of their work, effectively communicate their findings to policymakers (this differs from a scientific presentation), and advocate for policy implementation and changes when warranted.
<h1>INFLUENCING POLICY THROUGH GOVERNMENT SERVICE

Many roads lead to advocacy and politics. When people think of politics, they often visualize a single road, assuming it's a straight path to running for and being elected to public office. Typically, the offices that come to mind are high-profile state or national positions. However, elected positions represent only a small fraction of the political opportunities available. Political roles are less visible but crucial for nursing and healthcare policy development. Nurses currently hold—and many more can hold—appointed positions or volunteer roles. Individuals can be appointed to an office or a committee or elected. The following examples illustrate the range of governmental opportunities available and the influence that nurses can and do wield.
<H2>LOCAL GOVERNMENT

Carol Roe, JD, MSN, RN, always knew she wanted to help people and was inspired to become a nurse by reading Cherry Ames and Sue Barton novels as a child. She attended law school to advocate more effectively for nursing and patients in the public policy arena. She began her career as a diploma-prepared nurse, and each time she pursued further education, it was partly due to her dissatisfaction with leadership and the often-heard adage, “If you can’t beat them, join them.” Throughout her distinguished career, Roe served as a nurse administrator, clinical nurse specialist, faculty member, lobbyist, nursing regulator, compliance officer, risk manager, and mayor.

Roe served as the assistant director of medical–surgical nursing at University Hospitals of Cleveland from 1979 to 1989 and greatly enjoyed her role, especially the positive working relationships she fostered. While attempting to revamp the nursing documentation system to not only be medically directed but also incorporate nursing diagnoses, Roe collaborated with lawyers who objected to her intentions. During the same period, she testified to amend the Ohio Nurse Practice Act at the state capitol. This testimony was crucial as it marked the first effort to update the definition of nursing practice. The main opposition to the amended definition, which would recognize nurse practitioners, came from hospitals. These experiences prompted Roe to pursue a law degree.

Her nursing lens has always been, “What is in the best interest of the patient?” Her passion for healthcare policy and politics developed from her experiences in public health as a student. While making home visits to chronically ill children, she realized that some families struggled to afford necessary care. Through this experience, Roe learned about the role of insurance in the healthcare delivery system and came to believe that access to appropriate healthcare is a right, not a privilege.

While working, Roe was deeply involved in the Ohio Nurses Association (ONA) and involved in partisan politics. She believes that the best way for nurses to expand their influence is through professional organizations. Marta Reeder, the ONA president, served as an invaluable mentor, demonstrating that one can be a nursing administrator, genuinely understand and appreciate staff nurses, and effectively convey the positions of those staff nurses in the workplace. Roe participated in Democratic Party politics, including political campaigns for city and state legislators and presidential elections.

Roe’s commitment to increasing female representation in office led to her involvement in women’s campaigns, advocacy for women’s issues, and active participation in the National Organization of Women. She consistently provided financial support to candidates, which is essential for their success in elections.

Despite her extensive involvement in political campaigns, Roe never considered running for office, fully aware of the significant funding needed for a successful campaign. This perspective changed in 2015 when Roe felt her neighborhood lacked proper representation on the city council, and individuals she had developed relationships with through her previous political engagements reached out to her. She ran successfully for city council, serving from 2016 to 2019. In 2018, her fellow council members selected her as mayor of Cleveland Heights (2018-2019), in part due to her outstanding listening skills as a nurse.

Roe’s success as mayor stemmed from her perspective on leadership, which went beyond merely directing others. The most effective leaders inspire those around them and find joy in witnessing the success of those they have mentored. They emphasize systemic failures rather than individual shortcomings when things do not go as planned. As city councilwoman and mayor, she oversaw the city manager in governing Cleveland Heights, a city with a population of 46,000 and an annual budget of $78 million. Her responsibilities also included recommending legislation, addressing constituent concerns, representing the city at community events and meetings, chairing the Administrative Services Committee, serving as the city council president, and representing the city in the Ohio Mayors Alliance and the Northeast Ohio Mayors Association.
<H2>STATE GOVERNMENT

Sue Birch, MBA, BSN, RN, has over 35 years of extensive experience in healthcare administration across both the public and private sectors. She possesses a rich background in community, regional, and national healthcare transformation, focusing on service delivery, program reform, and population health initiatives. After earning her baccalaureate degree in nursing from the University of Colorado in 1982, she worked both as a staff nurse and a charge nurse in an inpatient medical-surgical unit. She later transitioned from inpatient care to concentrate on primary care and prevention, playing a key role in developing and implementing ambulatory services at Kaiser Permanente and St. Joseph Hospital from 1984 to 1989. Birch received her MBA in 1988, and from 1990 to 1992, she founded and operated a nurse consulting firm that provided consultation services to community agencies, including childcare centers, schools, and camps.

After moving to rural Colorado, Birch served as the executive director and CEO of Northwest Colorado VNA from 1992 to 2010. In this role, she managed a $9 million operating budget while leading and supervising a multidisciplinary management team and a staff of 150. During her tenure, the agency acquired the Haren Assisted Living Center, built a co-located community center, and received national recognition for its extensive aging well services.

Governor John Hickenlooper (D-CO) became acquainted with Birch’s track record and was aware of her work on the ACA. Recognizing the need for political balance on his team, he appointed her as the Executive Director of the Colorado Department of Healthcare Policy and Financing, where she oversaw public insurance, health delivery, health policy development, and the implementation of the ACA for the state from 2011 to 2017. Leading a department with a $9 billion budget and responsible for administering healthcare coverage for 1.4 million Colorado residents, her experience as a Robert Wood Johnson Executive Nurse Fellow (RWJENF) and subsequent collaborations with “social justice warriors” enabled her to effectively balance mission and margin. These experiences helped her understand both the clinical and programmatic aspects of issues.

A critical learning experience within Birch’s three-year RWJENF program involved collaborating with economists at the Brookings Institution to examine the quantifying costs of care and the significance of investments. She recognized that in policy work, it is essential to follow the money and build a compelling case. Under Birch’s leadership, the department successfully expanded coverage to over 400,000 low-income, previously uninsured Coloradans while emphasizing cost containment and improving service delivery. She takes great pride in having persuaded the governor to expand Medicaid coverage. In 2012 and 2013, the department received the highest state bonus for its innovation and modernization of eligibility and enrollment systems from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). In 2017, Colorado ranked sixth in the Commonwealth Fund’s State Health System Performance scorecard.

History repeated itself in 2018 when Governor Jay Inslee, impressed by her work in Colorado, persuaded Birch to relocate and serve as a cabinet member directing the Washington State Health Care Authority, a position she continues to hold today. Birch oversees initiatives aimed at transforming the healthcare system, ensuring that Washington residents have better access to care at lower costs. With a budget of $14 billion, Birch leads the agency, the state’s largest healthcare purchaser, serving nearly 2.7 million residents through Medicaid, the Public Employees Benefits Board Program, the School Employees Benefits Board Program, and the COFA Islander Health Care Program. Under her leadership, there have been numerous firsts, including the launch of the first state-based public option in the U.S. in collaboration with the Washington Health Benefit Exchange and the Office of Insurance Commissioner, as well as the implementation of the first Hepatitis C Elimination Program, partnering with AbbVie on a population health and modified subscription financing model. In 2019, Washington ranked fourth in the Commonwealth Fund’s scorecard on state health system performance, resulting from better alignment for population health, rewarding high-quality care, and controlling health costs.

Birch has honed her strategic timing and alignment skills, becoming adept at motivating her teams to act when opportunities arise and turning challenges into opportunities. In Colorado and Washington, strong political champions, such as health-focused legislators leading health and budget committees, enabled rapid policy implementation. Having the interest and support of her governors allowed for faster implementation of policies and significant transformations. Because of the tight relationships among the Health & Human Services cabinet members, Governor Jay Inslee witnessed firsthand the inequities and the value in his efficiently functioning Health and Human Services sub-cabinet, which Birch chaired.

This led to the creation of the Pro-Equity and Anti-Racism (PEAR) executive order, an explicit state function housed in his office. Birch established the Office of Equity within the Health Care Authority. Led by a fellow nurse leader, HCA’s PEAR team became exemplars for other state agencies, offering training on combatting racism, white supremacy, and implicit bias and involving community stakeholders. Their efforts helped advance Washington in incorporating equity standards into health system contracting. HCA was nominated for the PEAR STAR (Show, Transform, Act & Reflect) award, recognizing community organizations and state agencies that exemplify Pro-Equity and Anti-Racist qualities.

While state budgets have limitations, Birch inspired her team to implement public-private partnerships aligned with foundation leaders invested in health policy. These partnerships focused on innovations in coverage, affordability, cost containment, and addressing medical debt concerns. A key innovation, continuous Medicaid eligibility for children aged 0 to 6, scaled rapidly. Private funders supported a study on its cost-effectiveness, enabling the House Health Committee to approve blending this policy into federal waiver requests. With backing from the Biden administration, Washington rolled out this program in January 2024. Nearly 14 states have expanded coverage for children on Medicaid, and President Biden included this in his 2025 budget proposal.

Additionally, Washington State launched another innovative coverage initiative aimed at reducing disparities, becoming the seventh state to offer coverage for undocumented individuals through a program called Apple Health Expansion. This represents a significant achievement for the Health Care Authority team. Aligned and dedicated teams worked diligently to implement this initiative despite the challenges posed by the winding down of the Public Health Emergency. To date, over 13,000 undocumented residents have obtained health coverage, and Birch remains hopeful that more residents will enroll with additional state resources. These efforts specifically target the most vulnerable and disadvantaged populations, and provide the basis for optimism about reducing disparities and countering the marginalization that frequently occurs in the health and human services sector.

Birch remains committed to pursuing the best health opportunities for all individuals in Washington State and across the nation. Birch’s primary focus on care and prevention, shaped by her earliest clinical nursing experiences, originated from her public health work at the VNA, state government agencies, and her MBA. These experiences have informed her nursing lens on social justice, equity, and population health, emphasizing communities and the goal of providing high-quality care while managing costs and generating revenue. The Washington Department’s Health Home model and Medicaid Program saved nearly a quarter billion dollars in shared savings returned to the state. Birch exemplifies a nurse with strong systems skills and thinking, capable of impacting individuals and populations. On a personal level, Birch’s early experience with her diabetic grandmother instilled compassion and an understanding of the medical complexities necessary for delivering quality care. On a population level, she seeks to operationalize health by considering aspects beyond medical complexity and the importance of place. She has played a pivotal role in transforming two state health departments, leading them to fourth and sixth rankings for system performance.
Birch believes her success is related to developing open, transparent teams that engage in “productive conflict.”
“We cannot shy away from healthy tension. It does not have to be an ugly process, although sometimes it is. It is important to align energies,” she asserts.

A supportive environment and a flexible family enabled her to take on jobs in different states. Patience, tenacity, persistence, and her ability to gauge the system’s capacity for change allowed her to do transformative policy work.

Lastly, Birch is passionate about having healthy people everywhere. “I think that when we can find passion in someone and marry passion with the profession, then that is when the magic happens. Nurses’ perspectives are important.”
<H2>FEDERAL GOVERNMENT

Mary Wakefield, PhD, RN, FAAN, currently serves as a visiting professor and distinguished fellow of the Joseph H. Blades Centennial Memorial Professorship in Nursing at the University of Texas at Austin. She is a trailblazing role model for nurses' involvement in health policy, having served as the administrator for the Health Resources and Services Administration of the DHHS from 2009 to 2015 and as DHHS Acting Deputy from 2015 to 2017. As acting deputy secretary, she held the second-most senior position at DHHS, providing leadership and direction to an agency with a $1 trillion budget (almost one-fourth of federal spending) and approximately 80,000 employees and contractors globally. The DHHS administers more grant money than all other federal agencies combined. It is responsible for regulating new pharmaceutical drugs and food products, overseeing the largest government healthcare programs, and preventing the outbreak and spread of diseases. Its mission is “to enhance the health and well-being of all Americans, by providing for effective health and human services and by posturing sound, sustained advances in the sciences underlying medicine, public health and social services” (DHHS, 2018, “Mission Statement”). The DHHS has 11 operating divisions, including eight agencies, such as the AHRQ, the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, the Food and Drug Administration, the CDC, the Health Resources & Services Administration (HRSA), the Indian Health Service, the NIH, and the CMS. The CMS administers Medicare, Medicaid, the Marketplace, and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP).

The mission of HRSA is “to improve health outcomes and address health disparities through access to quality services, a skilled workforce, and innovative, high-value programs” (HRSA, 2019, para. 1). HRSA “provides healthcare to people who are geographically isolated and/or economically or medically vulnerable,” including those living with HIV/AIDS, pregnant women, mothers and their families, and individuals unable to access high-quality health care. HRSA supports the training of health professionals, the distribution of providers to areas where they are needed most (medically underserved areas), improvements in healthcare delivery, and the maintenance of databases that flag providers with a record of malpractice, waste, fraud, and abuse (HRSA, 2019). The agency comprises five bureaus: the Bureau of Health Workforce, the Bureau of Primary Health Care, the Healthcare Systems Bureau, the HIV/AIDS Bureau, and the Maternal and Child Health Bureau. It also includes the Federal Office of Rural Health Policy, the Office of Global Health, and the Office of Health Equity. As HRSA’s administrator, Wakefield led and directed the agency, overseeing a $10.3 billion budget with more than 1,850 civil service and commissioned officer employees, along with the overall management of all HRSA programs and activities.

Wakefield led these federal agencies with her nursing lens. She stated that when she graduated from her baccalaureate and master’s programs, she did not fully grasp the impact of health policy on patients, families, and communities. She did not realize how policy directly influenced what she could and could not do as a nurse. As she gained clinical experience, she became aware of how much policy affected virtually every aspect of health care—from details such as the width of hospital room doorways to issues like the mismatch between Medicaid eligibility and the necessary coverage for large segments of the uninsured population. As a nurse, she recognized the profession's impact on health, but she soon learned that state and federal health policy could sometimes be even more influential. One example that Wakefield recalls vividly illustrates this point. A woman, clearly distressed, explained that she had a job, a couple of kids, was a single parent, had chronic conditions, and lacked health insurance. The patient asked, “What can you do to help me?” and Wakefield remembers to this day a feeling that contradicted her professional training; she could do nothing. This experience revealed a broader context for caring for patients. Nurses understand what patients and their families face. Wakefield recognized from firsthand experience what is in the best interest of the patient. She noted that in every leadership position she has held since that pivotal experience, she considers decisions through the lens of how well we are serving those in need. Her “north star” is always, “What is in the best interest of the patient?” Wakefield’s nursing perspective also involves viewing individuals holistically, acknowledging people within their environments, and considering how an injury or illness will affect patients after they leave our healthcare settings and return to their families and communities. She also emphasizes prevention; how can we keep people from needing to return to the healthcare system? She cites her experience as an ICU nurse in a small hospital in North Dakota as shaping her thinking. Some of her patients were admitted with diagnoses such as preeclampsia and strokes. She witnessed many who would never have been in the ICU if upstream problems could have been resolved. She viewed the ICU as a temporary fix that exposed a failing primary care and public health system.

Wakefield has many examples of how she shaped policy and emphasizes the importance of having nurses in leadership positions, like those she has held, to ensure that the development and implementation of policies benefit from nursing expertise. She is especially proud of her role in reconfiguring nursing programs at the HRSA to be veteran-friendly, enabling retired military personnel to transition into nursing programs more easily. These programs continue to receive funding today.

Wakefield’s journey into policy work started with a dedicated faculty member in her BSN program who encouraged nursing students to get involved in the state nurses’ association. Students were urged to attend state nurses’ meetings and annual conferences. This served as a safe incubator for her to observe and learn from nurse leaders striving to impact healthcare beyond delivery settings. She believes that participating in professional nursing associations with a strong policy emphasis (e.g., the ANA, the AAN, the Emergency Nurses Association) helps nurses cultivate leadership skills and policy-related knowledge. Actively engaging in professional associations fosters vital connections and relationships, broadens understanding of health and healthcare, and enhances involvement in political and policy processes.

At 31 years old, Wakefield was teaching health policy content derived from state-level experience and published literature. Without any federal experience, she felt somewhat uncomfortable teaching material she did not know personally. Consequently, during her summer break, she volunteered to work in the Washington, D.C. office of one of her state’s U.S. Senators. She was informed that they would be happy to have her volunteer, but they also had a permanent legislative assistant position available. Wakefield secured the role of legislative assistant and later became chief of staff to Senator Quentin Burdick (D-ND) in 1987, followed by her position as chief of staff for Senator Kent Conrad (D-ND) from 1993 to 1996. She served as the director of the Center for Health Policy, Research and Ethics at George Mason University from 1996 to 2001, then returned to her first faculty position at the University of North Dakota in 2001. She led the expansion of the Center for Rural Health from 2001 to 2009, and the center became a nationally recognized rural health resource. The combination of Wakefield’s prior experiences in the health policy arena within academe, professional organizations, and government, coupled with excellent relationships in each sector, as well as her initiative in pursuing Capitol Hill experience, led to her appointments to top-level administrative posts in the federal government.

While working in the U.S. Senate, Wakefield routinely introduced herself as a nurse and often heard responses like, “Well then what are you doing here?”, to which she replied, “It’s because I am a nurse that I’m here working in health policy. This is why I’m here.” While Wakefield is clearly an extraordinary nurse policy expert, it would be wonderful if more nurses pursued their own paths to leadership at the national level.

The nursing lens is critically needed in local, state, and federal government service. It creates opportunities for advancing nursing’s values and agenda to improve health for more individuals. These nurse leaders, Carol Roe, Susan Birch, and Mary Wakefield, harnessed the values instilled in their early nursing experiences to influence policy. Their representation at each level of government benefited the communities they served. Nurses have also embraced the challenge of influencing policy through elected offices at the federal level. See Policy on the Scene 11.1 about nurses serving in the 118th Congress.

<H1>POLICY ON THE SCENE 11.1:
Nurses Elected to the 118th Congress and Key Government Position

Nurses in the 118th Congress represent their districts' constituencies and give voice to important healthcare issues that need to be addressed at the federal level. As nurses and healthcare professionals, they bring a unique lens to the policy discussions that have the potential to impact the health of millions.

Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-SC-03) was sworn into office in the U.S. Congress in 2024. Her diverse background and life experience in service as a nurse and in her career in the Air National Guard offer a unique perspective in Congress. Over three decades as a nurse, she worked in an intensive care unit, served as administrator of a licensed nursing home, worked as a dual board-certified Family Nurse Practitioner and Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner, and provided care to first responders addressing mental health needs.

A Lieutenant Colonel in the Air National Guard, Congresswoman Biggs, DNP, APRN, served with distinction that included as medical crew director of numerous combat and combat support missions while operating in hostile environments in support of Operation FREEDOM’S SENTINEL. She is the recipient of the Aerial Achievement Medal. Her congressional assignments include the Homeland Security, Foreign Affairs, and Science, Space, and Technology Committees (Congress.gov., n.d.-a).

Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-VA-02) was sworn into office in 2023 after serving three sessions in the Virginia State Senate. Previous public service included two deployments to the Persian Gulf in the U.S. Navy as a helicopter pilot. A graduate of Old Dominion University’s Nursing School and Vanderbilt University’s Nurse Practitioner program, Congresswoman Kiggans, DNP, APRN, worked in long-term care and nursing facilities as a board-certified Adult-Geriatric Primary Care Nurse Practitioner.

Congresswoman Kiggans came to Congress seeking to bring civility and competence to politics. Her congressional committee assignments include the House Armed Service Committee, House Committee on Natural Resources, and House Committee on Veteran’s Affairs. In the Virginia Senate, she advocated for patients, families, and caregivers in long-term care facilities and championed legislation establishing a Military Spouse liaison. Along with Senator Richard Blumenthal, Kiggans introduced a bipartisan, bicameral legislative package to improve services and benefits for military families (Congress.gov., n.d.-b).

Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-IL-14) is the youngest African American woman to serve in the House of Representatives. In efforts to decrease maternal healthcare disparities and improve maternal health outcomes, she cofounded and currently co-chairs the Black Maternal Health Caucus. Her proposed Black Maternal Health MOMNIBUS Act is a multifaceted approach designed to address all aspects of the maternal health crisis in America that disproportionately affect women of color. She taught future nurse practitioners at Georgetown University’s online master’s program and has helped to implement the ACA while working for the DHHS (Congress.gov., n.d.-c).

Congresswoman Underwood prioritizes accessible and affordable health care for all people and has introduced the H.R. 1010 bill to better protect those with preexisting conditions by giving them continued insurance coverage. Rep. Underwood is Co-Chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee and serves on the House Committee on Appropriations.

Mayor Karen Bass (D-CA-37) served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2011 to 2022 and is currently the mayor of Los Angeles. Bass was a vocational nurse and then worked as a physician’s assistant before being elected to Congress. This occupational shift transferred her bedside manner skills into diplomacy and allowed her to continue her passion for addressing human service issues (Daniels, 2015). One of her passions is advocating for the health of children, evidenced by her founding the bipartisan Congressional Caucus on Foster Youth (History Makers, 2022). With a focus on expanding healthcare access, she also chaired the Subcommittee on Africa, Global Health, Global Human Rights, and International Organizations under the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero, Guam, has served as governor since 2019. Before her governorship, she served five terms in the Guam Legislature. As a senator, she served as Majority Leader and Chair of the Committee on Health, with significant achievements in banning smoking in restaurants and bars. With her experiences as a nurse, she champions healthcare initiatives, resulting in Guam having one of the highest COVID vaccination rates in the nation. She established the island’s first-ever paramedic program and is working to rebuild Guam’s only decades-old public hospital. After obtaining her BSN and MPH in California, she worked as a nurse in California and Guam (see Chapter 1, Figure 1.1).

A background in nursing and health provides an essential lens for members of Congress regarding the development and passage of legislation impacting health. These legislators cannot only propose health-focused legislation but also identify the health implications of legislation designed for other purposes (Office of the Governor of Guam, n.d.). https://governor.guam.gov/.

<H2>EXPANDING YOUR INFLUENCE

Influence is the inherent or developed ability to inspire action. Combining influence with strategy means setting a vision and balancing it with realism. Expanding and enhancing personal influence can be achieved by understanding one’s value and work, gaining visibility, building relationships and partnerships, and being prepared. As Alicia Georges said, “show up, volunteer, speak out. Many elected officials don’t know or have a sense of the health issues and social determinants; nurses know the impact.”
Our policy exemplars provide advice and specific actions that can be taken to expand one’s influence. See Exhibit 11.1.

While expanding one’s influence on an individual level is important, influencing policy is often a collective endeavor. Many of the leaders highlighted so far have expanded their influence through active engagement in the ANA, state nurses’ associations, specialty associations, and interdisciplinary and community groups. Their participation has frequently extended beyond a single association or interest group. Engaging with multiple groups broadens one’s network and influence and creates opportunities for synergy in pursuing common goals.

<H1>POLICY SOLUTION
The Nursing Lens of a Millennial Preparing for Policy Leadership
Marcus D. Henderson MSN, RN, FNAP

I believe that nurses can and should be a part of all health and policy conversations, given the lens we provide. We have our own scope of practice and autonomy. I don’t think this is stressed enough in school. Nurses need to understand their worth.

My clinical experience postgraduation in community health and psychiatric–mental health nursing since 2018 added this set of knowledge and skills to my nursing lens. My work with children and adolescents in mental health and homeless individuals in the community has allowed me to witness firsthand the failures of our healthcare and social services systems, which fuels my continued service to my community and the profession. My nursing lens informs my practice, teaching, leadership, and scholarship. I consistently use my voice through professional organizations and individually to engage with federal policymakers, providing the nursing lens on policies to advance health and well-being for all.

My mentors saw my potential when I did not see it myself. This has been a key lesson for me about the importance of mentorship. Mentorship is a reciprocal process in which the mentor and mentee grow together. My mentors helped me to strengthen my voice. They have always brought me alongside them and kept me grounded so that I could be an agent for change and a role model to others. They taught me that in order to move our profession and nation forward we must ensure that all voices have a seat at the table. I carry these lessons with me every day. I want students and nurses to understand the complexity of SDOHs and health equity and that we have lots of work to do to impact policy in our communities. Our profession is 4.3 million nurses strong, and we practice in communities across the country. If we collectively come together, I don’t see how we can’t move the needle toward a more fair and just future for all.
</unnumberedbox>
<H1>LESSONS LEARNED

When discussing failures with the policy shapers in this chapter, it is clear that experiencing setbacks at some point is inevitable, but failure itself is not an option. The term "failure" is seen more as an opportunity to showcase resilience. Dr. Birch reflects that “patience, tenacity, and persistence are needed to pull off transformations.”

Dr. Jemmott’s lessons culminate in the understanding that when things do not go your way, “it hurts for a minute.” Her pain stems from experiences with structural racism. White students did not want her to be their teacher, and her published research received critiques—and she was not given the opportunity to respond with a published rebuttal. Dr. Jemmott advises, “The challenges continue, and you have to be strong and keep pressing on, we are not any better than we were before; now people are not hiding what they think. You can’t let oppression and structural racism block success.”

This candid and vulnerable look into the personal journey of nurses shaping policy through health reform is framed through a nursing lens, informed by personal experiences and the experiences of our patients. Health reform is an excruciatingly difficult process; people seek an easy answer, but there isn’t one, even from the highest office (Blumenthal & Morone, 2010). The lessons learned from nurse leaders, illuminated throughout this chapter, echo Trautman’s account in The Heart of Power: Health and Politics in the Oval Office (Blumenthal & Morone, 2010): be passionate, have a plan, be part of and deploy a talented team, go public to create momentum, recognize the importance of speed, be ready to overrule advisors, and be prepared to lose.
<H2>OUTCOMES

Nurses are influencing policy at the highest levels in collaboration with some of the most senior legislators. For example, Dr. Trautman’s leadership during the rollout of the ACA and Dr. Buerhaus’s research, which generated funding from the federal government, support the nursing workforce and full practice authority for APRNs. Dr. Dreher’s work addresses policy with health insurance companies to promote patient outcomes. Dr. Birch’s leadership expands coverage for low-income, previously uninsured patients. Dr. Jemmott’s work develops evidence-based programming to reduce sexually transmitted diseases in underserved populations. Sower’s efforts removes policy barriers that prevent patients from accessing the services they need across state lines. The resounding denominator for policy change among nurse leaders influencing policy at all levels and in all settings is unity. Together, we must confront social injustices and health inequities while advocating for our communities’ public health; the power resides in each of us.
<H1>IMPLICATIONS FOR FUTURE

Nursing’s long history is filled with seminal documents that identify the nursing profession’s preferred future. This includes Future of Nursing 2020–2030: Charting a Path to Achieve Health Equity (National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine, 2021). This future cannot be realized without all nurses using their lens to take part in policy to create that future. We assert that the actions of individual nurses are as important as the collective policy decisions that affect the nursing profession and the health of the communities we serve. We propose several essential actions for reform to advance the profession: understanding the complete history of nursing, recognizing the potential of HOSA-Future Health Professionals as a pipeline for nursing, increasing membership in the National Student Nurse Association (NSNA) and the American Nurses Association (ANA), embedding policy throughout nursing curricula, and continuing the effort to include nurses on boards.

Nurses’ knowledge and understanding of the true history of nursing are incomplete. Nursing’s history needs to be rewritten to include marginalized and underrepresented nurse leaders. This accurate history must be integrated into all nursing curricula.

Numerous potential pipelines to nursing remain untapped. HOSA, as exemplified in this chapter, with a membership of over 165,000 distributed across 3,000 chapters, serves as a prime example. Most nurses are not aware of HOSA or that approximately 45% of its members come from minority groups. If every college or school of nursing partnered with a local HOSA chapter or another pipeline group, it would undoubtedly help increase diversity in the nursing workforce.

Many of the leaders identified in this chapter reflect on their early involvement in professional nurses’ associations such as the ANA and others. All faculty members should serve as role models for policy activism and be members of professional nurses’ associations (at a minimum the ANA and the state nurses’ association). Additionally, it should be expected that all prelicensure students are members of the student nurses’ association and that all graduate students belong to the professional nurses’ association. Some programs cover memberships through student fees.

Policy content and discussions must be integrated into all nursing curricula, not just included in a standalone policy course. The effects of policy on patients, their families, and the community should be addressed in every clinical course and during each daily clinical conference. Exploring the political and economic implications of integrating policy dialogues into our teaching would enhance nurses’ preparedness for policy-related matters. This approach would equip nurses to attain clinical competencies, including the new advocacy standard for nurses outlined in the ANA’s (2021) Nursing: Scope and Standards.

As noted, the largest group of healthcare providers is nurses. The first Future of Nursing report (IOM, 2011) was a call to action for nurses to take on a greater role in reforming the healthcare system. This led to the formation of the Nurses on Boards Coalition (NOBC), which achieved the milestone of 10,000 nurses on boards (NOBC, 2021b). These efforts must continue. Nurses must be strategic in ensuring they are represented on the boards of the major multi-site health systems participating in partnerships and strategic alliances. Similar efforts should also be made for nurse representation on collegiate and university boards.

The leaders highlighted in this chapter had visions shaped by their nursing lens. Without a vision, roadmap, or bold, audacious goals, strategies are not developed, change cannot be measured, and the nursing profession will not advance (see Chapter 1). We propose this set of goals as an initial step in Exhibit 11.2.
<H1>KEY CONCEPTS

The power to shape policy is present in every role in nursing—from providers in the community and at the bedside, to advanced practice providers, researchers, academia, boards, PACs, and professional organizations.
In nursing history, the nursing lens has also been grounded and limited by a Eurocentric, White viewpoint that negates the experiences of a growing number of nurses and patients.

The distinct disparities of COVID-19, nursing’s historical focus on health, healthcare equity, and social justice, and adherence to the ANA Code of Ethics necessitate that the nursing lens be used to address structural racism in all healthcare settings, educational institutions, workplaces, government policies, laws, and regulations.
Nurses' engagement in the political process is differentiated from that of others by their nursing lens, which is based on understanding nursing history, education, and practice experience.
Nurse leaders have made extraordinary contributions to health policy in various roles in the public and private sectors.
The stories of nurse exemplars provide valuable guidance and inspiration to nurses who may be hesitant to embark on the path of policy leadership.
It is possible to blend one’s passion for nursing with serving the public through policy advocacy.
Advanced education and professional association involvement are commonalities among nurse policy leaders who successfully champion long-term policy advocacy.
Having mentors and serving as mentors are essential aspects of policy leadership development.
Involvement in policymaking leads to additional networking opportunities that may impact policy.
Leadership and advocacy are important in creating the preferred future for nursing and a healthcare system responsive to the needs of the public.
Nurses need to engage in voting and in voter registration unanimously.
Nurses need to assume their rightful place in policy leadership and work in partnership with others to shape our healthcare system.
<H1>SUMMARY

Our responsibility as nurses and the goal of governments around the world is to achieve better health by addressing the PDOHs and SDOHs at all levels. When asked to describe their “nursing lens,” nurse leaders have highlighted several important attributes and characteristics that nurses bring to policy development and reform. While responses were based on unique lived experiences, interprofessional engagement, and social context, common themes included a clear assessment of needs, a commitment to the health and wellness of patients, individuals, and populations, and the critical importance of communicating these needs to policymakers. Nurses must be at the table before policies are developed.

In 2020, citizens of the United States witnessed a crippling national response to a global pandemic as drug-related overdoses surged, and both tragedies disproportionately affected minorities. In 2021, racism-fueled, violent protestors stormed the U.S. Capitol. As Villarruel and Broome (2020) highlight, these “injustices in law enforcement and health inequities are not new occurrences—nor are they rare” (p. 375). This is the fabric of structural racism woven throughout our policies, practices, and cultural norms. The nursing lens is firmly grounded within the context of social justice and is essential to naming and dismantling structural racism and addressing these atrocities (Villarruel & Broome, 2020). Shaping policy is the responsibility of every nurse at all levels and is the salvation of our democracy. The prominent nurse leaders in this chapter have paved the way, but our work is clearly just getting started.

At times, situations and personal and professional values violations may be challenged and require individuals to be courageous and act. The policy has various pathways; be guided by your nursing lens, be courageous and act to address the situation, and hold to your professional values.
