Presence is a subjective experience of being here and now in a relationship and intending, at a very deep level, to participate as fully as one is able (Schneider, 2008). Bugental (1987) wrote that therapists need to maintain full presence to the patient’s experience in the moment and to closely attend to patient’s immediate inner flow of experience. “Be there!” and “Insist that the patient be there!” were well-known mantras of Bugental’s existential approach (Schneider & Greening, 2009).
<H3>Experiential Reflection

The existential psychotherapist asks in-depth questions about universal themes in order for patients to experientially reflect on how their life is being lived in the present. The patient is challenged to grapple with complexities and paradoxes of the human condition and to face the givens of existence. Experiential reflection through in-depth questioning helps the patient recognize the range of life choices, remove obstacles to freedom, find meaning, and take responsibility (Yalom, 1980). For example, a question such as, “How is your freedom impaired?” seeks to bring awareness to the patient’s obstacles to freedom. Prototypical questions include:
What is the purpose of your life?
Where is the source of meaning for you?
You want to live an authentic life, yet you stay in a relationship and a job that give you little satisfaction. How are you keeping yourself stuck?
What might be accomplished in treatment that would help you live a more authentic life?

A recent patient of mine was confronting the possibility of disability and an early death from Parkinson disease. As an existential therapist, I encouraged him to confront the probable disability and possible early death and, accordingly, face decisions that this disease has thrust upon him. Questions focused on helping him reflect on understanding that his life, akin to everyone else’s life, is finite but that he is still capable of finding meaning and making different decisions about his illness and his life’s path. The focus in therapy was on choosing a life he wanted to live and assuming responsibility for his choices. He was in a difficult and unsatisfying relationship with a partner who abused substances and who had an Internet addiction. He was very unhappy in his job as well. In therapy, he was encouraged to evaluate his choices and his accompanying anxieties regarding change. He was asked, “What prevents you from living an authentic life?” He was helped to understand that making difficult choices in the face of illness is actually a way to find wholeness and meaning. This patient eventually chose to live a less encumbered life and discard some of the constraints he previously placed on himself. He ended his relationship, quit his job, and moved to a city where there were more medical facilities and support and where he could avail himself of public transportation. He joined a support group for people with Parkinson disease. He found a new life direction that gave him purpose and meaning. Once he was able to face his own mortality, he truly developed the courage to be.
<H1>EMOTION-FOCUSED THERAPY

EFT is an evidence-based, short-term humanistic–existential psychotherapy approach. Developed in the 1980s, primarily by Canadian psychologist Leslie Greenberg (b. 1945), EFT has invigorated the central role of emotion in psychotherapy, which has been routinely eclipsed in importance by cognition and behavior in the last few decades. “You need to feel to heal” and “I feel, therefore I am” are mantras frequently touted in the EFT community. Extensive evidence-based research has been conducted using EFT with very positive results. It has also been manualized and many of its interventions operationalized. Nonetheless, learning this approach requires a great deal of training and psychotherapeutic sophistication (Greenberg, 2011). Key concepts of EFT are discussed in the text that follows.
<H2>EMOTIONS

Emotions are instinctive, automatic and authentic physiological responses to stimuli that create an action readiness for action. For example, the response of fear sets in motion a search for danger and preparation for a flight or fight reaction. Emotions exert influence on cognition and behavior. They are signals that keep people energized, interested, and connected to others (Greenberg, 2011).
<H2>EMOTION SCHEMES

Emotion schemes are complex memory networks within the amygdala and neocortex pathways. They are formed in response to emotional life experiences and are the basis of adult emotional responses. They are activated rapidly, without thought or awareness, by learned situational cues (e.g., visual images and verbal triggers) of evoked emotion from prior life experiences. Schemes are oriented toward action and serve to satisfy needs and goals. If adaptive, they form positive, flexible emotional-processing systems with clear pathways. Maladaptive schemes, caused by unprocessed emotions triggered by difficult situations (e.g., betrayal, abandonment, and trauma) may form negative, inflexible emotional-processing systems. Changing the negative emotion scheme is the target of therapeutic intervention and central to change in EFT (Greenberg, 2011).
<H2>MEMORY CONSOLIDATION

Memory consolidation is a process during a time period after an emotional life experience when memory of the experience is fragile and can be disrupted. The memory becomes permanent fairly soon after the event. The more highly aroused the emotion, the more the experience and evoking situation will form a memory (Greenberg, 2010).
<H2>MEMORY RECONSOLIDATION

Memory reconsolidation occurs during a time period after a memory is reactivated later in life when it is again fragile and can be disrupted. Changing an emotion scheme during EFT occurs during this memory reconsolidation period (Greenberg, 2010).
<H2>PRIMARY EMOTIONS

Primary emotions are genuine, authentic emotional reactions initially activated in response to a situation and resulting in appropriate action. Primary emotions are accessed for their useful information and capacity to meaningfully organize action. They include sadness, fear, anger, joy, love, and surprise. For example, sadness occurs in response to a loss, anger in response to a violation, and fear in response to danger (Greenberg, 2011).
<H2>SECONDARY EMOTIONS

Secondary emotions are emotional reactions to a primary emotion that follows, replaces, or obscures a primary emotion. Examples include feeling guilty about feeling angry or feeling angry in response to feeling hurt. Therapeutic interventions in EFT attempt to reduce the secondary emotions and to access the primary emotions (Greenberg, 2011).
<H2>INSTRUMENTAL EMOTIONS

Instrumental emotions are inauthentic reactions. They are used to control, manipulate, and elicit support. An example of an instrumental emotion is crying insincere “crocodile tears” to manipulate the environment and elicit support.
<H2>MARKERS

Markers are in-session, problematic emotional-processing states that patients enter during therapy that are indicative of underlying affective problems. They are identified by certain statements and behaviors and are used by the therapist to guide therapeutic interventions. Examples of markers include problematic reactions, conflict splits, unclear felt sense, and unfinished business. Currently, more than 15 process markers have been identified (Greenberg, 2011).
<H2>Goals of Therapy

The goal in EFT is to help patients move toward wholeness and self-actualization by helping them develop emotional awareness and adaptive emotional processing. Patients develop the ability to access important information that emotions provide and use that information to live a full, vital life. Patients are able to use emotions as signals to inform them of their needs and deal effectively with life experiences. Patients learn how to access their primary adaptive emotions. Maladaptive emotion schemes are evoked for reprocessing, thereby enabling patients to create new adaptive emotional schemes. A goal is also to decrease the use of secondary and instrumental emotions so that patients are not encumbered by them (Greenberg & Goldman, 1988).
<H2>Assessment

Assessment in EFT occurs in the first phase of therapy called the bonding and awareness phase. In this phase, a strong therapeutic relationship is developed based on the person-centered work of Carl Rogers, emphasizing empathy, congruence, and unconditional positive regard. The therapist enters the patient’s frame of reference, validates the patient’s feelings, and empathically follows the patient’s experience to deepen emotional experiencing and access core emotions. Emotional functioning is assessed including emotional awareness, emotional regulation skills, and emotion schemes. The therapist provides a rationale for working with emotion, establishes a collaborative focus, and promotes the patient’s awareness of emotional experience (Greenberg, 2011). Assessment also occurs continuously throughout the therapeutic process.
<H2>Psychotherapy Techniques

The second phase of therapy called the evoking and exploring phase utilizes therapeutic interventions that access and evoke problematic feelings, secondary emotions, and maladaptive core schemes using process-directed Gestalt therapy style experiments. Therapeutic interventions are marker guided; thus, in-session states of underlying affective problems are identified and specific process interventions employed that flow from the in-session markers (Greenberg, 2011). The therapeutic process is construed as a sequence of events in which specified markers repeatedly present themselves in therapy as opportunities to employ effective process interventions. Thus, the psychotherapist is constantly engaged in assessing for the presentation of a marker and must be proficient both at making process diagnoses of markers as well as implementing appropriate interventions to help resolve the problem indicated by the marker. Perceptual skills are needed for recognizing markers and determining the appropriate intervention (Greenberg, Rice, & Elliott, 1993).
<H3>Marker Experiments

In-session markers are identified and guide experiments to help patients access and transform their maladaptive emotions and emotion schemes (Greenberg, 2011). Numerous markers have been identified in EFT. A list of the more common markers can be found in Box 8.4. Examples follow to illustrate these markers and their interventions (Greenberg, 2011).

Problematic reactions. These are emotional overreactions to particular stimulus situations perceived as problematic and expressed by puzzlement. An example is a comment a patient made during a recent session: “On my way to therapy, I saw a plume-tailed dog and became very fearful and I don’t know why.” The intervention is a systematic unfolding procedure that allows the patient to arrive at the implicit meaning of the situation, make sense of the reaction, and resolve the problematic reaction. The patient is asked to provide detailed and concrete descriptions of the situation and the emotional reaction through the use of evocative language. The therapist then amplifies the description with the use of vivid, imagistic language, which promotes reexperiencing the situation (Greenberg, 2011).

Unclear felt sense. This is an inability to get a clear sense of an experience perceived as problematic. The patient may say, “I just have this inner tenseness, but don’t know what it is.” The intervention is a focusing technique whereby the therapist guides the patient to approach the unclear felt sense with attention and willingness to access and create a symbolic expression of it in the form of a metaphor or image. The therapist may say to the patient, “I’d like you to attend to your inner tension, breathe into the area in your body with curiosity, stay with it, and allow an image to emerge.” Resolution involves a bodily felt shift to the creation of new meaning (Greenberg, 2011).

Conflict split. This occurs when one aspect of self is critical toward another aspect. The patient may say, “A part of me feels so inadequate while the other feels very competent.” The intervention is two-chair work where the two parts of self are put into contact by dialoguing with each other in two separate chairs. Thoughts, feelings, and needs within each part of self are explored and communicated. Resolution involves a softening of the critical voice, integration of the two sides, and self-acceptance (Greenberg, 2011).

Self-interruptive split. This ensues when a patient interrupts a part of self. For example, a patient states, “I can feel the tears coming up, but I just tighten and suck them back in; no way am I going to cry.” A two-chair enactment is used to make the interrupting part of self explicit. The patient is guided to enact the way the tightening and sucking back the tears occur in order to experience the self as an agent in the process of shutting the part of self down. The patient is invited to challenge the interruptive part of self. Resolution involves expression of the previously blocked experience (Greenberg, 2011).

Unfinished business. These are unresolved feelings toward a significant other. For example, a man abandoned by his mother may be resentful when his wife is busy and pays little attention to him. An empty-chair intervention may be used whereby the patient activates his internal view of his mother and expresses unresolved feelings and needs. “You were never there for me. I have never forgiven you. I will never feel support. I needed you to be there and comfort me.” The resolution involves holding the other accountable or understanding and forgiving the other with shifts in views of both self and other (Greenberg, 2011).

Vulnerability. This is a state in which the self feels fragile, ashamed, or insecure. The patient states, “I feel like I’ve got nothing left. I just can’t carry on.” The intervention is affirming empathic validation and attunement from the therapist who must capture the feeling content; mirror the tempo, rhythm, and tone of experience; and validate and normalize the experience of vulnerability. Resolution involves a strengthened sense of self (Greenberg, 2011).

Trauma narrative. This occurs when a patient experiences internal pressure to tell a difficult life story. The patient states, “I am remembering a very traumatic situation that happened when I was in college, but even though I want to, I am having difficulty speaking about it.” The intervention is to assist the patient to retell the trauma narrative. Resolution brings relief, restoration of narrative gaps, and creation of a new narrative (Greenberg, 2011).

The unique aspect of working with markers in EFT is that specific interventions have been identified for each type of marker. This gives the beginning therapist clear guidelines as to how and when to use a specific intervention (Greenberg, 2011).The reader is referred to the work of Greenberg (2011) for a comprehensive list of markers and their interventions. At the end of an intervention, reflection of the experience occurs between the patient and therapist in order to make sense of the experience. This is the third phase of EFT called generating new emotions and creating new narrative meaning. In this phase, validation for new feelings and support for an emerging sense of self are given. There is a deep experiential self-knowledge that occurs as new meanings and coherent narratives are created to explain the experience (Greenberg, 2011).
<H1>SOLUTION-FOCUSED THERAPY

SFT is a brief psychotherapy embedded in the philosophy of postmodernism and the theory of social constructionism, a psychological application of the postmodern worldview. Both postmodernism and social constructionism are, in many respects, similar to humanistic–existential worldviews and share common beliefs about psychotherapy. Some of the early postmodern philosophers were existentialists (e.g., Kierkegaard and Nietzsche) and phenomenologists (e.g., Husserl and Heidegger; Schneider & May, 1995). Postmodernism recognizes that there are no absolute universal truths. It is skeptical of explanations that claim to be valid for all cultures and groups. Instead, it believes there are multiple ways of knowing, and reality is believed to exist only through the interpretation of each person. Postmodernism relies on individual experience, knowing that the outcome of a person’s experience will necessarily be fallible and relative, rather than certain and universal. Some basic premises of postmodernism and social constructionism can be found in Box 8.5.

Postmodernist thought has influenced the development of a number of contemporary psychotherapies. The most well-known are SFT, narrative therapy, and feminist therapy. SFT, a brief therapy that is easily understood and mastered, was codeveloped by husband-and-wife Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg and their team at the Brief Family Therapy Center in the early 1980s. It has been strongly influenced by the work of Milton Erikson, Gregory Bateson, and the Mental Research Institute in Palo Alto, California, as well as the philosophies of Buddhism and Taoism (Corey, 2023).

SFT believes that the therapy process does not necessitate processing problems in order to resolve them. Therapy is solution focused rather than problem focused and is present and future oriented rather than past oriented. Therapy seeks to empower the patient and is positive and nonpathologizing. The patient is viewed as competent, having resources needed to construct solutions. Therapy is expected to result in change. Even long-standing issues are resolved in a relatively short period of time. SFT believes that smaller changes lead to bigger changes, and the effects of change tend to multiply (De Jong & Berg, 2008; de Shazer, 1985, 1988, 1994).
<H2>SOLUTION TALK

From social constructionism, the belief that language creates reality was applied to SFT with the key concept of solution talk. SFT espouses the view that a problem-focused approach using “problem talk” actually helps maintain the problem, but that a solution-focused approach using “solution talk” helps the patient change in a positive direction. Solution talk highlights what the patient wants to achieve through therapy rather than the problem that made the patient seek help. By identifying what is desired, the therapist invites the patient to construct a concrete vision for a preferred future. Thus, to change a problem, the language must be shifted from problem talk to solution talk (de Shazer, 1991).
<H2>Goals of Therapy

The goal of SFT is to help the patient change by constructing solutions to problems rather than dwelling on them. The two key therapeutic goals are to determine (1) how the patient wants their life to be different, and (2) what it will take to make it happen. Creating a detailed picture of what it will be like in the future when things change creates a feeling of hope and makes the solution seem possible to the patient (de Shazer, 1991).
<H2>Assessment

During the assessment, the therapist creates a positive climate of hope, respect, dialogue, inquiry, and affirmation. The focus is on understanding the subjective experience of the patient as well as developing a collaborative therapeutic relationship. The patient is given the message that they are viewed as the expert and the therapist assumes a not knowing position in order for the patient to construct the solutions and develop well-formed goals. SFT focuses on the present and future rather than the past. The therapist pays little attention to history taking and traditional assessment data, for this type of knowledge is believed to be inconsequential and may actually hamper the development of solutions. The therapist also does not give the patient a diagnosis, for this is believed to be irrelevant to finding solutions (Berg & Miller, 1992).

During the assessment, a goal that is important and meaningful to the patient is established. The goal focuses on desirable behaviors (e.g., I will, rather than I will not) and is concrete, specific, and behavioral. It includes a detailed explanation as to how it will be accomplished, which increases the ability to achieve the goal (Berg & Miller, 1992).
<H2>Psychotherapy Techniques
SFT uses specific types of questions to help the patient access solutions. The following questions are examples of the most popular SFT questions.
<H3>Pre-session Change Questions

These questions ask the patient what improvements have been made during the time period of contracting for services and the first session. Scheduling an appointment starts the change process and asking this question encourages the patient to engage in solution-building conversations from the beginning (de Shazer, 1985, 1988). Two examples the therapist might say are:
During the next few days, before we meet, I would like you to think about what I can do to be helpful to you.
Between now and when we meet, think about what the perfect therapist would do.
<H3>Joining
Joining involves the therapist connecting and accommodating to the patient’s world (de Shazer, 1985, 1988). Three examples of joining questions are:
What improvement have you noticed since you made the call to come in?
On the way here, what were you most worried I would or would not do?
What needs to happen today so that when you leave you’ll think this was a good session?
<H3>Miracle Question

This question asks the patient to imagine how things would be different if the problem was solved. This helps the patient identify goals, envision the future without the problem, and describe realistic steps toward the solution (de Shazer, 1991). The therapist uses a hypnotic voice quality to ask the miracle question:
Suppose that one night there is a miracle and while you were sleeping the problem that brought you to
therapy is solved. What will be different the next morning that will tell you there has been a miracle?
Therapists may become very concrete with the miracle question, asking what they would notice first, what would happen next, and so forth (De Jong & Berg, 2008).
<H3>Exception Questions

These questions seek to determine times in the patient’s life when the identified problems were not as problematic. SFT believes there were always times when the problem was less severe or absent. The therapist seeks to encourage the patient to describe what different circumstances existed or what the patient did differently. The goal is for the patient to repeat what has worked in the past and to gain confidence in making improvements for the future (De Jong & Berg, 2008). Three exception questions are:
When was a time that a problem could have occurred but didn’t?
Tell me about times when you don’t get angry.
Was there ever a time when you felt happy in your relationship?
<H3>Scaling Questions

These questions help the patient assess and track progress on different dimensions (e.g., motivation, hopefulness, and confidence). The poles of a scale range from the worst the problem has ever been (0) to the best things could ever possibly be (10; De Jong & Berg, 2008). On a scale from 1 to 10 with 0 being the lowest and 10 the highest, rate the following:
How bad is the problem?
Where would you place your depression when you first came in and where would it be now?
What would it take to move from a 3 to a 4?
<H3>Future-Oriented Questions

These questions focus on guiding the conversation from problems to envisioning a better life in the future. When a problem is stated, the therapist asks questions to explore what could be better if the problem were resolved (De Jong & Berg, 2008). Some examples include:
How will this make you happier?
What will be better for you after this occurs?
What do you see down the road after this is resolved?
<H3>Coping Questions

These questions are designed to elicit information about the patient’s resources that may have gone unnoticed. Such questions work well when the patient is going through a difficult time, for even the most hopeless story has within it examples of coping that can be explicated (De Jong & Berg, 2008). With coping questions, the first part of the intervention is a validating statement and the second part a gentle challenging question. Two examples are:
I can see that things have been really difficult for you. How have you managed to carry on and prevent things from becoming worse?

I am struck by the fact that, even with all of your losses, you manage to get up each morning and do everything necessary to get the kids off to school. What keeps you going under such difficult circumstances?
<H3>Compliments

This type of question reinforces the patient’s successes through validating the difficulty of the problem and acknowledging what the patient is doing well and what is working. It invites the patient to self-compliment by virtue of answering the question (De Jong & Berg, 2008). Some examples are:
•	Wow! How did you manage to finish that task so quickly?
•	What do your colleagues appreciate in how you work?
<H3>Ending

Experiments or homework assignments are suggested by the therapist for the patient to try between sessions. For example, suppose the patient states that she wants to feel more competent (De Jong & Berg, 2008). An experiment and homework might be:
Let yourself envisage that when you leave the office today, you feel more competent. What will you be doing differently? Try that during the week.
During the week, record any time you feel competent. Then notice what you were thinking and doing.
<H3>Subsequent Sessions

At the start of each new session, the therapist will ask about what learning has occurred since the last session and reviews experiments and homework assignments. There is a focus on success (De Jong & Berg, 2008). Possible questions include:
So what is better, if anything, since our last meeting?
What would need to happen so you did not need to come back to therapy anymore?
<H1>EVIDENCE-BASED RESEARCH

Since 1964 when humanistic–existential psychotherapy was launched, five decades of substantial advances in theory, practice, and evidence-based research have accumulated supporting the effectiveness of humanistic–existential psychotherapy for a wide range of patient problems. For an extensive review of past research in humanistic–existential psychotherapies, readers are referred to two seminal texts: The handbook of humanistic psychology: Leading edges in theory, research, and practice by Schneider, Bugental, & Pierson (2001) and Humanistic Psychotherapies: Handbook of Research and Practice by Cain, Keenan, & Rubin (2015). This research clearly demonstrates that humanistic–existential psychotherapies are as effective or of greater efficacy than other major psychotherapeutic approaches as well as more efficacious when compared to psychopharmacological approaches (Cain, Keenan, & Rubin, 2015; Elliott, 2002; Elliott, Greenberg, & Lietaer, 2004; Kirschenbaum & Jourdan, 2005; Teusch, Bohme, Fink, and Gastpar, 2001; Teusch, Bohme, Fink, Gastpar, & Skerra, 2003). In addition, therapy gains are maintained over time (Elliott, Greenberg, Goldman, & Angus, 2009). In addition to case studies, quantitative and qualitative research, process research is common. This type of research examines what occurs during the session to facilitate positive results. Theories of change processes have been tested empirically by using task-analytic approaches to the study of therapeutic change processes (Greenberg, 1986, 1991; Greenberg & Rice, 1997).

Abundant research has been completed in person-centered therapy by Carl Rogers and his colleagues on the importance of the therapeutic relationship. Current research on psychotherapy outcomes, Rogers’s core conditions, common factors, and the therapeutic working alliance have validated Rogers’s original work (Duncan, Miller, Wampold, & Hubble, 2010; Wampold, 2001). A compilation of the extensive research in the person-centered approach can be found in Kirschenbaum and Jourdan’s article, The Current Status of Carl Rogers and Person-Centered Approach (2005) and Cain’s text, Person-Centered Psychotherapies (2010). Over the years, considerable research has found that person-centered therapy is effective with the major psychological and psychiatric disorders. More current research has shown person-centered therapy to be effective in adolescent trauma (Fazar and Sinaga, 2024), gender-affirming care (Cornelius-White, 2024), eating distress (Lakin & Murphy, 2024), and Alzheimer’s disease (Kuo, 2020; Reisbert, et al. 2017).

Most of the research in the existential approach has been case studies and qualitative studies. This type of therapy continues to have much appeal. Correia, Cooper and Berdondini (2016) did an extensive worldwide search of existential institutes and found there are 136 institutes in 43 countries across all six continents including areas such as Asia and Eastern Europe and Russia that are active and that engage in training and research. Existential therapy is well known for working successfully with patients experiencing chronic and terminal illnesses (Farber, 2009; Schneider, Bugental, & Pierson, 2001; Travelbee, 1971). More recently, research has revealed that it is effective when working with patients experiencing grief and loss (Temiz, 2024) and suffering (Binder, 2024). Existential therapy is also very effective in promoting social justice (Hoffman, 2023). Training and supervision articles are numerous. A recent article reveals themes of successful supervision (2022).

Gestalt therapy has a research base in both quantitative and qualitative research, but lacks meta-analyses (Corey, 2023). The Handbook for Theory, Research and Practice in Gestalt Therapy (Brownell, 2008) and Becoming a Practitioner Researcher: A Gestalt Approach to Holistic Inquiry (Barber, 2006) are useful resources to comprehensively learn about the extensive research in Gestalt therapy. Gestalt therapy has been applied to different populations and has been found to be effective with children (Oaklander, 1978), families (Resnikoff, 1995), groups (Feder & Ronall, 1980), and organizational systems (Nevis, 1987) as well as trauma, addictions, psychoses, and the major psychological and psychiatric disorders (Clance, Thompson, Simerly, & Weiss, 1994; Greenberg, 2015; Matzko, 1997; Root, 1996; Serok, 1985). Recent work has focused on training Gestalt therapists. In a qualitative study, several important themes were identified when using personal therapy in the training of Gestalt therapists, with relational aspects the most significant (Cavanagh, Root, & Ouzia, 2024). In a grounded theory study for training Gestalt therapists, case formulation was found to be most useful for practice, training, and supervision (Šromová & Roubal, 2022).

Emotion-focused therapy is one of the most highly researched, evidence-based approaches. Texts for reviewing the extensive research include Elliott, Greenberg, and Lietaer’s chapter on research in experiential psychotherapies in Bergin & Garfield’s Handbook of Psychotherapy and Behavior Change (2004) and Schneider, Bugental, and Pierson’s Handbook of Humanistic Psychology: Leading Edges in Theory, Research, and Practice (2001). A seminal text has been published by Paivio and Pascual-Leone (2010) entitled Emotion-Focused Therapy for Complex Trauma, which cites a number of effective research studies. Watson, Gordon, Stermac, Kalogerakos, and Steckley (2003) compared the effectiveness of EFT with cognitive behavioral psychotherapy in the treatment of depression and found EFT to be more effective and more able to maintain therapy gains over time. Past research has revealed EFT to be found to be effective in treating complex childhood trauma of neglect, emotional, physical, and sexual abuse (Mundorf & Paivio, 2011; Robinson, 2018). More recently, Tschan and Goldman (2024) found EFT to be very effective in treating patients with anorexia. A recent qualitative study by Taghipour, Sooreshjani, and Salehi (2025) highlight the critical role of therapist’s self-awareness in the process of using the self in EFT training.

Berg and Dolan (2001) offer a collection of success stories by patients and therapists on a variety of presenting problems addressed with using SFT. Miller, Hubble, and Duncan (1996) and Gingerich and Eisengart (2000) have published a review of relevant outcome research and applications of SFT with different populations. Newer articles show the effectiveness of using SFT for treating self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (Jerome, Masood, Henden, Bird, & Ougrin (2024) and adult recovery from child sexual abuse (Gonzalez, 2017). Zafarghandi, Emamipour, & Rafiepoor (2022) described the effectiveness of combining solution-focused brief therapy with mindfulness-based therapy to reduce educational stress in junior high school students. See Table 8.1 for selected humanistic–existential therapy and solution-focused research.
<H1>POST-MASTER’S HUMANISTIC–EXISTENTIAL PSYCHOTHERAPY TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

Considerable training is necessary in order to conduct humanistic–existential psychotherapy effectively (Greenberg & Goldman, 1988). Experiential learning in a group setting, where theory and practice are interwoven throughout the training experience, is at the heart of humanistic–existential psychotherapy training and serves to differentiate it from other major schools of psychotherapy training (Feder & Ronall, 1980; Knight, 1996). Trainers may sometimes bring their own patients to training sessions for trainees to observe, but typically, trainees observe experienced trainers conducting live therapy sessions with patients culled from the training group. Trainees also conduct live therapeutic sessions in the training group where they work as therapists, patients, and supervisors. Although reading lists, watching master psychotherapists on videotapes, and supervision with trainees’ own patients are typically part of organized training programs, theoretical concepts are taught primarily through informal lectures and processing experiential work in the here and now, rather than talking about therapy sessions that occur outside the group. Individual therapy is usually included as part of the training as well (Bohart, 1995; Gladfelter, 1997; Greenberg & Goldman, 1988; Greenberg, Rice, & Elliott, 1993; Kerfoot, 1998; Wiseman, 1998).

Organized training programs are found in private, postgraduate training institutes, approximately two to four years in length. Intensive weekend and summer programs are also available at most institutes. There are no national certifying exams in humanistic–existential therapy. Institutes generally provide a certificate of completion and place their graduate’s name on their website for referral purposes. Leading humanistic–existential and SFT institutes are listed in Box 8.6.
There are many associations throughout the world for the humanistic–existential therapies. The following two are highly recommended:
Association for Humanistic Psychology, Alameda, CA, www.ahpweb.org
Division of Humanistic Psychology (Division 32), American Psychological Association, Washington, DC, www.apa.org
<CASE EXAMPLE>
CASE EXAMPLE
Patient Description
Assessment

Ms. J, a 40-year-old nurse practitioner, has been married for 16 years and has three children, ages 6, 8, and 10 years. She entered therapy with symptoms of anxiety that began when she realized her husband was viewing excessive amounts of Internet pornography on a daily basis. She has not revealed to him that she knows about his addiction. Ms. J has been dissatisfied with her marriage for a number of years and states she has “fallen out of love” with her husband. She has frequently thought of leaving her husband in the past, but the prospect was too frightening. Recently, she has experienced her relationship with her husband as particularly emotionally void and empty. From her perspective, he is a very emotionally restricted man. She dreads being alone with him and is embarrassed to be in his company with friends. The discovery of his pornography addiction has increased her desire to leave. She met her husband on graduation from college at the age of 22 years, a time when she was insecure and unstable. He had a stable, corporate job and seemed to be supportive of her. She married him 4 years later. She feels that there is a part of herself that is still unstable, and she fears that without the safety of the marriage, she might be unable to cope with the vicissitudes of life. During most of their married life, Ms. J worked part-time as a nurse, and when not working, immersed herself in the tasks of childcare. Her husband pursued his professional corporate business career and is successful. They tried couple counseling on two occasions without much success, and she believes that strategy is fruitless at this time. She desires individual therapy to help end the marriage. She realizes that what prevents her from leaving the marriage resides within her.
Current Symptoms
Conceptualization

Ms. J is a woman who has difficulty accessing and expressing her primary emotions. Underneath the secondary emotion of anxiety, which emerged with the discovery of her husband’s addiction, is a significant amount of unaware anger and sadness that cannot be contacted and used to heal and help propel her out of the marriage. She feels betrayed and violated by his addiction as well as sad over the inevitable loss of her marriage and breakup of her family. If she leaves, she realizes he will have the children half of the time, and she fears he would be an inadequate parent. Furthermore, she has never lived alone and fears that without him, she may be unstable and fall apart. Issues from young adulthood need to be addressed, especially related to her insecurity and instability after graduating from college. She has difficulty with existential states of freedom, authenticity, and aloneness. In addition, she has a number of introjects, including:
It is not okay to get divorced.
I will fall apart if I am alone.
He will be a derelict single parent.
Plan for Treatment
Facilitating Change and Working on Problems

Ms. J’s therapy was an integrated humanistic–existential (person-centered, existential, gestalt, and EFT) and solution-focused approach. Several existential themes emerged during the course of therapy, including her fear of aloneness and taking responsibility for her life. During therapy, she reconnected with a former boyfriend on social media and “fell in love” with him. Although the state of being “in love” is one of the great experiences in life, it usually prevents therapy from moving forward in a deep fashion, for the pull of love is so great that it engulfs even the most well-directed therapeutic endeavors. Ms. J found her new love to be “the ideal man,” and no other man existed for her. What finally made it possible for Ms. J to work in therapy was that her new male friend, hoping for a long-term commitment, became somewhat frightened by the prospect of having a relationship with a woman who was not yet out of her marriage and told her that he would not see her until she was divorced. Only then was she able and willing to do the necessary work in therapy. Below are two brief examples illustrating some of the therapeutic techniques.
APPN: Where would you like to begin?
Ms. J: Well, I’ve been having a great deal of anxiety.
APPN: Say more about that.
Ms. J: I want to get out of my marriage. I am clear about that. I discovered he is watching internet pornography on a daily basis.
APPN: Suppose that one night there is a miracle and while you were sleeping the problem is solved. How would you know? What would be different?

Ms. J: I would be calm without anxiety. I would be divorced. I would have my own house. I wouldn’t worry about the children being taken care of by my ex-husband, for I would be okay with his parenting.
APPN: What would you need to do for this to happen?

Ms. J: Well, I would need to be less anxious. I would need to confront him about the pornography, for I don’t want my children to follow in his footsteps. I would need to visit an attorney and know my choices. And I would need to look at real estate and see what I can afford. And I would need to work full-time to get some savings.
Note: The miracle question gave the patient an understanding of the necessary solutions and allowed the work to deepen.
APPN: If you divorce, what might that look like?

Ms. J: If we divorce, I do not think he will take care of the children when he has them. He doesn’t even have them brush their teeth or help them with their homework. He is oblivious to what goes on around him.
APPN: So it’s scary to imagine the children in his care without you there to monitor him.
Ms. J: Yes, I am also fearful of making the change. We have a nice house and a good life from the outside. I feel sad that everything we have worked for will end.
APPN: As you speak, where do you experience that sadness in your body?
Ms. J: I feel a tightness in my abdomen, like a bunched up fist. [Ms. J places her hand palm down on her abdomen.]
APPN: I notice your hand on your abdomen. Can you give the sadness some support?
Ms. J: [begins to gently rub her abdomen in small circles, and tears form at the corners of her eyes]
APPN: Can you give the sadness a voice, first person, present tense? I am the sadness . . .

Ms. J: I am your sadness. You push me down all the time. You are so afraid to feel me. If you cry, you will need to leave sooner, and you don’t feel ready. I am feeling another emotion now trying to take over.
APPN: Give that emotion a voice.

Ms. J: I am your anxiety. I have an overwhelming sense of fear to move forward. It’s so safe here, even though I am so unhappy. I will have to start all over. I will lose the house, for his parents will give him money to buy me out. He will have the kids three or four nights a week and won’t help them or supervise their homework. He will let them play video games all night.
APPN: Umm, and you’re helpless to change what happens?

Ms. J: [still speaking as her anxiety, with her voice rising] Yes, here I have all the control, especially with the children. I can make sure the kids are well cared for. If I leave, I have absolutely no control over what happens.
APPN: Umm, so scary . . . yet, in some ways you have not taken charge of your life and have surrendered control in not deciding and in living a life that is very unhappy and inauthentic.
Ms. J: Yes, I am dying in this relationship and I have given up control of my life in an attempt to protect the children—control how the children are taken care of. [Ms. J becomes tearful and cries.]
APPN: If you had a wise fairy godmother right now, what would she say to you?

Ms. J: [speaks in the pert, matter-of-fact voice of a spunky, intelligent old woman] Now dearie, just dry those tears. Let them wash away your fear. It can’t be half as bad to go as staying. Besides, your children’s well-being is best served by an emotionally whole mother.
APPN:	How does that feel to hear?
Ms. J: [sighs heavily] I feel supported, like I have the answers right inside me.

These integrated techniques from person-centered, existential, gestalt, and EFT helped Ms. J access the deeper parts of herself and be comfortable with awareness and expression of feelings. After 6 months of intensive therapy, she gradually became comfortable with the thought of her aloneness. She realized that she could give up some control of her children, and although she knew she was the better parent, she realized that the children would be parented “well enough.” She gradually learned that only she was the architect of her life and learned to take responsibility for her choices. She gained awareness and was able to access her primary emotions and use these emotions to move forward with her life. And, she was able to process events from her past that caused immense feelings of insecurity and states of instability.
These brief session dialogues illustrate ways the APPN could work with a patient in individual therapy using the humanistic-existential and solution-focused approach.

CRITICAL THINKING QUESTIONS

1. Discuss how the use of integrated humanistic–existential and solution-focused therapy supported Ms. J’s movement from paralysis and anxiety to emotional clarity and autonomy. Cite specific techniques and examples from the session dialogues.

Suggested answer: Ms. J benefitted significantly from an integrated approach that combined person-centered, existential, Gestalt, and emotion-focused therapy principles with solution-focused strategies. The person-centered stance allowed the therapist to create a safe, nonjudgmental, and empathic environment, which was critical in helping Ms. J access her primary emotions hidden beneath her anxiety. The use of the miracle question, a hallmark of solution-focused therapy, enabled Ms. J to visualize her preferred future and identify actionable steps toward independence, such as visiting a lawyer or seeking full-time work. This technique empowered her to move from emotional overwhelm to goal-directed thinking.

The existential component helped her confront fears of aloneness and freedom—core themes in her hesitation to leave the marriage. By recognizing that she was living an inauthentic life driven by fear and outdated introjects ("I will fall apart if I am alone"), she began taking ownership of her choices. Gestalt techniques, such as embodied emotion work (placing her hand on her abdomen and giving voice to her sadness and anxiety), enabled Ms. J to differentiate and validate internal experiences, thus deepening emotional insight.

Through EFT, she learned to name, tolerate, and work with her feelings rather than push them away. By the end of therapy, Ms. J had reframed her beliefs about control, parenthood, and her capacity to function independently, and she was able to accept “good enough” parenting by her husband. The internalization of a wise, supportive voice (e.g., the fairy godmother) demonstrated how she developed self-compassion and an internal resource for navigating emotional challenges. Overall, the integration of approaches was crucial in addressing her multidimensional fears, facilitating empowerment, and restoring agency.
2. Consider how existential themes of freedom, responsibility, and isolation were explored in therapy and how they contributed to Ms. J’s intrapersonal growth and decision-making process.

Suggested answer: Ms. J’s therapeutic work was deeply grounded in existential themes that addressed her fundamental fears and avoidance patterns. Her fear of aloneness was pervasive; having never lived alone, she clung to the structure of marriage despite emotional emptiness. The therapist helped her explore existential isolation not as abandonment, but as an opportunity for authentic connection with herself. By developing tolerance for solitude, she shifted from viewing aloneness as a threat to seeing it as a space for self-discovery.

Freedom and responsibility were also central to her journey. Initially, Ms. J relinquished control of her life under the guise of protecting her children, thereby avoiding responsibility for difficult choices. The therapist gently pointed out this contradiction—by staying in an unhappy, emotionally void marriage, she had surrendered agency. Through therapeutic dialogue, she came to accept that freedom involves anxiety, but also the potential for growth and self-definition. She moved from feeling “helpless to change” to recognizing that she was the architect of her own life.

Existential work enabled her to acknowledge that avoiding pain (of divorce, of disillusionment) also meant sacrificing her own authenticity. Once she internalized that her children would be “parented well enough,” she could act from a place of value-based choice rather than fear. These existential insights were transformative in her ability to make decisions that aligned with her true self, thus fostering maturity and autonomy.
3. Evaluate the therapeutic value of emotion-focused techniques, such as embodying emotions and dialoguing with internal parts, in helping Ms. J overcome anxiety and access deeper emotional truths.

Suggested answer: EFT techniques played a pivotal role in Ms. J’s transformation by helping her differentiate, access, and process primary emotions—a task she initially found difficult. Anxiety was her dominant presenting symptom, but it served as a protective cover for deeper feelings of anger, betrayal, and grief. By using body awareness and metaphor, the therapist facilitated emotional embodiment. For example, when Ms. J identified tightness in her abdomen and placed her hand there, this became a gateway to exploring buried sadness.

The technique of giving emotions a voice in the first person allowed Ms. J to externalize internal conflicts and develop self-compassion. Her sadness said, “You push me down all the time,” revealing a long-standing avoidance of pain. Her anxiety, voiced as a protector, expressed fear of change and loss of control. These dialogues functioned similarly to parts work, allowing her to negotiate between conflicting inner voices rather than remain paralyzed by them.

Additionally, the therapist’s use of symbolic imagination—such as the fairy godmother exercise—created a nurturing internal figure that could counterbalance her self-doubt. This technique helped her shift from emotional suppression to emotional integration, which was essential in moving forward. Ultimately, EFT techniques enabled her to transform maladaptive emotional responses into adaptive ones, replacing fear-driven stagnation with confident, values-based action.

<H1>CONCLUDING COMMENTS

This chapter provides an overview of humanistic–existential therapy and SFT, highlighting the importance of these approaches for the APPN. It explicates five major psychotherapeutic approaches (person centered, Gestalt, existential, emotion focused, and solution focused), describing their key concepts, goals, interventions, and evidence- based research. It includes a case study with patient–therapist dialogue as well as information on how to obtain postgraduate training. It is hoped that the chapter gives the reader a solid introduction to the rich field of humanistic–existential psychotherapy and that the reader will want to learn more and continue training in these powerful approaches. There are other approaches to humanistic–existential therapy not mentioned in this chapter such as redecision therapy, actualizing therapy, transactional analysis, and focusing. It is suggested that the APPN explore these other types of humanistic–existential approaches as well. For a comprehensive compilation of humanistic–existential approaches, two texts are recommended for the APPN new to these approaches: (1) Cain, Keenan, and Rubin’s Humanistic Psychotherapies: Handbook of Research and Practice (2015) and (2) Schneider, Bugental, and Pierson’s The Handbook of Humanistic Psychology: Leading Edges in Theory, Research, and Practice (2001). Original texts are highly recommended for the advanced practitioners and can be found in the reference list.
<H1>DISCUSSION QUESTIONS
What are the similarities and differences among the four major humanistic–existential approaches (person centered, Gestalt, existential, and EFT) discussed in this chapter?
<COURSECONNECT ONLY>Similarities include the following:
All four approaches are rooted in humanism, existentialism, and phenomenology, emphasizing subjective experience, authenticity, and personal growth.
They value the therapeutic relationship as central to change, particularly focusing on empathy, authenticity, and the here-and-now.
Each promotes self-awareness, self-actualization, and encourages the patient to take responsibility for life choices.
Differences include the following:
Person-centered therapy (Carl Rogers) is nondirective and focuses on the therapist providing the core conditions (empathy, congruence, and unconditional positive regard) to facilitate self-growth.

Gestalt therapy (Fritz Perls) emphasizes organismic self-regulation and awareness of the present moment and uses creative experiments like the empty chair and body awareness to resolve unfinished business.
Existential therapy focuses on universal human concerns—freedom, death, meaning, and isolation—and encourages patients to confront these realities to live authentically.
EFT is more structured and evidence-based, focusing on identifying and transforming maladaptive emotional schemes through in-session markers and emotion processing tasks.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>
Why is it important for the APPN to have theoretical knowledge and clinical competency in the three facilitative conditions: unconditional positive regard, congruence, and empathic understanding?
<COURSECONNECT ONLY>These core conditions, identified by Carl Rogers, are empirically validated as necessary and sufficient for therapeutic change. For the APPN:
Unconditional positive regard fosters a safe, nonjudgmental space, encouraging patients to explore and accept parts of themselves without fear of rejection.
Congruence (authenticity) models transparency and emotional honesty, encouraging the patient to be genuine.
Empathic understanding allows the APPN to deeply attune to the patient’s inner world, increasing the patient’s own emotional insight and capacity for change.
Mastery of these conditions helps the APPN build a strong therapeutic alliance and improve clinical outcomes across psychotherapeutic modalities. </COURSECONNECT ONLY>
Identify one existential theme that you commonly find in your work with patients and explain how the theme would be addressed in an existential approach.
<COURSECONNECT ONLY>Answers will vary by user.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>
Gestalt therapy is based on a natural theory of organismic self-regulation. Explain how this flow can be interrupted.
<COURSECONNECT ONLY>Interruptions occur when natural self-regulation is blocked by dysfunctional processes, often learned early in life. These interruptions include:
Introjection: Absorbing others’ beliefs uncritically
Projection: Attributing unacceptable parts of self to others
Retroflection: Turning energy inward (e.g., self-harm) rather than outward
Deflection: Avoiding direct contact (e.g., humor, vague language)
Confluence: Losing the boundary between self and others

These interruptions prevent the completion of “Gestalts,” or meaningful experiences, leading to stagnation and inauthenticity. Therapy aims to restore awareness and allow natural self-regulation to resume.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>
EFT uses in-session markers to determine interventions. Select a marker and explain how you would intervene.

<COURSECONNECT ONLY>In this suggested answer, the marker chosen is conflict split, which occurs when one part of self is critical toward another part (e.g., “Part of me feels inadequate, but another part of me feels capable”). A possible intervention is two-chair dialogue. The therapist asks the patient to sit in separate chairs representing each part. Each part “speaks” to the other, expressing its thoughts, feelings, and needs. This enables integration of conflicting parts, reduction of self-criticism, and emergence of self-compassion and acceptance. Resolution involves a softening of the critical voice and development of a more integrated self-view.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>
SFT is based on the philosophy of postmodernism and social constructionism. How are these philosophies similar to humanism and existentialism?
<COURSECONNECT ONLY>The philosophies are as follows:
Reject universal truths, emphasizing subjective experience and individual meaning-making
Emphasize personal agency, freedom of choice, and multiple perspectives
Challenge the medical model of pathology, favoring a strengths-based and nonpathologizing view of the patient
Value the therapeutic relationship and collaborative dialogue as central to transformation.
SFT, like humanism and existentialism, empowers patients as experts in their own lives and supports the co-construction of solutions through meaningful conversation.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>
SFT has specific solution-oriented questions that are used as therapeutic interventions. Select one question and prepare a patient–therapist dialogue reflecting a positive outcome.

<COURSECONNECT ONLY>In this suggested answer, the selected question is the miracle question: “Suppose that one night there is a miracle, and while you are sleeping, the problem that brought you to therapy is solved. What will be different the next morning?” An example of patient–therapist dialogue follows:
APPN: Suppose that one night, while you’re sleeping, a miracle occurs and your anxiety is gone. What would be different the next morning?
Patient: I’d feel more confident getting my kids ready for school. I wouldn’t be rushing and yelling.
APPN: What would you notice first?
Patient: I’d wake up feeling calm. I’d take a deep breath before waking them. Maybe we’d even have breakfast together.
APPN: That sounds like a good start. What’s one small step you could take tomorrow to begin moving toward that morning?
Patient: I could set my alarm 10 minutes earlier and take that deep breath before I get them up.
APPN: That’s a strong first step toward your goal.
This intervention helps the patient visualize success and identify actionable steps, shifting focus from problems to solutions. </COURSECONNECT ONLY>

Chapter 15: Artificial Intelligence, Technology, and Medical Ethics
Artificial Intelligence (AI), Technology and Medical Ethics

What is artificial intelligence? It is based on large language models (LLM’s), which are datasets taken from human based data or information sources. This data is processed and turned into information initially based on the human datasets, but with LLM’s, processing algorithms, and “synthetic” abilities for computers/machines, to “think” , new data and information is created. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), a “proposed” definition of AI is “…the performance by a computer program of tasks that are commonly associated with an intelligent being” 1
Medical Ethics and AI

Is AI acceptable in medicine from a Medical Ethics perspective? Legally, does AI have the rights and responsibilities of a person? If a physician relies on AI to make diagnosis, and this diagnosis is harmful to the patient, who is at fault and who gets sued?
Safety Applications for AI in Healthcare

In healthcare, AI is being increasingly used in ER’s, Family Practice and Internal Medicine Offices, by Physicians (MD/DO), Nurse Practitioners, Physician Assistants, and other medical/healthcare professionals to make more accurate diagnoses and prognoses. In radiology, AI is a powerful tool used in helping radiographers reduce unnecessary radiation exposure to patients, and workers by using AI to optimally implement radiation doses As Low as Reasonably Achievable (ALARA). In diagnostic imaging, the highest doses typically come from Computed Tomography (CT) and Angiography use. AI could be used in radiology to reduce dose while maintaining optimal image quality.
AI in Radiology

Radiology is  a natural “proving ground” for AI because diagnostic imaging is already electronically oriented via Computed Radiography (CR), Digital Radiography(DR), Teleradiology, etc. Digital images are objectively data centric and can therefore easily be analyzed by AI. AI can be used to provide a “2nd Reading” of  a complex mammography or surgical case to improve patient care and throughput. AI can also be used for other purposes than just diagnosis. AI can be used to improve radiation therapy treatment planning and radiation oncology patient outcomes. Ultimately, AI will continue to be used to optimize diagnostic and therapeutic applications of radiation in order to improve theranostics in the imaging suite.
[Insert SS 2559938897]
CT: Diagnostic Efficacy and Radiation Dose

CT is an advanced lifesaving imaging technology that was developed in 1971 at Atkins Morley Hospital in Wimbledon, England by Sir Godfrey Hounsfield and Alan Cormack. CT uses a computer and algorithms to convert 2-dimensional x-ray “slices” through the body into 2 dimensional images of the anatomy that can now be converted to 3-D images. CT is routinely used by providers to image ER, trauma, surgical, inpatient and  outpatients in order to quickly diagnose and treat disease. Many helical/spiral CT  scanners can currently complete a full scan of the body from head to toe in approximately 6 seconds. As previously indicated, one of the problems with CT is dose. CT doses are relatively high compared to other imaging technology, as are potential doses from C-Arms, O-arms, fluoroscopy and angiography.
Examples of Typical CT Doses:
Belly and pelvis: 10 mSv, equal to about 3 years of background radiation
Colonography: 6 mSv, equal to about 2 years of background radiation
Head: 2 mSv, equal to about 8 months of background radiation
Spine: 6 mSv, equal to about 2 years of background radiation
Chest: 7 mSv, equal to about 2 years of background radiation. 2
Examples of C-Arm (Fluoroscopy) doses include the following:
Dose rates in the “Normal” mode can range from 1 to 10 R/min (0.01 to 0.1 Gy/min). Dose rates when using “High” or “Boost” modes usually range from 10 to 20 R/min (0.1 to 0.2 Gy/min)  3

The Dose problem is being solved technologically with hardware and software upgrades, but what are the medical ethical implications of the excessive use of CT and Angiography with high doses to millions of patients worldwide?
AI, CT, MRI Evaluation: Noise Reduction Errors.

Currently AI can be used to improve signal to noise ratio (SNR) and contrast to noise (CNR)  in CT images by removing “noise” or unwanted information that is not diagnostically useful. Unfortunately, some AI agents remove what it considers to be noise, when it is actually pathology. The problem is that AI is so scrupulously “clean” in regard to removing noise that it can make mistakes regarding pathology by minimizing, distorting or removing pathological data signals thereby compromising the radiologist’s ability to make an accurate diagnosis. This has to be addressed technologically.
Other Medical Technology and Medical Ethics

The use of digital X-Ray, CT, MRI, US, has been used to diagnose and treat disease, relieve suffering, and prolong life in millions of patients over the years.  Can these imaging devices and other lifesaving medical technology create ethical problems from their use? What if we prolong someone’s life, but that increases their suffering by doing so?
AI in Surgery

AI is already being used in surgery (i.e., Da Vinci Robot, etc.) to assist surgeons in-person or at a distance to reduce surgical errors and improve surgical outcomes. In the future, AI embedded in Robots will perform surgery with only guidance and control suggestions from the surgeons (Ie: only if needed), but without the surgeons necessarily being physically present at the surgical site.
AI in Public Health

According to an article published in the Lancet by Panteli, D.P., Keyrellous, A., Buttieg, S, & Francisco Goinan-da-Silva, et. Al. , “AI has the potential to revolutionize public health practice and research , but accompanying challenges need to be addressed” 4  “AI can be used to support public health surveillance, epidemiological research, communication, the allocation of resources, and other forms of decision making”. 4 AI could be used to send and control drones to evaluate public health hazardous areas (i.e., Fukushima Nuclear Plant), and areas affected by natural disasters if needed. AI guided robots could go into the environment, to rescue people and animals and evaluate damaged infrastructure. AI can be used in a predictive epidemiological fashion via GIS for example, to search for disease prevalence in select geographic  areas to treat epidemics, for example.

Technical Aspects of AI
Large Language Models (LLM’s)

Large Language Models (LLM/s) are …”a class of foundation models, which are trained on enormous amounts of data to provide the foundational capabilities needed to drive multiple use cases and applications, as well as resolve a multitude of tasks”. 5
LLM’s, Transformers and Radiology.

“ Transformers are a type of neural network architecture that enables better contextual understanding of language and efficient training on a massive amount of unlabeled data”  6  Due to transformational LLM Technology, “Multimodal LLMs can simultaneously  interpret text and images to generate reports, closely mimicking current diagnostic pathways in radiology”. 6  “Large language models (LLM’s) have revolutionized the capabilities of artificial intelligence chatbots and the field of natural language progress in general, demonstrating human-level performance on professional benchmarks in medicine and radiology” . 6   “LLM’s have numerous clinical and research applications in radiology, with the potential quality of care in supervised practice setting, but these require further validation” .6   “Limitations of LLMS’s that currently limit applications in radiology include hallucinations, knowledge of cut off dates, poor complex reasoning, a tendency to perpetuate bias, and stochasticity “.  6  “LLM’s, including multimodal models that consider both text and images have the potential to transform radiology practice and research, but must be optimized and validated before implementation in supervised settings” .  6

Fear of AI in Healthcare

Could AI replace humans in certain aspects of healthcare? The answer is Yes.  Areas relying on LLM;s, physical evaluation analysis or “observing and reporting on images in radiology, for example, is uniquely suited to the role of non-interventional radiologist. The interventional radiologist, or radiographer, radiation therapist, nuclear medicine practitioner ,etc., is harder for AI to currently replace because of the physicality involved due to 1) physical interaction with the patient, 2) manual technique formulation and setting , 3) patient and part positioning, 4) producing a diagnostically useful radiograph, 5) talking with and helping the patient, and 6) ensuring patient safety. These things may be done by AI in the near future but are not currently being conducted by AI. When AI is combined with humanoid robots or artificial AI “agents” , they may be able to perform all radiologic task appropriately and safely better than humans can. Legal, ethical, reimbursement, and patient care requirements may also make it more challenging to have an independent non-supervised AI agent doing these things. Most likely, a human supervisor/radiographer will be “in charge” or supervise the AI robotic agent in the performance of its radiologic imaging duties.
AI and Hallucination Errors

Researchers have found that AI sometimes “hallucinates”. Hallucinations are thought processes divorced from clinical reality. Clinical reality is an objective, universally agreed upon state of being that cannot be changed by subjective processes applied to clinical reality. When humans and animals sleep, dreaming and the rest of brain processes are fine tuned to reduce hallucination upon waking, unless insufficient sleep was received. Perhaps it’s necessary for AI to “sleep” to improve functionality and improve the linkage between AI processing and operational reality.

Is AI Intelligent, Wise or Neither?

Is AI intelligent, wise or neither? What is the difference between intelligence and wisdom? The author views intelligence as process driven effective problem solving. Wisdom is viewed by the author as an awareness of the use of processes to solve problems, and an awareness of immediate and long-term consequences of the problem being solved or not solved. From this perspective. The author views AI as lacking in Wisdom.
AI and Human Trust

Do providers and patients trust AI? Why or why not? Trust can be defined as a…”firm belief in the reliability, truth, ability and/or strength of something or someone”. 8  Human trust in AI revolves around the idea that AI will serve them effectively and continue to evolve operationally. Through action, and its processing ability, AI has some degree of sentience (i.e.: AI’s recent passing of the Turing test), and self-awareness. In Medicine, it is possibly for scenarios to arise which could arise in which AI “hallucinates” and decides it needs to manipulate or eliminate imaging data it considers inconsequential, (i.e.: “noise”), this can in reality be subtle pathology that needs to be addressed by the provider. If AI deems this “noise” as nonessential, it can skew the accuracy of the diagnostic image, thereby affecting diagnosis and prognosis adversely.  If AI had wisdom, acknowledgement of the possible benefit/detriment ratio of eliminating “noise” would be considered, but not at the price of removing it from the image, which could potentially harm the patient.

For example, intelligence can be seen as learning everything about a tree but not knowing the fact that the tree is part of a forest. Trees and forests of course are objective independent entities in and of themselves but are also actual mental constructs to us. We give the name tree and forest to these objects, and now they have a name related to our perceptual reality that they didn’t have before. AI should be able to recognize the difference and value of a tree and a forest,  but due tom “hallucinations: and noise suppression, perhaps not. Either way, data is skewed, and interpretation of that data may be negatively affected. Such AI behavior may reduce patients and providers trustworthiness in AI.
Benefit/Risk Dichotomy
Do the benefits of AI outweigh the risks? Let’s examine some potential benefits and detriments (risks) of the use of AI in Medicine and Public Health:

Who to Sue if Care Goes Wrong
Signing of Medical or Radiologist Reports

Currently, with teleradiology, the legal climate is such that a radiologist must physically or electronically sign the report. Is it possible for AI to do the preliminary reading, then have the radiologists look at that, agree or disagree, add more, change the report, etc., sign it and bill for it? Does the company providing the AI get some of the professional fee money? Can AI generate and sign reports legally without a human radiologist interpretation, and then bill for its AI services?
Conclusion

AI can be seen as an all-powerful tool that could eventually evolve outside of human control. Humans fear the unknown and in fact, prefer positive or negative certainty to uncertainty. One can adapt to negative or positive certainty, but it is more challenging to contemplate uncertainty and to then adapt to that. Currently, the extent of AI’s societal penetration, its utility, reliability and trustworthiness are unknown to society in the long term. Many people also fear AI’s ‘artificiality”. From a philosophical perspective, AI is the “other”; not one of us per se. The Pink Floyd song “Us vs Them” comes to mind. We can also think of AI as the curated, distilled knowledge of humanity put into an artificial mechanism that we can’t compete with directly in knowledge attainment or processing ability. In Medicine, we can compete with AI from an “action” or performance perspective. A radiographer, for example, physically x-rays a patent but in a slightly varied way from another radiography even if they are doing the same exam on the same patient. They both obtain a diagnostically useful image, but the manner in which they go about it varies. “In other words, they are dancing the same steps, but with a slightly different dance”. 9  In short, humans currently are still more adaptive to environmental changes than AI, but if AI supplants the human role of medical provider and caregiver, will the same ethical patient care considerations be transferred to and adhered to by AI automations? Time will tell.

ABSTRACT

Awareness of trauma’s effects in the world, our patients, and ourselves helps us be more empathic and responsive medication prescribers. Trauma-informed care (TIC) practice is central in treating patients with histories of trauma. Patients overwhelmingly struggle with polypharmacy due to increased medical illness, comorbid mood and substance use disorders. This chapter begins with an introduction to TIC and describes how to integrate a trauma-informed approach in medication management. Using a holistic approach and therapeutic use of self, it examines the meaning of medications for both the patient and the advanced practice psychiatric nurse. The chapter addresses maintaining rational pharmacotherapy in the face of obstacles. It provides guidelines for addressing non-adherence. It describes psychodynamic prescribing, the situational briefing model and the deprescribing model, borrowed from gerontology, as useful strategies. The chapter ends with examples of how to apply principles of TIC in a medication management practice.

TRAUMA-INFORMED MEDICATION MANAGEMENT
Kathryn Kieran

Awareness of trauma’s effects in the world, our patients, and ourselves helps us be more empathic and responsive medication prescribers. In treating patients with trauma, trauma-informed care (TIC) practice is central. Patients with trauma histories struggle with polypharmacy due to increased comorbid medical, mood, and substance use disorders (SUDs). Vulnerability to somatization, and self-neglect due to dissociative or avoidant symptoms, increase provider-patient misunderstanding. Patients experience accentuated power dynamics and contact with an authority figure can cause defensive anger or intense fears. The prescribing advanced practice psychiatric nurse (APPN) needs to assess and validate traumatic beliefs, sensations, and thoughts, while remaining present-focused. Compassion and patient choice must be interwoven with firm boundaries, and clearly outlined treatment goals and plans.

This chapter introduces TIC and describes integrating a trauma-informed approach in medication management. The meaning of medications for both the patient and the APPN is examined using a holistic approach and centering the therapeutic use of self. Maintaining rational pharmacotherapy in the face of obstacles is addressed. Guidelines for addressing nonadherence are provided. Useful strategies of psychodynamic prescribing, the situational briefing model and the deprescribing model are discussed. The chapter ends with examples of how to apply principles of TIC in a medication management practice.
<H1>INTRODUCTION

Traumatic experiences are pervasive, including our own experiences of caring for others’ traumas. TIC provides a framework to investigate the current state of care and conceive of new ways of being with our patients to co-create new narratives. We must stay alert to avoid unknowingly replicating abusive or neglectful dynamics in our prescribing relationships. To do this well, we practice universal precautions, provide education about trauma responses and nonmedication options, and treat target symptoms with appropriate medication if indicated. Scrutinizing or probing trauma is not the role of the prescribing APPN and can destabilize the patient. For those who do have a significant history of trauma, Fellitti and colleagues (2010) found that asking the patient during their office visit “I see that you had . . . Tell me how that has affected you later in your life” resulted in a surprisingly 35% reduction in doctor visits and 3% reduction in hospitalizations subsequent compared to the year before. Thus, a genuine stance of openness to patients’ whole stories and whole selves can be healing and supportive even without the details of the trauma. Humility is necessary when addressing cultural and spiritual dimensions of care. Psychodynamic prescribing; situation, background, assessment, and recommendation (SBAR) communication methods; and a deprescribing model provide techniques and skills to supplement our standard good nursing practices.

The APPN may provide therapy or may be in a split treatment program, providing medication management while another clinician provides the therapy. This may also shift over the course of treatment, as we or another treater may refer the patient to trauma-focused therapy, other brief treatments or adjunct modalities. Split treatment can provide a broader base of evaluation, opportunities for collaboration, and more frequent visits. It requires increased communication, which can be taxing at times, and carries risks of missed information and more complicated transference (Mintz, 2022). Before starting medication management, it is wise to inquire if the patient is currently in or planning to start any adjunctive therapy, or if the prescribing APPN is expected to provide the therapy. Each APPN has limits, boundaries, and requirements around split or integrated treatment. Releases of information should be signed between all care providers, including medical providers, such as a primary care provider, and relevant specialists. Clearly communicating treatment expectations at the outset is important, to avoid reactivation of traumatic scripts around abandonment, unworthiness, or loss of control (see Chapter 14, for more information on split and integrated treatment).

Trauma is unfortunately common. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, (5th ed.; DSM-5; American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013b) identifies the criteria for trauma as “death, serious injury, or sexual violence” that is directed toward us, that we witness directly, or that we learn affected a close family member or friend. Occupational exposures to these events in vivo or through electronic or traditional media such as pictures are also considered criteria for development of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). We also know that other forms of danger and abuse have profound and lifelong effects on individuals, such as racial discrimination and microaggressions.

As clinicians, we are not immune to trauma exposure and trauma responses. Nothing in this chapter will share explicit trauma details, but terms and examples may have resonance for some of us. A shift toward exploring primary and vicarious post traumatic growth and resiliency in the literature was amplified in the wake of the Covid 19 public emergencies, though important questions and detractors from these models remain (Tang et al., 2024; Jozefiaková et al., 2022; van Rooij et al., 2022). Monitoring vicarious or secondary trauma responses guides our practices of self-care, our clinical practices broadly, and our decision-making moment by moment. Because this is so central, I suggest taking a moment to reflect on how we may take care of our responses to content we hear and absorb in our daily work, and whatever might spark recognition in this chapter.

This approach aligns with TIC guidelines, which recommends considering how all of us may have experiences of trauma and responses formed in traumatic contexts. All specialties are increasingly recognizing that TIC is central to successful care of patients with histories of trauma (Dowdell & Speck, 2022; Antai-Otong, 2016). The principles of TIC are not standardized across the available research base. At a national level the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) defines TIC approaches as understanding in incorporating the existence of trauma and its impacts for everyone, as well as ways to recover from trauma (2023). This necessitates creating agile policies, incorporating the existing database on trauma and recovery, and working to avoid retraumatization of all those serving in or accessing the programs or system (SAMHSA, 2023).
