<H1>CONCLUDING COMMENTS

All medications have meaning. Taking opportunities to regularly assess for meaning is holistic and responsive treatment. It can be healing to offer interventions that are clear, with scheduled check-ins to ventilate concerns and future goals. Taking a thorough history of past experiences of medication will help to determine personalized titration schedules. To build trust and establish expectations when starting medications, normalize nocebo, placebo, and side effects, while offering guidance about warning signs to seek further care. When giving a prescription, make the medication contract explicit, and discuss harm-reduction plans for urges or actions to overtake, undertake, or suddenly stop medications. When medication behaviors do not match stated goals, an open discussion of how mis-taking medications may be a result of historical trauma beliefs guiding current behavior and helps increase both client and APPN awareness and understanding. Scheduling a “state of the state” discussion at 3- or 6-month intervals can help to preempt or to readily identify self-discontinuation or misuse patterns.

Medications serve so many functions, and in patients with trauma those themes can be buried under minutiae if we are not careful. Themes that come up repeatedly in medication meetings can often be covert communication about trauma. Many individuals with trauma experience numbing and flooding cycles of emotions and physical experiences. Medications can accentuate or dull physical sensations and emotions in ways that fuel these cycles, and thus increase avoidance of traumatic content and experience. There are many strategies to hold space for these cycles to be slowed down; no one technique will be sufficient for all patients. Just as trauma is a layered experience that affects our patients’ biology, psychology, and sense of meaning and place in the world, healing and wellness requires addressing all dimensions of the person’s experience.

The stance of curiosity, when paired with caring, is an effective combination to build a strong alliance with trauma survivors. Safety, pacing, and containment of symptoms must be prioritized to maintain that alliance. Rushing through a medication management session is potentially disastrous, as it can re-create reminders of coercion or disregard. Even within this cultural moment, with all its distractions and pressures, stabilization can be maintained if we bring ourselves fully to the task.

What seems like the most challenging aspect of implementing trauma-informed medication education? Write two Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Timed (SMART) goals to help you meet this learning need.

<COURSECONNECT ONLY>One of the most challenging aspects of implementing trauma-informed medication education is navigating patients’ deeply personal and often painful past experiences with medications—especially when those experiences involve coercion, betrayal, or bodily harm. Trauma survivors may associate medications with loss of control, somatic flashbacks, or betrayal trauma, making them highly sensitive to side effects or fearful of trying something new. This can complicate adherence and open discussion. Addressing these challenges requires empathic communication, patient empowerment, and a flexible, collaborative approach.
SMART goals might include the following:

Within the next 4 weeks, I will review and summarize three peer-reviewed articles on trauma-informed psychopharmacology to deepen my understanding of placebo, nocebo, and medication-related transference in trauma survivors.

By the end of this month, I will integrate at least one trauma-informed strategy (e.g., using the SBAR model to assess medication concerns) into my medication education sessions with two patients and document their responses for reflection and supervision.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>
Define placebo and nocebo. Think of some examples of each that you have encountered.

<COURSECONNECT ONLY>A placebo effect refers to beneficial outcomes that occur after the administration of an inert treatment, which arise from the patient’s expectations, the therapeutic relationship, and contextual cues rather than the pharmacological properties of the treatment itself. A nocebo effect is the opposite: it involves negative side effects or worsening of symptoms due to negative expectations or beliefs about a treatment, even when the treatment itself is inert. Both effects are especially pronounced in trauma survivors due to heightened sensitivity to bodily sensations and cognitive patterns rooted in past adverse experiences. Examples encountered will vary by user.</COURSECONNECT ONLY>

Write out a conversation between a patient and yourself in which you are hoping to start a prn medication for anxiety. List some of the fears, past experiences, and questions the patient may have.
<COURSECONNECT ONLY>The following is one example of this kind of conversation:

APPN: Thanks for coming in today. I want to check in about the anxiety you’ve been feeling lately. You mentioned that some days are harder than others—have you ever considered a medication you could take only when needed?
Patient: I’ve thought about it… but honestly, medication makes me nervous. I don’t like feeling out of control.

APPN: That makes sense. Feeling in control is really important, especially when you’ve had experiences in the past where control was taken from you. Can I ask—have you had any past experiences with medications that were difficult?

Patient: Yes, actually. Years ago, I was given something that made me feel like I couldn’t move or think clearly, and no one told me what was happening. It reminded me of when I was younger and... things happened that I didn’t understand.

APPN: Thank you for sharing that—it sounds like that experience was scary and disorienting. I want to make sure anything we consider now feels safe and collaborative. Would it be okay if we looked at an option together and you helped decide when, how, or if to use it?
Patient: Maybe. What are you thinking?

APPN: Something mild, like hydroxyzine. It’s non-habit forming and you’d only take it when you’re feeling especially anxious. We can start with a small dose, and if at any point it feels like too much, we can stop. I’d also like to hear about any other fears or questions you might have.
Possible Patient Fears and Questions:
Will it make me feel "drugged" or sedated like last time?
What if I become dependent on it?
Will I still be able to function at work or take care of my kids?
Is it okay to take this only occasionally?
Will this interfere with my trauma therapy?
What happens if it doesn’t work—or makes things worse?

APPN Response: Those are all excellent questions. I can provide written information, and we can check in weekly while you're trying it. You’re the expert on your body, and we’ll move forward at your pace. </COURSECONNECT ONLY>

The APPN communicates the following expectations:
Medication will not be shared with others or used to harm self or others.
